sources.title: Why bodies? Twelve reasons for including bodily expressions in affective neuroscience
key_findings: Over 95% of human emotion studies had used faces; a May-2009 PubMed count gave 3521 hits for emotion x faces vs 339 for emotion x bodies.
Bodily expressions are recognised about as reliably as facial expressions; dynamic clips are recognised roughly 10% better than stills; point-light displays are harder.
Bodies show emotion together with the action the person is preparing (fear body = escape) and can be read at a distance where faces cannot.
Body emotion biases how an ambiguous face is read; face-body incongruence is detected early (~115 ms).
Different emotions draw attention to different body parts (e.g. hands for aggression).
practical_applications: Faceless characters (Mint & Tao) can carry emotion through posture and movement; this is a research-backed channel, not a workaround.
Show the action tendency (approach, withdraw, freeze) rather than a static 'emotion pose'.
limitations: Narrative review by one author, partly built on her own lab's work; neuroscience parts are not directly needed for craft.
WebFetch read ~100k of ~116k characters (the end of the reference list not read).
sources.license: open access via PMC (Royal Society; check licence)

sources.title: Emotion expression in body action and posture
sources.authors: Dael, N.; Mortillaro, M.; Scherer, K. R.
key_findings: 10 professional actors x 12 emotions (GEMEP corpus), coded with the Body Action and Posture (BAP) system and reduced to 16 behaviour factors.
Hot anger was homogeneously expressed by frontal body lean / forward movement (one cluster contained all hot-anger portrayals).
Amusement: touching/manipulation and discontinuous movements with mid-action holds, head straight and oriented to the interlocutor.
Elated joy (70%) and pride (40%) shared symmetrical up-down repetitive arm action; panic fear (60%) shared symmetrical arm action with knee movement, overlapping with joy (30%).

Sadness (60%) and relief (50%) were grouped together by arms resting (in pockets); despair and anxiety shared an indistinct pattern; anxiety + panic fear also showed backward lean, upward gaze and lateral trunk lean.
Interest and irritation shared arms at side + trunk leaning forward + one-arm asymmetric action.
Discriminant classification: elated joy 90%, amusement and hot anger 70%, sadness and irritation 30%; sadness was classified as despair as often as sadness. Cross-validated accuracies only 10-60%.
Arousal (activation) was the first discriminating dimension; most emotions were expressed by several different patterns.
practical_applications: High-arousal emotions (anger, joy, amusement) are easy to stage with body alone; low-arousal ones (sadness vs relief, irritation vs interest) need context, props or a second cue.
Disambiguate pairs known to be confused: joy vs panic fear, sadness vs relief vs despair, interest vs irritation.
limitations: Acted portrayals by 10 Western-European actors, standing, filmed in a lab; not spontaneous behaviour.
Exploratory cluster analysis; small n per cell; classification not cross-validated in the main report.

sources.title: Affective Body Expression Perception and Recognition: A Survey
key_findings: Both form (posture) and motion carry affect; motion can be sufficient for basic emotions but recognition drops when form is disrupted; posture helps separate emotions with similar movement activation.
High-level features that matter: leaning direction, openness of the body, head position (up/down/tilted); angular/diagonal configurations read as threatening, rounded ones as warm (Aronoff, ballet).
Sadness core: arms straight down close to the body; happiness/elation: head bent back, arms often raised; hands raised = happy, low = sad; lateral opening separates happy and fear from sad.
Disgust and pride can both use crossed arms; head position separates them (forward for disgust, back for pride) - Wallbott.

Non-acted Wii postures: defeated and concentrating both had slumped shoulders and arms down/diagonal; frustrated and triumphant both had shoulders up/back and arms raised laterally - arousal separated better than valence.
Cross-cultural: Japanese, Sri Lankan and American observers agreed best on sad/depressed for a faceless genderless avatar, but Japanese rated animated postures as more intense.
Prototypical expressions are rare in real life (Russell); context changes how an emotion is expressed.
practical_applications: Use head position + openness + lean as the three main levers for a faceless puppet.
Expect triumph vs frustration and defeat vs concentration to be confused unless context or hands disambiguate.
limitations: Narrative survey (not systematic); most cited studies use acted expressions.
Read from a lecture-site copy of the published PDF; tables partly garbled in text extraction.

sources.title: Emotion perception from dynamic and static body expressions in point-light and full-light displays
sources.authors: Atkinson, A. P.; Dittrich, W. H.; Gemmell, A. J.; Young, A. W.
key_findings: 10 actors with faces covered portrayed anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness at 3 levels of exaggeration; 150 full-light and 150 point-light clips plus static peak frames.
Basic emotions were readily identified from body movement even in point-light displays; static images were less efficient than dynamic displays.

More exaggerated movement increased recognition accuracy (most clearly for dynamic point-light) and intensity ratings; intensity judgements relied more on movement than on static form (secondary summaries add: exaggeration did not help sadness).
practical_applications: Faces can be hidden entirely and emotion still reads - direct support for faceless characters.
In clips, exaggerate movement amplitude for clarity; in stills (carousels) expect lower accuracy and add context.
limitations: Abstract read via Europe PMC; per-emotion accuracies not read.
Acted, Western actors.

sources.title: Perception of emotion from dynamic point-light displays represented in dance
sources.authors: Dittrich, W. H.; Troscianko, T.; Lea, S. E. G.; Morgan, D.
key_findings: Two trained dancers conveyed fear, anger, grief, joy, surprise, disgust.
Full-body clips: 88% correct; upright point-light (13 dots): 63% correct, well above chance; inversion reduced point-light performance close to chance.
practical_applications: Movement pattern alone carries emotion - a simplified stick/pencil figure that moves well can read.
Keep characters upright and anatomically coherent; scrambled or inverted motion loses meaning.
limitations: Only two dancers; dance is stylised movement.
Abstract only.

sources.title: Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions
sources.authors: Aviezer, H.; Trope, Y.; Todorov, A.
key_findings: At peak intensity (e.g. winning/losing), positive and negative situations were discriminated from isolated bodies but not from isolated faces.
Viewers perceived illusory valence in non-diagnostic faces when shown with bodies; in face-body composites, perceived affect followed the body.
practical_applications: For big moments (win, loss, shock) the body pose decides how the moment reads - design the body first.
Body + context can make the same neutral/ambiguous face (or no face) read as joy or despair.
limitations: Real-life photos of athletes/people at peak intensity; generalisation to mild emotions not tested.
Abstract only.

sources.title: Attributing emotion to static body postures: Recognition accuracy, confusions, and viewpoint dependence
key_findings: 176 computer-generated mannequin postures, each from 3 viewing angles, forced choice of 6 emotions.
Agreement ranged from zero for many disgust postures to over 90% for some anger and sadness postures.
Anatomical features and viewing angle predicted responses; confusions suggested a circumplex, with happiness and surprise close together.
practical_applications: For static images of simplified figures: anger and sadness can read from posture alone; disgust needs props/context.
Pick the camera angle that shows the posture most clearly (viewpoint matters).
limitations: Wooden, faceless mannequins without hand detail; static only.
Abstract read; per-feature tables not read.

sources.title: Perceiving affect from arm movement
sources.authors: Pollick, F. E.; Paterson, H. M.; Bruderlin, A.; Sanford, A. J.
key_findings: Point-light drinking and knocking arm movements with 10 affects; perceived affect formed a circumplex: dimension 1 activation, dimension 2 pleasantness.
Activation correlated strongly with movement kinematics (speed) even in scrambled displays; pleasantness seemed carried by phase relations between limb segments.
Secondary summaries: anger/happiness judged from fast, jerky movement; sadness from slow, smooth movement.
practical_applications: Tempo controls arousal: speed up for anger/joy/excitement, slow and smooth for sadness/tiredness.
Valence needs coordination quality (smooth flowing vs jerky, disconnected), not just speed.
limitations: Two actors; arm-only point-light.
Abstract only; the fast/jerky detail comes from secondary sources.

sources.title: Critical features for the perception of emotion from gait
sources.authors: Roether, C. L.; Omlor, L.; Christensen, A.; Giese, M. A.
key_findings: Motion capture of neutral, angry, happy, sad, fearful gaits from 25 people; observers judged avatars animated with them.
Judgements rely on simple features such as overall speed and on posture/dynamic cues; emotion-specific features depended on only a few joints.
Artificial walkers with only the critical features produced after-effects like natural emotional walkers.
practical_applications: A walk cycle can carry emotion with a few changes: speed, head inclination, arm-swing amplitude (details in the Kleinsmith survey).
Matches rig.js walk timings (brisk vs slow) - a cheap emotion channel for every entrance.
limitations: Abstract only; exact joint-angle results not read.
Acted gaits.
sources.license: open access (Journal of Vision; check licence)

sources.title: Bodily expression of emotion
key_findings: (Per Dael2012 and Kleinsmith2013, which were read in full) Actors portraying 14 emotions; overall classification ~.54; movement quality (activity, expansiveness, energy) strongly aided differentiation.

(Per secondary sources) part of the movement differences are explained by activation; collapsed posture for shame/sadness; pride more in body than face; arms crossed for disgust and pride, separated by head forward vs back.
practical_applications: Use expansiveness and energy as first-order controls; head position as the tie-breaker.
limitations: Not read directly; findings stated only as reported by secondary sources.

sources.title: The spontaneous expression of pride and shame: Evidence for biologically innate nonverbal displays
key_findings: Judo athletes at the 2004 Olympic (sighted, 36 nations) and Paralympic (blind, 20 nations, 12 congenitally blind) Games.
After winning: head tilted back, smile, arms raised, hands in fists, arms out, chest expanded, torso out - in sighted and blind athletes; hands on hips NOT reliably displayed.
After losing: only shoulders slumped and chest narrowed increased (head down / face hiding not associated with losing in this photo set).
Shame display was weaker in more individualistic cultures (sighted only), suggesting cultural suppression; no moderation in blind athletes.
practical_applications: Triumph = expand and rise (head back, arms up/out, fists); defeat = narrow the chest, drop the shoulders.
In collectivist settings (including Thai audiences, plausibly) visible shame displays after failure are culturally acceptable - but this is an inference, Thailand not separately analysed.
limitations: No self-report of felt emotion; competition with audience; one photographer, limited angles; small congenitally blind sample.

sources.title: How do we recognize emotion from movement? Specific motor components contribute to the recognition of each emotion
sources.authors: Melzer, A.; Shafir, T.; Tsachor, R. P.
key_findings: Earlier work (Shafir et al. 2016) found Laban components that enhanced feeling: happiness = jumping, rhythmic, spreading, free flow, lightness, up, rising; sadness = passive weight, arms touching upper body, sinking, head dropping; fear = retreating, condensing, bound flow, backwards, enclosing; anger = strong weight, sudden time, advancing, direct.
Clips of Certified Movement Analysts moving those components (without intending emotion) were recognised as the associated emotion above chance; anger only 47.2% of anger-component clips.
Actor clips (Atkinson set) were recognised better for anger, fear and neutral.
practical_applications: A practical vocabulary for directing movement quality: e.g. 'sinking, passive weight' for sadness; 'retreat + condense + bound flow' for fear.
Useful prompt words for AI video and notes for puppet timing.
limitations: All movers adult Caucasian women; sample too small for cross-cultural analysis; Laban coding by its own practitioners.

sources.title: Assessing the reliability of the Laban Movement Analysis system
sources.authors: Bernardet, U.; Fdili Alaoui, S.; Studd, K.; Bradley, K.; Pasquier, P.; Schiphorst, T.
key_findings: Certified Movement Analysts annotated the most and second-most salient difference between a neutral and a varied movement in a custom tool.
Inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha) ranged from weak to acceptable depending on how the two rounds were combined.
Positioned as the first formal reliability assessment of a widely used system.
practical_applications: Treat Laban terms as a shared craft vocabulary, not as a validated measurement scale.
When two people disagree about Laban labels for a shot, that is normal - test with viewers instead.
limitations: One study, small expert sample, limited movement set.

sources.title: Do the eyes have it? Cues to the direction of social attention
sources.authors: Langton, S. R. H.; Watt, R. J.; Bruce, V.
key_findings: Gaze direction is processed rapidly and triggers reflexive shifts of the observer's attention, even when uninformative and when told to ignore it.
Perceived attention direction depends not only on the eyes but on head orientation, body posture and pointing; head orientation changes perceived gaze (Wollaston effect).
Head orientation and pointing may be more salient than eye gaze for young children; cues are processed automatically and in parallel.
practical_applications: Faceless characters can still 'look': turn the head (and body) toward the target and the viewer's attention follows.
Use head turn + point to steer the viewer to a product or object in the frame.
limitations: Review written 2000; later gaze-cueing literature not covered here.
sources.license: author accepted manuscript (University of Stirling repository)

sources.title: The eyes have it: the neuroethology, function and evolution of social gaze
key_findings: Gaze is a core social signal; its signal value depends on the status, disposition and emotional state of sender and receiver.
Brain regions respond selectively to faces, bodies and gaze; gaze following may be 'hard-wired' (STS-amygdala-OFC circuit).
practical_applications: Direct orientation toward another character = engagement/challenge; averted = deference/avoidance - read through status context.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly primate neuroethology.

sources.title: The many faces of a neutral face: Head tilt and perception of dominance and emotion
key_findings: Secondary sources disagree on what it found: one says direct gaze + upward head tilt expresses dominance and downward head + averted gaze submission; another attributes 'head down increases perceived dominance' to it.

Later work (2020, Perception, per search snippet) found both 30-degree up and 20-degree down postures read as more dominant and less trustworthy than level; Witkower & Tracy reported slightly-down heads read angrier.
practical_applications: Head pitch changes perceived status and emotion, but the direction depends on the rest of the face/body and the camera angle - test, do not assume.
limitations: Not read; secondary sources conflict - recorded as contested.

sources.title: Bodily communication of emotion: Evidence for extrafacial behavioral expressions and available coding systems
key_findings: (Abstract per search result) Reviews evidence that pride, joy, sadness, shame, embarrassment, anger, fear and disgust are shown and recognised through bodily behaviour.
No existing body coding system covers the full range of emotions.
practical_applications: Supports a pose library covering these eight emotions as the most evidence-backed set.
limitations: Abstract content seen only via search result text.

sources.title: When do gestures communicate? A meta-analysis
key_findings: 63 samples: speech + gesture gives a significant, moderate comprehension benefit over speech alone.
Gestures depicting motor actions help more than gestures about abstract topics.
Benefit is larger when gestures are not redundant with speech; children benefit more than adults.
practical_applications: Give characters gestures that add information (show the size, shape, action) rather than repeat the words.
In TTS clips, an iconic gesture of the action described helps viewers - especially for family/child audiences.
limitations: Abstract only; lab comprehension tasks.

sources.title: The prosodic characteristics of non-referential co-speech gestures in a sample of academic-lecture-style speech
key_findings: Summarises McNeill (1992): referential gestures = iconic, metaphoric, deictic; beats were defined mainly as 'not iconic, metaphoric or deictic'; McNeill distinguished single flick beats marking narrative points from rhythm-beating gestures.

1,334 stroke-defined gestures in 20 min of lecture speech: the stroke of non-referential gestures tends to align with a pitch-accented syllable, as for other gesture types (Loehr 2004 strokes align with pitch accents).
Cites Kendon (1972, 1980, 2004) for gesture phrase structure and kinematic constancy across prosodic constituents; non-referential gestures are not a homogeneous 'beat' class.
practical_applications: Time a gesture's stroke to the stressed syllable of the TTS line; preparation before, hold/retraction after.
Use beats sparingly as emphasis; use iconic gestures for content.
limitations: One speaker style (American English lectures); Thai is a tonal language - stroke-to-stress alignment in Thai not tested here.

sources.title: Hand and Mind: What Gestures Reveal about Thought
key_findings: (Per secondary sources read: ShattuckHufnagelRen2018 and search results) Classifies co-speech gestures as iconic, metaphoric, deictic and beats; categories are not mutually exclusive; builds on 'Kendon's continuum'.
practical_applications: Plan each gesture by type: show (iconic), idea-as-object (metaphoric), point (deictic), emphasis (beat).
limitations: Book not read; content stated only as reported by secondary sources.

sources.title: Preferred interpersonal distances: A global comparison
sources.authors: Sorokowska, A.; Sorokowski, P.; Hilpert, P.; et al.
key_findings: 8,943 participants in 42 countries chose preferred distances on a 0-220 cm graphic scale between two figures (stranger, acquaintance, close person).
Means: social (stranger) 135.1 cm, personal (acquaintance) 91.7 cm, intimate (close) 31.9 cm; the order held in every country, absolute values varied widely.
Women and older people preferred larger distances; warmer countries preferred closer stranger distances.
Hall's (1966) contact/non-contact split by geography (Asian populations as non-contact) is only partly supported; earlier evidence was often anecdotal.
Thailand was not among the sampled countries (checked the manuscript text).
practical_applications: Distance between Mint and Tao in frame is a relationship dial: ~1 body-width apart = close; 2-3 = acquainted; more = stranger/estranged.
Do not rely on Hall's culture labels; use the relative order, which is cross-culturally stable.
limitations: Self-report picture task, not observed behaviour; sex of the other person unspecified; ~200 per country.
sources.license: accepted manuscript, WRAP terms (personal research use)

sources.title: The Hidden Dimension
key_findings: (Per Sorokowska2017, read in full) Proposes four distance zones - intimate (0-46 cm), personal, social and public - and a contact vs non-contact culture distinction; cultural norms seen as the main factor.
practical_applications: Zone vocabulary for staging two-shots and for blocking real people in clips.
limitations: Not read; zone ranges beyond 'intimate 0-46 cm' not confirmed this session; theory partly anecdotal (Sorokowska2017).

sources.title: Thai Traditional Salutation
key_findings: Wai: palms joined, touching the body between face and chest; the higher the hands, the greater the respect; the junior in age or rank initiates and the senior reciprocates; less strict between intimates.
Movement is never sharp: raised and lowered gracefully, upper arms close to the body, elbows not extended; idealised hand shape is the 'budding lotus' (phanom mue).
A senior conscious of superiority returns the wai no higher than the chest, or just nods / raises the right hand (rap wai); monks do not return a layperson's wai.
When standing before a seated respected person one stoops or bends the head; simple folk crouch on their haunches before great personages until they pass.

Krap (kneel and bow, forehead to floor between the hands, three times) is for the Buddha/Triple Gems; mop krap (crouched bow) for parents, teachers, royalty; side-sitting posture 'nang phap phiap' with legs folded back.
The author stresses variation by class, locality and setting; his description is a generalisation.
practical_applications: Correct Thai respect choreography for characters: who wais first, hand height by status, slow tempo, elbows in.
A rushed, high-elbow or one-handed wai reads as careless or comic - use only on purpose.
limitations: Mid-20th-century description (exact year not confirmed); modern urban practice is looser (Thailand Foundation and guides).
Scanned text with OCR errors.

sources.title: Feet Low, Head High: A Guide to Thai Etiquettes
key_findings: Feet are the lowest/least clean part: do not point feet or soles at people or Buddha images; tuck feet or sit cross-legged; do not put feet on tables; do not step over pillows or books.
Head is the most sacred part: do not touch anyone's head, even children's; do not pass objects over a head; bow the head when walking past elders.
Do not position the body above an elder's head; crouch or move on knees to pass seated elders or monks.
Everyday wai: palms together at chest level with a slight head bow; on special occasions bow low with hands at the elder's feet.
practical_applications: Cultural checks for every Thai scene: feet direction when seated, no head pats, lower the body when passing elders.
limitations: Cultural-promotion article (states it does not reflect government views); normative, not observational.

sources.title: Facial Action Coding System (FACS) - product page
key_findings: FACS is an anatomically based system describing all visually discernible facial movement as Action Units; first published 1978 (Ekman & Friesen), revised 2002.
FACS codes are descriptive; EMFACS codes 'have to be interpreted into emotion categories'.
Self-study 50-100 hours; used by researchers, animators and computer scientists.
practical_applications: Use AU names as a precise vocabulary for faces when a character HAS a face (TTS clip puppets, AI video prompts), not as an emotion detector.
limitations: Vendor page.

sources.title: Model for predicting perception of facial action unit activation using virtual humans
sources.authors: McDonnell, R.; Zibrek, K.; Carrigan, E.; Dahyot, R.
key_findings: Blendshape rigs are usually built from FACS Action Units; some AUs are perceptually more noticeable than others (ordering table provided).
Perceived difference grew roughly linearly with activation for most AUs; almost no AU was distinguishable from neutral at 0.2 activation except eyes closed and mouth open.
Geometric RMS predicted visibility better than the image metric SSIM; character race/sex had some effects, no other-race effect.
practical_applications: Subtle face moves (<20% intensity) are invisible to viewers - at our small on-screen sizes push face changes harder or move the body instead.
limitations: Realistic virtual humans viewed close-up; stylised 2D puppets not tested.

sources.title: Principles of traditional animation applied to 3D computer animation
key_findings: Lists the Disney principles (squash & stretch, timing, anticipation, staging, follow-through/overlap, straight-ahead vs pose-to-pose, slow in/out, arcs, exaggeration, secondary action, appeal).
Staging in silhouette: early black-and-white characters showed that actions must read in silhouette; Andre's scratch was moved to the side for clarity.
Anticipation prepares the audience and can show weight (bend low before lifting a heavy object).
'All actions and movements of a character are the result of its thought processes'; a character does the same action differently in different emotional states.
Exaggeration must be balanced across design, action, sound; exaggerating only one element - or everything - looks wrong.
practical_applications: Silhouette test for every key pose of Mint & Tao; show the thought before the action.
limitations: Craft knowledge from a practitioner (Pixar), published at SIGGRAPH; not empirical evidence.

sources.title: Acting for Animators (5th edition)
key_findings: Publisher description/TOC: applies acting theory (Aristotle to Stanislavsky) to animation; action -> obstacle -> objective; 'acting is a process of exposing, not of hiding'; acting is doing and reacting; status transactions and power centres; psychological gesture; character rhythm; a scene is a negotiation; Laban movement analysis.
Earlier edition TOC (retailer listing, 4th ed. 2017) includes 'Thinking tends to lead to conclusions' and 'Emotion tends to lead to action'.
practical_applications: Give every character an objective and an obstacle per scene; stage status changes through posture and space.
limitations: Only publisher/retailer pages read; book content not read; practitioner tier.

sources.title: Hume's Aesthetics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Hume: verdicts of taste rest on sentiment, yet some critics are better than others.
True judge: 'strong sense, united to delicate sentiment, improved by practice, perfected by comparison, and cleared of all prejudice'.
Standard of taste = joint verdict of true critics; long-run agreement (test of time).
Objections: circularity (good art defined by good critics and vice versa), ideal vs real critics, blameless disagreement from temperament and culture.
practical_applications: A critic's authority comes from practice, side-by-side comparison and removing bias: build these into the review procedure (reference sets, blind comparison).
Some disagreement is 'blameless' (audience temperament/culture) and should not be 'fixed'.
limitations: Philosophical, not empirical; entry author/revision year not recorded this session.

sources.title: Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Three aesthetic judgements: agreeable (mere liking), beautiful (taste), sublime.
Judgement of beauty: disinterested pleasure, claims universal validity without concepts, 'purposiveness without purpose', exemplary necessity grounded in a sensus communis; cannot be proved by rules.
Free beauty (independent of what the object is for) vs adherent beauty (dependent on a concept of its kind/purpose); most representational art is adherent.
Criticisms: deduction dilemma, disinterestedness, formalism, unclear normativity.
practical_applications: Commercial images are adherent beauty: judge them against their purpose (sell, explain, move), not as free art.
Separate 'I like it' (agreeable) from 'it works as this kind of thing' (adherent judgement) in critique.
limitations: Philosophical; entry author/revision year not recorded this session.

sources.title: How Nothing Became Something: White Space, Rhetoric, History, and Meaning
sources.authors: Pracejus, J. W., Olsen, G. D., O'Guinn, T. C.
key_findings: Per abstract/press summary: white space has no inherent meaning; it means what it does because of a history (minimalist art/architecture, late-1950s corporate art).
Creative directors and ordinary consumers share a similar understanding of white space even without knowing its origin.
Related survey (Olsen, Pracejus, O'Guinn 2012, JBR; search summary): 31 creative directors use white-space ads to make ads look good and convey prestige.
practical_applications: White space reads as prestige/quality to audiences who share this visual convention; it is a learned code, so check it holds for the target audience.
limitations: Full text not read; North American samples; convention may differ in Thai discount retail culture.

sources.title: The Space-to-Product Ratio Effect: How Interstitial Space Influences Product Aesthetic Appeal, Store Perceptions, and Product Preference
key_findings: Per abstract/press summaries: more empty space around displayed products raises perceived aesthetic appeal of the products and prestige of the store, and product preference.
Alternative explanations (popularity, scarcity, messiness) were ruled out per the abstract.
One summary: low-priced products became more aesthetically appealing but not more valuable with more space.
Field sales figures differ between sources (50% revenue/shopper vs 98%); unverified.
practical_applications: Give the hero product breathing room in frame; crowding several frames into one image signals 'stock', not 'selection'.
limitations: Full text not read; JMR 53(5) per summary; retail displays, not social posts.

sources.title: Symbolically Simple: How Simple Packaging Design Influences Willingness to Pay for Consumable Products
sources.authors: Ton, L. A. N., Smith, R. K., Sevilla, J.
key_findings: Per The Conversation summary (read in full) and abstracts: across 1,000+ supermarket packages, rated simplicity was positively associated with price.
Experiments: simpler packaging raised willingness to pay via perceived purity (inferred fewer ingredients).
Boundaries: weaker/absent for store brands (simple = low investment); indulgence-motivated shoppers prefer complex packaging.
practical_applications: Minimal looks signal purity/premium for health, care and 'clean' categories; for indulgent/fun categories richness may sell better.
limitations: Journal article not read; US supermarket context.

sources.title: Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of Brand Prominence
sources.authors: Han, Y. J., Nunes, J. C., Drèze, X.
key_findings: Brand prominence = conspicuousness of logo/marks on a product (loud vs quiet).
Four groups by wealth x need for status: patricians (quiet signals to peers), parvenus (loud, dissociate from have-nots), poseurs (loud counterfeits), proletarians.
Market data: inconspicuously branded luxury goods cost more than the same maker's conspicuously branded goods (premium for understatement); counterfeits disproportionately copy loud designs.
practical_applications: Quiet branding (small logo, recognisable form/material) reads as higher-tier luxury to insiders; big logos read as aspirational/mass. Choose by audience.
limitations: US/European luxury fashion; pre-social-media data.

sources.title: Holistic Package Design and Consumer Brand Impressions
key_findings: Per abstract/summaries: package designs cluster into five holistic types - massive, contrasting, natural, delicate, nondescript.
Recommended pairing: sincere -> natural; exciting -> contrasting; competent -> delicate; sophisticated -> natural or delicate; rugged -> contrasting or massive.
Method included 160 wine bottles and 100+ design experts rating elements (per summary).
practical_applications: Use the five holistic types as a vocabulary for brand looks; 'delicate' (muted, sleek, thin) for competence/sophistication.
limitations: Full text not read; element-level definitions not verified; wine/package domain.

sources.title: Impression Management Using Typeface Design
sources.authors: Henderson, P. W., Giese, J. L., Cote, J. A.
key_findings: Per abstract: empirically based guidance for choosing typefaces for impressions (pleasing, engaging, reassuring, prominent) and their trade-offs.
Six underlying design dimensions: elaborate, harmony, natural, flourish, weight, compressed.
practical_applications: Describe type choices in these dimensions (e.g., 'harmony + natural, low weight' for calm/trustworthy).
limitations: Full text not read; Latin typefaces only; Thai typefaces untested.

sources.title: Dressed for the Occasion: Font-Product Congruity in the Perception of Logotype
sources.authors: Doyle, J. R., Bottomley, P. A.
key_findings: Per abstract: perceived font appropriateness depends on match of connotative meaning (potency, activity) between font and product, and also on the font's meaning alone.
Related 2004 study (search summary): brands in 10 categories chosen about twice as often with an appropriate font.
practical_applications: Font must 'dress for' the product: a heavy, active font on a gentle eye-care message is incongruent.
limitations: Full text not read; Latin typefaces.

sources.title: The Taste of Typeface
sources.authors: Velasco, C., Woods, A. T., Hyndman, S., Spence, C.
key_findings: People matched rounder typefaces with 'sweet' and more angular typefaces with 'bitter', 'salty', 'sour'.
Rounder typefaces were liked more and judged easier to read than angular ones; authors link roundness, ease of processing, liking and taste correspondence.
practical_applications: Rounded type for soft, sweet, friendly, playful messages; angular type for sharp, intense, technical ones.
limitations: Short report, online sample, 12 typefaces (10 custom); Latin script.

sources.title: The role of typeface on taste expectations and perception: A review (accepted manuscript)
sources.authors: Velasco, C., Hyndman, S., Spence, C.
key_findings: Reviews evidence that typeface features (roundness/angularity) correspond to taste expectations; more preferred visual features match sweetness, less preferred match bitter/sour.
Early two-typeface finding (2014) was later replicated with more typefaces, languages and countries.
practical_applications: Typeface carries sensory and emotional connotation beyond the words; pick type as part of the look, not after it.
limitations: Manuscript submitted to Food Quality and Preference (2016); final published title/year/DOI not verified this session; food domain.

sources.title: The Stopping Power of Advertising: Measures and Effects of Visual Complexity
sources.authors: Pieters, R., Wedel, M., Batra, R.
key_findings: Per abstract: feature complexity (dense perceptual detail: colour, edges, luminance) reduced attention to the brand and attitude toward the ad.
Design complexity (elaborate creative arrangement of objects, shapes, patterns) increased attention to the picture and the ad, comprehension and ad attitude.
249 eye-tracked ads.
practical_applications: Cut raw clutter (noise, many small details, many colours) but keep a rich, structured design idea; 'cluttered' and 'well-designed complex' are different.
limitations: Full text not read; print ads in magazines.

sources.title: Predicting Users' First Impressions of Website Aesthetics With a Quantification of Perceived Visual Complexity and Colorfulness
sources.authors: Reinecke, K., Yeh, T., Miratrix, L., Mardiko, R., Zhao, Y., Liu, J., Gajos, K. Z.
key_findings: 450 websites, 548 volunteers; image-feature models predicted perceived colourfulness (R2 .78) and complexity (R2 .65).
Appeal after 500 ms dropped strongly at high complexity and slightly at very low complexity; colourfulness played a minor role.
Age and native language affected appeal; even award-winning sites were disliked by many; model explained ~48% of appeal variance.
practical_applications: Visual complexity is the first lever on a split-second impression; keep complexity low-to-moderate for feed images, and test per audience.
limitations: Website screenshots, online volunteers; does not measure trust or long-term liking.

sources.title: The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites: Working towards understanding aesthetic judgments
sources.authors: Tuch, A. N., Presslaber, E. E., Stöcklin, M., Opwis, K., Bargas-Avila, J. A.
key_findings: 119 real website screenshots varying in visual complexity and prototypicality; effects appear within 17-50 ms.
Low complexity + high prototypicality = most beautiful.
Complexity acts earlier; prototypicality's influence grows with viewing time (consistent with Leder's stage model).
practical_applications: For instant impressions: simple and genre-typical first; novelty can be added where viewing time is longer (later slides, captions).
limitations: Websites, lab; preprint version read.

sources.title: Quicker, faster, darker: Changes in Hollywood film over 75 years
sources.authors: Cutting, J. E., Brunick, K. L., DeLong, J. E., Iricinschi, C., Candan, A.
key_findings: 160 English-language films 1935-2010: shots got shorter; more motion; shorter shots carry proportionately more motion in recent films; films got darker (mean frame luminance decreased).
Authors attribute all four trends to filmmakers increasing control of viewer attention; darker images with wider dynamic range allow more contrast control.
practical_applications: 'Cinematic' in contemporary terms correlates with darker overall key, controlled contrast, motivated motion and short shots; use as checkable features, not as a guarantee of quality.
limitations: Hollywood English-language sample; descriptive trends, not audience-preference tests.

sources.title: The Handmade Effect: What's Love Got to Do with It?
sources.authors: Fuchs, C., Schreier, M., van Osselaer, S.
key_findings: Per abstract/press: four studies show handmade products are more attractive, largely because they symbolically 'contain love'; effort, quality, uniqueness, authenticity and pride were controlled.
Effect stronger for gifts to loved ones; press reports willingness to pay up to 17% more.
practical_applications: Visible human making (hands, process, the optician fitting) adds warmth and authenticity, strongest for gift/love framings.
limitations: Full text not read.

sources.title: Humans versus AI: whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork
sources.authors: Bellaiche, L., Shahi, R., Turpin, M. H., Ragnhildstveit, A., Sprockett, S., Barr, N., Christensen, A., Seli, P.
key_findings: All paintings were AI-made; random 'Human-created' vs 'AI-created' labels.
Human-labelled art rated higher on liking, beauty, profundity and worth (Study 1, replicated in Study 2).
Perceived story and effort moderated label effects for liking/beauty; attitudes to AI moderated profundity/worth.
practical_applications: The label/provenance changes judgement independent of pixels; communicate human intent, story and effort when AI tools are used.
limitations: Online samples; paintings not commercial images; label manipulation only.

sources.title: AI-synthesized faces are indistinguishable from real faces and more trustworthy
key_findings: 315 participants: accuracy at telling StyleGAN2 faces from real was 48.2% (chance).
With training and trial-by-trial feedback (219 participants): about 59%, no improvement over time.
Trustworthiness: synthetic faces 4.82 vs real 4.48 (small effect).
practical_applications: Photoreal AI faces are not reliably detectable by viewers; 'AI-looking' cues come from styling, lighting and context more than face pixels; disclose honestly.
limitations: 2021-era GAN faces, cropped portraits; not full scenes or products.

sources.title: AI Hyperrealism: Why AI Faces Are Perceived as More Real Than Human Ones
key_findings: Per BPS Research Digest and abstracts: White AI faces were judged human more often than real White faces (N = 124 in Exp 1).
AI faces were more average/less distinctive; people relied on familiarity/memorability cues that did not help; higher attractiveness pointed to AI.
Least accurate participants were most confident / had least insight.
practical_applications: Over-averaged, over-attractive, frictionless faces are a statistical tell of AI imagery; add specific, characterful features.
limitations: Original article not read (403); White faces only effect; Psychological Science 34(12) per summary.

sources.title: AI-generated food stimuli match real counterparts in perceived healthiness and calorie content but not in realism or willingness to eat
key_findings: 87 participants rated 60 pairs of AI-generated vs validated real food photos.
AI images rated less realistic and lower willingness to eat; healthiness and calorie ratings did not differ.
Relative realism of an AI image predicted its relative healthiness and willingness-to-eat ratings.
practical_applications: AI product imagery can communicate category facts but loses appetite/desire when it looks unreal; realism drives desire.
limitations: Food domain, single online study; participants did not classify AI vs real.

sources.title: Disclaimer! This Content Is AI-Generated: How AI-Disclosures Influence Trust in Advertisements and Organizations
sources.authors: Koning, B., Voorveld, H. A. M.
key_findings: Between-subjects experiment (N = 304): GAI ad with vs without AI disclosure.
Disclosure raised AI knowledge and persuasion knowledge, which mostly lowered trust in the ad and organisation.
A positive indirect path also appeared (via attitudinal persuasion knowledge to higher trust).
practical_applications: Disclosure has a trust cost on average but is ethically and often legally required; pair it with human-intent framing (see Bellaiche2023).
limitations: Single ad, Dutch sample; Journal of Interactive Advertising 25(3).

sources.title: Blinded with Science or Informed by Charts? A Replication Study
key_findings: Per abstract/summary: four replications (total N = 623) of Tal & Wansink's claim that trivial charts make claims more persuasive failed; text with chart was no more (sometimes less) persuasive.
The chart slightly improved understanding.
practical_applications: A 'scientific look' (graphs, formulas) does not reliably add credibility; use charts only when they inform.
limitations: Full text blocked; crowdsourced samples.

sources.title: Are Men Seduced by Red? The Effect of Red Versus Black Prices on Price Perceptions
sources.authors: Puccinelli, N. M., Chandrashekaran, R., Grewal, D., Suri, R.
key_findings: Per abstract: men perceived greater savings when prices were shown in red vs black (low involvement); women showed better price recall.
practical_applications: Red price tags code 'deal/discount': useful for promos, but the same code pulls a premium look toward 'sale/cheap'.
limitations: Full text not read; magnitude figures differ between press sources.

sources.title: Recent theoretical, neural, and clinical advances in sustained attention research
sources.authors: Fortenbaugh, F. C.; DeGutis, J.; Esterman, M.
key_findings: Classic resource-depletion and mindlessness accounts of the vigilance decrement each fail to explain some findings.

Newer resource-control theory: attentional resources stay constant but executive control toward the task weakens and mind wandering takes more resources; opportunity-cost model: effort is reallocated by subjective value, not depleted.
A large reward withheld until the end of a 10-min run eliminated the vigilance decrement in one study.
In a web sample of 10,000+ (Fortenbaugh et al. 2015), sustained attention develops into young adulthood and does not decline until the mid-40s, later than processing speed.
practical_applications: Frame retention as an opportunity-cost decision each moment: give a reason to stay, not a demand to concentrate.
A promised payoff at the end can sustain attention if it is valued and credible.
limitations: Lab vigilance tasks (rare targets on screen), not entertainment video or social feeds.
Review focuses on 2012-2017 literature.

sources.title: Sustained attention across the life span in a sample of 10,000: dissociating ability and strategy
sources.authors: Fortenbaugh, F. C.; DeGutis, J.; Germine, L.; et al.
key_findings: As reported in Fortenbaugh2017: gradCPT web study of 10,430 participants; sustained attention peaks late and age-related declines begin around the mid-40s.
practical_applications: Audiences 45+ may need slightly calmer, clearer pacing; do not assume decline starts at 65.
limitations: Only read via the 2017 review; web-based self-selected sample.

sources.title: Busting the attention span myth
sources.authors: Maybin, S. (BBC World Service, More or Less)
key_findings: The 8-second / goldfish figure appears in a 2015 Microsoft Canada Consumer Insights report but did not come from Microsoft's own research; it cites Statistic Brain.
Sources listed by Statistic Brain (US National Library of Medicine/NCBI, Associated Press) could find no record of research behind the numbers; Statistic Brain did not respond.
Gemma Briggs (Open University): an 'average attention span' is pretty meaningless; attention is task-dependent and shaped by what viewers bring.
Shorter film shot lengths show film-makers got better at grabbing attention, not that attention spans shrank (per the researcher behind that work).
Goldfish are a model system for learning and memory (Felicity Huntingford).
practical_applications: Never cite the 8-second/goldfish statistic; describe swiping as choice, not incapacity.
limitations: Journalism, not peer-reviewed; read via a reproduction in a University of Wisconsin course PDF (bbc.com blocked for fetch).

sources.title: Is Your Attention Span Shorter Than a Goldfish's?
key_findings: Popular 8-second claims are not corroborated by science; attention is too complex to reduce to a span of time.
Edward Vogel: measures of college students have been remarkably stable across 20 years; Michael Posner: no real evidence of change since the late 1800s.
The Microsoft report credits Statistic Brain; NLM and AP could not locate the cited numbers.
practical_applications: Use as the citation when correcting the goldfish myth in team briefs.
limitations: Newspaper article; read via reproduction in a University of Wisconsin course PDF.

sources.title: Are attention spans really collapsing? Data shows UK public are worried - but also see benefits from technology
sources.authors: The Policy Institute & Centre for Attention Studies, King's College London (Duffy, B. et al.); fieldwork Savanta ComRes
key_findings: Online survey of 2,093 UK adults, 24-26 Sept 2021.
50% wrongly believe the average adult attention span is eight seconds; only 25% identify it as false.
Researchers: without long-term studies it is impossible to confirm attention spans have declined; Duffy calls the 8-second claim thoroughly debunked.
practical_applications: Expect clients and collaborators to believe the myth; correct it gently with this source.
limitations: UK sample; measures beliefs, not attention.

sources.title: Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more?
key_findings: The widely repeated 10-15 minute lecture attention span ultimately relies on a single key 1978 manuscript and thin evidence.
Treats the 8-second figure as a separate myth from the 2015 Microsoft-commissioned report.
practical_applications: Do not structure content around a fixed 'attention cliff' minute.
limitations: Personal View article in Adv Physiol Educ 40(4):509-513; full text blocked (403), read via search summary/abstract.

sources.title: Everyday attention: variation in mind wandering and memory in a lecture
sources.authors: Risko, E. F.; Anderson, N.; Sarwal, A.; Engelhardt, M.; Kingstone, A.
key_findings: In a video-recorded lecture, reported mind wandering increased with time on task and memory for lecture material decreased; mind wandering related to memory.
practical_applications: Long monotone segments lose viewers gradually; vary and re-hook rather than assume a fixed limit.
limitations: Lab lecture videos; a secondary summary reports other lecture studies did not find increases over time.

sources.title: States of curiosity modulate hippocampus-dependent learning via the dopaminergic circuit
sources.authors: Gruber, M. J.; Gelman, B. D.; Ranganath, C.
key_findings: Better memory for trivia answers people were curious about, and also for unrelated faces shown during high-curiosity anticipation, at immediate and one-day tests.
High curiosity enhanced midbrain and nucleus accumbens activity and hippocampus-reward circuit connectivity.
practical_applications: Place brand/product shots in the waiting period between question and answer, not only at the end.
limitations: Small fMRI sample, trivia and faces not brands; read via abstract/summaries.

sources.title: Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects
key_findings: The Ovsiankina effect (tendency to resume interrupted tasks) appears to be a general tendency; the Zeigarnik effect (better recall of unfinished tasks) lacks universal validity.
Authors suggest conditions that produced Zeigarnik effects (e.g., experimenter authority, involvement) were more common in historical studies.
practical_applications: Treat open loops as curiosity plus urge-to-complete, not as a memory booster; always close the loop.
limitations: Full text not reachable (nature.com redirect, unibe.ch DNS failure); pooled numbers reported by blogs not verified and not used.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications is open access; not confirmed on page)

sources.title: Absolute coding of stimulus novelty in the human substantia nigra/VTA
key_findings: Two fMRI studies: SN/VTA responses were driven by stimulus novelty rather than rarity, negative emotion or task relevance.
Novelty enhanced learning of familiar items presented in the same context.
practical_applications: Genuinely new visual information (a new angle, a new detail) can recruit reward/learning systems; repetition of the same frame does not.
limitations: Oddball lab paradigm; read via abstract/summary.

sources.title: The effects of edits on arousal, attention, and memory for television messages
sources.authors: Lang, A.; Zhou, S.; Schwartz, N.; Bolls, P. D.; Potter, R. F.
key_findings: Rate of edits (camera changes within the same scene) varied from slow to very fast; as edit rate increased, physiological arousal, self-reported arousal and memory increased.
Authors suggest edits can increase attention and encoding without substantially raising cognitive load.
practical_applications: Change angle/scale of the same product within a scene to hold attention; distinguish from cuts that introduce wholly new information.
limitations: Television era, horizontal screen; read via abstract only; full title may be longer than indexed slug.

sources.title: The limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing: meta-analytically summarizing two decades of research
sources.authors: Huskey, R.; Wilcox, S.; Clayton, R. B.; Keene, J. R.
key_findings: 142 articles, 683 effects: pooled effect sizes for LC4MP domains (cognitive load, motivation, memory) range r = .314-.398.
Self-report measures give the largest pooled effects, then behavioral, then psychophysiological; no clear evidence of publication bias.
LC4MP: attention to media is governed by viewer goals and involuntary orienting responses to structural features.
practical_applications: Use structural changes (cuts, motion, sound onsets) deliberately to orient attention, while respecting limited capacity.
limitations: Authors acknowledge a 'fruit salad' approach grouping heterogeneous constructs; does not test sub-processes or interactions; only 66 effects had directional information.

sources.title: Attention and the evolution of Hollywood film
sources.authors: Cutting, J. E.; DeLong, J. E.; Nothelfer, C. E.
key_findings: 150 popular films 1935-2005: shot lengths became more correlated with neighbours and their power spectra approached 1/f; authors suggest this may help harness attention.
A 2018 follow-up (295 films 1915-2015) found convergence on 1/f for several dimensions.
practical_applications: Vary shot length in patterns (not uniform rapid cuts) when editing longer story clips.
limitations: Critics (Cinemetrics) note dialogue length drives shot length and the attention link is hypothetical; read via abstract/press/commentary.

sources.title: How video production affects student engagement: an empirical study of MOOC videos
sources.authors: Guo, P. J.; Kim, J.; Rubin, R.
key_findings: 6.9 million video sessions across four edX courses: shorter videos are much more engaging.
Informal talking-head and Khan-style tablet drawings are more engaging; pre-recorded classroom lectures cut into segments engage poorly.
practical_applications: For explainer clips, keep segments short and personal; avoid repurposing long talks unedited.
limitations: Learners in MOOCs, not social-feed viewers; only abstract-level text read, so the length curve was not seen.

sources.title: Counting How the Seconds Count: Understanding Algorithm-User Interplay in TikTok via ML-driven Analysis of Video Content
sources.authors: Masood, M.; Kannan, S.; Liu, Z.; Vasisht, D.; Gupta, I.
key_findings: 68-user lab study plus data donation of 2.65 million videos.
Users spend most time on a few topics but topics change often; feeds individualise rather than converge to trending.
Recommendations do not reflect just-performed actions (contrary to folk theory).
Users like topic change: session novelty relates to perceived content quality; sequence of videos matters.
Content features predict watching >10% of a video with ~70% accuracy, leaving much behaviour unexplained.
practical_applications: Do not over-trust folk theories about 'the algorithm'; vary topics across a posting series; content quality explains only part of retention.
limitations: Participants mostly 18-34, browsing TikTok on macOS web browser, not the mobile app; VLM clustering choices.

sources.title: Measure key moments for audience retention (YouTube Help)
key_findings: Flat line = viewers watch that part start to finish; gradual decline is typical; spikes = rewatching/sharing (strong or confusing content); dips = leaving/skipping.
Intro metric = share of audience still watching after the first 30 seconds; align opening with title and thumbnail.
Typical retention compares a video with the channel's 10 latest videos of similar length; move compelling content earlier.
practical_applications: Read post-publication graphs against the RETENTION_REVIEW table; benchmark against own videos, not internet averages.
limitations: Platform documentation; no published methodology or effect sizes.

sources.title: Creative best practices for performance ads (TikTok Business Help Center)
key_findings: Prioritise the hook in the first 6 seconds; introduce the content proposition in the first 3 seconds.
Use sound/music; captions or text overlays at 5-10 words per second; 9:16 vertical, 720p+, inside UI safe zone.
Feature creators, employees or customers; end with a clear CTA; structure hook -> USPs -> CTA; refresh creatives when performance declines.
practical_applications: Use as craft defaults for product clips, labelled as platform guidance.
limitations: No studies or data cited on the page; written for paid performance ads.

sources.title: Best practices for Instagram video ads (Meta Business Help Center)
key_findings: Feature brand and key message within the first 3 seconds; 6-15 second videos are more effective in feed and stories; hook with motion or a compelling first frame.
Design for sound-off with subtitles and supers, but music/voiceover helps those who listen; Meta reports feed video ads have 2.25x higher CTA CTR when watched with sound on.
Provide key info early because many people interact before the video ends; native, non-ad-like creative performs better; test and iterate.
practical_applications: Brand and frame visible in first seconds; every clip must work muted and unmuted.
limitations: Platform guidance without methodology; retrieved through Meta's official help-article tool.

sources.title: Optimize your ad creative for Instagram (Meta Business Help Center)
key_findings: Showcase brand/product within the first 3 seconds; under 15 s in feed, under 10 s in stories.
Structured storytelling (problem > solution > result, transformation, day in the life) and product demos help performance.
Product-focused creative for lower-funnel results, people-focused creative for brand objectives; aim for frequency of 2-3 impressions per person per 7 days.
practical_applications: Choose product-focused vs people-focused clips by campaign goal; watch frequency to avoid fatigue.
limitations: Platform guidance, no methodology.

sources.title: Generational differences in work-related attitudes: a meta-analysis
key_findings: 20 studies, 18 pairwise comparisons, 19,961 subjects across Traditionals, Boomers, Gen X and Millennials.
Relationships between generation and work outcomes are moderate to small, essentially zero in many cases; meaningful differences probably do not exist on the variables examined.
A 2024 meta-analytic review (Ravid, Costanza, Romero, J Organ Behav) reportedly found few systematic meaningful differences.
practical_applications: Brief by life situation and age-related needs, not by generation label.
limitations: Work attitudes, not media habits; Gen Z not included; read via abstract/search summary.

sources.title: Are Generational Categories Meaningful Distinctions for Workforce Management?
sources.authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
key_findings: Committee charged to assess whether generational categories are meaningful for workforce management; notes advice on managing generations is prevalent but sometimes contradictory.
practical_applications: Cite as an authoritative caution against generation-based targeting.
limitations: Only front matter read; conclusions not read this session.

sources.title: How Pew Research Center will report on generations moving forward
key_findings: Generational analysis only when historical data allow comparing groups at the same life stage; age, period and cohort effects are hard to separate.
Demographic shifts can look like generational differences; great diversity within generations.
Labels like Gen Z/Millennial are reference points, not scientific facts; used sparingly to avoid reinforcing stereotypes.
practical_applications: Remove generation stereotypes from briefs; use age/life-stage and context.
limitations: Methodological statement, US focus.

sources.title: How to design font size for older adults: a systematic literature review with a mobile device
sources.authors: Hou, G.; Anicetus, U.; He, J.
key_findings: 12 studies: older adults prefer larger fonts, but there is a critical size beyond which readability declines ('bigger may not always mean better').
Reading speed declines sharply below roughly 9-18 arcmin and declines less steeply above roughly 60-180 arcmin.
Recommended sizes range ~8-22 pt across devices, languages and tasks; higher contrast and more line spacing help; inconsistent units across studies, arcmin proposed.
practical_applications: Subtitles for 45+ viewers: large, high-contrast, generous line spacing, but not so large that lines break every two words.
limitations: Mixed devices and languages (Chinese, Japanese, English); no Thai script; small study count.
sources.license: CC BY (Frontiers; not confirmed on fetched portion)

sources.title: Older Users and Web Accessibility: Meeting the Needs of Ageing Web Users
key_findings: Age-related impairments overlap with disabilities: reduced contrast sensitivity, colour perception and near focus; hearing loss for higher pitches and separating overlapping sounds (e.g., audio with background music); reduced short-term memory and easier distraction.
WCAG guidance for people with disabilities also serves older users.
practical_applications: Duck music under voiceover; high-contrast captions; simple, low-distraction layouts for presbyopia content.
limitations: Web-focused overview, not video-specific research.

sources.title: The recognition of time-compressed speech as a function of age in listeners with cochlear implants or normal hearing
sources.authors: Tinnemore, A. R.; Montero, L.; Gordon-Salant, S.; Goupell, M. J.
key_findings: Normal-hearing younger, middle-aged and older listeners performed similarly at normal rate; age-by-compression interactions were not significant at 20% but significant at 40% and 60% compression.
Middle-aged (52-64) and older groups did not differ at 40-60% compression, suggesting age effects begin before 65.
Processing-speed test (Symbol Search) did not predict performance.
practical_applications: Do not speed up TTS to fit a duration in content for 45+ customers; cut the script instead.
limitations: English sentences, artificial time compression (natural fast speech may be harder per other work); first ~100k characters read.
sources.license: CC BY (Frontiers; not confirmed on fetched portion)

sources.title: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language - Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines
key_findings: Four principles: relevant, findable, understandable, usable; identify readers and purpose; evaluate with readers.
Applies to printed/digital text, may help video creators; does not cover accessibility (points to WCAG and EN 301 549).
practical_applications: English clips for tourists: short plain sentences, numbers clear, visuals carry the story.
limitations: Paid standard; only publisher page and catalogue summaries read.

sources.title: Recommendation ITU-R BS.1770-5: Algorithms to measure audio programme loudness and true-peak audio level
key_findings: Current in-force version approved 2023-11; defines programme loudness (LKFS = LUFS) and true-peak measurement.
Annex 2 gives guidelines for accurate true-peak measurement (oversampling) because sample peaks miss inter-sample overs.
It is the measurement basis cited by EBU R128, Spotify, Apple Podcasts.
practical_applications: Every loudness number in our pipeline (ffmpeg ebur128/loudnorm) should be BS.1770 based so platform figures are comparable.
limitations: Only the ITU product page and search snippets were read; Annex details not checked.

sources.title: EBU R 128 (2020, v4.0): Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
key_findings: Normalise to Programme Loudness; Target Level -23.0 LUFS, tolerance +/-1.0 LU where target not practically achievable (live).
Measure the whole programme, not only speech or music (no 'anchor' emphasis); gated measurement per BS.1770 eq. 7.
Maximum True Peak -1 dBTP in production; lower limits may apply for distribution systems / data reduction (see EBU Tech 3344).
Loudness Range (Tech 3342), max momentary and max short-term loudness are descriptors, not targets.
practical_applications: Use -23 LUFS only for broadcast deliveries; social video uses streaming targets but the same metering method.
Keep TP <= -1 dBTP as an absolute ceiling; lower before lossy encoding.
limitations: Broadcast standard, not a social-platform spec. A 2023 v5.0 exists (seen in search, not read).

sources.title: Loudness normalization on Spotify (Spotify for Artists support)
key_findings: Default playback target -14 LUFS (ITU 1770); user modes Loud -11, Normal -14, Quiet -19 LUFS.
Positive gain is capped by the track's peak with 1 dB headroom for lossy encoding; loud mode uses a limiter (-1 dB, 5 ms attack, 100 ms release).
Advice: master to about -14 LUFS, keep true peak below -1 dBTP; if louder than -14 LUFS keep below -2 dBTP.
No normalization on the web player and some third-party devices.
practical_applications: Good reference for 'loud masters get turned down, quiet masters may not be fully raised' logic that also applies to video platforms.
limitations: Music-streaming platform, not a video platform. Undated support page; values can change.

sources.title: Apple Podcasts for Creators: Audio requirements
key_findings: Target around -16 LKFS +/-1 dB, true peak not above -1 dBFS, both per ITU-R BS.1770-5; condition loudness before encoding.
WAV/FLAC min 44.1 kHz, 16- or 24-bit; 24-bit recommended; mono masters must be delivered as dual-mono stereo for WAV/FLAC.
practical_applications: Use -16 LUFS for speech-only audio deliverables (podcast-style VO, audio-only posts).
limitations: Podcast spec; not a video-platform rule.

sources.title: AES TD1008: Recommendations for loudness of internet audio streaming and on-demand distribution (republished as AES77-2023)
sources.authors: Audio Engineering Society Technical Committee on Broadcast and Online Delivery
key_findings: Guidance for distributors (not producers) on distribution loudness for music streams, radio-style streams and podcasts; supersedes TD1004.
Per Shepherd's summary: music -16 LUFS distribution loudness (album/loudest-track at ~-14), speech-only and assorted content -18 LUFS.
practical_applications: Explains why platform targets cluster at -14 to -18 LUFS and why speech-only content is often played quieter than music.
limitations: Numbers taken from a practitioner summary (ProductionAdvice), not read in the AES document itself.

sources.title: AES TD1008 summary (ProductionAdvice)
key_findings: Summarises TD1008: music -16 LUFS; speech/podcast/'assorted' -18 LUFS; interstitials and assistant audio -18 LUFS.
practical_applications: Secondary reference for speech-only targets.
limitations: Practitioner summary; no true-peak figure stated in the summary.

sources.title: Are you confused about exactly what YouTube's playback volume normalization is doing to your music?
key_findings: YouTube 'Stats for nerds' shows 'content loudness' = difference between a video's loudness and YouTube's reference.
YouTube only turns loud videos down; quieter videos are not turned up.
practical_applications: Check an uploaded clip: right-click > Stats for nerds; positive content loudness means YouTube is attenuating it.
limitations: 2017 article; YouTube publishes no official loudness target (no Google help page found this session). The often-quoted -14 LUFS reference is practitioner-reported (e.g. MeterPlugs 2019).

sources.title: How Meta brought high-quality audio to Facebook and Instagram with the xHE-AAC codec
key_findings: xHE-AAC with MPEG-D DRC deployed for Facebook and Instagram Reels/Stories: loudness metadata, original audio untouched, client applies a context-dependent target loudness and DRC (headphones, speaker, noise).
No target LUFS value is published.
practical_applications: On Reels/Stories the final playback loudness is decided by the app; deliver a consistent, well-limited master and do not rely on extreme loudness.
limitations: Engineering blog, not a spec; no numbers.

sources.title: LUFS targets per platform 2026
key_findings: Lists TikTok / Instagram / Meta as having no published loudness target (approx. -14 internal, context-adaptive), -1 dBTP advised.
practical_applications: Supports our position: for TikTok/IG use a sensible default, not a 'required' number.
limitations: Vendor blog; snippets only; internal values are estimates.

sources.title: Preferred levels for background ducking to produce esthetically pleasing audio for TV with clear speech
sources.authors: Torcoli, M.; Freke-Morin, A.; Paulus, J.; Simon, C.; Shirley, B.
key_findings: J. Audio Eng. Soc. 67(12) 2019: for a pleasant mix with clear speech, recommends at least 10 LU between commentary and music, and at least 15 LU between commentary and ambience; non-experts preferred about 4 LU more than experts.
Recommendation: at least 10 LU between commentary and music, at least 15 LU between commentary and ambience.
Non-experts preferred LDs about 4 LU higher than experts (significant); preferences varied widely between listeners.
Earlier convention version: listeners over 50 preferred at least 7 LU (under 50 no clear preference).
practical_applications: Core number for our VO mix: music bed >= 10 LU below VO while speaking, ambience >= 15 LU below; we are 'experts' so err louder VO than we like.
limitations: 22 listeners, normal hearing, TV documentary material, German lab; LD measured on short items.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: target is preference with clear speech; venue JAES.

sources.title: [exact title not confirmed] JAES review of object-based audio personalisation for hard-of-hearing listeners
key_findings: Systematic review: spatial separation, speech-to-noise ratio and redundancy are evidenced to improve intelligibility; no single solution fits all hearing-impaired listeners.
practical_applications: Use all three levers in VO mixes: level difference, keep music out of the VO's centre/frequency space, redundancy (on-screen text = subtitles).
limitations: Exact title not confirmed; JAES vol. 67 pp. 584-597 per search snippets; content read only from snippets.

sources.title: ISO 226:2023 Acoustics - Normal equal-loudness-level contours
key_findings: Third edition (2023): equal-loudness contours for pure tones 20 Hz-12.5 kHz, otologically normal listeners aged 18-25.
practical_applications: Explains why bass and very high treble sound quieter at low playback levels -> mixes checked only loud sound thin when quiet on a phone.
limitations: Standard not read; product page/snippets only.

sources.title: [exact title not confirmed] Review of the ISO 226:2023 revision (Acoustical Science and Technology 45(1) 1-8)
sources.authors: Suzuki, Y.; Takeshima, H.; Kurakata, K.
key_findings: 2023 revision differs from 2003 by at most 0.6 dB; motivated by a 0.4 dB lower threshold at 20 Hz (ISO 389-7:2019) and an updated loudness exponent.
practical_applications: The 2003 curves remain fine for mixing intuition.
limitations: Title paraphrased from search result; snippets only.

sources.title: An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing (6th ed.)
key_findings: Ch.3 'Frequency selectivity, masking and the critical band': auditory filters, power-spectrum model of masking.
Masking spreads more upward in frequency than downward; critical bandwidth grows with centre frequency.
practical_applications: Why a bass-heavy or mid-heavy music bed masks VO consonants more than its level suggests; carve the music where the VO lives.
limitations: Only table of contents / search snippets read.

sources.title: Digital dynamic range compressor design - a tutorial and analysis
sources.authors: Giannoulis, D.; Massberg, M.; Reiss, J. D.
key_findings: Compressors are nonlinear systems with memory; compares peak vs RMS detection, feed-forward vs feedback; recommends feed-forward designs as stable and predictable.
practical_applications: Explains threshold / ratio / knee / attack / release used in our acompressor settings.
limitations: Abstract only. JAES 60(6) 399-408.

sources.title: 0 dBFS+ levels in digital mastering
key_findings: Inter-sample peaks can be considerably higher than 0 dBFS; consumer CD players reproduce such signals with distortion.
practical_applications: Reason to meter true peak (dBTP), not sample peak, and to leave >= 1 dB headroom before AAC encoding.
limitations: AES convention paper, abstract only.

sources.title: FFmpeg Filters Documentation (loudnorm, ebur128, sidechaincompress, acompressor, afftdn, agate, deesser, alimiter)
key_findings: loudnorm: EBU R128 normalisation with dynamic and linear modes; single pass and two pass; defaults I=-24, LRA=7, TP=-2; dynamic mode upsamples to 192 kHz so set -ar explicitly.
linear=true needs all measured_* values; reverts to dynamic if target LRA < source LRA or the gain would exceed target TP.
acompressor/sidechaincompress defaults: threshold 0.125, ratio 2, attack 20 ms, release 250 ms; afftdn default nr 12 dB, nf -50 dB.
practical_applications: All command examples in MIX_PLAYBOOK.md were run on ffmpeg 9.0 (gyan.dev build) on synthetic audio this session.
limitations: In our test, loudnorm pass-1 input_i differed from ebur128 by about 0.9 LU on a synthetic signal - always re-measure the output.

sources.title: Managing sibilance / Vocal de-essing (Sound On Sound techniques)
key_findings: Offending sibilance usually 5-8 kHz (SOS review); many vocal mics have a presence boost around 5 kHz; over-de-essing dulls the voice.
practical_applications: De-esser band for Thai/English TTS: start 5-8 kHz, then listen.
limitations: Snippets only; craft advice.

sources.title: Digitizing audio (EECS 4462 course notes)
key_findings: Sampling theorem: sample rate must exceed twice the highest frequency; bit depth sets quantisation noise floor ~6.02 dB per bit (+1.76 dB for a full-scale sine), 16-bit ~ 96 dB.
practical_applications: 48 kHz / 24-bit (or 32-bit float) for production files; 16-bit is fine for final delivery.
limitations: Read via search snippets only.

sources.title: GSMArena labs: smartphone loudspeaker test methodology
key_findings: Measures phone speaker frequency response with a sweep and reports loudness in LUFS; shows strong bass roll-off on phone speakers.
practical_applications: Motivation for a phone-speaker check (high-pass ~150 Hz preview) in QC.
limitations: No published cut-off numbers in what we saw; consumer-review methodology.

sources.title: Guidelines for Selecting or Modifying Logos
sources.authors: Henderson, P. W.; Cote, J. A.
key_findings: (As summarised by Kim & Lim 2019) Logo design characteristics (active, balance, cohesive, complex, depth, organic, parallel, proportion, repetition, representative, round, symmetric) were related to correct recognition, false recognition, affect and familiar meaning.
Three underlying design dimensions: elaborateness (complexity, activeness, depth), naturalness (representative, organic) and harmony (symmetry + balance).

Guidelines by objective: high-recognition logos = very natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; low-investment logos = less natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; high-image logos = moderately natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate.
Figurative logos depicting familiar objects need less learning and are recognised more easily than abstract ones.
practical_applications: Brief a new mark as 'harmonious + moderately elaborate'; choose figurative/natural when there is little media budget to teach an abstract mark.
limitations: Full text not read this session; findings come from Kim & Lim (2019) review footnotes.

US student sample, black-and-white logos, late-1990s stimuli; later cross-national work (Henderson et al. 2003; van der Lans et al. 2009) reportedly supports the three dimensions but colour/motion were not tested.

sources.title: Does Your Company Have the Right Logo? How and Why Circular- and Angular-Logo Shapes Influence Brand Attribute Judgments
sources.authors: Jiang, Y.; Gorn, G. J.; Galli, M.; Chattopadhyay, A.
key_findings: Five experiments: circular logos activate 'softness', angular logos 'hardness' associations, shifting attribute judgments (shoe rated more comfortable with a circular logo, more durable with an angular one; sofa softness; company customer-sensitivity).
Mechanism is mental imagery in visuospatial working memory: effect disappears under visual (not verbal) load and for people low in imagery disposition.
Shape works even as an incidental prime, not only as the logo.

No main effect on overall attitude; attitude/WTP rose only when the headline stressed the same attribute the shape implies (congruence). A headline stressing a different attribute removed/disrupted the shape effect.
practical_applications: Match shape language (round vs angular) to the attribute the brand claims (comfort/care vs durability/precision) and keep the headline on the same attribute.
limitations: Simple lab logos, fictitious brands, student/mTurk samples (N 69-306 per study); small effect sizes (partial eta-squared ~.04-.09).
Authors note real logos are complex and shape meaning depends on context (a cross means different things for a church vs a hospital).

sources.title: A comprehensive review on logo literature: research topics, findings, and future directions
sources.authors: Kim, M. J.; Lim, J. H.
key_findings: Reviews 124 logo studies (30 years) in six topics: theory, design/redesign, typeface/shape/colour, additional elements, outcomes, practical applications.

Redesign: new logos lose processing fluency; committed consumers judge redesigns more negatively (Walsh et al. 2010, 2011); remedies = figurative marks, repeated multi-channel exposure, launch communication.
Evolutionary (small) vs revolutionary (large) redesign; revolutionary used when strategy changes or to shed a negative image (Airey 2009, practitioner).

Shape: angular/heavy = more masculine, rounded/slender = more feminine (Lieven et al. 2015); logo frames feel protective under high risk (Fajardo et al. 2016); asymmetry linked to excitement (Bajaj & Bond 2018; Luffarelli et al. 2019).
Colour: Labrecque & Milne (2013) report a negative relation between colour differentiation from a dominant market leader and brand equity in some categories.
M&A/co-brand logo options: keep both, fuse, use the stronger one, or create new; little evidence on which is best.
practical_applications: Use as the map of logo evidence; check each claim against its primary study before treating it as fact.
limitations: Narrative (not meta-analytic) review; repeats popular colour statistics (e.g. '62-90% of judgments based on colour', 'colour raises recognition 80%') from non-peer-reviewed sources without critique.
sources.license: copyrighted (copy found on a university course site)

sources.title: Building a unique brand identity: measuring the relative ownership potential of brand identity element types
sources.authors: Ward, E.; Yang, S.; Romaniuk, J.; Beal, V.
key_findings: 1,281 in-market identity elements, 13 packaged-goods categories, 19 countries; 'Competitive Intensity' (HHI-based) measure of uniqueness potential.
Characters, logos and logotypes have the highest potential for unique ownership; colour is hardest because competitors share it heavily.
Competitive intensity varies within an element type, so execution matters.
practical_applications: Invest first in a character/mascot or a distinctive logo/logotype; treat colour as a supporting cue, not the only one.
limitations: Abstract only; FMCG categories; static, de-branded elements shown one at a time.

sources.title: Exploring the uniqueness of distinctive brand assets within the UK automotive industry
key_findings: Replicates Ward et al. (2020) in a high-involvement category: 44 de-branded assets of top-12 UK car brands, 206 respondents.
Logo is the most uniquely ownable asset; fonts, slogans and colours show low uniqueness concentration.
No gender or generational differences in uniqueness.
Reports an industry-wide lack of consistent use of non-logo assets and frames it as an opportunity for brands willing to use colour/font/slogan consistently.
practical_applications: Do not assume a font or colour is 'ours' — test whether people name the brand from it; protect the logo first.
limitations: Convenience/snowball sample (mean age ~29), one country and category; assets shown statically and individually; no sound or character assets tested.

sources.title: Building Distinctive Brand Assets
