key_findings: (Per search summaries of the book and its contents) A distinctive asset must be unique (evokes only this brand) and famous (most category buyers link it to the brand); chapters cover fame and uniqueness metrics and the fame x uniqueness grid.
Grid advice (secondary): invest in unique-but-not-yet-famous elements; avoid famous-but-not-unique elements that competitors share.
practical_applications: Run a simple fame/uniqueness test on each candidate asset before writing it into a brand book.
limitations: Book not read; publisher page blocked; content known only from secondary summaries. Practitioner-oriented book from the Ehrenberg-Bass school.

sources.title: Evidence concerning the importance of perceived brand differentiation
sources.authors: Romaniuk, J.; Sharp, B.; Ehrenberg, A.
key_findings: Existence confirmed; widely cited as Ehrenberg-Bass evidence that few buyers perceive their brand as different or unique, supporting 'distinctiveness over differentiation'.
practical_applications: Cite only as the origin of the distinctiveness-vs-differentiation debate.
limitations: Not read; year listed inconsistently (2004/2007/2010) across catalogues. Critics argue explicit self-report underestimates perceived differentiation.

sources.title: Answering critics
key_findings: Rebuts critiques: growth comes mainly from penetration but loyalty also rises slightly (double jeopardy); cites longitudinal work (2003, 2012, 2014 JBR) against 'cross-sectional only'.
Argues attitude-predicts-behaviour findings reflect regression to the mean; behaviour shapes attitudes more than the reverse.
Several replies are dismissive rather than evidential (e.g. 'pseudo-science', asking critics to publish data).
practical_applications: Shows the school's own position; pair with critics for a balanced view.
limitations: Self-defence by the institute, undated, informal tone.

sources.title: In the battle between salience and differentiation, bothism wins
key_findings: Argues Ehrenberg-Bass overstates by dismissing differentiation, and Thomaz overstates by saying distinctiveness does not work.
Reports Thomaz citing a Google/YouTube study of thousands of ads in which distinctiveness was not among the top-10 performance drivers.
Advice: keep a list of distinctive assets for salience AND a clear position for relative differentiation.
practical_applications: Brand book should hold both: distinctive assets (how we are recognised) and positioning (why choose us).
limitations: Opinion column; studies mentioned were not checked.

sources.title: 'Byron Sharp is ignoring 60 years of published work'
key_findings: (Search summary) Argues How Brands Grow rests on Ehrenberg's stable-market assumptions, that growth depends on perceived differentiation, and that mental/physical availability lack clear measurement.
practical_applications: Reminder that distinctiveness alone is not a growth strategy.
limitations: Page did not load; only search-snippet content; polemical.

sources.title: Recognisably You
key_findings: Database of 12,000+ assets from 900+ brands; only ~15% reach 'gold' (instant, unique link to the brand when shown alone).
Brands with many strong assets reported 31% more likely to be considered and 38% more likely to be used than brands with few.
Advice: test recognition without the logo; combine visual, verbal and sonic cues; set fixed vs flexible guardrails; track performance.
practical_applications: 'Cover the logo' test for every template; separate fixed elements from flexible ones in the brand book.
limitations: Vendor content, proprietary method, correlational (big brands have more famous assets — reverse causality likely), no sample details.

sources.title: Do logo redesigns help or hurt your brand? The role of brand commitment
sources.authors: Walsh, M. F.; Winterich, K. P.; Mittal, V.
key_findings: The greater the change in roundedness of a previously angular logo, the more negatively strongly committed consumers evaluate it; weakly committed consumers respond neutral-to-positive.
Negative logo evaluation spills over into lower brand attitude among committed consumers.
practical_applications: Before a rebrand, involve or pre-brief the most loyal customers; prefer evolutionary change for brands with a loyal base.
limitations: Abstract and press coverage only; 632 US undergraduates, two shoe brands, lab redesigns.

sources.title: 'Starbucks effect': Committed customers don't like logo redesigns
key_findings: Describes Walsh/Winterich/Mittal design: Adidas and New Balance logos, slight vs considerable redesign by a professional designer, 632 students, attitude measured before and after.
Researchers recommend asking committed customers for input, notifying them before reveal, making them feel like insiders.
practical_applications: Rebrand communication plan: loyal-customer preview first.
limitations: University press release; no effect sizes.

sources.title: Corporate rebranding failure and brand meanings in the digital environment
key_findings: Qualitative case of Gap's 2010 logo change (launched 6 Oct, old logo back 12 Oct 2010): 1,000+ Facebook posts plus Twitter and designer forums in under a week.
Brand meanings polarised (hostile and supportive) among managers, consumers, designers and marketers, shaping the failure; brand meaning is co-created online, so firms must expect public critique.
practical_applications: Treat a rebrand as a public conversation: explain the why, stage the change, monitor reactions daily in launch week.
limitations: Abstract + Lund University news summary only; single case.

sources.title: Is a Company Known by the Company it Keeps? Assessing the Spillover Effects of Brand Alliances on Consumer Brand Attitudes
sources.authors: Simonin, B. L.; Ruth, J. A.
key_findings: Main study (n=350) and two replications (n=150, n=210): attitudes toward a brand alliance spill over to later impressions of each partner brand.
Brand familiarity moderates these effects; partners do not necessarily gain or lose equally.
practical_applications: Co-branding/partner logos transfer meaning both ways; the less familiar partner is more affected — choose partners whose image you want to share.
limitations: Abstract only; product alliances (not retailer-carries-brand logos); 1990s US samples.

sources.title: Co-branding logo guidelines (Red Hat-led)
key_findings: Lead brand's template, fonts, colours and voice govern; partner logo goes second; partner colours and style stay out.
Lockups: horizontal (wide partner logos), stacked (tall), vertical (square/narrow); clear space minimum = height of the 'R'; logos matched in visual size and weight.
Three or more brands: tri-brand, co-brand + partner, or equal-weight logo wall.
Always get permission to use a partner logo, even if used before; misuse includes unequal weights, custom templates, mixing illustration styles, AI-generated co-brand logos.
practical_applications: Template for 'our logo + supplier/partner logo' rules in any brand book.
limitations: One corporation's internal rules; not evidence of effectiveness.

sources.title: Branded lockups
key_findings: Co-branded lockup: logos visually equal, vertically centred, partner logo not taller than the core symbol, thin grey divider equal to logo height, clear space = x-height of 'a'.
Defers to the partner's own co-branding standards when they exist.
Partner lockups max 1-2 per asset, placed in a corner related to the core logo, max twice core-logo height.
practical_applications: Concrete numbers to copy into a partner-logo section.
limitations: Single company practice.

sources.title: Voice and Tone — Mailchimp Content Style Guide
key_findings: Voice = constant personality; tone = adapts to situation and the reader's emotional state.
Four voice traits (plainspoken, genuine, translators, dry humour) written with 'X but not Y' pairs (e.g. smart but not snobbish; weird but not inappropriate).
Clarity over entertainment; consider reader's state (relieved, confused); when unsure, keep a straight face; mascot is not given its own voice.
practical_applications: Use the voice-trait + 'but not' pattern and a tone-by-situation table in any brand voice guide.
limitations: Company practice, no outcome data.

sources.title: Microsoft's brand voice: above all, simple and human
key_findings: Separates message (what) from voice (how); voice constant, tone adapts from serious to empathetic to light by context and customer state of mind.
Three principles: warm and relaxed; crisp and clear; ready to lend a hand.
Style tips: key takeaway first, talk like a person, short everyday words, cut every excess word, write for scanning.
practical_applications: Three-adjective voice principle with behavioural style tips is a compact model for small brands.
limitations: Company practice, English-language.

sources.title: How to create brand guidelines (Shopify blog)
key_findings: Typical sections: logos (variants, sizing, clear space, colour), typography, colour palette (names, hex, hierarchy, combinations), imagery (photo, illustration, icons), audience, voice and tone, grammar/style.

Small-business advice: define personality/point of view before colours; start with logo + palette + type; write how-to-use rules with do's/don'ts and examples; a preliminary guide can be a few pages, full ones 15-80 pages.
practical_applications: Basis for the section order of BRAND_GUIDE_TEMPLATE.md.
limitations: Vendor blog; craft advice.

sources.title: Designing Brand Identity: An Essential Guide for the Whole Branding Team
key_findings: (Per table-of-contents listings) Standard practitioner textbook; includes 'Standards + guidelines', 'Standards content', brand books and online brand tools within a 'Managing assets' phase. Multiple editions (3rd-5th).
practical_applications: Reference for full brand-book scope when a client needs more than the template.
limitations: Book not read; TOC only via search summaries.

sources.title: Conceptualizing, Measuring, and Managing Customer-Based Brand Equity
key_findings: Customer-based brand equity = differential effect of brand knowledge on consumer response to the brand's marketing; brand knowledge = awareness + image (associations).
Awareness = recognition (confirm prior exposure when shown the brand) + recall (retrieve the brand from a category/need cue); recognition matters more when decisions are made at the point of sale.

Associations should be favourable, strong and unique; information congruent with existing associations is learned more easily, though unexpected inconsistent information can sometimes create stronger associations; incohesive images reduce what is recalled.
Measurement: indirect (recall/recognition, free association, ratings of associations) and direct (compare response to branded vs unbranded/fictitious version) approaches are complementary.
practical_applications: Small-business brand check: unaided recall question + aided recognition + 'three words you link with us' free association.
limitations: Conceptual paper (no new data); the Ehrenberg-Bass school challenges the attitude-to-behaviour direction.

sources.title: Binet presents fast, cheap, predictive Share of Search metric
key_findings: Share of Search = a brand's organic searches / all brands' searches in the category, free from Google Trends.
Correlated with market share in cars, energy and mobile handsets and led it (up to ~12 months for cars); the gap 'Extra Share of Search' predicts share movement.
Caveats: not a silver bullet; conversion depends on price etc.; not all searches are positive.
practical_applications: Monthly Google Trends comparison of the brand name vs 2-4 local competitors as a free brand-health line.
limitations: Industry presentation, not peer-reviewed; small local brands may have too little search volume for Trends to register.

sources.title: Investigating the effects of consistent visual identity on social media
key_findings: 2x2 between-subjects experiment (consistent vs inconsistent corporate visual identity x organisation type) on social media.
Consistent visual identity significantly improved appreciation of the identity, attitude toward the company, perceived reputation and intention to commit to the company on social media.
practical_applications: Evidence for keeping templates, palette and logo use stable across a social feed.
limitations: Abstract only; sample and stimulus details not seen; single experiment, Indian context.

sources.title: (title not retrieved — Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights article on communication consistency and hotel brand equity)
key_findings: (Search summary) Survey of 223 five-star hotel guests: communication consistency positively related to all brand-equity dimensions, most strongly brand trust, image and perceived quality.
practical_applications: Supports one voice + one visual system across all touchpoints.
limitations: Only search snippet; title wording not confirmed; cross-sectional survey, one sector.

sources.title: Exciting red and competent blue: the importance of color in marketing
sources.authors: Labrecque, L. I.; Milne, G. R.
key_findings: (Per Kim & Lim 2019) Hue, saturation and value relate to brand personality dimensions (e.g. saturation positively, value negatively, with ruggedness), and colour can shape purchase intention via personality.
practical_applications: Choose palette by intended personality, then test — not by colour-meaning charts.
limitations: Not read; JAMS 40(5):711-728; colour meanings vary across cultures.

sources.title: Prompting guide: working without negative prompts
key_findings: States "FLUX models don't support negative prompts".
Naming an excluded thing can pull the model toward it.
Recommends describing the positive visual opposite (e.g. 'a street with no cars' -> 'a quiet pedestrian walkway with cobblestones').
practical_applications: Rewrite every 'no X' in FLUX prompts as what is there instead (plain unmarked paper, empty sky, hands in pockets).
limitations: Vendor guidance, no controlled study; applies to FLUX in general, version not specified.

sources.title: Photographic looks, camera and lens language, art styles, lighting, target colors, and text in FLUX images
key_findings: Recommends naming a style AND describing its visual traits; concrete descriptions beat vague labels such as 'aesthetic'.
Mood/style line at the end of the prompt (documented for FLUX.2 klein); multi-image style reference exists only in FLUX 3 Image.
Text in images: quote exact strings, describe placement and type, proofread output.
practical_applications: For FLUX.1 schnell: write style as traits (line weight, fill, shading, paper) rather than relying on a label alone.
limitations: Written mainly for FLUX 3 / FLUX.2; transfer to FLUX.1 schnell is an assumption to test (ai_tests T1/T2).
Says nothing about artist names.

sources.title: FLUX.1 [schnell] model card
key_findings: 12B rectified-flow transformer, trained with latent adversarial diffusion distillation, 1-4 steps; Diffusers example uses guidance_scale=0.0.
Apache-2.0: personal, scientific and commercial use.
Listed limitations: may not match prompt; prompt following depends heavily on prompting style; may amplify biases.
practical_applications: Keeps our setup legal for shop/client work; explains why steps stay at 4 and guidance is not a knob.
limitations: Card gives almost no prompting guidance.

sources.title: Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance
key_findings: Guidance can be obtained without a classifier by jointly training conditional and unconditional models and combining their score estimates.
The combination trades sample quality against diversity.
practical_applications: Mechanism behind negative prompts: the negative text takes the place of the unconditional branch; at guidance weight 1 the combination reduces to the conditional prediction alone, so the negative has no effect (our derivation from the CFG formula, see AI_CARTOON_GENERATION.md section 2).
limitations: Abstract only read; the cfg=1 consequence is derived from the standard CFG formula, not stated in the abstract.

sources.title: Fast High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation
sources.authors: Axel Sauer, Frederic Boesel, Tim Dockhorn, Andreas Blattmann, Patrick Esser, Robin Rombach
key_findings: Distilled student matches teacher quality with 'four unguided sampling steps'; teacher data generated at a constant CFG.
Trade-off: quality kept 'at the expense of prompt alignment'; common issues 'object duplication and merging'.
No adjustable guidance strengths in the student; in editing it sometimes adheres too closely to the input.
practical_applications: Explains schnell-type behaviour (no CFG knob, occasional duplicated limbs/characters, weaker prompt binding): keep scenes simple, one action per character.
limitations: Paper is about SD3-Turbo; the FLUX schnell card names the same method family but BFL has published no schnell-specific results.

sources.title: IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
sources.authors: Hu Ye, Jun Zhang, Sibo Liu, Xiao Han, Wei Yang
key_findings: ~22M-parameter adapter with decoupled cross-attention for image features; base model frozen.
Image and text prompts can be combined; reusable on models fine-tuned from the same base.
practical_applications: Image-as-prompt is the standard way to carry a character/style reference without training.
limitations: Abstract only; original work is on Stable Diffusion, not FLUX.

sources.title: flux-ip-adapter model card
key_findings: IP-Adapter for FLUX.1-dev, trained at 512 and 1024 px; beta, 'may take more attempts'.
Weights under the FLUX.1 [dev] Non-Commercial License; ComfyUI via x-flux-comfyui nodes; suggests true_gs=2 if results are poor.
practical_applications: Shows the FLUX IP-Adapter route exists but is dev-based and non-commercial -> not for client/shop output without a licence.
limitations: Behaviour with schnell not documented.

sources.title: FLUX.1 Redux [dev] model card
key_findings: Adapter for image variations and restyling; described as working with FLUX.1 base models.
Falls under the FLUX.1 [dev] Non-Commercial License.
practical_applications: Image-variation route for a character master, but the licence blocks commercial use without a BFL licence.
limitations: Card does not discuss schnell explicitly.

sources.title: ComfyUI Examples: Flux
key_findings: Schnell is 'a distilled 4 step model'.
Redux needs sigclip_vision_patch14_384 in clip_vision and flux1-redux-dev in style_models; it 'can be used to prompt flux dev or flux schnell'.
Fill (inpaint/outpaint), Canny and Depth models are dev-based.
practical_applications: Technically Redux runs with our schnell workflow after downloading two files; the licence, not VRAM, is the blocker.
limitations: No VRAM figures; an example page, not a spec.

sources.title: PuLID: Pure and Lightning ID Customization via Contrastive Alignment
sources.authors: Zinan Guo, Yanze Wu, Zhuowei Chen, Lang Chen, Peng Zhang, Qian He
key_findings: Tuning-free identity insertion with a Lightning T2I branch, contrastive alignment loss and ID loss (NeurIPS 2024).
Claims high ID fidelity while keeping background, lighting, composition and style close to the no-ID image.
practical_applications: Face-identity tool for real people; little use for faceless pencil characters.
limitations: Abstract only; the ID loss relies on face recognition, so faceless/cartoon characters are outside its design (our inference, untested).

sources.title: PuLID GitHub repository (PuLID-FLUX)
key_findings: PuLID-FLUX 'can run on a 16GB graphic card'; local gradio demo 'supports 12GB'; fp8 install notes reference flux-dev-fp8.
Code Apache-2.0; ComfyUI implementations are third-party.
practical_applications: Below the documented 12 GB minimum on a 6 GB RTX 3050 -> not feasible now.
limitations: Requirements stated by the authors, not independently tested.

sources.title: DreamBooth: Fine Tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven Generation
sources.authors: Nataniel Ruiz, Yuanzhen Li, Varun Jampani, Yael Pritch, Michael Rubinstein, Kfir Aberman
key_findings: 3-5 subject images typical; 4 gave the best DINO/CLIP-T in their test.

Metrics: CLIP-I and DINO (subject fidelity), CLIP-T (prompt fidelity); DINO preferred because CLIP-I cannot separate subjects with similar descriptions; DINO correlates 0.32 vs CLIP-I 0.27 with human preference.
Failure modes: context-appearance entanglement (colour shifts with the prompt), overfitting to the training context, hallucinated details.
practical_applications: Defines how to score character consistency (DINO similarity to the master) and warns that even a trained character drifts with context.
limitations: Correlations with humans are modest (0.27-0.32); results on Imagen/SD with A100/TPU hardware.

sources.title: FluxGym (FLUX LoRA trainer)
key_findings: 'LOW VRAM (12GB/16GB/20GB) support' via Kohya sd-scripts.
Supports Flux1-dev; schnell listed but the author 'Couldn't get high quality results, so not really recommended'.
practical_applications: Local LoRA training on 6 GB is below the documented minimum -> not feasible locally; a dev-trained LoRA would also carry the dev licence question.
limitations: Practitioner tool README; no benchmarks.

sources.title: ComfyUI-GGUF README
key_findings: GGUF loaders for ComfyUI; transformer/DiT models like Flux are less affected by quantization, enabling low-bit quants on low-end GPUs.
LoRA loading is 'experimental' and should work with the built-in LoRA loader nodes.
practical_applications: Explains why FLUX runs on our 6 GB card and that applying (not training) a LoRA is possible but experimental.
limitations: Work in progress; no quality numbers.

sources.title: DreamSim: Learning New Dimensions of Human Visual Similarity using Synthetic Data
sources.authors: Stephanie Fu, Netanel Tamir, Shobhita Sundaram, Lucy Chai, Richard Zhang, Tali Dekel, Phillip Isola
key_findings: NIGHTS: 20,019 human 2AFC triplets.
Agreement with humans: PSNR 57.1%, SSIM 57.3%, LPIPS 70.7%, CLIP B/32 83.1%, DINO B/16 90.1%, DreamSim 96.2%.
DreamSim focuses on foreground objects and semantic content, also sensitive to colour and layout; LPIPS/DISTS dominated by low-level cues like background colour.
practical_applications: Best available automatic proxy for 'do these two character images look like the same thing'; pixel metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are near chance for this.
limitations: Benchmark images come from Stable Diffusion (mostly photo-like); agreement on line-art cartoons is untested; layout sensitivity can reward near-identical poses.

sources.title: Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation (ConsiStory)
sources.authors: Yoad Tewel, Omri Kaduri, Rinon Gal, Yoni Kasten, Lior Wolf, Gal Chechik, Yuval Atzmon
key_findings: Shared subject-driven attention across a batch keeps a subject consistent without training (SDXL; SIGGRAPH 2024 / TOG).
Consistency measured with DreamSim on background-removed images (notes it can favour slight layout changes); text alignment with CLIP score; 2AFC user study with 3,000 responses.
Limits: appearance and style entangled (works best with one shared style); reduced layout diversity; localisation fails on unusual styles (<5%, fixed by re-seeding).
practical_applications: Evaluation recipe: mask the background, compute pairwise DreamSim within a character set, plus a prompt-alignment score; keep one style per series.
limitations: SDXL-only implementation; not available for our FLUX GGUF setup.

sources.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
key_findings: 'Copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements.'
'prompts do not alone provide sufficient control.'

Human authors keep copyright in their own work perceptible in outputs and in creative selection, coordination, arrangement or modification; an illustrator inputting their own drawing may have a 'greater claim to authorship'. Cites the Zarya of the Dawn comic decision (human text and arrangement registered, AI images not).
practical_applications: Hand-drawn layouts used as img2img input, human-written text in the HTML layer and documented selection/edits are what make a cartoon post protectable.
limitations: US law only; Thai law not covered; case-by-case.

sources.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training (Pre-publication)
key_findings: Style is not protected by copyright as such, but there 'may be cases where the replication of style does capture protectible elements'.

Treats stylistic imitation as a possible market harm ('market dilution') in fair-use analysis; cites 'in the style of' prompts naming artists and the flood of images imitating a Japanese animation studio's look.
Notes some AI systems are instructed not to create images in the style of living artists.
practical_applications: House rule: never name living artists, studios or franchises in prompts; describe generic traits of historical movements instead.
limitations: Pre-publication version; US fair-use analysis; not a court ruling.

sources.title: Qualitative Failures of Image Generation Models and Their Application in Detecting Deepfakes
key_findings: Five failure categories: body parts (hands/fingers, eyes, teeth, eyeglasses...), geometry (straight lines, perspective, symmetry), physics (shadows, reflections, support), semantics/logic (spatial reasoning, repeated objects/faces), text/noise/details (garbled text, fine details, crowds).
practical_applications: QC checklist for every AI cartoon panel before publishing.
limitations: Qualitative review drawn from papers and social media; models of 2022-23.

sources.title: เบื้องหลัง 'ขายหัวเราะ ฉบับ AI'
key_findings: Khai Hua Rao AI edition (Apr 2023), presented as the first Thai gag comic made with AI: AI wrote gags and drew images; a 5-6 person team prompted, selected, filled gaps and edited.
The team's own conclusion: AI cannot yet replace human creativity but can convey some humour.
practical_applications: Thai industry precedent: AI as draft generator, humans curate and edit - the same split as our pipeline.
limitations: News feature, publisher self-report; no audience data.

sources.title: The Wild Classics Of Rubber Hose Animation That Inspired 'The Cuphead Show!'
key_findings: Rubber hose: bouncy elasticity, floppy limbs, pie-cut eyes, white gloves, two-button pants; Bill Nolan credited with the approach (Felix, Krazy Kat).
Fleischer the 'rubber hose capital'; Disney moved away in the mid-1930s toward believable movement; out of favour by the mid-1930s; revived by Cuphead.
practical_applications: Trait list for prompting a rubber-hose look without naming characters or studios.
limitations: Trade journalism, not peer-reviewed.

sources.title: How Disney's Snow White became the first full-length animated feature (History.com)
key_findings: Premiere 21 Dec 1937; about 3 years, $1.4M, 750 artists; aimed to compete with live-action features.
Multiplane camera first tested in The Old Mill (1937) to create depth.
practical_applications: Anchor for the 'golden-age full animation' entry: naturalistic movement, depth, painted backgrounds.
limitations: Popular history; the 'first full-length animated feature' claim ignores earlier non-US features (contested).

sources.title: United Productions of America (Nick and Stephen Bosustow Film Collection exhibit)
sources.authors: Indiana University Libraries Moving Image Archive
key_findings: UPA founded 1943; modernism of simplified shapes, flat bold colour without shading, emphasis on the 2D picture plane.
Limited animation: about 12/8/6 drawings per second vs 24, redraw only moving parts, reuse movements; Gerald McBoing-Boing Oscar 1950.
Cites Bashara (Cartoon Vision): by the mid-1950s 'UPA style had become cartoon style'.
practical_applications: Basis for the 'mid-century flat / limited animation' style entry and for limited-animation tricks in our HTML rig.
limitations: Archive exhibit text summarising a scholarly book; Bashara not read directly.

sources.title: The Flintstones Popularizes Prime-Time Cartoons (EBSCO Research Starters)
key_findings: Hanna-Barbera cut costs with stationary backgrounds and about six facial movements; drawings for a half hour reduced by nearly 97% in some cases.
The Flintstones premiered 30 Sep 1960 on ABC as the first prime-time cartoon.
practical_applications: Model for TV limited animation: held poses, mouth swaps, repeating backgrounds - what rig.js puppets do cheaply.
limitations: Reference summary; drawing-count figures differ across sources.

sources.title: Manga, Media and Content in Postwar Japan (nippon.com)
key_findings: Astro Boy premiered 1 Jan 1963 on Fuji TV as Japan's first long-form TV anime; used fewer frames, reused drawings, moved only the mouth in some scenes.
Strong story-manga source material compensated for limited animation and set the manga-to-anime model.
practical_applications: Anime lineage = story strength + economical motion; supports strong scripts with limited rig animation.
limitations: Journalistic history article.

sources.title: Hergé & The Clear Line
key_findings: 'Klare Lijn' label used in Joost Swarte's 1977 booklet; roots in Hergé's Tintin; Brussels School; later Dutch, French, Spanish and Italian followers.
Hergé stressed clarity of drawing, composition and narrative and disliked a style-only reading.
practical_applications: Ligne claire entry: clarity and readability first - fits simple characters on calm backgrounds.
limitations: Critic's essay (expert, not peer-reviewed); the visual rules (uniform line, flat colour) come from secondary summaries.

sources.title: Snack Culture's Dream of Big-Screen Culture: Korean Webtoons' Transmedia Storytelling
key_findings: Webtoon portals from 2003 (Daum) and 2004 (Naver); smartphone era from 2009.
Web-focused attributes: vertical layout, colour drawing, fast production and consumption ('snack culture').
practical_applications: Vertical-scroll grammar for 9:16 story clips and carousels.
limitations: Korea-specific; 2019.

sources.title: ปัจจัยที่ส่งผลต่อศักยภาพภาพยนตร์แอนิเมชันไทยร่วมสมัย (Potential Factors Effecting Contemporary Animated Thai Films)
sources.authors: เขมพัทธ์ พัชรวิชญ์
key_findings: 12 Thai theatrical animated features 1979-2016: classical era = Sudsakorn (2522/1979); contemporary era from 2545/2002 (Pang Pond, Khan Kluay 2549/2006 in 3D, Yak 2555/2012 ...).
Payut Ngaokrachang made Sudsakorn on cels with a 16 mm camera, budget 5M baht; then a gap of more than 20 years; SIPA policy revived the industry.
Only Khan Kluay and Yak succeeded commercially; problems: narrow target audience, TV-to-cinema shift without quality, adapting Thai literature without fresh ideas, technical lag.
practical_applications: Thai audiences reward familiar Thai material told freshly; adaptation alone is not enough.
limitations: KMITL architecture journal; interviews with 4 directors; features only, no TV/web.

sources.title: อัตลักษณ์ทางศิลปกรรมไทยในผลงานภาพยนตร์การ์ตูนของ อาจารย์ปยุต เงากระจ่าง ตั้งแต่ปี พ.ศ. 2498
sources.authors: วิสิฐ จันมา (Vizit Junma)
key_findings: Payut's first Thai cartoon film 'เหตุมหัศจรรย์ในเช้าวันหนึ่ง' 2498/1955; หนุมานเผชิญภัย 2500/1957; Sudsakorn the first Thai feature.

Thai identity via simplified Thai physiognomy and dress, Thai settings and lai thai ornament; Hanuman characters adapted from traditional Thai mural painting with rounded soft forms; rubbery exaggeration in early work.
practical_applications: How to make a cartoon read as Thai without cliché: everyday Thai settings, dress and body types, ornament as accent.
limitations: Naresuan University journal; publication year not visible in the extracted text.

sources.title: วิวัฒนาการทางวัฒนธรรมของการ์ตูนไทยสู่จินตนาการอันก้าวไกลในโลกดิจิทัล (Cultural evolution of Thai cartoons to the far-reaching imagination in the digital world)
sources.authors: ณปภัช อโรชาสิริ (Napapat Arochasiri)
key_findings: Khrua In Khong called the first Thai cartoonist; first political cartoonist Khun Patiphak Pimlikit (Pleng Tripin) under Rama VI.

After 1932: Sawat Chutharop's serialised Sang Thong and comic sidekick Khun Muen (Popeye/Mickey influence); Prayoon Chanyawongse ('king of Thai cartoons', Magsaysay award); children's magazine Tukata (Pimon Kalasee, characters from 1952); Khai Hua Rao three-panel gags (Arwat); post-1967 TV-influenced superhero comics (Asawin Saifah); Chai Rachawat political strip after 14 Oct 1973.
Today: digital tools and manga influence; concern that a distinct Thai cartoon style may be lost; Wisut Ponnimit (hesheit) as a rough-line, idea-first Thai artist known abroad.
practical_applications: Thai lineage for style proposals: Thai gag strip, Thai political caricature line, Thai fable/jakkrawong comics.
limitations: Descriptive review relying partly on web sources; some dates not given.

sources.title: Die angeborenen Formen moeglicher Erfahrung
key_findings: Proposes the Kindchenschema (baby schema): large head relative to body, high forehead, large low-set eyes, round cheeks, short limbs, which releases caretaking/affection (as summarised by Glocker2009, Nittono2012, Borgi2014).
practical_applications: Origin of the cute-design levers used in chibi, kawaii, mascot and picture-book characters.
limitations: Not read; content known only via secondary sources. Ethological claim of innateness is debated.

sources.title: Baby Schema in Infant Faces Induces Cuteness Perception and Motivation for Caretaking in Adults
sources.authors: Melanie L. Glocker, Daniel D. Langleben, Kosha Ruparel, James W. Loughead, Ruben C. Gur, Norbert Sachser
key_findings: Parametric manipulation of real infant photos: high baby schema (round face, high forehead, big eyes, small nose/mouth) vs low (narrow face, low forehead).
n = 122 undergraduates: high-baby-schema infants rated cuter and elicited stronger caretaking motivation than unmanipulated and low versions.
Method (per Borgi2014): features adjusted within +/-2 SD of the natural range, so it does not test extreme cartoon exaggeration.
practical_applications: Quantified checklist for 'make it cuter': widen face, raise forehead, enlarge eyes, shrink nose and mouth.
limitations: Effects tested on photographic human infants inside natural range; generalisation to stylised cartoon proportions is inferred, not tested here.

sources.title: Baby schema in human and animal faces induces cuteness perception and gaze allocation in children
sources.authors: Marta Borgi, Irene Cogliati-Dezza, Victoria Brelsford, Kerstin Meints, Francesca Cirulli
key_findings: Six facial measures manipulated (face width, forehead length, eye width, nose length, nose width, mouth width) on human, dog and cat faces, following Glocker's method.
Children aged 3-6 (eye tracking, n = 50) looked longer at high-baby-schema faces across species; children (n = 32) and adults (n = 58) rated them cuter.
Eyes drew most fixations, then nose and mouth; children looked longer at the eye region of high-infantile faces.
practical_applications: Baby schema works on animal characters and on child audiences, not only adults; the eyes are the main lever.
limitations: Gaze effect near significance, driven by adult faces; photographic stimuli.

sources.title: The Power of Kawaii: Viewing Cute Images Promotes a Careful Behavior and Narrows Attentional Focus
sources.authors: Hiroshi Nittono, Michiko Fukushima, Akihiro Yano, Hiroki Moriya
key_findings: After viewing baby-animal images, fine-motor performance improved 43.9% vs 11.9% after adult animals (n = 48); visual search accuracy +15.7% vs +1.4% (adult) and +1.2% (pleasant food).
Global-precedence effect disappeared after cute images: attention narrowed to detail.
Pleasantness alone (food) did not produce the effect.
practical_applications: Cute characters can make viewers look closer and more carefully - useful before a detail-heavy panel or product close-up (DERIVED).
limitations: Small samples; Japanese university students; photographic animals, not drawn characters; replication not checked in this batch.

sources.title: The two-layer model of 'kawaii': A behavioural science framework for understanding kawaii and cuteness
key_findings: Splits kawaii into two layers: an emotion and a social value.
The emotion is a positive feeling tied to social motivation to stay close to appealing people/objects; most typical toward infants but not limited to them.
Argues the biological trait is not culture-specific, but Japanese culture has cultivated it.
practical_applications: Kawaii design need not rely only on baby proportions: approachability and closeness are the target feeling.
limitations: Only the abstract was read; survey details not checked.

sources.title: The evolution of the teddy bear
sources.authors: R. A. Hinde, L. A. Barden
key_findings: (Per search summary of the paper and citing works) Museum teddy bears from 1903 onward show a trend toward a larger forehead and shorter snout; interpreted as selection by human preference for baby features.
(Per citing work Morris, Reddy & Bunting 1995) 6- and 8-year-olds preferred baby-featured bears; 4-year-olds did not.
practical_applications: Commercial characters drift toward baby schema over time - a known pattern for mascots and toys.
limitations: Not read directly; small museum sample; correlational.

sources.title: Identification and ratings of caricatures: Implications for mental representations of faces
sources.authors: Gillian Rhodes, Susan E. Brennan, Susan Carey
key_findings: Computer line-drawing caricatures (exaggerating all metric differences from a norm face) of familiar faces were identified faster than veridical drawings, which were faster than anticaricatures; accuracy did not differ.
The best likeness was judged to be a caricature (about +16% by interpolation, as reported by Frowd2007).
Supports norm-based (distance-from-average) face coding.
practical_applications: Exaggerate what makes a character differ from the average face; pulling a design toward 'average' makes it slower to recognise.
limitations: Familiar real faces as line drawings; does not test invented cartoon characters.

sources.title: An application of caricature: how to improve the recognition of facial composites
sources.authors: Charlie Frowd, Vicki Bruce, David Ross, Alex McIntyre, Peter J. B. Hancock
key_findings: Review section: best-likeness caricature level ~16% (Rhodes 1987) to ~42% (Benson & Perrett 1994) for line drawings, but only ~4-6% for photographs.
Caricatured line drawings are identified as well as or slightly better than veridical; anticaricatures less well.
For error-laden composites an anti-caricature was best - exaggeration also amplifies errors.
practical_applications: Stylised/line work tolerates far more exaggeration than photoreal rendering; exaggerate only features that are correct/distinctive.
limitations: Forensic composite context; effects for invented characters inferred.

sources.title: A Study of Facial Features of American and Japanese Cartoon Characters
sources.authors: Kun Liu, Junhong Chen, Kang-Ming Chang
key_findings: 100 American and Japanese animation characters measured against real faces (angles, lengths, areas).
Both traditions exaggerate eyes, nose, ears, forehead and chin.
Eye area: American characters ~2x human, Japanese characters ~3.4x human.
practical_applications: Starting numbers for eye scale per style: Western TV/feature ~2x, anime/manga ~3.4x real eye area.
limitations: Abstract only; sample selection and per-style variance not checked; Symmetry is an open-access MDPI journal (moderate tier).

sources.title: The assessment of the biological age of children's characters created in the convention of Japanese animation in forensic practice
key_findings: 173 frontal anime faces (ages 10-18): eye-related ratios decrease and lower-face ratios (pupil-to-mouth, pupil-to-chin) increase with the character's stated age.
Age readable within +/-2 years for 67% of males but only 35% of females - female characters are drawn more paedomorphic.
Square chins appear only in the 16-18 male group; round/triangular chins in younger boys.
practical_applications: In anime-style design, age is signalled by eye size vs lower-face length and chin shape - use these to make age readable.
limitations: Forensic purpose; anime only; assigned ages imprecise.

sources.title: The vocabulary of manga: Visual morphology in dialects of Japanese Visual Language
key_findings: Catalogued 73 conventionalised graphic schemas in manga (e.g. nosebleed for arousal, nose bubble for sleep) across 20 shonen and shojo books.
Most schemas appear in both genres (shared Japanese Visual Language) but in different proportions - genres act as dialects.
practical_applications: Manga-style expression sheets should include symbolic emblems, not only facial anatomy; shonen and shojo share the vocabulary.
limitations: Abstract/publisher page only; frequencies per schema not read.

sources.title: The Uncanny Valley (translated by K. F. MacDorman and N. Kageki; original 1970)
key_findings: Affinity rises with human likeness, then dips sharply near (but short of) full human likeness; movement amplifies peaks and valleys.
Examples: toy robot (first hill), realistic prosthetic hand (valley), bunraku puppet (high affinity from a distance).
Recommends designers aim for the first peak - moderate human likeness - rather than risk the valley.
practical_applications: Clearly stylised characters are the safe default; near-photoreal characters need flawless detail and motion.
limitations: Essay/hypothesis, not data; the curve shape itself is weakly supported (see Katsyri2015).

sources.title: A review of empirical evidence on different uncanny valley hypotheses: support for perceptual mismatch as one road to the valley of eeriness
sources.authors: Jari Katsyri, Klaus Forger, Meeri Makarainen, Tapio Takala
key_findings: Naive uncanny dip for any human-likeness increase: weak (1 of 8 studies); linear rise of affinity with human likeness: 7 of 9.
Inconsistent realism across features (e.g. realistic face with mismatched eyes, face-voice mismatch): strongest support (4 of 4).
Atypical features on humanlike faces (e.g. enlarged eyes on realistic faces): good support (3 of 4). Movement amplification: not supported.
practical_applications: Keep one realism level across eyes, skin, shape, motion and voice; never put anime-size eyes on photoreal skin.
limitations: Small, heterogeneous, mostly self-report evidence base; morphing artefacts may confound.

sources.title: To Stylize or not to Stylize? The Effect of Shape and Material Stylization on the Perception of Computer-Generated Faces
sources.authors: Eduard Zell, Carlos Aliaga, Adrian Jarabo, Katja Zibrek, Diego Gutierrez, Rachel McDonnell, Mario Botsch
key_findings: Shape stylization drives perceived realism and expression intensity (expressions read as more intense on more stylised shapes); material/texture drives appeal, reassurance and attractiveness.
Strong mismatch between shape and material stylization lowers appeal and raises eeriness (abstract shapes + realistic materials = highly eerie).
Realism is a poor predictor of appeal (appeal and realism scales do not correlate); blurring realistic skin texture raises appeal and lowers eeriness with little realism loss.
practical_applications: For AI images: if the shape is cartoon, keep the surface cartoon (flat/soft), and soften textures rather than adding pores.
limitations: 3D CG faces of two people; lab ratings; generalisation to 2D drawing inferred.

sources.title: Render me Real? Investigating the Effect of Render Style on the Perception of Animated Virtual Humans
sources.authors: Rachel McDonnell, Martin Breidt, Heinrich H. Bulthoff
key_findings: (Per search summaries/citing papers) Render style affects appeal and perceived realism of animated humans; animation artefacts were more acceptable on cartoon-rendered than realistic characters; highly realistic and highly abstract styles were treated differently from middle styles.
practical_applications: Cartoon rendering buys tolerance for imperfect motion - relevant to cheap rig/AI-video animation.
limitations: Not read; details unverified.

sources.title: Iconic faces are not real faces: enhanced emotion detection and altered neural processing as faces become more iconic
sources.authors: L. N. Kendall, Quentin Raffaelli, Alan Kingstone, Rebecca M. Todd
key_findings: Five stimulus sets from photorealistic to fully iconic: at brief presentation, emotion identification was more accurate for more cartoonised faces; at the fastest times the simplest images were ~60% more accurate than realistic faces.
Higher contrast and lower featural complexity each improved accuracy independently.
Simpler/higher-contrast faces produced lower P1 amplitudes (less early cortical processing needed).
practical_applications: For feeds and thumbnails, simplified high-contrast cartoon faces communicate emotion faster than realistic faces.
limitations: Lab task with brief exposures; small set of basic emotions.

sources.title: Transfer between Picture Books and the Real World by Very Young Children
sources.authors: Patricia A. Ganea, Megan Bloom Pickard, Judy S. DeLoache
key_findings: 15- and 18-month-olds extended new labels between pictures and real objects more often with photographs and realistic drawings than with cartoons; iconicity aids transfer.
practical_applications: For toddler educational content where real-world transfer matters, prefer realistic illustration over heavy cartoon stylisation.
limitations: Very young children only; effect shrinks with age (Strouse2018).

sources.title: The Role of Book Features in Young Children's Transfer of Information from Picture Books to Real-World Contexts
sources.authors: Gabrielle A. Strouse, Angela Nyhout, Patricia A. Ganea
key_findings: Realism: photos easiest, cartoons hardest for 15-18-month transfer; iconicity still matters at age 3 in some tasks.
Anthropomorphic language/illustrations reduced factual learning and increased attribution of human traits to real animals (Ganea et al. 2014).
Sharing story with human characters increased children's sharing; the same story with a raccoon decreased it (Larsen et al. 2017).
Manipulative features (flaps, pop-ups) reduced learning in toddlers (Tare et al. 2010).
practical_applications: Teach facts or behaviours with human (or realistic) characters; keep talking-animal designs for entertainment/brand warmth.
limitations: Few studies per domain; small samples; mostly Western urban children.

sources.title: Color Psychology: Effects of Perceiving Color on Psychological Functioning in Humans
sources.authors: Andrew J. Elliot, Markus A. Maier
key_findings: Colour can carry meaning and affect affect, cognition and behaviour, but the literature is nascent; boundary conditions and real-world generalisability are needed before strong application recommendations.
practical_applications: Treat character colour-personality coding as craft convention, not science.
limitations: Abstract only; not specific to characters.

sources.title: The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation
key_findings: Source of the 12 principles incl. 'appeal', 'exaggeration' and 'solid drawing' (as summarised in CHARACTER_DESIGN.md and SHAPE_LANGUAGE.md).
practical_applications: Vocabulary for appeal, exaggeration, twinning avoidance.
limitations: Not read this session; practitioner (craft) knowledge.

sources.title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: Proposes 'amplification through simplification': simplified iconic faces invite reader identification (theory cited as motivation by Kendall2016, which tested a related claim).
practical_applications: Rationale for simple faces on protagonists + more detailed environments.
limitations: Not read this session; theory, partly supported by Kendall2016 for emotion speed only.

sources.title: Model Sheets for Character Designers (Clip Studio guide)
key_findings: A model sheet set = construction sheet (proportions in heads), head + body turnaround, colour sheet, expression sheet, pose sheet.
Turnaround minimum: front, back, profile, three-quarter; horizontal guide lines for eye centres, brows, chin, shoulders keep views aligned.
Expression sheet: at least joy, sadness, anger, surprise; ~6 samples; pose sheet 4-5 poses.
practical_applications: Template for the turnaround/model-sheet section and AI master images.
limitations: Single practitioner; numbers are recommendations, not standards.

sources.title: Early studio animation before rubber hose (animationstudies 2.0 blog)
key_findings: Pre-1928 studio style (from Bray, 1914) had single brisk speed, little squash/stretch, animation on 4s, cycles; rubber hose era marked by rubberised limbs and synchronised sound from 1928.
practical_applications: Context for rubber hose spec card: fluid limbs paired with music timing.
limitations: Blog by an animation scholar; brief.

sources.title: Rubber hose animation
key_findings: Limbs drawn as flowing unjointed curves; rounder smoother bodies (Bill Nolan, Felix shorts, 1920s); style suited sound/music sync; declined in the 1930s with the move to anatomical realism; revived in later TV and games.
practical_applications: Spec card for rubber-hose style.
limitations: Community source; gloves/pie-eyes traits not covered and so not asserted.

sources.title: Chibi (style)
key_findings: Super deformed: head roughly 1/3 to 1/2 of total height vs ~7-8 heads for a typical anime character; oversized head and eyes, tiny nose, stubby limbs, details dropped, signature hair/accessory emphasised; widely used in merchandise and for exaggerated reactions.
practical_applications: Spec card for chibi/SD.
limitations: Community source; proportions are convention.

sources.title: Character Design and Visual Development for LINE Stickers: 'Yoga Teacher'
key_findings: Thai LINE sticker character built with persona research + silhouette-first design + Super Deformed proportion + split-complementary bright colours with grey/white; large face for clear emotion.
40 stickers; 30 target users: 93.3% understood the messages, 90.0% satisfied, 96.7% felt it could represent them.
practical_applications: Workflow for Thai sticker/mascot characters: persona -> silhouette -> SD proportion -> palette -> expression set with short Thai phrases.
limitations: Practice-based design research; satisfaction survey without control.

sources.title: Brand Communication by Using Spoke-characters Featured in LINE Stickers in Thailand
key_findings: Content analysis of 5 popular 2018 sponsored LINE sticker sets: characters created specifically for stickers, usually more than one per brand, mostly gender-unidentifiable, all humorous.
Focus groups (n = 18): a duck character linked to a restaurant's roast-duck dish built brand association; characters with no link to the brand did not.
Users favour cute, funny, often animal characters behaving like everyday life (as reported).
practical_applications: A brand character must carry a visible link to the product/service; casts of 2+ characters are the norm in Thai brand stickers.
limitations: Small sample; one year; qualitative.

sources.title: Thai Comics in the Twenty-First Century: Identity and Diversity of a New Generation of Thai Cartoonists (research project)
key_findings: Early Thai long-story comics (1930s) were stylistically inspired by American newspaper/animation cartoon strips; a realistic illustrative style was introduced by Hem Vejakorn (1938) via Siamese-Italian academic painting.

Kai Hua Roh (gag magazine, 1973, slogan 'household humour') and Maha Sanook (1976, younger readers, short comic stories) from Banlue; pocket format; one-baht comics with simple moral plots peaked in the late 1970s-80s.

Mainstream Thai comics of the 1990s-2000s were strongly manga-influenced; the 21st-century independent generation shows 'freedom of style' (European, American and Japanese influences); individual gag cartoonists' styles vary widely (one is compared with loose European illustrators).
practical_applications: Thai cartoon tradition = plural, not one look; when prompting 'Thai gag comic' describe concrete traits (format, line, humour) rather than a single house style.
limitations: Academic research report; no systematic analysis of proportions or line in Kai Hua Roh.

sources.title: Khan Kluay (2006 film)
key_findings: First Thai 3D animated feature (Kantana Animation, 2006), directed by a former Disney/Blue Sky animator; title character a brave blue elephant who becomes a royal war elephant; budget 115 M baht, 3-year production; multiple Thai and international awards.
practical_applications: Reference point for Thai CG feature style: stylised animals in a historical Thai setting with non-natural signature colour.
limitations: Encyclopedia; no design analysis available.

sources.title: From Webtoon to Apptoon: Changes of Korean Webtoon's Displaying code
key_findings: First-generation webtoons used vertical layout for mouse scrolling with extended panels and creative gutters; app versions shrink frames to phone size and use zoom/pan/vertical movement transitions as directing grammar.
practical_applications: Webtoon characters must read in small, tightly framed panels viewed one at a time while scrolling.
limitations: Short essay; does not discuss character drawing directly.

sources.title: Navigating comics: an empirical and theoretical approach to strategies of reading comic page layouts
key_findings: 145 participants numbered empty panels on 12 layouts; Z-path used ~94% in a canonical grid
Blockage: 91/145 read the left vertical stack first instead of the Z-path
Separation Z-path ~0.72; staggering ~0.90 (trend only); inset: outer dominant panel first 60%
Upper-left panel almost always starts the page (0.96); left-to-right preferred 93 vs 21
Proposes Assemblage (grouped areas, smooth paths, no jumping, no gaps) and ordered preference rules
Frequent comic readers used blockage paths more; frequent manga readers used L->R entry less
practical_applications: Use plain grids for broad audiences
Avoid or cue blockage layouts
Start the page with a clear top-left panel
limitations: Self-selected Comic-Con sample (2004)
Empty panels, no content
Self-reported expertise

sources.title: Navigating comics II: constraints on the reading order of comic page layouts
key_findings: All departures from a grid (blockage/staggering, separation, overlap) pushed readers off the Z-path
Deviation was graded: the lower the rightward gutter, the less the Z-path; at full blockage Z-path <10%
Wider gutters increased group-by-group reading
Notes written Japanese can run right-to-left in vertical columns, unlike L->R English
practical_applications: Keep gutters contiguous when you want rows to read as rows
Use gutter width deliberately to group panels
limitations: Empty-panel task
Author preprint read; published in Applied Cognitive Psychology 29:193-199

sources.title: The architecture of visual narrative comprehension: the interaction of narrative structure and page layout in understanding comics
key_findings: Z-path in grid 95%, staggered 89%, separated 71%, blockage 31% (synthesis)
Narrative constituents and layout tiers are not isomorphic; they operate in parallel
Suggests (untested) Initials at page ends drive page turns and splash pages act as Peaks
practical_applications: Align scene changes and cliffhangers with page/slide boundaries as a hypothesis to test
limitations: Focused review of the author's own work
Layout-narrative mappings are observations, not tested

sources.title: Framing attention in Japanese and American comics: cross-cultural differences in attentional structure
sources.authors: Neil Cohn, Amaro Taylor-Weiner, Suzanne Grossman
key_findings: 30 books (US mainstream, US indy, Japanese manga), ~300 panels each, coded Macro/Mono/Micro/Amorphic
US comics: Macro ~ Mono, few Micro/Amorphic; manga: Mono dominant, more Micro and Amorphic
Shot types track genre more than country
Interpreted as manga using panels as a spotlight of attention; convention is an alternative explanation
practical_applications: Vary attentional framing: Amorphic for mood pauses, Micro for product/detail inserts
limitations: 10 books per group; translated shonen only
Moderate shot-coding reliability (kappa 0.54)
Cognition link inferred

sources.title: Your brain on comics: a cognitive model of visual narrative comprehension
key_findings: PINS model: semantics (mental model, updating) and narrative structure (categories, constituents) processed in parallel
Categories: Establisher, Initial, (Prolongation), Peak, Release; plus conjunction and Refiner (head-modifier) schemas
People delete Establishers/Releases more than Peaks/Initials; missing core panels are detected more accurately
N400 indexes semantic access; anterior negativity narrative structure; P600 updating/inference
Visual language fluency (VLFI) modulates ERPs, reaction and viewing times; manga readership changes processing of Environmental-Conjunction
practical_applications: Plan each panel's narrative role; cut peripheral panels first
Keep inference load low for non-comic audiences
limitations: Model synthesises mostly one lab's work
Mostly wordless Western strips
sources.license: CC BY (open access, Topics in Cognitive Science)

sources.title: Zooming in on visual narrative comprehension
key_findings: Panels zoomed to the regions fixated by earlier readers (about 13% of the panel area) were rated easier to understand than non-fixated or incongruous controls (7-point scale: 4.2 vs 1.8; full panels 6.1) and were viewed more similarly to the originals.
Non-fixated or incongruous crops were harder
Fixation-based inset panels also highlighted key content; modifications affected subsequent panels
practical_applications: Crop tightly to the informative region; use inserts/Refiners for product details
limitations: Self-paced lab task, six-panel strips
Memory & Cognition 49:451-466
Spot-check C1 2026-11-25: corrected.

sources.title: Reading without words: eye movements in the comprehension of comic strips
sources.authors: Tom Foulsham, Dean Wybrow, Neil Cohn
key_findings: Panels in original order were understood faster with fewer fixations than in random order
Random order produced more regressions
Narrative context changed where people looked inside panels
practical_applications: Coherent order lowers effort; scrambled or unclear order costs attention
limitations: Wordless Peanuts strips
Lab eye tracking

sources.title: Being explicit about the implicit: inference generating techniques in visual narrative
key_findings: Speech balloons and motion lines are bound morphemes (affixes) that attach to stems; framing out the stem triggers inference
Peak Drop: deliberate omission of the Peak, inferred from Initial + Release
Suppletive panels (action stars, fight clouds, poof clouds) and text substitution (a sound effect replaces the Peak)
practical_applications: Use Peak Drop for before/after and gentle handling of sad or violent beats
SFX can stand in for an action
limitations: Theoretical/descriptive, corpus examples; not exhaustive

sources.title: (Pea)nuts and bolts of visual narrative: structure and meaning in sequential image comprehension
sources.authors: Neil Cohn, Martin Paczynski, Ray Jackendoff, Phillip J. Holcomb, Gina R. Kuperberg
key_findings: Compared Normal, Semantic-only, Structural-only and Scrambled strips
Reaction times fastest for Normal, slowest for Scrambled, intermediate for the others
N300/N400 smallest for Normal sequences: structure + meaning together ease processing
practical_applications: Both a coherent narrative arc and related content are needed
limitations: Only abstract read in detail; DOI and Cognitive Psychology 65 (2012) 1-38 confirmed from the PDF header

sources.title: The limits of time and transitions: challenges to theories of sequential image comprehension
key_findings: Critiques McCloud's six transitions as linear panel-to-panel relations without hierarchy
Argues closure is an additive inference made at the next panel, not in the gutter
Critiques Groensteen's arthrology as making no testable predictions; proposes hierarchic grouping (grammar)
practical_applications: Treat McCloud transitions as a planning vocabulary, not a cognitive model
limitations: Theoretical argument; Studies in Comics 1(1)

sources.title: Beyond speech balloons and thought bubbles: the integration of text and image
key_findings: Four text-image interfaces: Inherent, Emergent (balloons/tails), Adjoined (captions near), Independent
Integration tempered by Gestalt grouping and semantic features
Balloon carriers link text content to a root (speaker)
practical_applications: Balloon-free captions are Adjoined: speaker must be signalled by position, colour or font
limitations: Theoretical, Semiotica 197

sources.title: The vocabulary of manga: visual morphology in dialects of Japanese Visual Language
key_findings: Described and categorised 73 conventional graphic schemas in manga (e.g. nosebleeds, sleep bubbles)
Corpus of 20 books: most schemas recur in shonen and shojo, at different proportions ('dialects')
practical_applications: Use recognised symbols to carry emotion for faceless characters
limitations: Only abstract read in this session

sources.title: Pow, punch, pika, and chu: the structure of sound effects in genres of American comics and Japanese manga
sources.authors: Nimish K. Pratha, Natalie Avunjian, Neil Cohn
key_findings: US mainstream comics used 100% onomatopoetic SFX, indy comics also some descriptive SFX (Punch!)
Shojo manga used more gitaigo (state-mimicking) and hiragana; shonen more giongo and katakana
In English a similar function is carried by font stylisation
practical_applications: Choose SFX type (sound vs state word) and lettering style by genre and tone
limitations: Small genre corpora; Multimodal Communication 5(2)

sources.title: Navigating meaning in the spatial layouts of comics: a cross-cultural corpus analysis
sources.authors: Irmak Hacimusaoglu, Bien Klomberg, Neil Cohn
key_findings: Corpus of 134 annotated comics (North America, Europe, Asia)
Within-row transitions change the situation least; across rows and pages more
Page boundaries align with spatial-location changes; Asian comics less constrained by layout
practical_applications: Put scene/location changes on page or slide boundaries
limitations: Only abstract read (publisher blocked); correlational

sources.title: Navigating the narrative: an eye-tracking study of readers' strategies when reading comic page layouts
sources.authors: Clare Kirtley, Chris Murray, Phillip B. Vaughan, Benjamin W. Tatler
key_findings: Eye tracking replicated the dominant influence of panel external structure on navigation
Text location inside panels affected order in ambiguous layouts
practical_applications: Use balloon position to cue reading order when a layout is irregular
limitations: Only abstract read (publisher blocked)

sources.title: Reading comics: the effect of expertise on eye movements
key_findings: 14 experts vs 17 non-experts; experts made more and larger saccades
Experts attended more to images; non-experts needed more and longer fixations on text
practical_applications: For general audiences keep text short; images should carry the story
limitations: Small sample; GLMM with layout/text controls
sources.license: CC BY (Journal of Eye Movement Research)

sources.title: Picturing words: the semantics of speech balloons
key_findings: Speech and thought bubbles analysed as quotational event modification in a dynamic picture semantics
Balloons are symbolic elements inside iconic pictures; non-verbal affixes (motion lines, lightbulbs) can be analysed similarly
practical_applications: Balloon content is read as a quotation attached to the depicted speaker/event
limitations: Formal semantics proceedings paper (Amsterdam Colloquium); no empirical data

sources.title: The secret art of comedy manga: analisis struktur kishotenketsu pada komik populer Jepang
sources.authors: Ni Kadek Karisma Dewi, Ni Nyoman Puspa Dewi, Luh Putu Leoni Pramesti, I Nyoman Larry Julianto
key_findings: Yonkoma structure: Ki = intro (panel 1), Sho = development (2), Ten = unexpected twist/climax (3), Ketsu = conclusion that makes the reader rethink the twist (4)
Qualitative analysis of Gekkan Shojo Nozaki-kun ch.101: structure gives a clear, consistent message and scales to longer plots
practical_applications: Use ki-sho-ten-ketsu for 4-slide gentle gags and reflective stories
limitations: Descriptive qualitative study of one manga; Indonesian design journal

sources.title: Review of 'The Art of Thai Comics: A Century of Strips and Stripes' by Nicolas Verstappen
key_findings: Thai comics peaked 1980s-2000s; first Siamese comic strip late 1920s (Pong Gab Priaw)
Temple-mural tradition: panels with minimal captions and detailed backgrounds, colour with narrative codes
Manga has dominated Thai comics since the 1980s; Thai comics characterised by eclectic mixing (lai rot)
practical_applications: Detailed, meaningful backgrounds and folk-tale retelling fit Thai visual heritage
limitations: Book review, not primary research; Journal of the Siam Society 110(1)

sources.title: The symbolization of sounds in Thai onomatopoeic words
key_findings: Data from Thai dictionaries and 40 Japanese-to-Thai translated comics
Most Thai sound-symbolic words are monomorphemic or reduplicated
Meanings relate to human behaviours, activities and surroundings
practical_applications: Thai SFX design: use single syllables and reduplication
limitations: Only the abstract page read; full PDF blocked by a bot check

sources.title: Memes in a digital world: reconciling with a conceptual troublemaker
key_findings: Internet memes = groups of related items circulated, imitated and transformed by many users
Three dimensions: content, form, stance (participation, keying, communicative function)
Spread through mimicry and remix; form is copied most faithfully while content/stance shift
practical_applications: Design comic templates with fixed form and swappable content; match stance to brand
limitations: Two qualitative case studies; 2013 platforms

sources.title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: Closure and six panel transitions (moment, action, subject, scene, aspect, non-sequitur) as described in Cohn2010TimeTransitions
practical_applications: Vocabulary for planning transitions
limitations: Book not read this session; content known via Cohn2010TimeTransitions and a 1998 IEEE review record (the URL/DOI is that 1998 review, not the book)

sources.title: Comics and Sequential Art: Principles and Practices from the Legendary Cartoonist
key_findings: Existence of 1985/1990 and 2008 editions confirmed via OpenAlex records
practical_applications: Classic practitioner textbook on sequential art
limitations: Not read this session; no findings claimed

sources.title: The System of Comics (trans. Bart Beaty, Nick Nguyen)
key_findings: Per search summaries: spatio-topia (space + place of panels), arthrology (relations among images), restricted vs general arthrology, braiding (tressage)
practical_applications: Motif repetition across distant panels/episodes
limitations: Only search summaries read; French original 1999, English 2007 (University Press of Mississippi)

sources.title: Sticker guidelines (static) - LINE Creators Market
key_findings: Sets of 8/16/24/32/40; sticker max 370x320 px, <=1 MB; main 240x240; tab 96x74; PNG transparent; >=72 dpi RGB; even dimensions; ~10 px margin; ZIP <=60 MB
Recommended: everyday expressions/messages; not recommended: objects/scenery, overly long images, low variety
Prohibited: advertising, requests for personal info, sexual/violent content, under-age drinking/smoking
practical_applications: Spec sheet for sticker sets
limitations: Platform rules change; re-check before submission

sources.title: Animated sticker guidelines - LINE Creators Market
key_findings: Sets of 8/16/24; max 320x270 px (one side >=270); 5-20 frames; <=4 s; 1-4 loops; APNG with .png; <=1 MB each; main 240x240; tab 96x74
practical_applications: Spec sheet for animated stickers
limitations: Platform rules change

sources.title: Creator's Resource Handbook and Before You Publish Checklist (WEBTOON CANVAS)
key_findings: Vertical format: reader sees one panel at a time; max 2 panels on screen; <=3 balloons/panel; 1-2 sentences per balloon; diamond stacking
Min 200 px between panels in a scene; 600-1000 px for location/scene transition; vary panel size; impact panels
Images <800 px wide and <1280 px tall, <=2 MB each, <=20 MB / 100 images; JPG/PNG
Thumbnails 1080x1080 (<500 KB) and 1080x1920 (<700 KB), no text; launch with 3 episodes; font 12-30 px typical
practical_applications: Pacing and spec rules for webtoon and scroll-pan clips
limitations: Editorial guidance from the platform, not reader research; year not printed

sources.title: Tips for Creating Vertical Scrolling Webtoons
key_findings: Canvas 800 px wide per WEBTOON spec; export in sections <=1280 px
Spacing gives readers rest and time for text; larger gaps mark scene change
Gradient maps (e.g. sepia) for flashback; colour can extend beyond panels; dialogue before character suggests thought
practical_applications: Practical webtoon production tips
limitations: Practitioner tutorial; no pixel values for spacing

sources.title: Comic Book Grammar & Tradition
key_findings: Tails point to the mouth and end ~50-60% of the way to the head; joined balloons = one train of thought
Off-panel: tail to border or none; thought balloons largely replaced by captions
Burst = shout; dashed = whisper; lightning tail = radio; caption types: location/time, internal, spoken, editorial; avoid tangents
Bold italic for emphasis; double dashes for interruption; ellipses for trailing
practical_applications: Lettering conventions for balloons and captions (adapt for Thai: no caps)
limitations: US English conventions; craft, not research

sources.title: Instagram Now Allows Up to 20 Photos and Videos for Carousel Posts
key_findings: Instagram raised the carousel limit from 10 to 20 photos/videos, rolling out worldwide on 8 Aug 2024
practical_applications: Carousel comics can run up to 20 slides
limitations: News report, not Instagram's Help Center; aspect-ratio rules not covered

sources.title: A Non-Photorealistic Lighting Model for Automatic Technical Illustration
sources.authors: Amy Gooch, Bruce Gooch, Peter Shirley, Elaine Cohen
key_findings: Observed in technical illustrations: edge lines (boundaries, silhouettes, discontinuities) drawn in black; matte objects shaded with intensities far from black or white, warmth/coolness indicating surface normal; single light gives white highlights; cast shadows usually not shown.

Core idea: if black edge lines and white highlights are drawn, shading must stay in the mid-tones or the lines and highlights get lost; hue shift (cool to warm) carries orientation instead of a large luminance range.

Model: I = ((1+l.n)/2) k_cool + (1-(1+l.n)/2) k_warm, with k_cool = k_blue + alpha*k_d and k_warm = k_yellow + beta*k_d; shown with b=0.4, y=0.4, alpha=0.2, beta=0.6 and also b=0.55, y=0.3, alpha=0.25, beta=0.5 - authors say exact values are not crucial.
Objects keep their colour name under tone shading, so colour can still code categories.
Metal convention: alternating dark/light anisotropic bands, used by illustrators even for smooth metal.
Light placed up and to the right because vision assumes light from above (cited, not tested here).
practical_applications: Cool-to-warm shading for any lined illustration: shadows go to cool hue, lit side to warm, never to black.
Reserve pure black for lines and pure white for highlights; clamp fills to mid-tones.
Metal glasses frames in line art: banded light/dark stripes along the frame.
limitations: Exploratory model, no user study; claims about shape perception lean on cited perception studies.
Hue shift can interfere with albedo (true colour) perception - authors accept this for illustration.

sources.title: Suggestive Contours for Conveying Shape
sources.authors: Doug DeCarlo, Adam Finkelstein, Szymon Rusinkiewicz, Anthony Santella
key_findings: Suggestive contours = lines on visible parts of a surface where a true contour would appear with a small change of viewpoint (zero crossings of radial curvature, filtered for stability).
Contours alone convey limited shape; adding suggestive contours makes sparse drawings easier to read - argued from images, not from a user study.
Artists draw view-dependent lines: a nose in profile gets a ridge line, in front view lines on the sides of the nose.
Not all viewpoints are equal - some views produce much clearer drawings.
practical_applications: In minimal line art, add a few short lines where the form is about to turn away (side of nose, under cheek, fold of sleeve) instead of outlining every crease.
Pick the camera angle that makes the silhouette informative before adding interior lines.
limitations: Needs good curvature estimates; noisy on scanned meshes.
Effectiveness shown qualitatively; quantitative test came later (Cole2009).

sources.title: Where Do People Draw Lines?
sources.authors: Forrester Cole, Aleksey Golovinskiy, Alex Limpaecher, Heather Stoddart Barros, Adam Finkelstein, Thomas Funkhouser, Szymon Rusinkiewicz
key_findings: Art students drew 3D models to 'convey the shape'; 75% of their line pixels were within 1 mm of another artist's line - strong agreement, especially along occluding contours.
Exterior boundary alone accounted for 35-50% of classified line pixels; interior occluding contours 10-20%.
Most non-contour lines lie on large image-intensity gradients and match CG definitions (apparent ridges, ridges/valleys, suggestive contours); no single definition matches all drawings.
Mechanical models: ridge/valley-like lines dominate the remaining lines; smooth/blobby models: fewer non-contour lines, suggestive contours relatively more.
About 14% of lines were not explained by any local property tested; artists differ in style (one artist had far more unexplained lines).
practical_applications: Line budget: silhouette first (it carries roughly half the lines), then interior occluding contours, then a few ridge/fold lines.
Hard-edged objects (glasses frames, furniture) need crease/ridge lines; soft forms (faces, cloth) need few interior lines.
limitations: 12 models, art students, drawings registered to a faint photoreal prompt - may bias toward shading-based lines.
Grey-scale, single lighting; no colour or cartoon stylisation.

sources.title: How Well Do Line Drawings Depict Shape?
sources.authors: Forrester Cole, Kevin Sanik, Doug DeCarlo, Adam Finkelstein, Thomas Funkhouser, Szymon Rusinkiewicz, Manish Singh
key_findings: Gauge-figure study, about 275,000 surface-normal settings, 12 objects x 6 rendering styles (shaded, human drawing, contours only, apparent ridges, ridges/valleys, suggestive contours).
For some shapes people interpret line drawings almost as well as shaded images; computer line drawings can match artists' drawings.
Contours alone were considerably worse than the other line styles.
Smooth blobby shapes were hard to read even when shaded; errors for the best drawings were still around 35-40 degrees for difficult models; shaded prompts had lower average error.
practical_applications: Outline-only cartoon art reads shape poorly on smooth forms - add a shadow shape or a few interior lines.
For blobby subjects (bodies, cushions, food), give shading or texture, not lines alone.
limitations: Lab task with grey renderings of 3D models; not cartoon characters, colour or story context.
Measures shape reading, not appeal or emotion.

sources.title: Line Drawings from 3D Models: A Tutorial
sources.doi_isbn: Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision; arXiv:1810.01175
key_findings: Tutorial/survey of occluding contours, visibility and stylisation of lines from 3D, plus a survey of other line types and artistic shading.
Occluding contours are the core of line rendering; suggestive contours, apparent ridges and highlight lines extend them; image-space edges from depth/normal buffers are a cheap alternative.
Hatching directions: principal curvature, texture or illumination gradients; perceptual work suggests hatching strokes are read as curvature directions (Mamassian & Landy 1998, as cited).
History: toon shading and contour edges spread into games and films after 2000.
practical_applications: For 3D product renders of glasses: render a normal/depth pass and run edge detection to get clean contours, then composite over a toon-ramp shading pass.
Hatch along the form (cross-contour) when shading by lines.
limitations: Technical; focuses on 3D input; I read the introduction and the shading/hatching sections, not every chapter.

sources.title: Illustrative Rendering in Team Fortress 2
sources.authors: Jason Mitchell, Moby Francke, Dhabih Eng
key_findings: Codified conventions of early-20th-century commercial illustration: warm-to-cool hue shift, shadows go cool not black; saturation rises at the terminator (often reddened); high-frequency detail omitted; interior folds echo silhouette shapes; silhouettes emphasised with rim highlights instead of dark outlines.
Characters designed to be identifiable in pure silhouette; this was used to validate designs.
World textures: painterly, loose visible brush strokes, minimal visual noise and minimal repetition; muted colours dominate with small saturated areas.
Shading: diffuse light warping (half-Lambert then a 1D warp ramp) plus a rim term.
practical_applications: Rim light instead of outline for characters on dark backgrounds.
Silhouette test for every character and product shape.
Keep backgrounds lower in detail and saturation than characters.
limitations: Industry paper for one game; claims about readability come from production experience, not controlled studies.

sources.title: Stylization with a Purpose: The Illustrative World of Team Fortress 2 (GDC 2008 slides)
key_findings: Read hierarchy: team (colour) -> class (silhouette, proportions) -> selected weapon.
Value gradient on characters: dark feet to light chest; highest contrast at chest level where the weapon is held.
Character creation order: silhouette -> interior shapes solved with shadow shapes -> model sheet -> 3D.
Half-Lambert: scale the cosine term by 0.5, bias by 0.5 and square, to wrap light around the form.
practical_applications: Put the highest value contrast where the story object is (hands holding glasses, face).
Design interior detail as shadow shapes, not extra lines.
limitations: Slides, not a paper; practitioner claims.

sources.title: What line drawings reveal about the visual brain
key_findings: There are no lines around objects in nature, yet line drawings are recognised by infants, people without picture experience and chimpanzees - evidence against a purely cultural account.
Orientation-tuned neurons that evolved for edges respond to lines too, so lines stand in for solid edges.
Lines in a drawing stand for depth or slant discontinuities ('object contours'); drawing shadow borders as lines promotes them to object contours and corrupts the image.
Artists' intuitions go beyond current vision science (perspective article).
practical_applications: Never outline cast-shadow or shading borders with the same black line as object edges - use a shape of colour (cel shadow) or a lighter, coloured line.
In line art, every line should mean an edge, fold or occlusion.
limitations: Perspective/opinion article citing studies, not new data.

sources.title: Simple line drawings suffice for functional MRI decoding of natural scene categories
