sources.authors: Dirk B. Walther, Barry Chai, Eamon Caddigan, Diane M. Beck, Li Fei-Fei
key_findings: Scene category (beach, city, forest, highway, mountain, office) decoded from fMRI as well from line drawings as from colour photos, from V1 to PPA and RSC; decoding was above chance, not perfect.
Error patterns for drawings resembled those for photos in PPA/RSC.
Behaviour: removing long contours hurt category matching more than removing short contours - long contours carry global scene structure.
practical_applications: Background line art: keep the long structural lines (horizon, floor/wall edges, big masses) and drop short detail lines first.
A simple line BG is enough to tell 'where' the scene is.
limitations: 10 participants, 6 categories; line drawings traced from photos by trained people.

sources.title: Non-Photorealistic Rendering and the Science of Art
key_findings: NPR can serve as a 'third pillar' (simulation) for studying how artists make images and how viewers respond.
Theories must be tested against data, not judged by looking at pictures; Cole et al. 2008 cited as the model.
Line thickness example: stroke thickness proportional to isophote distance, clamped - nearer/less curved forms thicker, consistent with many illustrations (Goodwin et al. 2007).
practical_applications: Treat style rules as testable hypotheses: render A/B versions and measure, rather than trust a rule because it looks right once.
limitations: Position paper.

sources.title: Computer-Generated Watercolor
sources.authors: Cassidy J. Curtis, Sean E. Anderson, Joshua E. Seims, Kurt W. Fleischer, David H. Salesin
key_findings: Catalogue of watercolour effects from artists' practice: dry-brush, edge darkening, backruns, granulation and pigment separation, flow patterns, glazing.
Edge darkening: pigment migrates to the edge of a wet area as it dries, leaving a dark rim.
Granulation: pigment settles in the hollows of rough paper, strongest when the paper is very wet; varies by pigment.
Glazing = thin transparent layers over dry layers; layers composited optically with the Kubelka-Munk model.
practical_applications: To fake watercolour in HTML/SVG: transparent fills (multiply), a darker rim at the edge of each shape, paper grain modulating opacity, and a few backrun blooms.
Prompt words that map to real effects: 'edge darkening, granulation on cold-press paper, soft backruns, transparent glazes'.
limitations: Physical simulation, heavy; effects list is the transferable part.

sources.title: Learning to Cartoonize Using White-box Cartoon Representations
key_findings: From observing cartoon painting and consulting artists, cartoon images are decomposed into: surface (smooth low-frequency colour, edges/details ignored), structure (sparse flat colour blocks, celluloid style), texture (high-frequency contours and details).
Common features of cartoon images: global structure of sparse colour blocks; details outlined by sharp clear edges; flat smooth surfaces.
Different workflows weight these differently (some palette-led, some colour-block-led).
practical_applications: A cartoon look = flatten colour into a few blocks + smooth surfaces + keep only clear edges; control each separately.
Code is CC BY-NC-SA (non-commercial) - do not use the model commercially; use the idea.
limitations: GAN method trained on anime frames; user study scale small.
sources.license: CVF open access (paper); code CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

sources.title: CartoonGAN: Generative Adversarial Networks for Photo Cartoonization
sources.authors: Yang Chen, Yu-Kun Lai, Yong-Jin Liu
key_findings: Cartoon styles have high simplification and abstraction; cartoon images have clear edges, smooth colour shading and relatively simple textures.
These traits break texture-statistics style losses; an edge-promoting adversarial loss was needed to keep clear edges.
practical_applications: When FLUX output looks 'painted not cartoon', the missing ingredients are usually clear edges and flatter shading - ask for them explicitly.
limitations: Trained on specific anime directors' films; describes features, not perception.

sources.title: Locally Controllable Stylized Shading
sources.authors: Hideki Todo, Ken-ichi Anjyo, William Baxter, Takeo Igarashi
key_findings: The canonical toon shader often creates unwanted shadow areas (e.g. a dark patch over an eye) from geometry or lighting complexity.
Directors want to remove some dark areas and add fictive ones (shade under an eye for fierceness, under the nose for depth) - shadow shapes are designed, not physically computed.
Paint-brush local edits integrated with global lighting and animated smoothly between keyframes.
practical_applications: Cel shadow shapes are a design layer: delete shadows that cover eyes/mouth, add small designed shadows for expression.
For SVG puppets, draw shadow shapes per pose instead of computing them.
limitations: Technical tool paper; artistic rationale from production (OLM Digital).

sources.title: The Role of Book Features in Young Children's Transfer of Information from Picture Books to Real-World Contexts
sources.authors: Gabrielle A. Strouse, Angela Nyhout, Patricia A. Ganea
key_findings: Highly iconic (realistic) pictures help young children link book depictions to real objects; cartoons were the hardest for transfer in the reviewed studies, improving with age.
Simcock & DeLoache 2006 (as cited): 18-month-olds imitated actions from photo books more than from colour drawings; colour drawings worked by 24 months, black-and-white line drawings by 30 months.
Anthropomorphised animals and fantastical content can make it harder for children to separate facts that generalise from story-only features.
practical_applications: For teaching real facts to small children (eye care, real objects), use more realistic depiction; cartoon stylisation is fine for story and emotion with older audiences.
For adult audiences this effect is not shown - do not overgeneralise.
limitations: Review of toddler/preschool studies; not about adults, ads or social media.

sources.title: Transfer between picture books and the real world by very young children
sources.authors: Patricia A. Ganea, Megan Bloom Pickard, Judy S. DeLoache
key_findings: As described by Strouse2018: 15- and 18-month-olds extended a new word from a book to the real object more readily when the book had realistic drawings or photos rather than cartoons.
practical_applications: Same as Strouse2018.
limitations: Not read; only secondary description.

sources.title: XDoG: An eXtended difference-of-Gaussians compendium including advanced image stylization
sources.authors: Holger Winnemoller, Jan Eric Kyprianidis, Sven C. Olsen
key_findings: Extended DoG edge operator with soft thresholding gives line, pencil-shading, pastel, hatching and woodcut looks from one operator.
Canny gives lines whose thickness is independent of edge scale (looks mechanical); DoG lines vary in thickness with edge scale, closer to drawn lines.
Also produces negative edges, ghosting, speed-lines, indication and abstraction effects.
practical_applications: To turn a FLUX/photo background into line art: DoG/XDoG (OpenCV GaussianBlur difference + threshold) rather than Canny for a hand-drawn line feel.
limitations: Image-based; lines follow intensity edges, not object meaning (see SayimCavanagh2011 on shadow edges).

sources.title: Stylized Rendering Techniques for Scalable Real-Time 3D Animation
sources.authors: Adam Lake, Carl Marshall, Mark Harris, Marc Blackstein
key_findings: Real-time cartoon shading via a 1D texture indexed by the Lambertian term, simulating the limited palette of painted cels; pencil-sketch variant; silhouette inking (per indexed abstract and as summarised in Mitchell2007_TF2).
A few bright texels at the lit end of the ramp give a view-independent pseudo-highlight (per Mitchell2007_TF2).
practical_applications: Toon ramp = posterise the light term into 2-3 bands; in SVG use feComponentTransfer type='discrete'.
limitations: Original paper not read; content from abstract index and a citing paper.

sources.title: X-Toon: An Extended Toon Shader
sources.authors: Pascal Barla, Joelle Thollot, Lee Markosian
key_findings: Extends the 1D toon ramp to a 2D lookup indexed by light and a second attribute (depth, orientation) to get level-of-abstraction, aerial perspective, depth-of-field, backlighting and specular effects (search summary of abstract).
Fresnel-like term gives a hard 'virtual backlight' = rim light (per Mitchell2007_TF2).
practical_applications: Depth-based abstraction: farther objects get fewer tone bands, lower contrast and lighter values - a rule for cartoon backgrounds.
limitations: Abstract/summary only.

sources.title: Stylized Highlights for Cartoon Rendering and Animation
key_findings: Highlight shader for cel animation: starts from a Blinn specular shape, then artists translate, rotate, split and square the highlight shape per keyframe; animated automatically without texture maps (per search summary of abstract).
practical_applications: Cartoon highlights are designed shapes (squares, bars, split dots) - in SVG draw them as separate shapes on top, keyed per pose.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: GuiltyGearXrd's Art Style: The X Factor Between 2D and 3D (GDC 2015)
key_findings: Custom cel shaders plus 3D models built specifically for those shaders; in-engine shader editor for iteration (search snippet of handout).
Cel shading is hard because a surface is either lit or not; a tiny change in surface normal can create a large shadow blotch (search snippet).
practical_applications: In cel shading, shadow shapes must be art-directed (edit normals or paint shapes) - same lesson as Todo2007.
limitations: Handout not reachable this session; only search snippets.

sources.title: Surface versus edge-based determinants of visual recognition
key_findings: As cited by SayimCavanagh2011 and Gooch1998: line drawings of objects are recognised about as fast and accurately as colour photographs; surface colour/texture plays a secondary role in fast recognition of intact objects (per secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Clean line art is enough for fast object recognition at feed-scroll speed; colour serves mood and category, not recognition.
limitations: Not read; objects with diagnostic colour (fruit, food) may depend more on colour - later work debated this.

sources.title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: 'Amplification through simplification': cartooning focuses on chosen details rather than just removing detail; the simpler the icon the more universal (per secondary summaries).
Picture plane triangle: realistic - iconic - abstract.
Widely cited but debated; theoretical, not empirical.
practical_applications: Simple faces (Mint & Tao) invite projection; render settings and objects more fully when they must feel real ('masking' idea - craft claim).
limitations: Book not read this session; claims about identification are untested craft theory.

sources.title: Redesigning Animation: United Productions of America (chapter: UPA Films as Case Studies for a Simplified Visual Language in Animation)
key_findings: Book and chapter exist (CRC/Taylor & Francis); chapter title frames UPA films of the 1940s-50s as case studies of a simplified visual language influenced by modernist painting, graphic design and poster advertising (per publisher listing and search summaries).
practical_applications: Flat TV-style backgrounds descend from modernist graphic design: shapes and colour fields, not rendered space.
limitations: Only listing seen; no content read.

sources.title: The Vital Background Art: Interview with Background Company Studio Pablo Vol. 1
key_findings: Anime background pipeline: art director sets world style -> art setting (line drawing, 'blueprint of the stage') -> art board (coloured version shared with staff) -> final backgrounds painted from the art board -> art director check.
A 30-minute episode has about 250-400 cuts; about 70-80% need new backgrounds (about 180-300 images); reuse ('multi-use' backgrounds) decided at storyboard to save time for key cuts.
practical_applications: Make one line 'art setting' and one colour 'art board' per location, then generate all angles from them (matches STYLES.md 'write the place once').
limitations: Interview with one company; year 2013 inferred from the page id timestamp (0x51b76057 = June 2013), not printed on the page.

sources.title: Filmmaking Process: Layout
key_findings: Layout turns storyboards into the first full staged version: lenses, camera moves, angles, composition, how shots cut; requires cinematography, staging and rough animation.
Layout finaling after animation: camera polish, framing, focus, continuity.
practical_applications: Decide camera, horizon and floor line (layout) before painting or generating a background.
limitations: Brief studio page; 3D pipeline.

sources.title: Ben Day Dots Part 8: 1930s to 1950s - the Golden Age of Comics
key_findings: Golden Age comics (approx. 1938-1955) printed with Ben-Day tints of only 25% and 50% (colourists reported ~20%/40%): 63 colours plus white = 64 (65 counting black); 1948 Craftint names the plates red, yellow and blue.
Colourists marked colour guides with codes (e.g. YR2); separators made the plates; Craftint replaced hand-laid Ben Day for speed.
Some publishers limited the palette further (one avoided yellow tints until 1969, about 32 colours).
Interiors were line art (Ben Day = line etching, not halftone); line and dot irregularities came from etching, press pressure and newsprint, not intention.
practical_applications: A real 'vintage comic' palette = CMY at 0/20-25/40-50/100% combinations only; dots visible in the light tints; slight misregistration and paper yellowing.
Avoid smooth gradients in a retro-comic recipe - they did not exist.
limitations: Expert blog by a comics-printing researcher, not peer-reviewed; I read the first ~65% of the page.
Spot-check C1 2026-11-25: corrected.

sources.title: What's a Risograph? (print guide)
sources.authors: University of Illinois School of Art and Design
key_findings: Riso = stencil duplicator, one colour per pass, bright spot inks; uncoated paper only.
Files are separated into one grayscale image per ink; 100% black prints as 100% of that ink, 90% as 90%.
Ink is rice-oil based and never fully dries (smudges); large 100% areas cause set-off - use 80-90%.
Print light colours (yellow, pink) first, darker (blue, black) last; allow drying between layers.
practical_applications: Digital riso look: 2-3 spot inks as separate grayscale layers combined with multiply, overprint colours where they overlap, slight registration offset, grain.
limitations: One institution's machine guide; misregistration figures (1-3 mm) come from other vendor guides seen only in search snippets.

sources.title: Nail Your Comic Book Artwork With Precision Color Printing
key_findings: RGB shows a wider gamut than CMYK; CMYK cannot reproduce neon colours; RGB-to-CMYK conversion often looks flatter/duller.
Total ink limits differ by press/paper: sheetfed 300% (270% with UV), coldset web 260% offset / 245% groundwood / 235% newsprint, heatset web 310%, digital 320%.
Line screens: coldset 100-133, heatset 133-175, sheetfed 120-200; images at 1.5-2x line screen, 300-350 ppi default.
G7 grey balance and ICC profiles to keep colour consistent across devices; ask for a printed proof.
practical_applications: Design screen-first cartoon colours knowing which ones will die in print (neon pinks, electric blues, saturated greens) and check a CMYK soft-proof before print jobs.
limitations: Printer's blog; numbers are that printer's recommendations.

sources.title: Anime Skin Tutorial: Makeup, Light, Colour, Tones
key_findings: Use coloured shadows, not grey/black (which make skin dull); first shadow cel-shaded in a warm peach; optional second darker shadow; cool shadows in purple/blue.
Soften only the hard edge of the cel shadow with a small blending brush; blending the whole area looks smudged.
Small highlight dots/wavy lines on cheekbone, eyelid, lip, nose side; colour the line art locally (lighter/brighter at lashes, lips, skin lines).
practical_applications: Cel shadow colour = hue-shifted, more saturated darker version of the base, not base + black.
Coloured line art inside skin areas.
limitations: Single practitioner tutorial (date not stated).

sources.title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Summarised evidence that the immediate memory span of young adults is about seven items
Emphasised that effective capacity can be extended by recoding/chunking
practical_applications: Historical anchor only; use Cowan's ~4 chunks as design ceiling
limitations: Not read; 'seven' described by later authors as partly rhetorical

sources.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity
key_findings: When rehearsal and long-term-memory chunking are prevented, a single central capacity limit averages about 4 chunks (population range about 3 to 5)
Miller's 7 reflects rehearsal and grouping; capacity is counted in chunks, not raw items
Some theories place the limit in duration/decay rather than number (debated in the article)
practical_applications: Max ~4 meaning units per slide/shot
Lists of 3-4 items; group longer lists into categories
Limit new names/numbers per spoken sentence
limitations: Lab tasks with digits/words/shapes, not narratives
Defining a 'chunk' in real sentences is hard

sources.title: Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
sources.authors: Daniel J. Simons; Christopher F. Chabris
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Many observers engaged in an attention-demanding counting task failed to notice an unexpected person in a gorilla suit
Noticing depends on primary-task difficulty and on similarity of the unexpected event to attended items
practical_applications: Give price/CTA its own moment, not during long captions or main action
limitations: Read via search summaries only; feed-context magnitude unknown

sources.title: Faces and text attract gaze independent of the task: Experimental data and computer model
sources.authors: Moran Cerf; E. Paxon Frady; Christof Koch
key_findings: In free viewing, faces were fixated ~16.6x and text ~11.1x more than comparable regions (size/position normalised)
Participants found it hard to avoid faces and text even when costly
Adding face/text channels to a bottom-up saliency model improved fixation prediction
practical_applications: Place the product near faces/text, which capture gaze first
Text in speech bubbles is the gaze magnet for faceless Mint & Tao
limitations: Static desktop images; no cartoon or faceless characters tested

sources.title: Individual differences in face salience and rapid face saccades
sources.authors: Maximilian Davide Broda; Petra Borovska; Benjamin de Haas
key_findings: 77 participants: saccades were faster to faces, face features and text than to cars; the advantage was largest for full faces
Isolated eye regions were not sufficient to produce face-like rapid saccades
Stable individual differences in face saccade speed, weakly correlated with face fixations in free viewing
practical_applications: Full faces beat partial faces for instant capture; text also has a speed advantage
limitations: Lab saccadic choice task, not a feed

sources.title: Gaze cueing of attention: Visual attention, social cognition, and individual differences
sources.authors: Alexandra Frischen; Andrew P. Bayliss; Steven P. Tipper
key_findings: Reviews the gaze-cueing paradigm: observers shift attention in the direction another face is looking
Covers social-cognitive, developmental and clinical individual differences
practical_applications: Have the model look at the glasses or key text at least once
limitations: Only abstract read; effect sizes not extracted

sources.title: Motion onset captures attention
sources.authors: Richard A. Abrams; Shawn E. Christ
key_findings: Across three experiments, the onset of motion (not motion per se) captured attention
Debated: Franconeri & Simons argued some motion captures attention by itself; a later account linked the effect to jerky animation (disputed)
practical_applications: Stagger element entrances so the key element starts moving alone
limitations: Abstract only; simple lab displays

sources.title: Top-down and bottom-up control of visual selection (Acta Psychologica 135) - read only via Egeth, Leonard & Leber commentary
key_findings: (Per commentary) Theeuwes argues an initial feedforward sweep is stimulus-driven so salience dominates early orienting; top-down control acts afterwards
Commentators argue capture is much smaller when target and distractor are known in advance, implying some top-down control
practical_applications: Make the first frame win on salience alone
limitations: Target article itself not read; only commentary snippet

sources.title: Top-down versus bottom-up attentional control: a failed theoretical dichotomy
sources.authors: Edward Awh; Artem V. Belopolsky; Jan Theeuwes
key_findings: The goal vs salience dichotomy is inadequate; selection history (past selections/rewards) also shapes an integrated priority map
practical_applications: Keep series visual identity stable so followers' selection history works for us
limitations: Abstract level; later debate continues on terminology

sources.title: Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
sources.authors: John Sweller; Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer; Fred Paas
key_findings: Reviews 20 years of cognitive load theory: manage load so processing irrelevant to learning is minimised and germane processing optimised within capacity
Grounds the theory in evolutionary psychology and extends it to course-level design and measurement
practical_applications: Cut extraneous load: split-attention, redundancy, transient information
limitations: Full text not reached (login redirect); effects come from instructional settings

sources.title: Research-based principles for designing multimedia instruction (chapter in: In Their Own Words, APA Division 2)
key_findings: Median effect sizes from Mayer (2021): multimedia d=1.35 (13 tests); coherence 18/19 d=0.86; signaling 26/28 d=0.70; redundancy 8/12 d=0.10; spatial contiguity 9/9 d=0.82; temporal contiguity 8/8 d=1.31; segmenting 7/7 d=0.67; pre-training 10/10 d=0.78; modality 18/19 d=1.00; personalization 13/15 d=1.00; voice 6/7 d=0.74; embodiment 16/17 d=0.58; image 7 tests d=0.19; generative activities 37/44 d=0.71
Redundancy effect diminishes or reverses when the lesson is slow/learner-paced, on-screen text is short or reworded, learners use a second language, or there are no graphics

Signaling works best used sparingly, for low-knowledge learners and complex material; coherence strongest for low working-memory learners, system-paced lessons and highly interesting extraneous material
practical_applications: Captions with VO are acceptable (small redundancy cost); keep any extra on-screen headline to keywords
Place text next to what it describes; sync narration with visuals
Use a conversational script and the most human-sounding TTS voice
limitations: Author's own meta-analysis of mostly his lab's studies; outcome is learning transfer, not engagement

sources.title: The past, present, and future of the cognitive theory of multimedia learning
key_findings: Reviews four decades of CTML; core ideas (dual channels, limited capacity, active processing) constant over time
Lists 15 evidence-based multimedia design principles
practical_applications: Framework for clip and carousel design reviews
limitations: Abstract/introduction level only

sources.title: Meta-analysis of the modality effect
key_findings: 43 independent effects; strong modality effect (spoken text + graphics beats written text + graphics), especially under system-paced conditions
practical_applications: In clips (system-paced) let voice carry the explanation while visuals show
limitations: Abstract only; moderators not extracted

sources.title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis
sources.authors: Olusola O. Adesope; John C. Nesbit
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Spoken+written presentations outperformed spoken-only; condensed on-screen key words added to narration were associated with better learning; negative effects most likely when spoken and written text are identical and accompanied by pictures
practical_applications: Subtitles are not harmful for short social clips; on-screen headlines should be condensed keywords
limitations: Not read beyond secondary summaries

sources.title: Cognitive load theory and the effects of transient information on the modality effect
key_findings: Longer audio text was inferior to equivalent visual text (modality effect reversed) because transient speech overloads working memory; shortening the audio restored the usual modality effect (modality x length interaction)
Earlier paper (Leahy & Sweller 2011, Applied Cognitive Psychology 25(6):943-951) reported the same reversal
practical_applications: Keep VO sentences short; move dense facts to persistent on-screen text or visuals
limitations: Abstract only; sample sizes unverified

sources.title: A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media
sources.authors: Sascha Schneider; Maik Beege; Steve Nebel; Gunter Daniel Rey
key_findings: (Secondary summary) 103 studies, 12,201 participants; retention g+=0.53, transfer g+=0.33
Benefit larger for low prior knowledge learners; moderated by pacing and signal type
practical_applications: One clear highlight per slide; design for novices
limitations: Numbers from secondary sources, not checked against original

sources.title: A meta-analysis of the segmenting effect
sources.authors: Gunter Daniel Rey; Maik Beege; Steve Nebel; Maria Wirzberger; Tobias H. Schmitt; Sascha Schneider
key_findings: 56 investigations, 88 comparisons: segmenting has small-to-medium effects on retention and transfer, lowers overall cognitive load and increases learning time
High prior knowledge learners gained more retention from segmentation
practical_applications: One story beat per slide; clear segment breaks in clips
limitations: Abstract only

sources.title: A review of research and a meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect
key_findings: Existence and bibliographic data confirmed; Mayer (2023) cites it for coherence boundary conditions (stronger when extraneous material is highly interesting)
practical_applications: Remove interesting-but-irrelevant decorations
limitations: Content not read

sources.title: Keep it coherent: A meta-analysis of the seductive details effect
key_findings: Existence confirmed (Educational Psychology Review, 2020); cited by Mayer (2023) as support for the coherence principle
practical_applications: Same as Rey2012
limitations: Content not read

sources.title: Processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure: Is beauty in the perceiver's processing experience?
sources.authors: Rolf Reber; Norbert Schwarz; Piotr Winkielman
key_findings: The more fluently an object is processed, the more positive the aesthetic response; figural goodness, symmetry, figure-ground contrast, repetition and prototypicality all raise fluency
Fluency is hedonically marked and used as information unless attributed to an irrelevant source (then discounted)
Figure-ground contrast affected prettiness only at short exposures (0.3-3 s), not at 10 s (Reber & Schwarz 2001, as reported)
Same statements judged more likely true in high contrast (Reber & Schwarz 1999, as reported); repetition increases both liking and truth judgments
practical_applications: High text/background contrast and readable fonts for feed viewing
Consistent, recognisable brand style
Do not exploit repetition for unsupported health claims
limitations: Theoretical review; preference for complexity explained via attribution, not directly tested

sources.title: Uniting the tribes of fluency to form a metacognitive nation
sources.authors: Adam L. Alter; Daniel M. Oppenheimer
key_findings: Reviews fluency as a general metacognitive cue influencing judgments across perceptual, linguistic and conceptual forms
practical_applications: Simple wording and clear layout make claims feel truer and nicer - use responsibly
limitations: Abstract only

sources.title: The truth about the truth: A meta-analytic review of the truth effect
sources.authors: Alice Dechene; Christoph Stahl; Jochim Hansen; Michaela Wanke
key_findings: 51 studies; repetition increases judged truth: d=0.39 within-items, d=0.50 between-items (random effects)
A 2021 registered report notes original data unavailable and that bias correction might give smaller effects
practical_applications: Ethics: never use repetition to push unproven claims
limitations: Search-summary level; meta-analysis quality questioned

sources.title: Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems
sources.authors: Andrew Meyer; Shane Frederick; et al.
key_findings: Pooling the original experiment with 16 replications: no effect of hard-to-read fonts on solution rates under any tested condition; disfluent fonts only slightly slowed responses
practical_applications: Never use hard-to-read fonts as a 'make them think' device
limitations: Abstract only; specific to reasoning problems

sources.title: Levels of processing: A framework for memory research
sources.authors: Fergus I. M. Craik; Robert S. Lockhart
sources.doi_isbn: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 11:671-684
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Memory depends on depth of processing at encoding, from shallow sensory to deep semantic analysis; offered as a framework, not a complete theory
Criticised for not defining depth independently of memory outcome
practical_applications: Make jokes/messages hinge on meaning, not just visuals
limitations: Not read in full

sources.title: Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention
sources.authors: Henry L. Roediger III; Jeffrey D. Karpicke
key_findings: Restudy beat testing at 5 minutes, but prior testing produced substantially better retention at 2 days and 1 week, even though restudy raised confidence more
practical_applications: End carousels with a question to answer before the reveal
limitations: Abstract only; educational prose, not ads

sources.title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis
sources.authors: Nicholas J. Cepeda; Harold Pashler; Edward Vul; John T. Wixted; Doug Rohrer
key_findings: 839 assessments in 317 experiments: spaced beats massed; the optimal inter-study interval grows with the retention interval
practical_applications: Re-surface key health messages across episodes days/weeks apart in new forms
limitations: Abstract only; verbal recall in lab

sources.title: Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology
sources.authors: John Dunlosky; Katherine A. Rawson; Elizabeth J. Marsh; Mitchell J. Nathan; Daniel T. Willingham
key_findings: Practice testing and distributed practice rated high utility; elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaving moderate; summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery for text, rereading low
practical_applications: Prefer retrieval prompts over repeated summaries
limitations: Abstract/press-release level

sources.title: Chunking mechanisms in human learning
sources.authors: Fernand Gobet; Peter C. R. Lane; Steve Croker; Peter C-H. Cheng; Gary Jones; Iain Oliver; Julian M. Pine
key_findings: Distinguishes deliberate, goal-oriented chunking from automatic perceptual chunking; illustrated with verbal learning, expert memory and language acquisition
practical_applications: Keep a fixed episode/slide structure so followers chunk the format
limitations: Abstract only

sources.title: Mental models and human reasoning
key_findings: People reason by building models of possibilities; models represent what is true and omit what is false, reducing working-memory load but producing systematic errors
practical_applications: Keep character world rules consistent; use one correct comparison visual for lens functions
limitations: Abstract level; reasoning theory applied to narrative by analogy

sources.title: Whatever next? Predictive brains, situated agents, and the future of cognitive science
key_findings: Examines the hierarchical prediction-machine view of the brain as a candidate unifying account of perception and action, and lists evidential, methodological and conceptual challenges
practical_applications: Craft metaphor only: set up an expectation before a twist
limitations: Theory; abstract level

sources.title: The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?
key_findings: Proposes that free-energy minimisation (an upper bound on surprise) accounts for action, perception and learning and may unify several brain theories
practical_applications: Do not cite as scientific proof in published content
limitations: Highly theoretical and contested; abstract level

sources.title: Unification by fiat: Arrested development of predictive processing
key_findings: Argues PP's status as a unifying theory is asserted rather than earned; gaps between theory and its biological/computational bases have arrested its development
practical_applications: Treat predictive processing as low-confidence theory
limitations: Abstract level

sources.title: Perception of intersensory synchrony: A tutorial review
key_findings: Reviews measurement of audiovisual synchrony (temporal order and simultaneity judgments) and ways the brain handles lags: wide integration window, compensation, recalibration of perceived synchrony, shifting one stream toward the other
practical_applications: Sound slightly late is tolerated more than sound early
limitations: Search summary only; numeric windows not read here

sources.title: Temporal window of integration in auditory-visual speech perception
sources.authors: Virginie van Wassenhove; Ken W. Grant; David Poeppel
key_findings: 43 participants: audiovisual speech integration spans an asymmetric window of about 200 ms favouring visual lead; speech tolerates larger asynchrony than non-speech
Later work cites roughly 50 ms audio-lead to 200 ms visual-lead as perceived synchronous
practical_applications: Lip-sync: mouth may start slightly before audio, never audio clearly before mouth
limitations: Abstract and citing sources only

sources.title: The construct of the multisensory temporal binding window and its dysregulation in developmental disabilities
sources.authors: Mark T. Wallace; Ryan A. Stevenson
key_findings: Defines the temporal binding window as the span within which multisensory inputs are likely integrated; the window is altered in autism, dyslexia and schizophrenia and is malleable
practical_applications: Expect individual differences in sync tolerance; aim inside the tightest thresholds
limitations: Abstract level

sources.title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1: Relative timing of sound and vision for broadcasting
key_findings: Subjective tests: detectability thresholds about +45 ms (sound advanced) to -125 ms (sound delayed); acceptability about +90 ms to -185 ms
practical_applications: Never let audio lead picture by more than ~45 ms (about 1 frame at 30 fps)
limitations: Read via quoted search snippets of the official text; broadcast TV tests from the 1990s

sources.title: Embodied Cognition (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Cognition is embodied when deeply dependent on bodily features beyond the brain; distinguishes embodied from embedded and extended cognition; critics argue the body's role may be causal rather than constitutive
practical_applications: Use bodily acting for characters; avoid strong claims about body-to-mind effects
limitations: Search snippets only; archived edition

sources.title: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988)
key_findings: 17 labs, same protocol: pen-in-teeth vs pen-in-lips cartoon funniness difference 0.03 points (95% CI -0.11 to 0.16) vs 0.82 in the original
practical_applications: Do not claim 'just smile and you'll be happy' as science
limitations: Abstract level

sources.title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration
key_findings: 3,878 participants in 19 countries: facial mimicry and voluntary smiling amplified and initiated happiness; pen-in-mouth evidence less conclusive; lead author notes the effect is small
practical_applications: Eye-break clips may invite a relaxed face but must not overclaim
limitations: Abstract/press level

sources.title: Eye movements when reading spaced and unspaced Thai and English: A comparison of Thai-English bilinguals and English monolinguals
sources.authors: Heather Winskel; Ralph Radach; Sudaporn Luksaneeyanawin
key_findings: Thai sentences with inserted interword spaces were read slightly slower (1834 vs 1746 ms, marginal) with more fixations (9.27 vs 8.62, significant) than normal unspaced Thai
Spaces facilitated recognition of target words but did not change initial landing positions in Thai; removing spaces severely disrupted English
Authors suggest Thai-specific segmentation cues (e.g. vowel letters written before the consonant, tone marks) may guide skilled readers
practical_applications: Do not insert spaces between every Thai word in slides or captions; break lines at phrase boundaries
limitations: Single-line sentences on desktop; bilingual university readers

sources.title: Eye movements while reading an unspaced writing system: The case of Thai
sources.authors: Benjawan Kasisopa; Ronan G. Reilly; Sudaporn Luksaneeyanawin; Denis Burnham
key_findings: 30 Thai adults: higher position-specific frequency of word-initial and word-final characters moved landing sites closer to word centre, suggesting readers use character-position statistics for eye guidance
practical_applications: Use common spelling; avoid unusual abbreviations that break familiar word boundaries
limitations: Search summary only

sources.title: Adding spaces to Thai and English: Effects on reading
sources.doi_isbn: Proceedings of the 19th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society, 388-393
key_findings: Thai readers were faster and made fewer errors with added spaces; meaning helped independently; no transfer of unspaced reading skill to English (not eye-tracking)
practical_applications: Conflicts with Winskel 2009 - treat spacing advice as medium confidence
limitations: Conference paper; abstract only

sources.title: Viewers can keep up with fast subtitles: Evidence from eye movements
key_findings: 74 English/Polish/Spanish viewers at 12, 16, 20 cps: comprehension and scene recognition unaffected by speed
Share of time on subtitles rose ~50% to ~60% (Exp.1) and ~40% to ~45% (Exp.2) from slow to fast
Slow subtitles caused far more rereading (about 2 in 3 vs 1 in 5) and more frustration; interviews suggested synchronisation mattered more than speed
practical_applications: Do not over-slow Thai subtitles; prioritise precise sync with speech
limitations: European languages, not Thai; speed confounded with text reduction

sources.title: Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension
sources.authors: Pablo Delgado; Cristina Vargas; Rakefet Ackerman; Ladislao Salmeron
key_findings: 54 studies (2000-2017, ~171,000 participants): comprehension better on paper than screens in both between- and within-subject designs
Screen inferiority larger for expository texts and under time limits (as summarised by later review)
practical_applications: Keep informational carousels shorter than narrative ones
limitations: Abstract/summaries; mostly longer texts than our slides

sources.title: Headlines, pictures, likes: Attention to social media newsfeed post elements on smartphones and in public
sources.authors: Anna-Theresa Mayer; Jakob Ohme; Ewa Maslowska; Claire M. Segijn
key_findings: Eye-tracking, 201 students, dynamic Facebook newsfeed: less attention to visuals on mobile; in public settings more attention to textual post elements
practical_applications: Always pair images with a short text carrying the message
limitations: Search summary only; student sample; Facebook not IG/TikTok

sources.title: Capturing attention in feed: The science behind effective video creative
sources.authors: Facebook IQ (tests by Fors Marsh Group, commissioned by Facebook)
key_findings: (As reported) people spend on average 1.7 s with a piece of mobile feed content vs 2.5 s on desktop; recall significant after 0.25 s exposure
practical_applications: Hook must be readable within the first 1-2 s
limitations: Industry-commissioned; method not public; 2016 Facebook feed

sources.title: Thai Timed Text Style Guide
key_findings: Thai subtitles: max 17 cps adult (13 children); SDH 20/17
35 characters per line excluding tone marks and upper/lower vowels; max two lines; prefer one line; bottom-heavy pyramid; avoid two short lines
No sentence-final periods; separate sentences with a single space
practical_applications: Caption timing and layout rules for Thai story clips
limitations: Industry practice, not empirical research; page revision date unknown

sources.title: Timed Text Style Guide: General Requirements
key_findings: (Search summary) Minimum subtitle duration 5/6 s (~0.83 s), maximum 7 s
practical_applications: Each caption cue stays at least ~0.8 s
limitations: Not opened directly

sources.title: Bridging cultures through letters: Typotheque's typographic journey in Thailand (with ATypI 2025 talk summary)
key_findings: (As reported) a Chulalongkorn study (180+ readers) found looped Thai improved paragraph reading speed; an ATypI 2025 study found no performance difference but all ages perceived looped fonts as more legible; younger readers associate loopless with modernity
practical_applications: Prefer looped Thai fonts for long dialogue/subtitles (weak evidence)
limitations: Foundry-produced summaries; peer-reviewed originals not located

sources.title: How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate
key_findings: (Search summary) 190 studies: average adult English silent reading 238 wpm non-fiction, 260 fiction; wpm depends on word length so cross-language wpm comparisons are not valid
practical_applications: Do not import English wpm targets into Thai captions
limitations: Search summary only; no Thai data

sources.title: Cross-linguistic investigations of oral and silent reading
sources.authors: Christophe Coupe; Yoon Mi Oh; Francois Pellegrino; Egidio Marsico
key_findings: Eight languages including Thai: oral and silent reading rates are well correlated, suggesting syllabic complexity affects both
practical_applications: Candidate source for Thai reading-rate figures (next research)
limitations: Abstract only; Thai figures not extracted

sources.title: Philosophy of Humor (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, substantive revision 2024)
key_findings: Three classic theories: superiority (Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes), relief (Shaftesbury, Spencer, Freud), incongruity (Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer); incongruity is dominant in philosophy and psychology today.
Superiority is neither necessary nor sufficient (Hutcheson): people laugh at wordplay and their own mistakes without feeling superior.
Relief theory's hydraulic 'nervous energy' model is outdated; few scholars defend it.
Incongruity alone is not sufficient: violated expectations can also produce fear, disgust or anger; refinements add resolution (Shultz, Suls) and enjoyment of incongruity (Clark, Martin).
Author proposes humour as play; laughter as a play signal derived from the primate relaxed open-mouth display.
Ethics: humour is objectionable when it treats as a joke something that should be taken seriously; stereotype jokes keep stereotypes in circulation.
practical_applications: Use incongruity + a safe 'play frame' as the base model for wholesome jokes.
Treat superiority/aggression as a risk lever, not a default.
limitations: Philosophical overview, not empirical; final ~1% of page not read.

sources.title: Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny
key_findings: Psychological Science 21(8):1141-1149. Five experiments: benign moral violations elicit laughter/amusement in addition to disgust.
Three conditions make a violation benign: an alternative norm that makes it acceptable, weak commitment to the violated norm, psychological distance.
Perceiving the behaviour as both wrong and not wrong partially mediated displays of amusement (Study 2, Sobel t = 2.1).

Examples: harmless vs harmful version of the same disgusting act - amused 61% vs 28% (Study 3, N=36); church raffling a Hummer - non-churchgoers amused 92% vs churchgoers 62% (Study 4, N=39 in that comparison).
practical_applications: Joke check: is there a violation? is it clearly benign for THIS audience?
Lower commitment/raise distance (fictional characters, small stakes) to keep a joke benign.
limitations: Small US student samples (N = 36-80 per study), self-reported amusement or coded smiles; written by the theory's proponents.

sources.title: Differentiating What Is Humorous From What Is Not
key_findings: JPSP 110(3):407-430 (online Dec 2015). Incongruity is defined in at least 4 ways in the literature: surprise, juxtaposition, atypicality, violation - and none alone separates humorous from non-humorous experiences well.

Six studies (entertainment, consumer products, social interaction): a benign violation - something that threatens well-being, identity or normative beliefs but simultaneously seems okay - differentiates humorous from non-humorous experiences better than common incongruity conceptualisations.
Main gain: fewer false predictions that joyous, amazing or tragic situations would be funny.
practical_applications: Incongruity alone can just confuse; add a 'mild threat that is OK' for laughs.
limitations: Authored by the theory's proponents; mostly US online/student samples.

sources.title: Too Close for Comfort, or Too Far to Care? Finding Humor in Distant Tragedies and Close Mishaps
sources.authors: A. Peter McGraw, Caleb Warren, Lawrence E. Williams, Bridget Leonard
key_findings: Psychological Science (OnlineFirst 31 Aug 2012). Five studies: tragedies (severe violations) are funnier when temporally, socially, hypothetically or spatially distant; mishaps (mild violations) are funnier when psychologically close.
Study 2 (N=87): 99% said being hit by a car would be funnier if it happened 5 years ago than yesterday; only 18% said so for stubbing a toe.
Interpretation: distance reduces threat for tragedies; closeness keeps some threat for mishaps.
practical_applications: Small everyday mishaps (spilled coffee, lost glasses) can be joked about up close; real suffering needs distance or no joke.
limitations: Mostly US MTurk/student samples; hypothetical or recalled events.
The 'rise then fall over time' (comedic sweet spot) finding is NOT in this paper - it is McGrawWilliamsWarren2014 (Hurricane Sandy). Corrected 2026-11-25.

sources.title: Are Benign Violations Necessary for Humor? (commentary/extension)
key_findings: As summarized in search results: BVT is one of few models claiming necessary and sufficient conditions; the necessity question is treated as open; results suggest BVT can extend beyond moral content.
practical_applications: Treat BVT as a useful checklist, not a proven law.
limitations: Only a search snippet seen; publication venue and year unconfirmed.

sources.title: You Must Be Joking! Benign Violations, Power Asymmetry, and Humor in a Broader Social Context
key_findings: As summarized in search results: some jokes whose violations are not seen as benign are still found funny; BVT does not explain why people disagree about whether something is funny; argues for power asymmetry and social context.
practical_applications: Who is joking about whom matters: a shop joking about customers is not the same as a customer joking about themself.
limitations: Full text blocked by captcha; content from search snippet; author first names and year from listing, not confirmed.

sources.title: A two-stage model for the appreciation of jokes and cartoons: an information-processing analysis
key_findings: In Goldstein & McGhee (eds.) The Psychology of Humor. Stage 1: the ending does not follow from the setup (incongruity); stage 2: the listener finds a cognitive rule that makes the ending fit (resolution).
Became the standard reference for cognitive/neuro humour studies (per Encyclopedia of Humor Studies summary).
practical_applications: Every joke needs a findable rule: the audience must be able to 'get it' within the medium's time.
limitations: Bibliographic + encyclopedia summary only; resolution need not remove incongruity fully (Ritchie).

sources.title: Variants of Incongruity Resolution
key_findings: Snippet: traditional incongruity-resolution is highly sequential and typically assumes full resolution; Suls and Shultz were highly influential.
practical_applications: Allow partial resolution (absurd humour) but know it is riskier for broad audiences.
limitations: Search snippet only.

sources.title: Individual differences in uses of humor and their relation to psychological well-being: Development of the Humor Styles Questionnaire
sources.authors: Rod A. Martin, Patricia Puhlik-Doris, Gwen Larsen, Jeanette Gray, Kelly Weir
key_findings: Journal of Research in Personality 37:48-75. HSQ: 32 items, 7-point scale, four styles: affiliative, self-enhancing (adaptive), aggressive, self-defeating (maladaptive).
Adaptive styles relate to extraversion, openness, self-esteem; maladaptive to aggression and neuroticism (secondary summary).
practical_applications: Give wholesome characters affiliative + self-enhancing humour; avoid self-defeating as a running gag for a lead.
limitations: Read via test-bank listing and secondary summaries; translated versions show reliability issues.

sources.title: The Psychology of Humor: An Integrative Approach (2nd ed.)
sources.authors: Rod A. Martin, Thomas E. Ford
key_findings: Standard textbook: definitions and theories, cognition, personality, physiology, social functions, development, health, applications in therapy/education/work.
practical_applications: Reference text for future deep-dives (not read this session).
limitations: Publisher page only.

sources.title: Cultural Differences in Humor Perception, Usage, and Implications
sources.authors: Tonglin Jiang, Hao Li, Yubo Hou
key_findings: Westerners treat humour as a desirable trait; Easterners (mostly Chinese samples) are more ambivalent, partly via Confucian devaluation.
Easterners use humour less for coping (Chinese, Japanese, Singaporean students); reportedly less aggressive and more affiliative humour, depending on collectivism/harmony.
Adaptive vs maladaptive HSQ pattern holds East and West but strength varies.
Thailand not covered; most Eastern data are Chinese samples; mainly correlational surveys.
practical_applications: For Thai/Asian audiences favour affiliative, harmony-keeping humour; be careful with aggressive teasing in brand voice.
limitations: Does not include Thailand; generalising East Asia to Thailand is DERIVED.

sources.title: The evolution and functions of laughter and humor: a synthetic approach
key_findings: Quarterly Review of Biology 80(4):395-430. Distinguishes Duchenne (spontaneous, stimulus-driven) from non-Duchenne (volitional, strategic) laughter.
Duchenne laughter hypothesised as a medium for playful emotional contagion; non-Duchenne co-opted for many functions incl. derision and embarrassment.
practical_applications: In TTS/animation, a warm genuine laugh and a polite social laugh are different acts; direct them separately.
limitations: Evolutionary hypotheses; abstract-level reading.

sources.title: Prosodic markers of saliency in humorous narratives
sources.authors: Lucy Pickering, Salvatore Attardo, et al.
key_findings: Acoustic measures: punchlines are not louder than preceding text, are delivered at lower pitch and more slowly, often with laughing/smiling voice, and are NOT preceded by significant pauses.
Folk belief 'it's all about the pause' was untested before and largely unsupported for told narratives.
practical_applications: For TTS punchlines: slightly lower and slower, smile in the voice; do not insert a long dramatic pause by default.
limitations: Author list from listing; small corpora of narrated jokes; abstract-level.

sources.title: Prosodic/multimodal markers of humor in conversation (Attardo, Pickering & Baker 2011; Attardo, Pickering, Lomotey & Menjo 2013)
sources.authors: Salvatore Attardo, Lucy Pickering, et al.
key_findings: As summarized in search results: in conversation, humorous turns show no higher pitch, volume or speed and no significant pauses; smiling/laughter accompany humour.
2013 dyadic study: lower-pitch punchline effect did NOT replicate; smiling seems to set up the humorous frame before the joke.
practical_applications: Signal the play frame early (smile voice, playful face) rather than relying on a pause before the line.
limitations: Two papers merged under one key; exact titles/venues not confirmed; search summary only.

sources.title: Timing is Everything: Temporal Scaffolding of Semantic Surprise in Humor
key_findings: 828 professional Chinese stand-up performances: temporal features (pause patterns, punchline timing) outweighed semantic incongruity in predicting audience appreciation.
Proposes 'dual prediction violation': a content surprise and a rhythm break together; example of a ~1.5 s pause before a distant punchline.
practical_applications: In performed/edited comedy, establish a rhythm then break it on the punch; contrasts with conversation findings above.
limitations: Conference paper (CogSci 2026), search summary only; stand-up genre, Chinese language.

sources.title: A meta-analysis of humor in advertising
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 369 correlations: humour enhances attitude toward the ad, attention and positive affect, and purchase intention; it reduces source credibility; no evidence it raises liking of the advertiser. Also raises brand attitude (ABR).
practical_applications: Use humour for stopping power and liking; never as the vehicle for medical/expert credibility claims.
limitations: Abstract-level; effect sizes not read; mostly Western ad studies.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: "liking" narrowed to attitude toward the ad (no effect on liking of the advertiser).
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

sources.title: How humor in advertising works: A meta-analytic test of alternative models
key_findings: Marketing Letters 22(2):115-132. Tests how earlier explanations of humour effects may be integrated (findings not read).
practical_applications: Pending: read to know whether humour works via affect transfer or via cognition.
limitations: Bibliographic only.

sources.title: The Impact of Humor in Advertising: A Review
sources.authors: Marc G. Weinberger, Charles S. Gulas
key_findings: Journal of Advertising 21(4):35-59. Humour does not guarantee better ads; effect depends on objectives, audience, situation and humour type.
Cited later as: humour attracts attention and raises likability but does not reliably improve comprehension or persuasion.
practical_applications: Decide the job first (attention? liking? understanding?) before adding a joke.
limitations: Abstract + secondary citation; 2019 update by the same authors not read.

sources.title: Humor and cultural values in print advertising: a cross-cultural study
sources.authors: Leonidas Hatzithomas, Yorgos Zotos, Christina Boutsouki
key_findings: 12,351 UK and Greek magazine ads (3,828 humorous). Higher uncertainty-avoidance Greece leaned to informative humour.
Suggests individualistic/low-UA audiences prefer humour-dominant messages; collectivistic/high-UA audiences use humour as a vehicle for required information.
practical_applications: For Thai (collectivist, Hofstede-high UA) audiences, DERIVED: let humour carry the information rather than replace it.
limitations: Content analysis of ad supply, not audience response; Thailand not studied; search summary.

sources.title: CDC's Use of Social Media and Humor in a Risk Campaign — 'Preparedness 101: Zombie Apocalypse'
key_findings: Journal of Applied Communication Research 43(2):222-241. Campaign met reach goals, but in the experiment students shown the comical zombie version reported weaker intentions to take protective action; authors: a light tone can trivialise perceived importance.
practical_applications: Health-related calls to action (eye exams, UV protection) should not be wrapped in a joke that makes the risk feel unreal.
limitations: Student sample; search summary; other studies (e.g. measles/MMR humour) found humour reduced reactance — mixed field.

sources.title: Lessons learned: match your humor to your message
sources.authors: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Health Communication
key_findings: Harvard Chan Center for Health Communication 'Lessons Learned' (3 Sep 2024) summarising a Health Communication study (DOI 10.1080/10410236.2023.2218532): 882 participants saw COVID memes paired with prevention- or promotion-focused messages.
Prevention messages (avoid a bad behaviour) were shared/engaged with more when paired with inoffensive humour that points out something unexpected.
Promotion messages (adopt a good behaviour) were shared more with AGGRESSIVE humour that makes fun of people who don't adopt the behaviour - explained by psychological-distance 'fit'.
Outcome = self-reported intention to share/engage, not behaviour change.
practical_applications: Use gentle surprise humour, not mockery, around health topics.
limitations: Institutional blog summarising one study; original paper not read. Earlier entry wrongly said 'playful > aggressive' - corrected 2026-11-25.

sources.title: Effects of humor on sentence memory
key_findings: JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. Humorous sentences better remembered than non-humorous versions in free and cued recall.
Later work: advantage appears in mixed lists, not pure lists (distinctiveness); Schmidt & Williams 2001 argued against pure distinctiveness/rehearsal — mechanism contested.
practical_applications: One funny slide among plain ones is memorable; a whole feed of jokes loses the advantage (DERIVED from mixed-list finding).
limitations: Search summary; lab sentences, not ads.

sources.title: A Computational Model of Linguistic Humor in Puns
key_findings: Cognitive Science 40(5):1270-1285. Two information-theoretic measures from a noisy-channel model of sentence processing: ambiguity (both meanings active) and distinctiveness (each meaning supported by different words).

435 sentences (phonetic puns with identical or near homophones, plus matched non-puns, from 'Pun of the Day'); funniness rated by MTurk participants (100 raters for the 195 identical-homophone sentences).
Both measures correlate with funniness; ambiguity separates puns from non-puns, distinctiveness separates exceptionally funny puns from mediocre ones.
practical_applications: A good pun needs BOTH meanings supported by different words in the line; Thai homophone puns can be checked the same way (DERIVED).
limitations: English homophone puns only; read via Europe PMC full-text XML.

sources.title: Spoonerism: a Creative Way of Communication in Thai
key_findings: Search summary: Thai spoonerism (คำผวน) is both a speech error and intentional wordplay; used for taboo avoidance in polite register; describes the 'Luu' secret spoonerist language (often gossipy, impolite casual talk).
practical_applications: คำผวน is a native Thai humour device, but swaps often surface hidden rude/sexual readings — every คำผวน must be checked in both directions.
limitations: Conference paper; PDF returned 403; only search summary.

sources.title: สุนทรียะคำผวน: เพศ พฤติกรรมการสมสู่ การสร้างคำใหม่และการสื่อสาร (Aesthetic of Spoonerism: Sex, Behavior of Sexual Intercourse, Word Formation and Communication)
sources.authors: Mallika Phumathon (มัลลิกา ภูมะธน), Dirak Duangloy (ดิเรก ด้วงลอย), Nakhon Sawan Rajabhat University
key_findings: Journal of Interdisciplinary Innovation Review 4(2), Jul-Dec 2021 (TCI). Academic article built from documents, prior research and conversations with colleagues skilled at คำผวน - not an empirical study.

Summarised functions of คำผวน: (1) creates new words, (2) a communication tool, (3) a linguistic trick, (4) avoids impolite words / makes them polite, (5) creates humour and language entertainment; methods: swapping vowels and final consonants, multi-syllable swaps, selective tone shifts.

Discusses classical examples (e.g. Sunthorn Phu) and the large share of คำผวน that resolve to sexual meanings; the author notes that frequent sexual spoonerisms at work start to feel excessive ('ผวนจนเกินงาม').
practical_applications: Confirms that sexual double meaning is a central register of คำผวน — red line for a wholesome brand.
limitations: Essay-style academic article with personal observation; no audience data.

sources.title: An Analysis of Linguistic Humor in the Humorous Scenes of Pee Mak Phra Kanong
key_findings: Trends of Humanities and Social Sciences Research 7(2):106-124 (Univ. of Phayao). Pee Mak Phra Kanong has 76 humorous scenes (identified by the producers, GDH); every fifth scene was analysed - 15 scenes, 16 humour instances.
Techniques (Berger 1997 + Pinit-Phuwadol 1998): analogy 4 (25%), pun 3 (18.75%), loanwords 3 (18.75%); ridicule, slang, explanation, mispronunciation, facetiousness, over-literalness 1 each (6.25%).
Analogy worked best combined with pun and exaggeration; slang, explanation and mispronunciation are outside Berger's taxonomy but drew laughs - Thai-specific categories needed.

Spoonerism appears only in the literature review (as phonological deviation); it was not among the techniques found in the sampled scenes. Most humour came from conversations of the added supporting characters.
practical_applications: Thai mainstream comedy leans on wordplay and analogy — fits Mint & Tao dialogue.
limitations: One film, 15 scenes, analysis of the producers' intended humour - not audience response.

sources.title: A Linguistic Strategies to Express Humor in Thai Context
key_findings: International Journal of Social Science and Humanity 6(6), June 2016. Data: five Thai situation comedies; frameworks: speech acts, Grice's cooperative principle, implicature.
Six categories of humour-related speech acts: boasting, expressing condescension, threatening, blaming, teasing and satire.
Humour in Thai sitcoms is closely associated with superiority and aggression created by the speaker; humour also arises from non-observance of Gricean maxims (violating or flouting).
practical_applications: Mainstream Thai sitcom humour is often put-down based; a wholesome brand should consciously NOT copy that default.
limitations: Qualitative analysis of scripted TV; no audience measure; 4-page conference-style paper.

sources.title: (Laughter in American English and Central Thai television talk)
key_findings: Search summary: laughter use varies cross-linguistically between American English and Central Thai TV, aligning with linguistic patterns and cultural values.
practical_applications: Thai laughter placement in VO should follow Thai norms, not dubbed-English habits.
limitations: Title not confirmed; snippet only.

sources.title: Pie and Chase: Gag, Spectacle and Narrative in Slapstick Comedy
key_findings: Search summary: frames slapstick as a tension between the gag (spectacle, 'pie') and narrative ('chase'); rethinks the gag's role in classical comic film.
practical_applications: Physical gags in clips should either push the story or be a deliberate pause from it — know which.
limitations: Snippet and blog summary only; open-access chapter not read.

sources.title: The comedy rule of 3s (blog post)
key_findings: Ken Levine blog (16 Jul 2017): the rule of three (comic triple) establishes a pattern and ends with something unexpected ('We serve lasagna, spaghetti, and poi').
Two items are usually enough to set the pattern; more than three feels wrong.
Traps: the first two items must clearly establish the pattern; keep setups straight (a funny setup cancels the payoff); don't make setups convoluted.
practical_applications: Template for 3-slide carousel jokes.
limitations: Craft, tier D. Callbacks and A/B-plot structure are NOT in this post (other practitioner pages).

sources.title: What Makes Things Funny? An Integrative Review of the Antecedents of Laughter and Amusement
sources.authors: Caleb Warren, Adam Barsky, A. Peter McGraw
key_findings: Personality and Social Psychology Review 25(1):41-65. More than 20 psychological humour theories draw on five candidate antecedents: surprise, simultaneity, superiority, a violation appraisal, and conditions for a benign appraisal.
Against the evidence, simultaneity, violation and benign appraisals help distinguish humorous from non-humorous experiences; surprise and superiority do not.

Surprise is too broad (muggings, diagnoses surprise without amusement) and too narrow: expected punchlines were rated funnier (Kenny 1955; Pollio & Mers 1974), partial prior exposure made jokes funnier (Topolinski 2014), rewatch enjoyment equals first viewing (O'Brien 2019); callbacks and running gags work.
When surprise and violation were manipulated orthogonally (candy offered vs thrown, warned vs not), violations increased laughter; surprise did not.
Failed attempts at humour make people/organisations seem incompetent or insensitive and can elicit disgust, anger and disapproval.
practical_applications: Don't chase 'surprise' as the core of a joke: build two simultaneous readings + a small violation + a clear 'it's okay' signal.
Running gags and callbacks are evidence-compatible; a known punchline can still land if it is a benign violation.
limitations: Written by BVT proponents; integrative (not systematic) review; underlying studies mostly Western students.

sources.title: The Rise and Fall of Humor: Psychological Distance Modulates Humorous Responses to Tragedy
sources.authors: A. Peter McGraw, Lawrence E. Williams, Caleb Warren
key_findings: Social Psychological and Personality Science 5(5), starting p. 566 (online Dec 2013). Longitudinal: about 100 different participants at each of 10 time points rated three Hurricane Sandy joke tweets (from one day before landfall to 99 days after).

Humour fell as the reality set in (day -1 M = 3.5 to day 8 M = 2.9), was lowest at day 15 (M = 2.7, 'too soon'), peaked at day 36 (M = 3.4), and fell again by day 99 (M = 2.6) - a comedic sweet spot, not a monotonic rise with time.
Changes in humour were mediated by perceived offensiveness (threat).
practical_applications: Topical jokes about a bad event have a window: not while it is fresh, and not once it no longer matters to the audience.
limitations: One US event, online samples, three tweets; 7-point ratings.

sources.title: Failure to detect changes to attended objects in motion pictures
sources.authors: Daniel T. Levin, Daniel J. Simons
key_findings: Per Smith 2012 (full text read): a short film of two women talking at a dinner table contained nine deliberate continuity errors (e.g. a scarf or plate changing colour across a cut); on first free viewing no viewer reported anything odd; on a second viewing with instructions to look for changes, viewers found on average 2 of 9, mostly those nearest the actors' faces.

Per Simons & Levin 1998 and Smith 2012 (full texts read): when one actor was replaced by a different actor across a cut (matched exit/entrance), only 33% of 40 participants reported the change, even though the actor was the centre of attention.
practical_applications: Small prop/colour slips far from faces in a single viewing are usually missed; spend continuity effort on what sits near faces and on what the story points at.
Spatiotemporal continuity (position, movement direction) does much of the work of making a cut feel continuous.
limitations: Original paper not read (publisher page only); findings are as reported by later papers by the same authors and by Smith 2012.
Lab clips viewed once; does not model rewatching, pausing, or comment-section crowds on social video.

sources.title: Change blindness
sources.authors: Daniel J. Simons, Daniel T. Levin
key_findings: Trends in Cognitive Sciences 1(7), Oct 1997. Unless a change produces a localisable transient, people generally do not detect it.

Box 3 'Insights from film makers': because scenes are shot out of order, 'almost every movie - in fact, almost every cut - has some continuity mistake', yet most of the time people are blind to these changes.
Same box: filmmakers are still justified in removing glaring errors because if one viewer notices, media and the internet publicise it and others then hunt for the error instead of watching the film.

Quotes Dmytryk: a mismatch far from the viewer's centre of interest (e.g. an arm when the viewer watches the actor's eyes) is 'ignored nine times out of ten'; quotes Kuleshov: good montage hides minor costume defects, bad montage makes the blunder 'leap to the eye'.
Viewers encode scene gist (the action, a few traits of the actor); changes that keep the gist are rarely detected; schema-inconsistent objects are more likely to be noticed.
practical_applications: Prioritise continuity of gist-level facts (who, where, what action, character identity markers) over background details.
Expect viral audiences to find errors once one person points them out: fix anything a pause-frame would show near faces/hands/products.
limitations: Narrative review, 1997; filmmaker quotes are craft lore, not data.
Course-hosted copy of the published article.

sources.title: Failure to detect changes to people during a real-world interaction
sources.authors: Daniel J. Simons, Daniel T. Levin
key_findings: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 5(4), 644-649. An experimenter asking a pedestrian for directions was swapped for a different person while a door was carried between them; only about half of pedestrians detected the change.
Detection depended on social group: pedestrians from the experimenters' own social group noticed; those from a different group mostly did not.
Summarises Levin & Simons 1997: only 33% of 40 participants noticed an actor swap in a motion picture.
Conclusion: provided the meaning of the scene is unchanged, changes to attended objects can escape detection.
practical_applications: Identity is carried by category-level cues (role, outfit type, silhouette) for most viewers; give recurring characters strong, simple category markers.
Audiences close to a character (fans, in-group) encode more detail: long-running series audiences are less forgiving than one-off viewers.
limitations: Small field samples; DOI not shown on the PDF copy, left empty.
Real-world interaction, not edited film.

sources.title: Change blindness: Past, present, and future
sources.authors: Daniel J. Simons, Ronald A. Rensink
key_findings: Trends in Cognitive Sciences 9(1), Jan 2005. Change blindness is a general failure to retain and/or compare information from moment to moment, not an artefact of lab disruptions.
Effects are stronger when changes are unexpected; most observers do not notice an actor replaced during a camera position change.
'Change blindness blindness': most people firmly believe they would notice such large changes (cites Levin et al. 2000).

Warns against over-inference: failing to detect a change does not prove the visual representation is absent or sparse (some studies show accurate visual memory for fixated objects, e.g. Hollingworth & Henderson 2002).
practical_applications: Creators overestimate what viewers will notice; don't overspend on invisible background continuity.
But memory for fixated, story-relevant objects can be good: hero props and character markers must stay exact.
limitations: Opinion/review article; does not quantify film-specific error tolerance.

sources.title: Edit Blindness: The relationship between attention and global change blindness in dynamic scenes
sources.authors: Tim J. Smith, John M. Henderson
key_findings: Journal of Eye Movement Research 2(2):6. Viewers asked to detect edits in excerpts of seven feature films while eye-tracked.
Overall 15.8% of edits were missed even when viewers were explicitly looking for them.
Within-scene cuts (25.1% missed) and match-action cuts (32.4% missed) produced more edit blindness than between-scene cuts (9.4%) and gaze-match cuts (10.9%).
Blinks coincided with very few missed cuts (about 1%); most edit blindness is attributed to attention being absorbed by the narrative, not to blinks/saccades.
Cut detection time averaged 489 ms.
practical_applications: Cut on action and keep spatial continuity within a scene to make cuts invisible; between-scene jumps are noticed and should be signalled deliberately.
In 2D puppet/AI clips, a match-action cut is a cheap way to hide a change of generated image.
limitations: Small sample of films and participants; viewers were instructed to detect edits, so free-viewing blindness is likely higher.

sources.title: The Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity
key_findings: Projections 6(1), 1-27 (author manuscript dated 2011 read). Continuity is the intended outcome of the continuity editing rules, not the style itself.
Over 90% of surveyed Hollywood shots adhere to continuity editing rules (citing Bordwell et al. 1985; Levin & Wang 2009).
AToCC: perceptual expectations can be matched across cuts without a coherent representation of the depicted space; attention (largely on faces and moving characters) decides what must match.
Explains match-action, matched exit/entrance, shot/reverse-shot, the 180-degree rule and POV editing in attentional terms; crossing the 180-degree line reverses screen direction.
Reports Levin & Simons' nine-error dinner scene (2 of 9 detected on a primed second viewing).
practical_applications: Match what attention will be on at the cut (face, hand, moving object, screen direction); the rest can drift.
Use the 180-degree rule and consistent screen direction as cheap continuity anchors for 2D series.
limitations: Theory paper; author manuscript may differ from the published version.

sources.title: The impact of continuity editing in narrative film on event segmentation
sources.authors: Joseph P. Magliano, Jeffrey M. Zacks
key_findings: Per search summary: Cognitive Science 35(8), 1489-1517. Edits classified as continuous in space/time/action; discontinuous in space or time but continuous in action; or discontinuous in action.

Per search summary: action discontinuities had the largest effect on where viewers perceive event boundaries; space/time discontinuities had minor effects; edits produced transient increases in early visual brain areas (fMRI).
practical_applications: Viewers chunk a story by action; a jump in location/time inside the same action reads as continuous, while breaking the action reads as a new event.
limitations: Full text blocked (PMC bot check); only a search summary was available, so findings are as stated by that summary.

sources.title: Continuity Job Descriptions 2024 - Script Supervisor
key_findings: Script supervisor duties: prepare the script, verify actors' lines, time takes, note deviations from the script, take and keep continuity photos, keep detailed notes of action, positions, camera angles and progression, note coverage, list pickups.
Sends continuity notes with a complete lined script to the editor after each shooting day; gives production a daily report (set-ups, picture time, scenes and pages shot).
practical_applications: The two classic outputs map to a small studio: a per-shot continuity log (what each shot shows) and a per-day/per-episode report (what was made, what changed).
limitations: Union job description (Canada); one page; describes duties, not methods.

sources.title: What IS a script supervisor? (script supervision handout and forms)
sources.authors: Vassar College Film department page (author not named)
key_findings: Films are shot out of sequence, so the script supervisor makes hair, make-up, costume and lighting match across scenes shot weeks apart; photos taken after the first take are the main memory aid.
Breakdown data per scene: scene number, location, action summary, time of day, page count (in 1/8 pages), cast, extras, props, costumes.
Continuity sheets per take record take number, lens, stop, filter, timings and action catchwords; delivered to the editor.
Continuous actions (smoking, drinking, eating) are the hardest to match.
Workflow: pre-production (breakdown, continuity report, wardrobe & prop summary), production (shot notes, daily reports), post (marked-up script, chronological scene report).
practical_applications: Template fields for a per-episode continuity breakdown; flag 'progressive' states (a drink level, a wound, dirt) as high-risk.
limitations: Practitioner handout hosted by a college page; author not stated; craft advice, not research.

sources.title: Tablets of Stone or DNA? TV series bibles
key_findings: Journal of Screenwriting 9(1), 3-23 (accepted manuscript read). Professional UK TV writers define 'Bible' vaguely; lengths range from 3-10 pages to 50-60 pages (House of Cards season bible) or 79 pages (The Wire selling bible).

Bible types include selling bible, season bible (development tool, with wall chart of character/storyline grid) and a later production bible that codifies 'case law' to keep long-running series consistent; it can become a database of 'fictional facts' and a human 'walking bible'.
A bible is 'less a tablet of stone, and more like a DNA code'; it is never fixed, so one must ask 'which version?'.

Common contents: premise, place/settings, locations (cost), character biographies, rationale, structure & style, research, production detail (case law such as where people live, what they drink), and episode storylines.
practical_applications: Keep two layers: a short stable 'DNA' (premise, rules, tone) and a growing case-law log of facts established on screen.
Version the bible and note which episode introduced each fact.
limitations: Interviews with seven UK writers and a sample of UK bibles; mostly UK practice.

sources.title: Situation models in language comprehension and memory
sources.authors: Rolf A. Zwaan, Gabriel A. Radvansky
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 123(2), 162-185. Readers build situation models indexed on at least five dimensions: time, space, causation, intentionality (goals) and protagonist.

Readers track protagonists and properties associated with them: an action inconsistent with an earlier trait (a vegetarian ordering a hamburger) raises reading time compared with a control (citing Albrecht & O'Brien).
Calls for treating situation models as multidimensional.
practical_applications: Use the five dimensions as the backbone of a continuity check: when/where/why/what goal/who for every scene.
Character trait contradictions are noticed even when not on screen recently; log traits, not only looks.
limitations: Mostly text-reading experiments; transfer to short video is plausible but not directly tested here.

sources.title: IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
sources.authors: Hu Ye, Jun Zhang, Sibo Liu, Xiao Han, Wei Yang
key_findings: Lightweight adapter (~22M parameters) adds image-prompt capability to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model via decoupled cross-attention for text and image features.
