Image prompt can be combined with a text prompt; transfers to custom models fine-tuned from the same base and works with existing controllable-generation tools.
practical_applications: Tool class 'reference-image conditioning': steer a new image toward a character/style reference without training.
limitations: Abstract only; arXiv preprint; consistency of identity across many images is not quantified in the abstract.

sources.title: IP-Adapter (Diffusers documentation, v0.43)
key_findings: set_ip_adapter_scale: 1.0 = full strength; 0.5 usually balances text and image prompts.
Variants: Plus (more reference detail), Plus-Face, FaceID (InsightFace identity embeddings instead of CLIP).
Masks can assign different reference images to different regions (e.g. two characters in one frame).

Can be combined with ControlNet (pose/depth) for structure, InstantStyle (layer-selective scale) for style vs layout, and multiple IP-Adapters (face + style); image embeddings can be precomputed and saved for reuse.
Available for Flux and SD3 as well as SD/SDXL.
practical_applications: Save the reference embedding of a master character image once and reuse it every episode; use masks for two-character scenes.
limitations: Vendor library docs; no quantitative consistency guarantees.

sources.title: Reproducibility (Diffusers documentation, v0.43)
key_findings: Use a torch Generator with manual_seed for repeatable outputs; a CPU Generator is more stable across machines; a GPU Generator can diverge from CPU results.
A Generator's state is consumed on use; reseed before each call to get the same result again.
enable_full_determinism() turns on deterministic algorithms (slower).
Reproducibility is not guaranteed even with an identical seed.
practical_applications: Log seed + model + sampler + steps + size + prompt for every kept image; a seed alone does not reproduce an image if anything else changes.
limitations: Library-specific (Diffusers/PyTorch); ComfyUI and hosted tools behave differently.

sources.title: DreamBooth: Fine Tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven Generation
sources.authors: Nataniel Ruiz, Yuanzhen Li, Varun Jampani, Yael Pritch, Michael Rubinstein, Kfir Aberman
key_findings: Fine-tunes a text-to-image model on a few images of a subject, binding a unique identifier token to it (CVPR 2023).
Class-specific prior preservation loss lets the model render the subject in new scenes, poses, views and lighting while keeping key features.
practical_applications: Tool class 'subject fine-tuning': strongest identity lock when a character must appear in hundreds of images; costs training time per character.
limitations: Abstract only; needs GPU training per subject; style drift and overfitting not covered in abstract.

sources.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
sources.authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen
key_findings: Freezes pretrained weights and trains small low-rank matrices per layer; on GPT-3 175B cuts trainable parameters ~10,000x and GPU memory ~3x versus full fine-tuning with comparable quality and no extra inference latency.
practical_applications: The same low-rank idea is what image-model 'character LoRAs' use: a small file per character/style that can be loaded on demand.
limitations: Paper is about language models; its use for image diffusion is community/tool practice, not shown in this paper.

sources.title: Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation (ConsiStory)
sources.authors: Yoad Tewel, Omri Kaduri, Rinon Gal, Yoni Kasten, Lior Wolf, Gal Chechik, Yuval Atzmon
key_findings: SIGGRAPH 2024 (TOG). Generates a consistent subject across a batch of images by sharing internal activations (subject-driven shared attention, feature injection) with no optimisation step.
Claims state-of-the-art subject consistency and text alignment versus baselines; prior methods need per-subject optimisation or large-scale pre-training and struggle with multi-subject scenes.
practical_applications: Tool class 'batch-shared attention': generate all frames of one episode in one batch to keep the subject aligned.
limitations: Abstract only; consistency holds within a batch, not necessarily across separate sessions/episodes.

sources.title: FLUX.1 Kontext: Flow Matching for In-Context Image Generation and Editing in Latent Space
sources.authors: Black Forest Labs (S. Batifol, A. Blattmann, P. Esser, R. Rombach, A. Sauer et al.)
key_findings: One flow-matching model for generation and editing with text + image context via sequence concatenation.
Claims better preservation of objects and characters over multiple edit turns than other editing models; introduces KontextBench (1,026 image-prompt pairs incl. a character-reference category).
practical_applications: Tool class 'in-context editing': edit the previous approved frame (new pose/place) instead of regenerating from text, to keep identity.
limitations: Vendor-authored preprint, abstract only; benchmark built by the same vendor.

sources.title: Image generation guide (OpenAI API docs)
key_findings: One or more images can be used as references to generate a new image; in edits the first image is edited and others serve as references.
Masking with GPT Image is prompt-based and may not follow the mask shape precisely.
input_fidelity controls how strongly input-image details are preserved; for gpt-image-2 it cannot be changed and all inputs are processed at high fidelity.
Stated limitation: 'the model may occasionally struggle to maintain visual consistency for recurring characters'; also text placement and precise layout.
practical_applications: When using Codex/GPT image generation, always attach the approved master image(s) as reference and still QC identity markers by eye.
limitations: Vendor docs change often; read on 2026-11-25.

sources.title: Introducing Runway Gen-4
key_findings: Vendor claims Gen-4 can 'precisely generate consistent characters, locations and objects across scenes' from 'a single reference image', without fine-tuning.
practical_applications: Represents the 'reference-image video model' class; plan to feed the same master reference to every shot.
limitations: Marketing claim, no independent evaluation; page undated.

sources.title: Creativity
key_findings: APA presidential address (American Psychologist 5(9):444-454) credited with starting psychological creativity research; Guilford's later Structure-of-Intellect model separates divergent from convergent production.
practical_applications: Separate a 'generate many' phase from a 'pick one' phase.
limitations: Known through secondary sources only; full text not read.

sources.title: Divergent Thinking as an Indicator of Creative Potential
key_findings: Divergent-thinking (DT) tests estimate creative potential, not achievement; DT is not the same as creative thinking; tests are reliable and moderately predictive, 'far from perfect'.
practical_applications: Many ideas is a means, not the goal: judge final work on originality + fit, not idea count.
limitations: Abstract/excerpts only; later papers flag psychometric problems of DT scores.

sources.title: The associative basis of the creative process
key_findings: Creativity = combining associative elements into new useful combinations; the more remote the elements, the more creative; proposed flatter associative hierarchies in creative people (basis of the Remote Associates Test).
Benedek & Neubauer (2013, PMC3924568) found hierarchies did not differ, but creative people showed higher associative fluency and more uncommon responses.
practical_applications: Deliberately pair distant domains (eyewear x temple fair, glasses x weather) to push past first associations.
limitations: No abstract; content via secondary sources; core hierarchy hypothesis only partly supported.

sources.title: Analogical problem solving
sources.authors: Gick, M. L.; Holyoak, K. J.
key_findings: People who read a military story often transferred its solution to Duncker's radiation problem only when hinted; without a hint analogous solutions dropped markedly; Gick & Holyoak 1983: two analogues improve transfer (schema induction).
practical_applications: Analogies do not arrive by themselves: explicitly ask 'what else works like this?' and give 2+ source examples from different domains.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; exact transfer rates not captured.

sources.title: Conceptual Integration Networks
key_findings: Blending is a general cognitive operation: two input spaces, a generic space and a blended space with emergent structure; network types simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope. Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors (lens = window, frame = character) as deliberate blends; check the blend's emergent meaning reads clearly.
limitations: Secondary summaries only; theory, little predictive experimental test.

sources.title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle
key_findings: Four experiments: production blocking (waiting to speak) accounted for most of the productivity loss of interactive vs nominal groups; free riding and evaluation apprehension were minor.
practical_applications: Generate alone first, then pool (nominal group / brainwriting).
limitations: Abstract/secondary only; lab tasks, students.

sources.title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: A Meta-Analytic Integration
sources.authors: Mullen, B.; Johnson, C.; Salas, E.
key_findings: Interactive brainstorming groups produce fewer and lower-quality ideas than nominal groups; losses grow with group size, experimenter presence and spoken (vs written) ideas.
practical_applications: Classic 'everyone shout ideas' brainstorming is the weakest format; write ideas individually.
limitations: Abstract only; Diehl & Stroebe disputed some mechanism conclusions.

sources.title: Idea Generation in Groups: A Basis for Creativity in Organizations
key_findings: In a brainwriting paradigm (writing ideas on slips and passing them on), idea-sharing groups outperformed nominal groups both during the session and in a later individual session.
practical_applications: Brainwriting style: read others' written ideas, then extend silently - works for Claude-vs-user idea exchange too.
limitations: Abstract only; Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 82(1):76-87.

sources.title: Idea Generation and the Quality of the Best Idea
sources.authors: Girotra, K.; Terwiesch, C.; Ulrich, K. T.
key_findings: Hybrid structure (work alone, then pool and evaluate as a team) beat team-only on number of ideas, quality, and ability to discern the best idea; building on others' ideas did not yield more or better ideas.
Best-idea quality depends on mean quality, number, variance, and selection ability.
practical_applications: We need the best idea, not the average: maximise variance in generation, then select carefully with criteria.
limitations: Abstract only; lab product-idea task.

sources.title: Productivity is not enough: A comparison of interactive and nominal groups on idea generation and selection
sources.authors: Rietzschel, E. F.; Nijstad, B. A.; Stroebe, W.
key_findings: J. Exp. Soc. Psych. 42:244-251. Related dissertation abstract: productivity was not related to the quality of selected ideas; a 2009 article by the same authors says using the right selection criteria is essential.
practical_applications: Selection is a separate skill: score ideas against explicit criteria, otherwise people pick the safe/feasible one.
limitations: Bibliographic only; finding linked to this paper via related abstracts.

sources.title: Does Incubation Enhance Problem Solving? A Meta-Analytic Review
sources.authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
key_findings: 117 studies, positive incubation effect (mean d about 0.29 per Gilhooly 2016).
Longer preparation -> larger effect; high-demand filler tasks -> smaller; low-demand tasks beat rest for linguistic insight problems; effects differ by problem type.
practical_applications: Work the brief hard first, then switch to a low-demand task and come back before final selection.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; lab puzzles.

sources.title: Creativity and Innovation Under Constraints: A Cross-Disciplinary Integrative Review
sources.authors: Acar, O. A.; Tarakci, M.; van Knippenberg, D.
key_findings: Constraint research across management fields is fragmented with conflicting findings; builds a taxonomy of constraints and mediating mechanisms (motivation, cognition, social context).
practical_applications: Constraints are not automatically good or bad; pick constraints that force search away from defaults (e.g., 'no coffee shop, no sunset').
limitations: Abstract only; taxonomy categories not verified; the common 'inverted-U' summary was not confirmed this session.

sources.title: The Effectiveness of Creativity Training: A Quantitative Review
sources.authors: Scott, G.; Leritz, L. E.; Mumford, M. D.
key_findings: 70 studies; well-designed creativity training typically yields gains that generalise across criteria; programmes focused on cognitive skills and heuristics did better.
practical_applications: Heuristic-based methods (problem finding, combination, idea evaluation) are the trainable core.
limitations: Abstract/secondary; see SioLortieForgues2024 on publication bias.

sources.title: Creativity Enhancement Methods for Adults: A Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Haase, J.; Hanel, P. H. P.; Gronau, N.
key_findings: 332 effect sizes, 12 method categories, overall g = 0.53; complex training courses, meditation and cultural exposure strongest (g = 0.66); drugs g = 0.10 n.s.; reported no publication bias.
practical_applications: Exposure to varied culture/references is a legitimate input step (moodboards from different eras/countries).
limitations: Abstract only; publication-bias conclusion contradicted by SioLortieForgues2024.

sources.title: The Impact of Creativity Training on Creative Performance
key_findings: 169 studies (844 effect sizes, 48 unpublished); unadjusted 0.53 SD; converging evidence of strong publication bias, adjusted estimates 0.29-0.32 SD; many methodological shortcomings, little improvement over time.
practical_applications: Expect modest gains from any named creativity method; don't promise big effects.
limitations: Abstract/preprint summary only.

sources.title: Thinking hats and good men: Structured techniques in a problem construction task
key_findings: Six hats and 'six men' (5W1H) both improved fluency and originality in problem construction vs controls; published abstract and preprint disagree on which technique had the more robust effect.
Authors' 2016 follow-ups: order of hats had no effect (possibly underpowered); a placebo-controlled study found active techniques beat placebo.
practical_applications: Six hats is acceptable as a perspective-switching prompt, but evidence is a handful of small studies; 5W1H questions work about as well.
limitations: Small samples, one lab; search summaries only; no large independent trial found.

sources.title: Experimental assessment of TRIZ effectiveness in idea generation (J. Mechanical Design version: TRIZ ideation effectiveness study)
sources.authors: Vargas Hernandez, N.; Schmidt, L. C.; Okudan Kremer, G. E.
key_findings: TRIZ improved novelty and variety but slightly reduced quantity vs ad-hoc ideation; conference version: method fit depends on the outcome sought.
practical_applications: TRIZ suits engineering contradictions (lens thin AND strong); limited relevance to story ideation.
limitations: Search summary only; engineering students; exact JMD title not captured.

sources.title: General morphological analysis as a basic scientific modelling method
key_findings: GMA (extending Zwicky) structures a problem space ('morphospace') into parameters and values, then synthesises solutions by combining values and removing inconsistent pairs (Technological Forecasting and Social Change 126:81-91).
practical_applications: Story matrix: setting x conflict x glasses role x ending -> forced distinct combinations.
limitations: Method description by its main proponent; no controlled efficacy evidence found.

sources.title: Doing Design Thinking: Conceptual Review, Synthesis, and Research Agenda
key_findings: Systematic review + card sort with designers: 10 attributes and 8 tools of design thinking; substantial disagreement between promoters and critics on attributes, applicability and outcomes.
A later paper reports the reviewed literature is 15% conceptual, 38% anecdotal, 44% qualitative (secondary).
practical_applications: Use design-thinking tools (user empathy, prototyping, iteration) as craft, not as a proven method.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

sources.title: Design Thinking: Critical Analysis and Future Evolution
sources.authors: Verganti, R.; Dell'Era, C.; Swan, K. S.
key_findings: JPIM editorial summarising critiques: design-thinking studies judged empirically unconvincing and theoretically disconnected from innovation-management theory.
practical_applications: Do not cite 'design thinking' as evidence that an idea works.
limitations: Search summary only.

sources.title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
sources.authors: Dow, S. P.; Glassco, A.; Kass, J.; Schwarz, M.; Schwartz, D. L.; Klemmer, S. R.
key_findings: Novices designing web ads: parallel prototyping beat serial on all performance measures, produced more diverse prototypes (independent raters), increased self-efficacy, and more positive reactions to critique.
Murphy et al. 2022 reports similar advantages in engineering design.
practical_applications: Make 3 rough directions side by side before polishing one; compare, then iterate the winner.
limitations: Abstract/summaries only; novice sample; one task type.

sources.title: Design fixation
sources.authors: Jansson, D. G.; Smith, S. M.
key_findings: Showing an example solution made designers (incl. professionals) repeat its features, even flawed ones; instructions to avoid the features did not reduce fixation.
Mixed later evidence: Purcell et al. 1993 replications largely unsuccessful, effects tied to familiarity; Chrysikou & Weisberg found defixation instructions helped.
practical_applications: Reference images and AI drafts anchor us; generate own directions before looking at references or AI output.
limitations: Known via secondary papers (Design Studies); replication mixed - medium confidence.

sources.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
sources.authors: Doshi, A. R.; Hauser, O. P.
key_findings: 293 writers, 600 evaluators; conditions 0, 1 or 5 GPT-4 ideas. Novelty +5.4% (1 idea) and +8.1% (5 ideas); usefulness +3.7% / +9.0%.
Gains largest for less creative writers (novelty up to +10.7%), roughly equalising them with more creative writers.
Stories became more similar to each other (+10.7% / +8.9% of similarity range) and about 5% more similar to the AI ideas - a social dilemma: individuals better off, collective diversity down.
practical_applications: AI ideas raise the floor but pull everyone toward the same stories: use AI for volume/critique, but force divergence (different seeds, constraints, human-first idea) and check against our own past output.
limitations: 8-sentence stories, one LLM, no interaction with the model, UK online sample, opt-in idea use.

sources.title: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
sources.authors: Anderson, B. R.; Shah, J. H.; Kreminski, M.
key_findings: 36 participants, four TTCT-style divergent tasks: different users produced less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT than with a non-AI creativity support tool (ACM Creativity & Cognition 2024).
practical_applications: Same model + similar prompt = similar ideas across users; vary the input, not just ask again.
limitations: Small sample; abstract only.

sources.title: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance
sources.authors: Meincke, L.; Mollick, E.; Terwiesch, C.
key_findings: GPT-4 with minimal prompting produced less diverse idea pools than groups of humans; personas and creativity-technique prompts helped somewhat; chain-of-thought prompting gave the highest diversity, close to human groups.
Authors suggest using multiple models to add variety.
practical_applications: Ask the model to first list many distinct concepts briefly, then develop each; mix models (Claude/Codex/FLUX) and seeds.
limitations: Working paper (SSRN/arXiv); diversity measured by embeddings, not by audience response; product-idea domain.

sources.title: Critical Thinking (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Common core of 17 conceptions: critical thinking = 'careful goal-directed thinking'; Dewey called it reflective thinking ('active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief').

Abilities listed include observing, questioning (turning puzzlement into a clear question), inferring, testing hypotheses, consulting and judging source credibility, argument analysis, and imagining alternative explanations.
Dispositions: attentiveness, habit of inquiry, open-mindedness, willingness to suspend judgment, seeking the truth; subject knowledge is also required.
Reports Abrami et al. 2015: dialogue, anchored instruction and mentoring help, combination best; evidence that instruction transfers across domains is described as scanty.
practical_applications: Use the ability list as the skeleton of the pre-delivery check (question, evidence, source credibility, alternatives).
Do not assume a generic 'think critically' instruction transfers; use domain-specific checklists.
limitations: Philosophical overview, not an empirical review; the last ~13% of the page text was not read.
Author not shown in the text read; first published 2018-07-21, last substantive revision 2022-10-12.

sources.title: Fallacies (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: A fallacy can be treated as an argument that seems better than it really is; academic writers favour this 'deceptively bad argument' view over 'false popular belief'.
Discusses textbook tradition (Copi's 18 informal fallacies) incl. equivocation, composition/division, begging the question, complex question.
practical_applications: Check our own captions/scripts for arguments that only look strong (e.g., one testimonial presented as proof).
limitations: Only a search summary was read; archived editions 2016-2025 exist, original year not captured.

sources.title: Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Abrami, P. C.; Bernard, R. M.; Borokhovski, E.; Waddington, D. I.; Wade, C. A.; Persson, T.
key_findings: 341 effect sizes, weighted mean g = 0.30 (range about -1 to +2), learners from elementary to adult (per SEP supplement and Clearinghouse commentary).
Dialogue, anchored (authentic problem) instruction and mentoring each helped; combinations worked best (per SEP).
practical_applications: Critical thinking is trainable but effects are small-moderate; build it into routines (checklists, dialogue/critique) rather than relying on intention.
limitations: Read via secondary summaries; most studies lack long-term follow-up.

sources.title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
key_findings: Three heuristics: representativeness, availability, adjustment from an anchor; economical and usually effective but lead to systematic and predictable errors.
Representativeness ignores factors such as base rates and sample size that should affect probability.
practical_applications: When judging 'which idea will work', ask for base rates (how did similar posts perform?) instead of how vivid/typical the idea feels.
limitations: Abstract and excerpts only; classic lab vignettes.

sources.title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises
key_findings: Confirmation bias = seeking or interpreting evidence in ways partial to existing beliefs; review states a great deal of empirical evidence shows it is extensive, strong and appears in many guises.
practical_applications: Before delivery, actively look for evidence against the chosen claim/idea, not just support.
limitations: Only abstract and opening pages read; narrative review, not meta-analysis.

sources.title: Considering the opposite: A corrective strategy for social judgment
sources.authors: Lord, C. G.; Lepper, M. R.; Preston, E.
key_findings: Two experiments (biased assimilation of evidence; biased hypothesis testing): inducing a 'consider the opposite' strategy corrected bias more than instructions to be 'as fair and unbiased as possible'.
practical_applications: Pre-delivery item: write the strongest case that the opposite is true; 'be objective' instructions are weaker.
limitations: Abstract only; 1980s student samples; no large modern replication found this session.

sources.title: Giving Debiasing Away: Can Psychological Research on Correcting Cognitive Errors Promote Human Welfare?
sources.authors: Lilienfeld, S. O.; Ammirati, R.; Landfield, K.
key_findings: Reviews what is known and unknown about debiasing confirmation bias and barriers to real-world effectiveness; research cataloguing biases far outweighs research on debiasing.
practical_applications: Treat any debiasing step as uncertain; prefer structural safeguards (checklists, second reviewer) over self-exhortation.
limitations: Abstract/introduction only; specific technique evidence not read.

sources.title: Debiasing Decisions: Improved Decision Making With a Single Training Intervention
sources.authors: Morewedge, C. K.; Yoon, H.; Scopelliti, I.; Symborski, C. W.; Korris, J. H.; Kassam, K. S.
key_findings: Two longitudinal experiments: one-shot training (video game or instructional video) produced medium to large debiasing effects immediately, persisting at least 2 months.
Games with personalized feedback and practice beat videos; effects were domain-general across taught and untaught formats.
practical_applications: Practice with feedback beats reading about biases: log our own wrong calls in LEARNING-LOG and review them.
limitations: Abstract only (full text blocked); games cost ~USD 7M to build (BU note); biases targeted were those relevant to intelligence analysis.
Published in Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences 2(1):129-140; DOI not captured this session.

sources.title: Debiasing Training Improves Decision Making in the Field
sources.authors: Sellier, A.-L.; Scopelliti, I.; Morewedge, C. K.
key_findings: Field experiment, 290 French business graduate students; one-shot confirmation-bias game before an unannounced Challenger-style business case.
Trained students were 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming option; write-ups suggest less confirmatory hypothesis testing.
practical_applications: Evidence that debiasing can transfer to a realistic case; supports building a habit of testing the rival hypothesis.
limitations: Single field experiment by the authors' own account; one population; abstract/summary only.

sources.title: The Trouble With Overconfidence
sources.authors: Moore, D. A.; Healy, P. J.
key_findings: Overconfidence is three distinct constructs: overestimation (own performance), overplacement (vs others), overprecision (excess certainty).
Hard tasks produce overestimation and underplacement; easy tasks the reverse; overprecision is the most persistent (later summary).
practical_applications: State uncertainty ranges and confidence labels rather than single confident claims (targets overprecision).
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

sources.title: Investigating Variation in Replicability: A 'Many Labs' Replication Project
sources.authors: Klein, R. A.; Ratliff, K. A.; Vianello, M.; et al.
key_findings: 13 effects, 36 samples, 6,344 participants; 10 replicated consistently; flag priming and currency priming did not; imagined contact weak.
Replicability depended more on the effect than on sample/setting.
Effects tested included anchoring, gain-vs-loss framing, sunk costs, retrospective gambler's fallacy; Nature coverage says anchoring was substantially stronger than the original study suggested.
practical_applications: Classic judgment effects (anchoring, framing) are among the more robust; subtle priming claims are not - do not build content on them.
limitations: Full text blocked (403); per-effect outcome for framing/sunk cost not confirmed this session.

sources.title: Timid Choices and Bold Forecasts: A Cognitive Perspective on Risk Taking
key_findings: Decision makers treat problems as unique; overly optimistic forecasts come from an 'inside view' anchored on specific plans and scenarios; the 'outside view' (later: reference-class forecasting) uses outcomes of similar past cases.
practical_applications: Estimate time/performance of a new clip from how similar past clips actually went (our render logs, past reach), not from the plan.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
sources.authors: Mellers, B.; Ungar, L.; Baron, J.; et al.
key_findings: In the IARPA tournament, probability training (correcting biases, using reference classes, averaging estimates), teaming and tracking each improved calibration and resolution.
practical_applications: Probabilistic language ('likely ~70%') plus reference classes is trainable and improves judgment.
limitations: Abstract only; geopolitical forecasting domain.

sources.title: Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events
sources.authors: Mitchell, D. J.; Russo, J. E.; Pennington, N.
key_findings: Secondary sources (premortem write-ups) report that imagining an event as having already happened ('prospective hindsight') increased the number of reasons generated by about 30%.
practical_applications: Basis for the pre-mortem item: 'it is next week and this post flopped/misled people - why?'.
limitations: Existence confirmed (J. Behavioral Decision Making 2(1):25-38); content not read; the 30% figure is from secondary sources only.

sources.title: Performing a Project Premortem
key_findings: HBR 85(9):18-19. Team assumes the project has failed and each member lists plausible reasons; held at the start so the plan can be fixed; claimed to prime people to notice early warning signs.
practical_applications: 2-minute pre-mortem before shipping a clip or a factual carousel.
limitations: Practitioner article; read via secondary summaries; effectiveness claims rest on small studies (Veinott2010, Mitchell1989).

sources.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence
sources.authors: Veinott, E. S.; Klein, G.; Wiggins, S.
key_findings: Secondary accounts: 178 students evaluating an H1N1 response plan; premortem reduced (over)confidence more than simple critique or pros-and-cons.
practical_applications: Premortem is a reasonable cheap tool to lower overconfidence in a plan.
limitations: Conference proceedings (ISCRAM); measured confidence, not real-world plan failure; content known only via secondary sources.

sources.title: The problem with '5 whys'
key_findings: 5 Whys has value as a teaching tool ('aha' of systems safety) but is weak for root cause analysis: oversimplifies complex problems, the number five is arbitrary, no objective stopping rule, tends toward a single causal chain.
practical_applications: Use 5 Whys only for quick single-chain glitches (render bug); for audience/performance problems list multiple contributing causes.
limitations: Commentary in a healthcare context; read via PSNet summary and excerpts (full text 403).

sources.title: The problem with root cause analysis
sources.authors: Peerally, M. F.; Carr, S.; Waring, J.; Dixon-Woods, M.
key_findings: The term 'root cause' implies a single cause and promotes reductionism; RCA applied without adaptation; eight challenges incl. single-point causation focus and weak feedback.
practical_applications: When a series underperforms, record several contributing factors (hook, timing, topic, format) and test one at a time.
limitations: Healthcare context; abstract and summaries only.

sources.title: The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?
key_findings: Nine viewpoints (strength, consistency, etc.) for judging whether an association is causal; commentators stress Hill did not call them criteria.
Core practical question: will changing A change the frequency of B?
practical_applications: Before saying 'X causes Y' (e.g., 'screens cause myopia'), check strength, consistency, dose-response and plausible alternatives; otherwise write 'linked with'.
limitations: Read via summaries (Wakeford, Milbank, ASU) not the full text.

sources.title: Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability
key_findings: Secondary sources describe it as an accessible summary/guide to Wald's WWII memoranda on estimating aircraft survivability from returning planes (the classic survivorship-bias case).
practical_applications: When copying 'what viral posts do', remember we only see survivors; flops that did the same thing are invisible.
limitations: JASA 79(386) per a single secondary source; content not read; popular retellings embellish the story (AMS 'Legend of Abraham Wald').

sources.title: Hofstede's model of national cultural differences and their consequences: A triumph of faith - a failure of analysis
key_findings: Questionnaire was designed for workplace satisfaction, not culture; sample was IBM employees (educated, mostly male).
Rejects national culture as a systematically causal factor of behaviour (as summarised by Williamson 2002).
Hofstede's reply 'Dimensions do not exist' (Human Relations 55(11):1355-1361) says McSweeney misses the point; McSweeney calls the reply evasive.
McSweeney 2013 'Fashion founded on a flaw' extends the critique to GLOBE: applying national scores to individuals is an ecological fallacy.
practical_applications: Use national dimensions only as rough hypotheses about a market, never to predict one customer.
limitations: Abstract/search summary; the 2002 article itself was not read. Check 2026-11-25: the Royal Holloway PDF at this URL is a different paper (McSweeney, Brown & Iliopoulou 2010 working paper) - now a separate source McSweeneyBrownIliopoulou2010 (read in full).

sources.title: Examining the Impact of Culture's Consequences
sources.authors: Taras, V.; Kirkman, B. L.; Steel, P.
key_findings: 598 studies, >200,000 individuals; overall absolute weighted effect rho = 0.18 at individual level.
Values relate most to emotions, then attitudes, then behaviours, least to job performance.
Effects larger in culturally 'tight' countries, for managers vs students, older/male/more educated respondents.
Related Steel & Taras 2010: up to ~90% of variance in cultural values lies within countries.
practical_applications: Culture shifts feelings/attitudes toward a message more than it decides behaviour: adapt tone and imagery, keep the offer clear.
limitations: Figures from abstract and secondary citations, not full text.

sources.title: Culture, Leadership, and Organizations: The GLOBE Study of 62 Societies
sources.authors: House, R. J.; Hanges, P. J.; Javidan, M.; Dorfman, P. W.; Gupta, V. (eds.)
key_findings: ~17,000-18,000 middle managers in three industries across 62 societies.

Nine dimensions: performance orientation, uncertainty avoidance, humane orientation, institutional collectivism, in-group collectivism, assertiveness, gender egalitarianism, future orientation, power distance.
Each scored as 'as is' (practices) and 'should be' (values) - the two often diverge.
practical_applications: Practices vs values gap is creatively useful: show the world the audience wishes for ('should be') rather than mirroring 'as is'.
limitations: Publisher page and summaries only; Thailand scores not retrieved; same ecological-fallacy critique (McSweeney 2013).

sources.title: A Critique of Hall's Contexting Model
key_findings: Reviewed 224 articles (1990-2006): high/low context is the most-cited intercultural framework.
Few propositions tested empirically; the most-tested ones (esp. directness) largely failed to support the model.
Recommends measures, more countries, and studying when cultures use both HC and LC messages.
Related: Kittler, Rygl & Mackinnon 2011 review (Int. J. Cross Cultural Management) finds no valid, reliable country classification for HC/LC.
practical_applications: Do not assume 'Thai = high-context so be vague'; context use depends on situation, relationship and channel.
limitations: Abstract and a blog review; full text not read.

sources.title: Psychology of the Thai People: Values and Behavioral Patterns
key_findings: Survey 1978-1981 of 2,469 Thais (per secondary summary); a 2016 review lists ten value dimensions incl. self-centeredness/individual emphasis, debt of gratitude (bunkhun) and social relations; tourism papers cite it for 'caring-considerate', 'friendly' hospitality.
Attributes values more to agrarian, relationship-centred society than to Buddhism; rural respondents weighted gratitude, obedience, forgiveness more.
practical_applications: Thai audiences respond to relationship, gratitude and face-saving framing; avoid humiliation humour.
limitations: Book not read; NIDA Bangkok; dated 1990/1991 inconsistently; data are 40+ years old.

sources.title: A discourse analysis of the Thai experience of 'being krengjai'
key_findings: Krengjai described as the Thai concept hardest for Westerners to grasp.
Historical research + questionnaire: 15 general meanings identified, back-translated, rated by 471 Thai people.
practical_applications: Characters who refuse indirectly or hesitate to ask are culturally legible to Thais; foreigners may read it as vague.
limitations: Abstract only (same key used in knowledge/emotions/sources.json).

sources.title: Customer deference to service providers in ordinary service encounters
key_findings: Critical incident technique, 253 Thai participants describing being deferential (kreng jai) to service providers.
Deference rises when customers perceive the provider's well-being is compromised; it involves aversive feelings, coping strategies and avoiding future contact.
practical_applications: Thai customers may not complain - they leave. Messaging that makes asking easy ('ถามได้เลย ไม่ต้องเกรงใจ') removes a real barrier.
limitations: Abstract; service-encounter setting.

sources.title: Bunkhun: The Ideology Effect of Thai Business Management
key_findings: Bunkhun translated as reciprocity of goodness / exchange of favours; strongly affects business relationships.

Related: corpus study of katanyu (gratitude) in the Thai National Corpus links gratitude discourse to reciprocity expectations and power inequality (doi 10.18848/2327-7882/CGP/v22i02/191-214); Chula thesis: speakers perform some face-threatening speech acts less toward people they owe bunkhun.
practical_applications: Gratitude stories (parents, teachers, long-time customers) resonate; avoid framing a gift as creating debt or obligation pressure.
limitations: Search summary; regional business journal.

sources.title: The Anatomy of Thai Face
key_findings: Ethnographic social-anthropology study: five abstract social constructs - nata (หน้าตา), kiat (เกียรติ), saksi (ศักดิ์ศรี), chuesiang (ชื่อเสียง) and barami (บารมี) - form the 'anatomy' of Thai face.
Thais think of the five together, but field data show they are distinct though not mutually exclusive; the author offers a visual model of their dynamic relationship.
From earlier search only: Ukosakul's work on Thai face idioms and politeness.
practical_applications: Never make a recognisable customer/staff member look foolish; humour targets situations, not people's status.
limitations: Abstract only (Manusya 11(1):53-75); the model itself not read.

sources.title: Thai Culture: Communication (The Cultural Atlas)
key_findings: Indirect refusals; bluntness only among close acquaintances.
Raising the voice implies loss of control and can cause loss of face.
Smiles can mask awkwardness/sadness; nodding = acknowledgement, not agreement.

Pointing with one finger is rude; beckon palm-down; never touch the head; feet are dirtiest - don't point with them or show soles; head higher than Buddha image is disrespectful; dramatic gestures may read as anger.
practical_applications: Direction notes for actors/puppets and for foreign-facing etiquette content.
limitations: Generalised cultural profile (Mosaica); not empirical.

sources.title: Feet Low, Head High: A Guide to Thai Etiquettes
key_findings: Daily wai: palms at chest, slight head bow; deeper wai/prostration for revered persons and ceremonies.
Head most sacred - don't touch heads or pass things over heads; feet lowest - don't point soles at people or Buddha images, don't rest feet on tables, step over pillows/books.
Remove shoes in chapels; don't step on temple thresholds (guardian spirit); bow/crouch passing seated monks; keep Buddha images above head height.
practical_applications: Staging rules for scenes with elders, monks, Buddha images and homes.
limitations: States it does not reflect Royal Thai Government views; royal topics not covered.

sources.title: The Hofstede model: Applications to global branding and advertising strategy and research
key_findings: Describes the dimensions most relevant to branding/advertising and reviews studies applying them.
Includes cautionary remarks on applying the model.
practical_applications: Use as a vocabulary for briefing (e.g. collectivist family framing vs individual achievement), then test.
limitations: Abstract only; written by the model's author (not independent).

sources.title: (Meta-analysis of adapting advertising appeals to cultural values - exact title not captured)
key_findings: Adapted cultural-value appeals are generally more persuasive and better liked than unadapted ones (as cited by later work).
No adaptation effects in studies with participants from Europe or Central/South America.
practical_applications: Adapting to values helps a little on average; don't expect it to rescue a weak offer.
limitations: Known via citing works (Radboud thesis page); exact title and statistics not verified.

sources.title: Cultural Value Adaptation in Advertising is Effective, But Not Dependable (meta-analysis)
key_findings: ~120 comparisons, studies 1994-2018: adaptation effects exist but are small (persuasion mean r = .049; ad liking mean r = .055).
When researchers' cultural background matched the audience's, adapted appeals were significantly more persuasive (r = .081).
practical_applications: Local creators who share the audience's culture are a real asset - have a Thai (or target-market) reviewer, not just a translator.
limitations: Publisher page blocked by bot check; numbers from search summaries; authors not captured.

sources.title: Harm and offence: Gender stereotypes (CAP/BCAP rule, in force 14 June 2019) and 12-month review
key_findings: CAP announced the rule on 14 Dec 2018; CAP Code rule 4.9 and BCAP rule 4.14 took effect 14 June 2019: ads 'must not include gender stereotypes that are likely to cause harm, or serious or widespread offence', following an ASA review of gender stereotyping in ads.

Guidance: the rule is not intended to stop ads featuring glamorous, attractive, successful, aspirational or healthy people or lifestyles, one gender only, or stereotypes used to challenge their negative effects.
Guidance covers five problem areas: stereotypical roles and characteristics; sexualisation and objectification; humour; contrasting stereotypes; other stereotypical depictions.
From earlier search only (not on this page): 12-month review kept the rule; Eisend (2010) meta-analysis of gender roles in ads (bibliographic).
practical_applications: Test: does the scene imply a role is ONLY for one gender or mock someone for not fitting it? Rewrite.
limitations: UK regulator advice page (CAP Executive, non-binding advice) - not Thai law; used as a good-practice benchmark.

sources.title: The Ethics of Cultural Heritage (sec. 4 Cultural Appropriation)
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author not captured)
key_findings: Appropriation = taking/using cultural products (stories, styles, motifs, artefacts, religion-related practices) by outsiders; wrongful cases usually sit on social inequality.

Arguments for wrongness: profound offence (prima facie, can be outweighed), harm/exploitation (profit without permission/reciprocity, stereotype, silencing), violation of group intimacy, oppression accounts.
Counterarguments: offence easily outweighed; insiders also misrepresent; cultural exchange is creative; essentialism about group boundaries.
practical_applications: Appreciation test: credit, context, consent/collaboration, no caricature, no sacred items as decoration, share benefit.
limitations: First published 2018, revised Sep 2025; ~100k of 130k characters read; authors not in fetched text.

sources.title: Correlates of Colorism: Freedom of Speech and Discriminatory Advertising in Thailand
key_findings: January 2016: Seoul Secret's 'Whiteness makes you win' skin-whitening ad went viral on Thai social media, drew international coverage (CNN, the Guardian) and local calls for legal action.
Content analysis of Thai print, online and social-media coverage: the value of free speech appears to be absent from Thai discourse about 'discriminatory advertising'.
From earlier search only: the ad was pulled and the company apologised; earlier Thai cosmetic/toothpaste ads were also criticised.
practical_applications: Colourism (fair = winner) is a live backlash risk in Thailand; never use skin tone as before/after or status cue.
limitations: Abstract only (International Journal of Social Sciences 6(2):63-76).

sources.title: Thailand welcomes 32.9m foreign tourists in 2025
sources.authors: The Nation Thailand (quoting Ministry of Tourism and Sports)
key_findings: 2025: 32,974,321 foreign arrivals; 1.53 trillion baht revenue (MOTS figures, published 6 Jan 2026).
Top 5 markets 2025: Malaysia 4,520,856; China 4,473,992; India 2,487,319; Russia 1,898,837; South Korea 1,555,227.
Arrivals down ~7% vs 2024; Malaysia overtook China from April 2025.
practical_applications: Tourist-facing content: plan for Malay/Muslim, Chinese, Indian (Hindu/other), Russian and Korean viewers, not only 'Western'.
limitations: News report of official figures; MOTS statistics page itself (mots.go.th/news/category/411) listed no data when fetched; markets 6-10 not captured. Hua Hin/local mix may differ.

sources.title: Localization vs. Internationalization
key_findings: Localization (l10n) = adapting content for a specific locale; internationalization = designing so localization is easy.

Localization covers number/date/time/currency formats, symbols, icons and colours, references that may be misread or insensitive, legal requirements, name/address order, script readability, and sometimes rethinking visual design and logic.
practical_applications: Translation is one line of the localisation checklist, not the whole job.
limitations: Web/software focus; no last-updated date.

sources.title: Criminal Code (Thailand), Wikisource translation of the 1956 (B.E. 2499) promulgated text
key_findings: 1956 text (Wikisource, read): s.112 defaming, insulting or expressing malice towards the King, Queen, Heir to the Throne or Regent - up to 7 years; s.118 any act against a flag or other symbol of the State in order to desecrate the Nation - up to 1 year / 2,000 baht; s.135 same for a friendly foreign state's flag; s.206 any act against an object or place of religious reverence that desecrates the religion - up to 3 years / 6,000 baht; s.207 disorder at a lawful religious meeting; s.208 wrongfully dressing as or using a symbol of a bhikkhu, novice, ascetic or cleric in order to make others believe one is such a person - up to 1 year / 2,000 baht.

Current consolidated Thai text (legardy.com / thailawonline.com, read 2026-11-25): s.112 imprisonment 3-15 years; s.118 and s.135 up to 2 years or 40,000 baht or both; s.206 1-7 years or 20,000-140,000 baht or both; s.208 up to 1 year or 20,000 baht or both - fines as amended by Criminal Code Amendment Act (No. 26) B.E. 2560 (2017).
s.208 needs intent to make others believe one is a monk/cleric; s.118/135 need intent to desecrate ('เพื่อเหยียดหยาม').
practical_applications: Any royal reference, Buddha image, monk costume or temple setting in content needs a respect check; satire of the monarchy is a criminal risk.
limitations: Wikisource is an unofficial translation of the original 1956 text; current penalties taken from two private law-database sites quoting the Thai consolidated text (Krisdika not checked). Supreme Court has applied s.112 broadly (press summaries). Not legal advice.

sources.title: Thailand 2024 Advertising Matrix
key_findings: Ads must not contain elements that denigrate or insult the King or other heads of state.
Ads should never insult or defame any religion or sacred person, place or thing.
All ads must follow the Consumer Protection Act 1979 as amended; Advertising Association of Thailand self-regulatory code also applies to broadcasters.
practical_applications: Baseline content rules for any Thai-market ad, including social posts and boosted posts.
limitations: Industry summary (PDF metadata dated Mar 2025); text extracted locally from the PDF.

sources.title: Thailand's Advertising Guidelines Targeting AI-Generated Content
key_findings: Law-firm summary (12 Mar 2026) of an OCPB notification under the Consumer Protection Act B.E. 2522, described as already in effect: AI/software-made or edited ad images/video that may cause material misunderstanding about the product must match real size/quantity/volume/composition, get regulator approval where the law requires, and carry clear disclosures; example labels include 'Image created by AI', 'Video created by AI', 'Real image or simulation edited using AI'.
Exact trigger is not fully clear from the summary: the label bullet speaks of AI used to create or edit images generally; safest practice = label any AI-made/edited ad image showing a product.
practical_applications: Our AI scenes with real frames: label AI images; never AI-alter the product itself (shape, colour, lens) beyond reality.
limitations: Law-firm summary; penalties not stated in fetched page.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: no in-force date given (12 Mar 2026 is the article date); label wordings are examples; trigger scope ambiguous - read the Royal Gazette notice before relying on details.

Primary check 2026-11-25: OCPB's own article (OCPB2025_AIAdGuidance) and OCPB news (OCPB2025_AINews) read in full - they confirm the three duties and the Thai label wordings; Gazette text still unread (Cloudflare block).

sources.title: Garuda emblem on shoes clear violation of law: Wissanu
key_findings: 16 Mar 2021: Deputy PM Wissanu said using the national emblem on shoes violates the Garuda Emblem Act; anyone wanting to use it must first seek permission from the Prime Minister's Office.

The manufacturer would be summoned and face legal action in Thailand; people who wear the shoes would not face criminal charges. No penalty amounts given (see KhrutPhaAct2535: up to 1 year / 6,000 baht for unauthorised use implying right).
practical_applications: Never put the Garuda, royal crests or 'By Royal Appointment' style marks in our designs.
limitations: News report of an official's statement.

sources.title: ปัญหาการกำหนดความผิดฐานเหยียดหยามธงชาติ (Problems of criminalizing flag desecration) - LL.M. thesis, Chulalongkorn University; also Chula Law Journal 42(1), March 2024
sources.authors: จินต์จุฑา บำเพ็ญวัฒนา (Bumpenvattana, Jinjutha)
key_findings: Thesis studies flag desecration under Penal Code ss.118 and 135 and Flag Act B.E. 2522 s.54, comparing the US, India, Germany and South Korea.
Finds four problems: out of step with social/political context, contrary to lex certa (vague wording), over-criminalised, and disproportionate limits on free expression.

PROPOSALS (not current law): repeal Flag Act s.54 as redundant with s.118; narrow the act to removing, destroying, damaging, rendering useless or defiling a flag/State symbol publicly or in a meeting; keep 'desecrate' as specific intent. Current s.118 covers 'any act' done to desecrate the nation.
practical_applications: Show the Thai flag intact, upright and clean; no flag on floors, shoes, trash or as a wipe.
limitations: Abstracts (Thai + English) read on Chula ETD and in the CLJ article PDF; the PDF body's Thai text could not be extracted (font encoding), so Flag Act s.54 wording and penalty remain unread. The earlier entry wrongly presented the proposed list of acts as the current law.

sources.title: From tattoos to toilet seats, 'misused' Buddha images make some blood boil
key_findings: 27 Apr 2018 feature: Buddha images on tattoos, toilet seats, swimwear, flip-flops, rugs, beer bottles, mugs and keychains, cut-off heads/hands/feet as spa or home decor, items on or near the floor or in bathrooms, and nightlife branding (Buddha Bar) anger many Buddhists.

The billboard campaign was run by Knowing Buddha, a private group funded entirely by individual donations (founded about six years earlier, ~20,000 members in 25 countries) - not a government ministry.

Quotes: 'A cut-off head or hands is always wrong, it's like cutting your national flag into pieces'; Knowing Buddha: 'It's especially offensive to put those items on or near the floor.' A monk quoted: the image is 'only a symbol'.
Article says s.206 can bring up to 7 years and/or 14,000 baht; the Wat Arun 'butt bros' photographers were nearly charged and were deported after a fine.
practical_applications: Buddha images: never as props, decor, product backgrounds, cropped heads, or comic elements.
limitations: Feature journalism (2018); its s.206 fine figure predates/does not match the current text (20,000-140,000 baht after the 2017 amendment - see ThaiPenalCode).

sources.title: Thailand's National Office of Buddhism Calls Foul on Supreme for Using Photo of Late Monk
key_findings: 22 Feb 2021: the National Office of Buddhism (statement 19 Feb 2021) was weighing legal action against Supreme for using an image of the revered late monk Luang Phor Koon (d. 2015) and yant script on its 'Blessings Ripstop Shirt' (SS21) without seeking or receiving permission.

Department of Intellectual Property (DG Vittikrai Leewiraphan): no copyright registration exists for the image or yant; the temple would have to prove authorship; protection would last 50 years from creation.
No outcome reported; the temple planned to discuss the issue with Supreme first.
practical_applications: Revered monks' faces, amulets and yant designs are off-limits for product design.
limitations: Trade-press report; outcome unknown.

sources.title: ชี้นำความคิด…ถูกผิดต้องรู้(กฎหมาย) [OCPB article on influencer/native ads and AI-made ad images]
sources.authors: กฤดิกร แจ่มตระกูล (นักประชาสัมพันธ์, สำนักงานคณะกรรมการคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค)
key_findings: OCPB's own article ties the AI rule to ประกาศคณะกรรมการว่าด้วยการโฆษณา เรื่อง แนวทางการใช้ข้อความโฆษณาที่มีลักษณะเป็นการยืนยันข้อเท็จจริงอันยากแก่การพิสูจน์ และแนวทางการพิสูจน์เพื่อแสดงความจริงเกี่ยวกับข้อความโฆษณา พ.ศ. ๒๕๖๕: it controls ads for goods or services whose still or moving images are created or edited with programs or AI so that the pictured product/service does not match what is actually sold, causing misunderstanding about its condition, quality, quantity or other material aspects.

Duties: (1) get permission from the relevant agency where a specific law already requires approval before advertising; (2) any size, quantity, volume, number or composition shown in still or moving images must match the product/service actually sold; (3) if a still or moving image is created or edited with programs or AI, the business/advertiser must show a message telling consumers so.

Example wordings (Thai, verbatim): 'ภาพจริงหรือภาพจำลองจากของจริง โดยใช้ปัญญาประดิษฐ์ (AI) ปรับแต่งภาพ'; 'ภาพถ่ายจากสถานที่จริง หรือภาพจำลองจากของจริงโดยใช้ปัญญาประดิษฐ์ (AI) ปรับแต่ง'; 'ภาพถ่ายจากสินค้าจริงหรือภาพจำลอง จากของจริง โดยมีการปรับแต่ง'; 'ภาพสร้างโดย AI'; 'ภาพเคลื่อนไหวสร้างโดย AI' - shown so it can be clearly seen, heard or read for the type of medium.
Same article: influencer posts without a 'Sponsored' disclosure are native advertising that can mislead.
practical_applications: Any ad/promo post or clip whose image or video was made or edited with AI or editing software: put a clear Thai label such as 'ภาพสร้างโดย AI' / 'ภาพเคลื่อนไหวสร้างโดย AI' (an English line may be added) in the picture or caption, readable on a phone.
Never let AI change the real product's size, shape, colour, lens or what is included.
limitations: Public-relations article by OCPB staff (1 page, Nov 2025), not the Gazette text. Wording 'created or edited with programs' is broad - read literally it covers ordinary retouching too; the examples include 'ภาพถ่ายจากสินค้าจริง... โดยมีการปรับแต่ง' for edited real photos.

The Royal Gazette PDF (ratchakitcha.soc.go.th) was blocked by a Cloudflare check on 2026-11-25, so the exact clause number and start date of the AI wording were not read. OPT News (28 Jul 2025) instead reports a NEW OCPB notification 'แนวทางการโฆษณาสินค้าหรือบริการที่อาจก่อให้เกิดความเข้าใจผิดในสาระสำคัญเกี่ยวกับสินค้าหรือบริการ ตามพระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค พ.ศ. 2522' with the same three AI duties - the two descriptions of the instrument conflict.

sources.title: เลขาธิการคณะกรรมการคุ้มครองผู้บริโภคสั่งออกประกาศควบคุมการโฆษณา ภาพเสมือนจริงที่สร้างด้วย AI เพื่อคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค
sources.authors: สำนักงานคณะกรรมการคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค (สคบ.)
key_findings: OCPB news, 18 Jun 2025: NESDC data showed consumer complaints up almost 40% in a short period, mainly fake ads, especially AI-made images of goods, services or places that consumers could not tell from real.
Secretary-General Ronnarong Phoolpipat ordered Consumer Protection Division 1 to prepare a notification on advertising guidelines and to enforce strictly.
Using AI to create images or content that mislead consumers about material aspects of goods/services may be unfair advertising under section 22 of the Consumer Protection Act B.E. 2522.
Consumer tips: check the source, look for AI errors in backgrounds, faces, hands and text, read real reviews, avoid paying in advance; report via hotline 1166 / OCPB Connect.
practical_applications: Even before any label rule, misleading AI product images are already actionable as unfair advertising (s.22).
limitations: Announcement of intent (June 2025), not the notification itself.

sources.title: สคบ.เตือนโฆษณาที่ใช้คนดัง/ภาพAIอย่าหลงเชื่อ
sources.authors: อปท.นิวส์ (OPT News)
key_findings: 28 Jul 2025 report: OCPB Secretary-General ordered a notification 'แนวทางการโฆษณาสินค้าหรือบริการที่อาจก่อให้เกิดความเข้าใจผิดในสาระสำคัญเกี่ยวกับสินค้าหรือบริการ ตามพระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค พ.ศ. 2522', aimed at celebrity/influencer and AI-image ads.

Item 2 (AI or photo-editing images/clips): 2.1 get permission from the relevant agency before publishing; 2.2 size, quantity, number or composition must match reality; 2.3 state clearly if the image or clip was created or edited, e.g. 'ภาพจำลองโดยใช้ปัญญาประดิษฐ์ (AI)', 'ภาพเคลื่อนไหวสร้างโดย AI', 'ภาพถ่ายจริง หรือปรับแต่งด้วย AI', readable/audible/visible for the medium.
Item 1 (non-edible products imitating food): permission shown, Thai-language text (foreign text needs a Thai translation) and clear warnings such as 'สินค้านี้รับประทานไม่ได้'.
practical_applications: Cross-check for OCPB2025_AIAdGuidance; note item 2.1 is phrased more broadly here than in OCPB's own article ('where a specific law requires').
limitations: Local news paraphrase; Gazette text not read; publication/in-force date of the notification not given.

sources.title: Khrut Pha Emblem Act (No 2), 2535 BE (1992) - Wikisource translation of Royal Gazette vol. 109 issue 10, 14 Feb 1992
sources.authors: National Legislative Assembly of Thailand (trans. Wikisource)
key_findings: Amended s.4: 'khrut pha emblem' = any emblem portraying a garuda, in whatever pose, with or without other text, picture or symbol; 'warrant of appointment emblem' = the khrut pha with the text 'by royal charter' (or foreign-script equivalent) usable only after receiving a warrant.

Warrants: apply to the Bureau of the Royal Household; after royal charter the Prime Minister (as commander of the Bureau) issues the warrant and publishes it in the Royal Gazette; it is personal and can be recalled or revoked.

Penalties: breaching the royal decrees on reproduction/use - up to 6 months and/or 3,000 baht (s.12); reproducing or using the khrut pha emblem, a warrant or the warrant emblem without right so as to make another person believe one has the right - up to 1 year and/or 6,000 baht (s.13).
practical_applications: No garuda (any style, even 'decorative') in logos, merch, posts or AI scenes.
limitations: Unofficial translation of the 1992 amendment only; later amendments (if any) and the royal decrees not checked.

sources.title: How not to do cross cultural analysis: predictive failure and construction flaws in Geert Hofstede's case study (Royal Holloway School of Management Working Paper SoMWP-1004)
sources.authors: McSweeney, B.; Brown, D.; Iliopoulou, S.
key_findings: Tests Hofstede's 'validating' case study (masculine cultures such as the US, Britain and Ireland fight out industrial conflict; feminine cultures such as the Netherlands, Sweden and Denmark negotiate) against cross-sectional and longitudinal industrial-conflict and homicide data: no even weak association - neither explanatory nor predictive power; authors call it a 'projective fiction'.

Notes Hofstede's own figure that his four dimensions account for 49% of the variance in country mean scores of IBM survey answers - leaving 51% unexplained, and these are questionnaire answers, not behaviour.

Applying national averages to organisations or individuals is the ecological fallacy ('fallacy of the wrong level'); flaws also include non-equivalent country sets and asserted rather than demonstrated causality.
practical_applications: Never write 'Thais are X' from a Hofstede score; test with the real audience.
limitations: Working paper by a known Hofstede critic; one case study; refereed internally.

sources.title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
sources.authors: Andrew J. Reagan, Lewis Mitchell, Dilan Kiley, Christopher M. Danforth, Peter Sheridan Dodds
key_findings: EPJ Data Science 5. Sentiment trajectories of Project Gutenberg fiction cluster into six core arcs (rags-to-riches rise, tragedy fall, man-in-a-hole fall-rise, Icarus rise-fall, Cinderella rise-fall-rise, Oedipus fall-rise-fall) as building blocks.
Some arcs associated with higher download counts.
Robustness via matrix decomposition, supervised and unsupervised learning.
practical_applications: Pick an arc shape deliberately per piece; 'man in a hole' (fall then rise) fits problem→solution content.
limitations: Text sentiment (word valence) only, not audience feelings; corpus size reported inconsistently (1,327 vs 1,737); downloads ≠ quality; arc names here from general knowledge of the paper, abstract confirms six arcs only.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (EPJ Data Science, open access)

sources.title: All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect
sources.authors: Balca Alaybek, Reeshad Dalal, et al.
key_findings: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 170:104149. 174 effect sizes; peak-end effect on retrospective evaluations large (r = .581, 95% CI .487-.661), robust across tested boundary conditions.
Peak-end effect about as strong as the overall average of the experience, and stronger than trend and variability effects.
practical_applications: Design one clear peak and a deliberate ending; but do not ignore the average — the whole piece must be decent.
limitations: Search summary; peak-end not a replacement for average; day-long experiences may not follow it (secondary).

sources.title: Patterns of Affective Reactions to Advertisements: The Integration of Moment-to-Moment Responses into Overall Judgments
sources.authors: Hans Baumgartner, Mita Sujan, Dan Padgett
key_findings: Overall ad judgments driven mainly by the peak emotional moment and the final moment, plus how fast moment-to-moment reactions improved (trend).
Duration only weakly related to overall judgments; longer ads have an advantage if they build toward a peak.
Adaptation may explain preference for delayed peaks and high endings; longer ads can both raise and lower liking.
practical_applications: In ads/clips put the peak late-ish and end high; an upward trend helps; extra length only if it builds.
limitations: Abstract-level; 1990s TV ads; journal (Journal of Marketing Research) from general knowledge, not confirmed in snippet.

sources.title: Affective Forecasting: Knowing What to Want
sources.authors: Timothy D. Wilson, Daniel T. Gilbert
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 14(3):131-134. Impact bias: people overestimate intensity and duration of future emotional reactions.
Causes: focalism (attending to one aspect of the future), immune neglect, failure to anticipate how quickly they will make sense of events (speeding recovery).
practical_applications: Creators over-predict how strongly an audience will feel a moment: test with real viewers; brief negative beats fade faster than feared, so audiences recover — but do not rely on predicted 'wow'.
limitations: Abstract/excerpts; about life events, applied to media by analogy (DERIVED).

sources.title: Mood management through communication choices
key_findings: American Behavioral Scientist 31(3):327-341 (per secondary). People select media to regulate mood: bored people choose exciting content, stressed people calming content.
Content dimensions: excitatory potential, absorption potential, semantic affinity, hedonic valence (fourth dimension named in other secondary sources).
Challenged by the popularity of sad/tragic media (see OliverBartsch2010).
practical_applications: Match the opening energy of a post to the likely state of the viewer (late-night feed = calm), then move them.
limitations: Only secondary sources seen (Wikipedia and reference lists).

sources.title: Appreciation as Audience Response: Exploring Entertainment Gratifications Beyond Hedonism
key_findings: Human Communication Research 36(1):53-81. Three studies develop measures of gratifications beyond fun and suspense: moving and thought-provoking experiences (appreciation).
Appreciation is a response distinct from enjoyment and from emotional valence.
practical_applications: A piece can succeed by being moving/meaningful rather than pleasant; sad-but-meaningful Mint & Tao stories are a legitimate target.
limitations: Abstract-level; film genres.

sources.title: Toward a general psychological model of tension and suspense
key_findings: Domain-general model: tension arises from conflict, instability, dissonance or uncertainty that trigger predictions about emotionally significant future events.
Tension scales with how much the outcome matters, strongest when possible outcomes span very positive to very negative; lack of control adds tension.
Suspense = two clearly opposed outcomes; tension = more diffuse; surprise happens after an event, tension before.
Outcomes can become the next initiating event: chains of tension-resolution at multiple timescales; optimal delay is an open empirical question.
Examples: deceptive cadence delaying resolution, dramatic irony.
practical_applications: Build tension by an open, meaningful question + delayed answer; chain resolutions into new questions for series.
limitations: Hypothesis & theory article; ~70% of page text read; empirical data on delay scarce.

sources.title: Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation
key_findings: ITPRA theory: Imagination, Tension, Prediction, Reaction, Appraisal response systems to expected events; tension linked to uncertainty.
Chapters on creating predictability, surprise and tension.
practical_applications: Music and edit beats: establish predictability before surprise; tension rises before an expected event.
limitations: Publisher/library descriptions only.

sources.title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
sources.authors: Valorie Salimpoor, Mitchel Benovoy, Kevin Larcher, Alain Dagher, Robert Zatorre
key_findings: Nature Neuroscience 14(2):257-262. PET + fMRI: caudate more involved during anticipation, nucleus accumbens during peak emotional experience (chills).
Anticipation of an abstract reward releases dopamine along a pathway distinct from peak pleasure.
practical_applications: Anticipation is itself rewarding: a build-up before a peak (drop, reveal) is part of the pleasure, not dead time.
limitations: Small sample of selected listeners with chills; abstract-level.

sources.title: Emotional responses to music: The need to consider underlying mechanisms
key_findings: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 31:559-621. Six induction mechanisms: brain stem reflex, evaluative conditioning, emotional contagion, visual imagery, episodic memory, musical expectancy; later extended to eight (BRECVEMA, adds rhythmic entrainment and aesthetic judgment).
Commentaries dispute mechanism boundaries and cultural context.
practical_applications: Music cues act through several routes: a sudden loud hit (brain stem reflex) startles regardless of story; a known song triggers memory (nostalgia).
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries.

sources.title: Effects of Musical Tempo and Mode on Arousal, Mood, and Spatial Abilities
key_findings: Music Perception 20(2):151-171. Same Mozart piece in fast/slow and major/minor versions: tempo changed arousal but not mood; mode changed mood but not arousal.
practical_applications: Use tempo as the arousal knob and mode (major/minor) as the valence knob when choosing or briefing music.
limitations: One piece, Western listeners; abstract-level.

sources.title: The role of structure in the musical expression of emotions
key_findings: In Handbook of Music and Emotion (2010) pp. 367-400. Related later chapter by Gabrielsson: tempo, loudness, mode etc. can each signal several emotions; perceived emotion depends on many factors acting together additively or interactively.
practical_applications: No single music parameter = one emotion; brief music by combined profile (tempo + mode + loudness + articulation).
limitations: Bibliographic + abstract of related chapter only.

sources.title: Film Structure and the Emotion System
key_findings: Mood-cue approach: films set a longer-lasting mood that orients viewers; brief emotion cues must recur to sustain the mood; tonal shifts work if the audience is cued to expect them.
practical_applications: Set mood in the first seconds; keep a steady drip of small cues; foreshadow a tonal change before it happens.
limitations: Film-theory (cognitive) book; publisher excerpts and summaries only.

sources.title: Enhancement of experienced sexual arousal in response to erotic stimuli through misattribution of unrelated residual excitation (excitation-transfer test)
sources.authors: Joanne Cantor, Dolf Zillmann, Jennings Bryant
key_findings: Excitation transfer (per secondary): residual arousal from one event intensifies the next emotional reaction, mainly when people cannot attribute the arousal to its real source.
Later study: effect disappeared when people were self-aware of their arousal; an MSU dissertation on TV programs and commercials found no support (assimilation instead).
practical_applications: A high-arousal beat can amplify the beat that follows (e.g. relief/joy after suspense) — keep the gap short; evidence mixed.
limitations: Only Wikipedia/search summaries; title from search listing; mixed replication in media settings.

sources.title: Factors involved in generating suspense
key_findings: Human Communication Research 9:49-58 (per reference list). Snippet (attribution likely, unconfirmed): suspense increased with more positive dispositions toward the protagonist.
practical_applications: Make the audience like the character before putting them in peril; no liking → no suspense.
limitations: Bibliographic; finding attribution unconfirmed.

sources.title: The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 116(1):75-98. Information-gap theory: curiosity arises when attention focuses on a gap in one's knowledge, producing a feeling of deprivation.
practical_applications: Open a specific, answerable gap in the hook; close it in the body; a vague gap does not pull.
limitations: Secondary/abstract summaries only.

sources.title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
key_findings: Cognition & Emotion 17:297-314. Prototype of awe: perceived vastness + need for accommodation; can be unsettling (not always pleasant).
practical_applications: Awe needs scale (wide shot, small figure) AND something that does not fit existing understanding.
limitations: Theoretical paper; abstract-level. Also in M02 sources.

sources.title: Nostalgia: Past, Present, and Future
sources.authors: Constantine Sedikides, Tim Wildschut, Jamie Arndt, Clay Routledge
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 17(5):304-307. Nostalgia is not only about the past; related work: self-oriented, existential and social functions; ambivalent but more positive than negative; supports meaning via social connectedness; future-oriented (approach, optimism).
practical_applications: Nostalgia beats should end in connection or forward motion, not only loss.
limitations: Snippets of several papers by the same group; full texts not read.

sources.title: Universal Patterns in Color-Emotion Associations Are Further Shaped by Linguistic and Geographic Proximity
key_findings: Psychological Science 31(10):1245-1260. 4,598 participants, 30 nations, 22 languages, 20 emotion concepts × 12 colour terms.
Strong cross-national similarity (mean r = .88) plus nation-specific differences, larger similarity for linguistically/geographically close nations.
practical_applications: Colour-emotion associations are largely shared but locally tuned: check Thai associations; colour terms, not rendered colours, were tested.
limitations: Specific colour-emotion pairs not read; colour words not images; Thailand participation not confirmed.

sources.title: Attention and the evolution of Hollywood film
sources.authors: James E. Cutting, Jordan E. DeLong, Christine E. Nothelfer
key_findings: Psychological Science. 150 popular films 1935-2005: shot-length sequences increasingly approximate 1/f patterns; average shot length fell (press: ~8-10 s in 1960s to ~3-4 s by 2005); variation pattern independent of mean.
practical_applications: Vary shot lengths in a structured way (clusters of short shots, then longer holds) rather than uniform cuts.
limitations: Secondary coverage; ASL as a measure criticised.

sources.title: The evolution of pace in popular movies
key_findings: Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. 180 films 1930-2015: shot duration, motion and luminance across film structure; snippet: altered patterns affect pace, with increasing shot durations and decreasing motion in the setup.
practical_applications: Openings (setup) can be slower and calmer; pace increases toward climaxes (DERIVED from pattern).
limitations: Snippet only; feature films, not short social video.

sources.title: (Camera angle and product evaluation in advertising, 1992)
key_findings: As cited by Schuldt, Konrath & Schwarz 2012: products photographed from a low camera angle were evaluated more positively than from high or eye level.
Twente thesis (2009): moderation by need for cognition not reproduced; camera-angle effect significant for faces but only one of six objects.
practical_applications: Low angle = more power/positivity is a weak, fragile effect; treat as CRAFT-plus, not law.
limitations: Original paper not seen; title/journal unconfirmed; partial replication failure.

sources.title: Emotional Contagion
sources.authors: Elaine Hatfield, John T. Cacioppo, Richard L. Rapson
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 2(3). Automatic mimicry of expressions, voices, postures → feedback → emotions converge (per secondary summaries). Covered in depth in M02.
practical_applications: The on-screen character's/narrator's emotion is the lowest-level route to the viewer's.
limitations: Bibliographic; see M02 (Hatfield1993, ManySmiles2022) for evidence strength.

sources.title: How does an editor control the rhythm of a film
key_findings: Practitioner guide on edit rhythm (pace via shot length, cutting on action/beat, holding shots for emotion).
practical_applications: Craft reference for edit-rhythm cells in the matrix.
limitations: Tier D, only search listing seen.

sources.title: Emotional Expressions Reconsidered: Challenges to Inferring Emotion From Human Facial Movements
sources.authors: Barrett, L. F.; Adolphs, R.; Marsella, S.; Martinez, A. M.; Pollak, S. D.
key_findings: Tests the 'common view' that anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise can be read from facial configurations; evidence does not support using them as diagnostic of emotion.
Four criteria: reliability, specificity, generalizability, validity.
People do scowl/smile/frown more than chance in the matching emotion, but the link is weak: meta-analysis cited (Duran et al. 2017) average r = .32, average proportion .19 (category range .15-.25).
Posed expressions match the prototypes better than spontaneous ones; e.g. only 8 of 55 winning judo fighters produced a Duchenne smile (Study 1), all during social interaction.
Context (situation, culture, internal state) is largely unmeasured and is a likely reason for weak reliability; automated detectors drop below ~83% accuracy outside the lab.
practical_applications: Rule for the studio: never state or caption a character's inner emotion from face or voice alone; give context (situation, words, action).
Faceless Mint & Tao fit this science: emotion is carried by situation, posture and dialogue, not a stereotyped face.
limitations: Only the first ~100k of ~560k characters of the PMC page were read; the closing recommendations section was not read in full.
Critics from basic-emotion tradition dispute how strongly to read the results (not reviewed here).

sources.title: The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization
key_findings: Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 12(1). Presents the theory of constructed emotion (formerly the conceptual act theory) as a brain-based computational account.
The brain uses prediction (predictive coding) and interoception, and categorizes sensations with learned emotion concepts to construct instances of emotion.
Emotion categories show degeneracy: dissimilar brain representations can produce instances of the same category, so no one-to-one emotion-circuit mapping is expected.
practical_applications: Supports showing emotion through situation + concept (words, culture) rather than fixed facial templates.
Explains why Thai emotion words (jai-compounds) may shape what viewers feel and name.
limitations: PMC full text blocked by a browser check this session; content known only from search summaries and Wikipedia.
Published online Oct 2016 in SCAN 12(1); page range differs between sources (Ovid lists 1-23).
