sources.title: Appraisal Theories of Emotion: State of the Art and Future Development
sources.authors: Moors, A.; Ellsworth, P. C.; Scherer, K. R.; Frijda, N. H.
key_findings: Appraisal theories define emotions as processes (episodes), not states; componential: appraisal, motivational (action tendencies), somatic, motor (expression) and feeling components.
The process is continuous and recursive; changes in one component feed back to others; several episodes may run in parallel.
Appraisal detects significance for well-being = satisfaction/obstruction of concerns (needs, attachments, values, goals, beliefs).

Core appraisal variables: goal relevance, goal congruence, certainty, agency (self/other/circumstance), coping potential/control; some add novelty, urgency, intentionality, fairness, norm compatibility.
practical_applications: Write story beats as appraisal changes: same event, different appraisal -> different emotion (e.g. Tao blames himself = guilt; blames the shop = anger).
Use the appraisal variables as a checklist when designing a turning point in a carousel.
limitations: Introduction to a special section; summarises rather than tests theories.
Appraisal lists are not claimed to be exhaustive or universal.

sources.title: The dynamic architecture of emotion: Evidence for the component process model
key_findings: Emotion as an emergent dynamic process based on subjective appraisal of significant events; emphasis on the sequence of appraisal checks (stimulus evaluation checks) and synchronisation of response systems.
practical_applications: Sequence for a reaction shot: novelty -> pleasantness -> goal relevance -> coping -> norms; animate the change in that order.
limitations: Only abstract and secondary descriptions seen.

sources.title: Cognition and Motivation in Emotion
key_findings: American Psychologist 46(4), 352-367.
Primary appraisal (is this relevant to my well-being: harm/benefit) and secondary appraisal (coping options).
Core relational themes summarise the emotion-producing person-environment relation, e.g. anger: unfairly slighted; anxiety: anticipated harm with doubt about coping; shame: personal failure.
practical_applications: One-line 'core relational theme' per scene makes the intended emotion explicit for writers and voice directors.
limitations: Read via an HTML copy hosted on a university site; themes for envy, pride, hope etc. are in the 1991 book, not this article.

sources.title: Appraisal in the Emotion System: Coherence in Strategies for Coping
key_findings: Emotion Review 5(2), 141-149. Emotions form an organised system of coping strategies guided by appraisals, for threats and opportunities.
practical_applications: Frame each emotion by what it makes the character DO (coping strategy), useful for action beats.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: An argument for basic emotions
key_findings: Emotions evolved for adaptive value; characteristics include rapid onset, short duration, unbidden occurrence, automatic appraisal and coherence among responses.
Emotion 'families' share expression, physiology, antecedents and perhaps appraisal.
practical_applications: Basic-emotion families are still a useful coarse index for libraries (joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise).
limitations: The PDF link returned 404 this session; content from abstract and secondary summaries.
Strong universality claims contested (Barrett2019, Jack2012).

sources.title: Core affect and the psychological construction of emotion
key_findings: Core affect = neurophysiological state consciously accessible as the simplest raw feeling; a single blend of pleasure-displeasure and activation (a point on the circumplex).

Core affect can be free-floating (mood) or attributed to an Object, beginning an emotional episode; prototypical episodes such as fear/anger = core affect attributed to something plus non-emotional processes.
Defines affective quality (a stimulus' power to change core affect), attributed affect, affect regulation, emotional meta-experience.
practical_applications: Images/clips set core affect (pleasant/calm etc.) through 'affective quality'; the caption/dialogue supplies the Object that turns it into a named emotion.
Explains 'mood' entries (visual.coziness) as affective quality, not character emotion.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted PDF copy (keyword excerpts).

sources.title: Pleasure-arousal-dominance: A general framework for describing and measuring individual differences in temperament
key_findings: Current Psychology 14, 261-292. Three nearly orthogonal dimensions (pleasure, arousal, dominance) describe emotional states; temperament = average emotional state across situations.
practical_applications: Dominance axis separates anger (high D) from fear (low D) at the same valence/arousal - useful for posture and camera height.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

sources.title: Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients
key_findings: PNAS 114(38), E7900-E7909. Reported emotional states elicited by 2,185 short videos.
Videos reliably elicited 27 distinct varieties of reported emotional experience; category labels (e.g. amusement) captured reports better than valence/arousal dimensions.

Boundaries between categories are fuzzy, linked by gradients (anxiety-fear-horror-disgust; calmness-aesthetic appreciation-awe) that track smooth variation in dimensions such as valence and dominance.
practical_applications: Reference list for gap analysis of the studio's emotion libraries.
Gradients suggest designing transitions along neighbouring states, not jumps.
limitations: Abstract-level; US English-speaking sample; Barrett et al. published a constructionist reply.

sources.title: The brain basis of emotion: A meta-analytic review
sources.authors: Lindquist, K. A.; Wager, T. D.; Kober, H.; Bliss-Moreau, E.; Barrett, L. F.
key_findings: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 35(3), 121-143. Meta-analytic summary of human neuroimaging studies of emotion experience and perception.
Little evidence that discrete emotion categories are consistently and specifically localized to distinct brain regions (locationist hypothesis).
Evidence fits psychological construction: a set of interacting, domain-general networks is active across emotion categories and in non-emotional operations.
practical_applications: Science basis for treating emotion labels as useful categories, not brain modules.
limitations: Findings not read this session; only the framing from search results.

sources.title: Emotion (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Three traditions: feeling, evaluative (incl. appraisal), motivational.
Basic emotion theory vs psychological constructionism; appraisal theories answer the differentiation problem via appraisal patterns but do not by themselves say what emotions are.
practical_applications: Orientation map for writers choosing which theory to lean on for a given task.
limitations: Read first ~100k characters plus footer; first published 25 Sep 2018, revision date not seen.

sources.title: Putting the Self Into Self-Conscious Emotions: A Theoretical Model
sources.authors: Tracy, J. L.; Robins, R. W.
key_findings: Psychological Inquiry 15(2), 103-125. Self-conscious emotions require self-awareness and self-representations, emerge later, are cognitively complex and show weaker evidence of universal expressions.
Model: attention to self -> identity-goal relevance -> internal attribution; shame = internal stable/global ('I'm a dumb person'), guilt = internal unstable/specific ('I didn't try hard enough').
Embarrassment: public self, identity-goal incongruence, internal attribution; argued less cognitively elaborated, emerges earlier in childhood.
Two prides: achievement-oriented (unstable/specific) vs hubristic (stable/global). Humiliation proposed as public focus + stable/global blame (flagged as under-researched).
practical_applications: Write shame vs guilt lines by the attribution: 'I'm hopeless' (shame) vs 'I forgot your glasses' (guilt).
Pride beats: credit the effort ('I practised') not the self ('I'm the best') to keep a character likeable.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted copy (keyword excerpts).
Theoretical model; predictions tested later by others.

sources.title: Moral emotions and moral behavior
sources.authors: Tangney, J. P.; Stuewig, J.; Mashek, D. J.
key_findings: Annual Review of Psychology 58, 345-372. Reviews shame, guilt, embarrassment and positive moral emotions (elevation, gratitude, pride), plus other-oriented empathy.
Self-conscious emotions function as an 'emotional moral barometer' and can be anticipated before acting as well as felt afterwards.
On balance guilt (about a behaviour) appears more adaptive than shame (about the self); guilt-proneness consistently correlates with perspective-taking and empathic concern.
practical_applications: Guilt (repair) is the prosocial self-conscious emotion; brand stories should invite repair, never shame the viewer.
limitations: Only abstract-level summaries read (PMC blocked).

sources.title: Signs of Appeasement: Evidence for the Distinct Displays of Embarrassment, Amusement, and Shame
key_findings: JPSP 68(3), 441-454. Five studies: embarrassment has a distinct nonverbal display that differs from amusement and is identified by observers.
Embarrassment markers: gaze down, gaze shifts, smile controls, head turn, face touches; nearly all embarrassed targets looked down (94% vs 72% of amused).
Appeasement hypothesis: display more readily perceived from lower-status individuals.
practical_applications: Animate embarrassment as a 2-3 s sequence (look down -> suppressed smile -> head turn -> touch face) for faceless puppets via body and head.
limitations: Lab sample, US students; display is a tendency not a diagnostic (see Barrett2019).
Read via text extraction (keyword excerpts).

sources.title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
key_findings: Cognition and Emotion 17, 297-314. Prototype approach: perceived vastness + need for accommodation; peripheral flavours.
Proposed evolutionary origin in low-rank members' response to powerful leaders.
practical_applications: Awe images need scale (small figure, vast scene) and something that does not fit expectations.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; theoretical paper.

sources.title: The Science of Awe (white paper for the John Templeton Foundation)
sources.authors: Allen, S. (Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley)
key_findings: Summarises Keltner & Haidt: vastness + accommodation; five flavours: threat, beauty, ability, virtue, supernatural causality.
Awe often accompanied by 'small self', connectedness; cultural differences in elicitors (personal accomplishment more in US, awe of another person more in China).
practical_applications: Threat-flavoured awe (storm, huge wave) vs beauty awe (sunset at Hua Hin) need different palettes and music.
limitations: Funded white paper, narrative review; read via text extraction (excerpts).

sources.title: Awe, the small self, and prosocial behavior
sources.authors: Piff, P. K.; Dietze, P.; Feinberg, M.; Stancato, D. M.; Keltner, D.
key_findings: JPSP 108(6). Five studies; dispositional and induced awe linked to more prosocial behaviour, mediated by a sense of small self (per press release).
practical_applications: Awe scenes can precede a kindness beat in a story.
limitations: Press-release level; a student replication reported failure to replicate the small-self finding (unpublished).

sources.title: The relationship between awe and prosocial behavior: Three-level meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling
sources.authors: Lin, R.; Yu, Q.; Hu, T.; Zhang, J.; Ye, Y.; Lian, R.
key_findings: Acta Psychologica Sinica 57(4), 631-651. Subgroup estimates seen in snippets: self-report prosocial measures r ~ .41, lab behavioural measures r ~ .24.
practical_applications: Expect awe->kindness effects to be modest in real behaviour.
limitations: Pooled estimate not seen; snippet-level only.

sources.title: Find, Remind, and Bind: The Functions of Gratitude in Everyday Relationships
key_findings: Social and Personality Psychology Compass 6(6), 455-469. Gratitude helps find new relationship partners, reminds of existing ones and binds (maintains) them.
practical_applications: Thank-you posts to customers work as relationship 'bind' moments, not just politeness.
limitations: Secondary summaries only.

sources.title: Leveling up and down: The experiences of benign and malicious envy
sources.authors: van de Ven, N.; Zeelenberg, M.; Pieters, R.
key_findings: Emotion 9(3), 419-429. Benign envy -> moving-up motivation (self-improvement); malicious envy -> pulling-down motivation; found in Dutch (two words) and US/Spanish (one word) samples.
practical_applications: Marketing should evoke benign envy (I could have that too) and never malicious envy or mockery of others.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Emotional Contagion
sources.authors: Hatfield, E.; Cacioppo, J. T.; Rapson, R. L.
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 2(3). Primitive emotional contagion: automatic mimicry of face, voice, posture, then feedback from the mimicry shapes one's own feeling, producing convergence (as summarised by secondary sources).
practical_applications: A calm, warm narrator voice and relaxed body language in clips are the low-level route to a calm viewer.
limitations: Full text behind login; mechanism details from secondary summaries.

sources.title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration
key_findings: Nature Human Behaviour 6, 1731-1742. Preregistered adversarial multi-lab study, n = 3,878 participants in 19 countries.
Facial mimicry and voluntary facial action tasks could both amplify and initiate feelings of happiness.
Evidence was less conclusive when facial feedback was manipulated unobtrusively via the pen-in-mouth task.
practical_applications: Feedback (part of contagion) is real but small: do not promise 'smile and you will feel happy' in health content.
limitations: Effect sizes not read this session.
Only the abstract on the publisher page was read (full text paywalled at session time).

sources.title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
sources.authors: Kramer, A. D. I.; Guillory, J. E.; Hancock, J. T.
key_findings: PNAS 111(24), 8788-8790. News Feed experiment with N = 689,003 Facebook users.
Reducing positive posts: positive words in users' updates fell by 0.1% (d = 0.02) and negative words rose 0.04% (d = 0.001); reducing negative posts had the opposite pattern (d = 0.02 and 0.008).
Authors note effects are small (as small as d = 0.001) but argue they matter at scale; a withdrawal effect also appeared (fewer emotional posts seen -> less expressive).
practical_applications: Feed tone spreads in text form even without faces; keep the shop's feed warm, not anxious.
limitations: Effect sizes very small (not verified here); Editorial Expression of Concern over consent - ethically contested.
Effect sizes are tiny; consent/ethics of the experiment were widely criticised (secondary).
PNAS published an Editorial Expression of Concern (111(29):10779) about consent.
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

sources.title: The emerging field of emotion regulation: An integrative review
key_findings: Review of General Psychology 2(3), 271-299. Defines emotion regulation as how people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them; distinguishes it from coping, mood regulation, defence and affect regulation.

Process model: antecedent-focused strategies (situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change/reappraisal) vs response-focused strategies (response modulation, e.g. suppression).
Reviews early evidence that reappraisal and suppression have different consequences, with reappraisal acting earlier in the emotion process.
practical_applications: Five regulation points = five places a story character can change an emotion: choose the situation, change it, shift attention, rethink it, hide it.
limitations: Abstract-level; full text not read.

sources.title: Emotion regulation: Affective, cognitive, and social consequences
key_findings: Psychophysiology 39(3), 281-291. Reappraisal (early) decreases experience and expression with no memory cost; suppression (late) decreases expression but not experience, impairs memory and increases physiological responding for suppressors and their partners.
Suppressing negative expression does not reduce negative experience, but suppressing positive expression does reduce amusement.
practical_applications: 'Holding back tears' = suppression: the feeling stays, the body leaks (breath, jaw, hands).
Reappraisal lines ('maybe it's a chance to...') are the healthy turn in Mint & Tao stories.
limitations: Read via text extraction of a course-hosted PDF (abstract + excerpts); mostly US student samples.

sources.title: Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes: Implications for affect, relationships, and well-being
sources.authors: Gross, J. J.; John, O. P.
key_findings: JPSP 85(2), 348-362. Five studies; introduces the ERQ. Habitual reappraisal relates to better well-being and interpersonal functioning; habitual suppression to worse.
practical_applications: Characters who habitually suppress can be shown as more distant in relationships - a gentle arc toward sharing feelings.
limitations: Correlational; abstract only.

sources.title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
key_findings: Psychological Inquiry 26(1), 1-26. Extended process model: regulation as valuation with stages identification, selection, implementation.
practical_applications: Story arcs of regulation: notice the feeling -> pick a strategy -> carry it out.
limitations: Search summaries only; commentary notes co-regulation is underplayed.

sources.title: Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation
sources.authors: Webb, T. L.; Miles, E.; Sheeran, P.
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 138(4), 775-808. 306 comparisons: attentional deployment overall d+ = 0.00 (distraction 0.27, concentration -0.26); response modulation small (0.16; suppressing expression 0.32, suppressing experience/thoughts not effective); cognitive change small-medium (reappraising stimulus 0.36, perspective taking 0.45, reappraising response 0.23).
practical_applications: Perspective-taking is the strongest listed strategy - ideal for Mint helping Tao see it from another side.
limitations: Figures from abstract/secondary snippets; lab manipulations.

sources.title: Emotion regulation and culture: Are the social consequences of emotion suppression culture-specific?
sources.authors: Butler, E. A.; Lee, T. L.; Gross, J. J.
key_findings: Emotion 7(1), 30-48. Suppression's negative social effects (less responsiveness, hostile partner perceptions) were smaller for participants with stronger Asian values.
practical_applications: Thai polite restraint should not automatically be written as cold or fake; in-culture it can read as considerate.
limitations: Female US college students (European vs bicultural Asian values); not Thai samples.

sources.title: Unpacking Emotion Differentiation: Transforming Unpleasant Experience by Perceiving Distinctions in Negativity
sources.authors: Kashdan, T. B.; Barrett, L. F.; McKnight, P. E.
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 24, 10-16. Emotion differentiation (granularity) - distinguishing fine-grained negative states - supports regulation and is a component of interventions.
practical_applications: Precise emotion words in Thai captions (e.g. 'น้อยใจ' vs 'เสียใจ') are more useful to viewers than 'sad'.
limitations: Abstract-level; measurement validity debated.

sources.title: Eliciting mixed emotions: a meta-analysis comparing models, types, and measures
sources.authors: Berrios, R.; Totterdell, P.; Kellett, S.
key_findings: 63 experimental studies (N = 7,157): mixed emotions reliably elicited, d = 0.77 (PET-PEESE corrected ~0.53); similar across discrete vs dimensional models and across mixed-emotion types.
Happy-sad is the most studied pair; methods include films, music, ads, autobiographical recall.
Supports the Evaluative Space Model (positive and negative affect as separable) over strictly bipolar circumplex.
practical_applications: Bittersweet endings (farewell, last day of a season) are a scientifically real target, not a contradiction.
limitations: Experimental studies only; self-report and memory biases; first ~100k characters read.

sources.title: Which emotions last longest and why: The role of event importance and rumination
key_findings: Motivation and Emotion 39, 119-127. 233 Belgian high-school students recalled recent episodes of 27 emotions and reported duration, appraisals and regulation.
Sadness lasted longest (median ~120 h in the paper's figure); shame, surprise, fear, disgust, boredom, being touched, irritation and relief were shortest.
Fear was shorter than anxiety (t(1647) = 4.12, p < .0001) and guilt longer than shame (t(1647) = 2.71, p = .0067).
Event importance and rumination together accounted for 43% of the between-emotion variance in duration.
practical_applications: Sadness/guilt beats can linger across slides; fear/surprise resolve fast.
limitations: Retrospective self-report; Belgian adolescents; specific hour figures from press coverage only.
Retrospective self-reports from one adolescent sample; the press figure of ~35 h for joy was not confirmed from the text.

sources.title: Emotion dynamics
key_findings: Current Opinion in Psychology 17, 22-26. Study of trajectories, patterns and regularities of emotional change over time; inertia (resistance to change) cited from this line of work.
practical_applications: Character design: high-inertia character (slow to change mood) vs high-variability character.
limitations: Bibliographic record + citing papers only.

sources.title: Duration neglect in retrospective evaluations of affective episodes
key_findings: JPSP 65(1), 45-55. Study 1: 32 participants rated pleasant and aversive film clips of varied length in real time and globally; Study 2: 96 participants ranked the clips from memory or online.
Effects of duration on retrospective evaluations were small, fully explained by changes in real-time affect, and smaller when made from memory (duration neglect).

Retrospective evaluations behave like a weighted average of 'snapshots'; the paper cites a reanalysis of Varey & Kahneman (1992) where peak + end discomfort explained 94% of variance and duration added only 3%.
practical_applications: Design every clip and carousel with a deliberate peak and a warm last slide; length matters less than the ending.
limitations: Lab film clips; peak-end does not hold well for day-long experiences (Miron-Shatz).
The 94% figure comes from the cited reanalysis of judgments about another person's schematic discomfort reports, not from these film studies.

sources.title: Cognitive neuroscience of emotional memory
key_findings: Nature Reviews Neuroscience 7(1), 54-64. The amygdala mediates emotional learning and boosts memory operations in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex across encoding, consolidation and retrieval.
practical_applications: Emotional (arousing) moments in a story are remembered better - put the product/brand inside the emotional beat, not after it.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories
sources.authors: Talarico, J. M.; Rubin, D. C.
key_findings: Psychological Science 14(5), 455-461. 54 students after 9/11: consistency of flashbulb and everyday memories declined equally; only vividness/confidence stayed high for flashbulb memories.
practical_applications: Emotional memories feel vivid but are not more accurate: characters can be confidently wrong about the past - a good story device.
limitations: Small sample; up to 32 weeks.

sources.title: Facial expressions of emotion are not culturally universal
sources.authors: Jack, R. E.; Garrod, O. G. B.; Yu, H.; Caldara, R.; Schyns, P. G.
key_findings: PNAS 109(19), 7241-7244. Reverse-correlation with a generative face grammar: 15 Western Caucasian and 15 East Asian observers each categorized 4,800 animations.
Western mental models formed six distinct clusters for the six 'basic' emotions; East Asian models did not form distinct clusters.
East Asian observers represented emotional intensity with distinctive dynamic eye activity; authors argue this refutes the universality hypothesis.
practical_applications: Do not rely on Western-coded facial clichés for Thai audiences; context matters more.
limitations: Debated (Sauter & Eisner comment and reply); summaries only.
Small observer sample (30); later critiques (e.g. Sauter & Eisner, secondary) dispute the strength of the conclusion.

sources.title: The fear gasping face as a threat display in a Melanesian society
sources.authors: Crivelli, C.; Russell, J. A.; Jarillo, S.; Fernández-Dols, J.-M.
key_findings: PNAS 113(44). Two studies with adolescents of the Trobriand Islands (Papua New Guinea), with researchers speaking the vernacular.
Study 1: mixed, variable attribution with much lower agreement than in Western samples; the gasping 'fear' face was consistently matched to anger and threat.
Study 2: asked to pick the threatening face, Trobrianders chose the gasping 'fear' face, Spaniards the scowling 'angry' face.
practical_applications: Face-to-emotion mappings are culture-dependent.
limitations: Small-scale society; definitional critique of 'gasping face'.

sources.title: On the universality and cultural specificity of emotion recognition: a meta-analysis
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 128(2), 203-235. Emotions recognised above chance across cultures, with an in-group advantage (better accuracy for same-culture expressors).
practical_applications: Thai actors/voices are read more accurately by Thai viewers - favour Thai talent and Thai TTS.
limitations: Matsumoto (2002) disputes the in-group advantage on design grounds.

sources.title: Cultural variations in emotions: A review
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 112(2), 179-204. Cultural differences and similarities appear in every phase of the emotion process; which appears depends on level of description; differences arise from event schemas, appraisal propensities, behaviour repertoires, regulation.
practical_applications: Localise emotion at each phase: what triggers it in Thai life, how it is appraised, how it is shown, how it is regulated.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Emotion semantics show both cultural variation and universal structure
sources.authors: Jackson, J. C.; Watts, J.; Henry, T. R.; List, J.-M.; et al.
key_findings: Science 366(6472), 1517-1522. Colexification analysis of emotion concepts across 2,474 spoken languages.
Emotion colexification networks vary significantly across language families, and the variation is predicted by the geographic proximity of the families.
Universal structure too: all families differentiate emotions primarily by hedonic valence and secondarily by physiological activation.
practical_applications: Translate emotions by meaning, not word-for-word; valence/arousal is the safe common ground.
limitations: Abstract/press-level.

sources.title: Cultural variation in affect valuation
sources.authors: Tsai, J. L.; Knutson, B.; Fung, H. H.
key_findings: JPSP. Ideal affect (how people want to feel) is shaped by culture more than actual affect; European Americans value high-arousal positive states more, Hong Kong Chinese value low-arousal positive (calm) more; a 2025 meta-analysis reports these differences persist.
practical_applications: Thai/Asian audiences may respond to calm-positive (LAP) imagery; test rather than assume.
limitations: No Thai samples; secondary summaries.

sources.title: A comparative study of smiling facial expressions and display rules of the Thai and the Japanese
key_findings: Asian Review 29(1), 101-121. Interviews: when not happy, Thais smiled more when greeting or apologising; Japanese smiled more to fit in with a group; Thais raised cheeks (AU6) more when smiling with sadness.
practical_applications: A Thai smile in a story is a social act (greeting, apology, kreng jai), not proof of joy.
limitations: Abstract only; sample size not seen.

sources.title: A discourse analysis of the Thai experience of 'being krengjai'
key_findings: Intercultural Pragmatics. Historical research + questionnaire of 471 Thai people mapping the many meanings of krengjai (consideration, deference, reluctance to impose).
practical_applications: Kreng jai lines need a relational context (status gap, debt, closeness).
limitations: Publisher page returned an error; known from search summary only.

sources.title: Psychology of the Thai People: Values and Behavioral Patterns
key_findings: Bangkok: NIDA. Nine Thai value clusters from a survey of 2,469 Thais (1978-81), including interdependence and fun-pleasure (sanuk) orientations (per secondary sources).
practical_applications: Sanuk and interdependence as content tones for the shop.
limitations: Not read; year given as 1990 or 1991 in different records.

sources.title: Basic Emotion Words Derived from Physiological Effects in Thai
sources.authors: ต๊ะวิชัย ศ. (as listed on the journal page)
key_findings: Journal of the Faculty of Arts, Silpakorn University 37(2), 182-221. 195 Thai basic emotion words from the Royal Institute Dictionary 2011 + survey of 200 speakers; prototypes include ชื่นใจ (happiness), ต้องใจ (affection), น้ำตาตกใน (sorrow), เสียวสันหลัง (fear), เลือดพล่าน (anger); seven lexicalisation processes; meaning extended via metonymy/metaphor.
practical_applications: Use bodily Thai idioms in captions and VO for vivid, culturally native emotion naming.
limitations: Abstract only; issue labelled 2015 but published online 2020.

sources.title: A Review of Studies in Heart or Jai Metaphor in Thai Language
key_findings: Manutsat Paritat: Journal of Humanities 45(2), 68-85. Jai (heart) metaphors fall into four groups: heart as person, object, space, container; central to everyday Thai emotion talk.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors for Thai emotion (a 'cool' or 'wide' heart) can be drawn from these mappings.
limitations: Abstract only; DOI shown on page looked malformed, omitted.

sources.title: Assessing Equanimity in a Thai Buddhist Context: Psychometric Validation of the Thai Equanimity Scale-16
key_findings: Journal of Socio-Buddhist Analytics 11(1), 162-175 (Jan-Mar 2026). Thai Equanimity Scale-16 validated with 437 Thai mindfulness-oriented adults; 211 from monastic-university networks retested after one week.
Two-factor model (Experiential Acceptance, Non-Reactivity) fit well: CFI = 0.994, TLI = 0.990, RMSEA = 0.020; internal consistency .84; one-week test-retest r = .89.

Higher equanimity associated with greater benevolence and fewer aversive tendencies (SOFI); authors argue Western scales reduce upekkha to emotion regulation/reduced reactivity, missing its insight- and compassion-based meaning.
practical_applications: 'Jai yen'/equanimity is valued in Thai culture and is more than suppression.
limitations: Search snippet only; authors not captured.
Sample is mindfulness-oriented Thai adults, not the general public.

sources.title: Thai Culture: Core Concepts (The Cultural Atlas)
key_findings: Describes face, hierarchy, harmony (calm demeanour, avoiding outbursts), sanuk (finding enjoyment in what one does) linked to 'mai pen rai'.
practical_applications: Background for tone; not evidence about emotion processes.
limitations: Cultural guide, no in-text citations; generalises a diverse country.

sources.title: Better, Bolder B2B Branding: Category Entry Points in a B2B world
sources.authors: Romaniuk, J. (LinkedIn B2B Institute / Ehrenberg-Bass Institute)
key_findings: Category entry points (CEPs) are the cues category buyers use to access memories in a buying situation.
Mental availability = being easily thought of in buying situations; more CEPs linked to a brand raise the chance it is selected (citing Romaniuk & Sharp 2000; Romaniuk 2001).
Distinctive brand assets act as memory shortcuts; assessed by fame and uniqueness (Distinctive Asset Grid).
practical_applications: List the shop's CEPs (beach glare, presbyopia onset, lost glasses on holiday) and tie each piece of content to one.
limitations: Industry paper for B2B; peer-reviewed originals not read; read via search summary.

sources.title: Dimensions of brand personality
key_findings: As described by secondary sources: adapts the human five-factor model into a five-dimension brand personality framework; the most cited and applied brand personality scale.
practical_applications: Use the dimensions as shared team vocabulary for tone (e.g., sincerity + sophistication).
limitations: Not read this session; existence and content known only via critiques (Journal of Marketing Research).

sources.title: Do brand personality scales really measure brand personality?
key_findings: Existing brand personality scales merge several dimensions of brand identity, personality being only one of them.
Aaker's trait selection is criticised as an all-encompassing potpourri drifting from the meaning of personality.
Other critiques question use for individual brands or within a category; a 2018 review notes the scale remains most cited.
practical_applications: Do not treat brand personality scores as precise measurement; consistency of tone matters more.
limitations: Read via abstract and secondary summaries (Journal of Brand Management 11(2):143-155).

sources.title: The Hero and the Outlaw: Building Extraordinary Brands Through the Power of Archetypes
key_findings: Proposes 12 brand archetypes drawn from Jungian ideas; defenders say Mark used Young & Rubicam BrandAsset Valuator data (per Researchscape).
practical_applications: Use archetypes only as a character-writing aid for Mint & Tao, never as science.
limitations: Practitioner book; not read; no independent replication found.

sources.title: Brand Archetypes (doctoral dissertation, University of Washington)
key_findings: Empirically examines Mark & Pearson's model and proposes a refined classification of the 12 archetypes into four clusters based on consumer perceptions.
Separately, a Croatian online-survey study (English abstract) found the 12 archetypes do not form unidimensional constructs.
practical_applications: Treat the 12-archetype system as unvalidated.
limitations: Read via search summary; year not confirmed; Croatian study authors not recorded.

sources.title: How advertising works: what do we really know?
key_findings: Reviews 250+ articles and books; builds a taxonomy from no-intermediate-effects to hierarchy and non-hierarchy models.

Supports a space of intermediate effects (cognition, affect, experience) but finds little support for a fixed temporal hierarchy; AIDA-type hierarchy cannot be empirically supported (as quoted by citing work).
practical_applications: Use AIDA as a completeness checklist, not a model of how customers move.
limitations: Journal of Marketing article not read; URL is the related 1996 MSI working paper; findings via secondary summaries.

sources.title: How advertising shapes what we think and buy (HEC Paris Knowledge@HEC summary of Valenti, Yildirim, Vanhuele, Srinivasan & Pauwels)
sources.authors: Vanhuele, M. (summary author); study by Valenti, A.; Yildirim, G.; Vanhuele, M.; Srinivasan, S.; Pauwels, K.
key_findings: Kantar Worldpanel data: 178 FMCG brands, 18 categories, 7 years of monthly advertising, mindset and sales metrics.

Most brands show a clear dominant sequence of advertising effects; the most common is affect -> cognition -> experience (about half of brands), more prevalent for utilitarian and non-differentiated brands.
Awareness responds most to advertising; experience metrics correlate most strongly with sales; advertising has long-term effects.
practical_applications: Entertainment/affect content (Mint & Tao) can come before product information; in-store experience content matters for sales.
limitations: Business-school summary; journal and year of the underlying paper not identified; FMCG not eyewear.

sources.title: (Article on the origin of the AIDA model) Japan Marketing History Review 3(2)
key_findings: The dominant hypothesis that E. St. Elmo Lewis invented and formulated AIDA is unsupported or based on weak evidence; stronger claims for Arthur Frederick Sheldon and Frank H. Dukesmith.
Attribution to Lewis became common after Strong's 1925 book, which dated Lewis's slogan to 1898 without naming a source.
practical_applications: Avoid repeating 'Lewis invented AIDA in 1898' as fact.
limitations: Exact title not captured; read via search summary of the J-STAGE abstract.

sources.title: The consumer decision journey
sources.authors: Court, D.; Elzinga, D.; Mulder, S.; Vetvik, O. J. (McKinsey Quarterly)
key_findings: Replaces the narrowing funnel with a circular journey: initial consideration, active evaluation, moment of purchase, post-purchase experience, and a loyalty loop.
A 2015 McKinsey follow-up says the journey needs updating; firms that compress or eliminate consideration/evaluation gain advantage.
practical_applications: Map the eyewear journey including post-purchase fitting and loyalty loop content.
limitations: Consulting publication; full text not read; no public quantitative validation.

sources.title: Best practices for A/B tests in Meta Ads Manager
key_findings: Test only one variable; set a specific measurable hypothesis.
Audience large enough and not used by other concurrent campaigns (overlap contaminates results).
Run at least 7 days (up to 30); shorter tests may be inconclusive; longer if conversion lag exceeds 7 days.
Budget must produce enough results to determine a winner confidently.
practical_applications: Small shop: test big concept differences only, 7+ days, equal budget, non-overlapping audiences.
limitations: No sample-size numbers given; retrieved via Meta's official help-article tool.

sources.title: About A/B testing for Meta ads
key_findings: A/B testing splits audiences so nobody sees both versions; measures cost per result or cost per conversion lift.
Use the same budget for both versions.
Meta does not recommend informal testing by manually turning ad sets on and off (overlapping audiences, unreliable results).
practical_applications: Use the built-in A/B tool, not on/off comparisons, before calling a winner.
limitations: Platform documentation.

sources.title: arXiv 2305.16459 (paper on A/B test sample-size rule of thumb)
key_findings: States the widely adopted rule of thumb n ≈ 16σ²/δ² per group for α = 0.05 (two-sided) and power 0.8.
Related sources: the factor 16 rounds (z_{α/2}+z_β)² × 2; Kohavi notes it becomes about 24 at α = 0.01 (formula attributed to van Belle 2002).
practical_applications: For low base rates (e.g., 2% chat rate) detecting small lifts needs tens of thousands of people per arm; small shops should test large differences.
limitations: Preprint; title and authors not captured; read via search summary only.

sources.title: Signaling status with luxury goods: the role of brand prominence
sources.authors: Han, Y. J.; Nunes, J. C.; Drèze, X.
key_findings: Brand prominence = extent of visible markings that help observers recognise the brand.
Four groups by wealth and need for status: Patricians prefer quiet goods recognisable only to peers; Parvenus prefer loud; Poseurs buy loud counterfeits; Proletarians do not seek status.
Luxury brands charge more for quieter items; counterfeiters mostly copy cheaper, louder items.
practical_applications: Premium frame content: show craftsmanship details rather than enlarged logos.
limitations: Journal of Marketing 74(4):15-30; handbags, cars, shoes in Western markets; read via abstract/press/summary.

sources.title: Subtle signals of inconspicuous consumption
key_findings: Four studies: people with domain knowledge often prefer subtle branding to differentiate from the mainstream, even though subtle markers raise misidentification risk.
Effect stronger for identity-relevant categories and more public consumption.
practical_applications: Eyewear is public and identity-relevant: understated presentation can signal premium to knowledgeable buyers.
limitations: Journal of Consumer Research 37(4):555-569; read via abstract.

sources.title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
sources.authors: Mathur, A.; Acar, G.; Friedman, M. J.; Lucherini, E.; Mayer, J.; Chetty, M.; Narayanan, A.
key_findings: ~53K product pages from ~11K shopping websites; 1,818 dark pattern instances on 1,254 sites (~11.1%), 15 types in 7 categories.
183 websites engaged in deceptive practices; 22 third-party entities offer dark patterns as turnkey solutions.
Develops a taxonomy of dark pattern characteristics by influence on and harm to decision-making.
practical_applications: Avoid fake scarcity, urgency timers and similar patterns in posts, chats and ads.
limitations: US-centric English shopping sites in 2019; read via abstract (attribute names not confirmed).

sources.title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report)
sources.authors: US Federal Trade Commission, Bureau of Consumer Protection
key_findings: Four groups: design elements that induce false beliefs; hide or delay disclosure of material information (e.g., drip pricing); lead to unauthorized charges; obscure or subvert privacy choices.
Appendix examples include baseless countdown timers, deceptive consumer testimonials, undisclosed paid endorsements and hidden costs/drip pricing.
Dark patterns have stronger effects when combined.
practical_applications: Use as the ethical checklist for promotions and testimonials even outside the US.
limitations: US regulator staff report, not Thai law.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 25 Online interface design and organisation
sources.authors: European Parliament and Council of the EU
key_findings: Prohibits online platform providers from designing, organising or operating interfaces that deceive or manipulate users; Recital 67 links this to dark patterns.
Applies to online platforms only; Commission may issue guidelines under Art. 25(3).
practical_applications: Reference standard for ethical interface/promotion design.
limitations: EUR-Lex not reachable; read via search summaries and a secondary legal-text site.

sources.title: Commission Notice - Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2005/29/EC (Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), C/2021/9320
key_findings: Non-binding guidance adopted December 2021 replacing the 2016 guidance; contains a dedicated section on dark patterns as unfair commercial practices deployed through interface design.
States the UCPD does not require intention for a dark pattern to be unfair (per commentary).
practical_applications: Intent does not excuse a manipulative design: judge by effect on the consumer.
limitations: Primary text not read; secondary commentary only.

sources.title: Does Clickbait Actually Attract More Clicks? Three Clickbait Studies You Must Read
sources.authors: Molina, M. D.; Sundar, S. S.; Rony, M. M. U.; Hassan, N.; Le, T.; Lee, D.
key_findings: Study 1 (quasi-experiment, MTurk N=149) and Study 2 (controlled experiment varying one clickbait characteristic, N=249): clickbait did not generate more curiosity than non-clickbait; participants clicked read-more/share as often or more for non-clickbait.
Study 3: four clickbait detectors agreed only 47% of the time, questioning their validity.
practical_applications: Write specific, honest hooks; curiosity gaps tied to real content, closed in the same piece.
limitations: News headlines, US online samples; read-more intention not real clicks on articles.

sources.title: พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค พ.ศ. 2522 (ฉบับรวมแก้ไขถึงฉบับที่ 4 พ.ศ. 2562, สำนักงานคณะกรรมการกฤษฎีกา)
sources.authors: Kingdom of Thailand; compiled by Office of the Council of State; hosted by Office of the Consumer Protection Board (สคบ.)
key_findings: s.3: 'ข้อความ' includes letters, pictures, film, light, sound, signs or any act making the meaning understandable.

s.22: advertising must not use statements unfair to consumers; listed as unfair: (1) false or exaggerated; (2) causing misunderstanding of material facts, whether or not citing academic reports or statistics; (3) supporting illegal/immoral acts or damaging national culture; (4) causing division; (5) others by ministerial regulation; statements the public knows cannot possibly be true are exempt from (1).

s.27: advertising committee may order amendments, bans on statements or methods, and corrective advertising; s.28: may order the advertiser to prove claims, suspend ads, and claims citing research/statistics/certification that cannot be proven are deemed false or exaggerated.

Penalties: s.47 intentional misleading advertising up to 6 months or 100,000 THB (repeat up to 1 year or 200,000 THB); s.48 up to 3 months or 60,000 THB; s.49 non-compliance with s.27/28 orders up to 6 months or 100,000 THB.
practical_applications: Keep evidence for every claim (UV400, blue-cut, 'best'); avoid health cures and unprovable superlatives.
limitations: Compilation may lag later amendments; legal interpretation not provided.

sources.title: อย. เข้มตรวจจับ 'โฆษณาเครื่องมือแพทย์เสริมความงาม' ผิดกฎหมาย ... คุก 6 เดือน ปรับ 5 หมื่น
key_findings: Thai FDA: advertising a medical device that shows a trade name/trademark or states indications, efficacy, quality, standards, ingredients or origin requires prior FDA approval.
Approved ads must show licence number ฆพ. XX/YYYY; unlicensed advertising: up to 6 months prison or 50,000 THB fine or both; hotline 1556.
practical_applications: Contact lens content with brand names or benefit claims needs a ฆพ. number.
limitations: News report (19 Aug 2023) quoting the FDA; no statute section cited; focus on beauty devices.

sources.title: (MGR Online news) Thai FDA: all contact lenses classified as medical devices
key_findings: Medical Device Committee resolved that all contact lenses (corrective, cosmetic, therapeutic) are medical devices under the 2008 Act, with import and sale controlled and import licences required.
practical_applications: Treat contact lens advertising as medical device advertising.
limitations: Old news (around 2009); read via search summary; current notices not checked.

sources.title: Country Overview: Medical Devices - Thailand
key_findings: (Older scheme) Thai devices in Class I (licence), II, III; contact lenses listed among Class I licence devices; unlisted devices default to Class III.
Some products classified as devices elsewhere may not be devices in Thailand; applicants can ask the TFDA.
practical_applications: Spectacle lens/frame status must be confirmed with the Thai FDA.
limitations: Dated (around 2011-2012) and Thailand moved to risk-based classification notices in 2020; read via search summary.

sources.title: (Thansettakij news) Ministry of Public Health drafts ministerial regulation placing eye testing for glasses under the Healthy Establishments Act
key_findings: Published 17 June 2026: draft regulation would make 'กิจการตรวจวัดสายตาประกอบแว่น' a licensed business under the Healthy Establishments Act; testers trained and registered.
Scope: refractive testing (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia) for ages 12+, excluding eye-muscle testing; effective 180 days after Royal Gazette publication; still a draft.
practical_applications: Monitor; future rules may affect how the shop advertises eye-testing services.
limitations: News on a draft; no advertising provisions mentioned.

sources.title: คู่มือการคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล (PDPA Guideline) incl. พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล พ.ศ. 2562 (Royal Gazette text)
sources.authors: Department of Intellectual Property, Ministry of Commerce, Thailand
key_findings: s.6: personal data = data identifying a person directly or indirectly (photos/video of customers qualify).
s.19: consent required unless another basis (s.24/s.26); must be explicit, in writing or electronic, purpose stated clearly in easy language, freely given, withdrawable.
s.26: sensitive data includes health data and disability -> eye prescriptions/exam results are health data.

Administrative fines: s.82 up to 1 million THB; s.83 up to 3 million THB (incl. obtaining consent by deception); s.84 up to 5 million THB (sensitive data); civil liability s.77 and punitive damages up to 2x s.78.
practical_applications: Written/chat consent form for customer photos, videos and testimonials, with separate tick for paid ads and for any health data; no prescriptions in posts.
limitations: Agency guideline for its own operations; PDPC marketing/photo guidance not read; not legal advice.

sources.title: About Meta's health and wellness advertising policy
key_findings: No ads that imply or try to generate negative self-perception to promote health-related products.
For weight and cosmetic products/procedures: no statements of inferiority about appearance; before-and-after cosmetic transformations allowed only when targeting 18+.
No clickbait in health contexts (sensational language, extreme claims, promised outcomes in a timeframe without qualifiers); no claims to cure listed incurable diseases.
practical_applications: 'Before/after glasses' content shows experience, not shamed appearance; label vision simulations.
limitations: Platform policy can change; retrieved via official help-article tool.

sources.title: About Meta's privacy violations and personal attributes advertising policy
key_findings: Ads must not assert or imply personal attributes of the viewer, including age, physical or mental health, medical condition and disability, including by asking questions about them.
'You/your' allowed if not tied to a prohibited attribute; Meta reports such ads lead to negative experiences and lower engagement.
practical_applications: Write 'After 40, many people...' instead of 'Are you over 40? Your eyes are failing.'
limitations: Applies to paid ads; interpretation of borderline wording is ours.

sources.title: About Meta Advertising Standards
key_findings: Lists topic policies including personal attributes, sensational content, and personal health and appearance (no negative self-perception or unrealistic/unexpected results); ads must also follow Community Standards and commerce/branded content policies.
practical_applications: Check each paid post against the topic list before boosting.
limitations: Overview page; full policies at Meta Transparency Center not read.

sources.title: Emotional responses to music: the need to consider underlying mechanisms
key_findings: Target article (BBS 31(5) 559-575): research had neglected the mechanisms by which music induces emotion; proposes six mechanisms beyond cognitive appraisal (brain stem reflex, evaluative conditioning, emotional contagion, visual imagery, episodic memory, musical expectancy).
practical_applications: A music brief must say WHICH mechanism we rely on (e.g. contagion via tempo/timbre, expectancy via a build), not just 'make it emotional'.
limitations: Theoretical; commentaries contest parts. Abstract-level access.

sources.title: From everyday emotions to aesthetic emotions: towards a unified theory of musical emotions
key_findings: Revised framework with eight mechanisms: Brain stem reflex, Rhythmic entrainment, Evaluative conditioning, Contagion, Visual imagery, Episodic memory, Musical expectancy, Aesthetic judgement (BRECVEMA).
practical_applications: Checklist for music direction: which of the 8 does the cue use?
limitations: Physics of Life Reviews 10:235; snippet/abstract level.

sources.title: A review of music and emotion studies: approaches, emotion models, and stimuli
key_findings: Review of 251 studies: self-report dominates; ~70% use discrete or dimensional emotion models; stimuli lean on a small set of familiar Western classical pieces.
practical_applications: Results generalise poorly to Thai pop, lo-fi or library music; test our own cues on our audience.
limitations: Music Perception 30(3) 307-340; abstract only.

sources.title: Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation
key_findings: ITPRA theory: five expectation response systems - Imagination, Tension, Prediction, Reaction, Appraisal.
Devices such as syncopation, cadence, meter, tonality and climax exploit these responses; accounts for chills, laughter, awe.
Critics (e.g. Zilberg, Leonardo 2007) question universality claims from an ethnomusicology view.
practical_applications: Build tension (uncertainty) before a reveal, reward with a predictable resolution on the product shot; a 'wrong' surprise works for comedy.
limitations: Publisher page and reviews only; Western tonal bias.

sources.title: Modeling tonal tension
key_findings: Tonal Pitch Space model predicts listeners' tension ratings from prolongational structure, pitch-space distance, surface dissonance and voice-leading attraction; extended to chromatic music.
practical_applications: Tension rises with distance from the home chord and dissonance; resolution = return home. Use at endings.
limitations: Music Perception 24(4) 329-366; summaries only; Western tonal music.
Check 2026-11-25: the Zenodo PDF previously linked is Wagner (2014) 'Cognitive Models of Tonal Tension', a University of Amsterdam student paper that reviews this model - not the original article.

sources.title: Universal recognition of three basic emotions in music
key_findings: Mafa listeners (Cameroon) with no Western music exposure recognised happy, sad and scared/fearful Western piano excerpts above chance (about 2/3 happy, ~1/2 sad and fearful per press reports).
Authors warn against the 'universal language of emotion' idea.
practical_applications: Broad happy/sad/scary cues travel across cultures; finer moods (nostalgia, kreng-jai warmth) do not necessarily.
limitations: Current Biology 19(7) 573-576; 21 participants per coverage; summary-level access.

sources.title: Mode and tempo relative contributions to 'happy-sad' judgements in equitone melodies
key_findings: Mode and tempo each affect happy-sad judgements; tempo was the more salient cue.
practical_applications: If we can't change the track's mode, tempo/energy is the stronger lever for 'happy vs sad'.
limitations: Cognition & Emotion 17:25-40; abstract-level summary.

sources.title: Effects of musical tempo and mode on arousal, mood, and spatial abilities
sources.authors: Husain, G.; Thompson, W. F.; Schellenberg, E. G.
key_findings: 36 undergraduates; Mozart K.448 as MIDI in 4 versions: 165 vs 60 bpm x major vs minor.
Tempo changed arousal but not mood; mode changed mood but not arousal; spatial-task scores followed arousal/mood (arousal-mood account of the 'Mozart effect').
practical_applications: Two independent knobs: tempo = energy/arousal, mode = valence/mood. Brief them separately.
limitations: Small sample; one piece; Western students.

sources.title: Communication of emotions in vocal expression and music performance: different channels, same code?
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 104 vocal-expression and 41 music-performance studies; emotions are communicated with similar cue patterns (tempo/rate, loudness, pitch, timbre) in voice and music.
practical_applications: Match VO prosody and music cues (both fast/bright for joy, slow/soft/low for sadness) so they don't fight.
limitations: Psychological Bulletin 129:770-814; secondary summaries only for cue details.

sources.title: The relationship between musical structure and perceived expression (Oxford Handbook of Music Psychology, 2nd ed.)
key_findings: Any structural factor (tempo, loudness, pitch, timbre, mode, rhythm, harmony...) can point to several emotions; effects are additive or interactive.
Clearest results for basic auditory/motion variables (loudness, timbre, pitch, tempo); typical musical variables less clear.
practical_applications: Write briefs in tempo/loudness/register/timbre first, harmony second.
limitations: Chapter abstract only.

sources.title: The emotional connotations of major versus minor tonality: one or more origins?
key_findings: The major-positive / minor-negative valence association is psychologically robust in Western tonal music but has no single accepted explanation; Parncutt compares six partly related theories.

Theories: dissonance (minor passages rougher / less harmonic on average); alterity-markedness (major and positive emotion are the common norm, minor and negative the marked 'Other'); uncertainty (minor triad has a more ambiguous root; minor scale has three forms because degrees 6 and 7 vary); speech (minor scale degrees 3 and 6 are lower than expected, like sad speech); salience of flats; familiarity/cultural learning (differences emerged by accident in the 14th-16th centuries and were reinforced by composers).
Conclusion: there are arguments for and against each theory; the truth may be a mixture - not immediately clear which to privilege.
practical_applications: Minor = sad is a learned Western-tonal association, strong for our audience (Thai pop is largely Western-tonal) but not universal.
limitations: Theoretical review of Western tonal music; does not establish cross-cultural universality.

sources.title: The impact of background music on adult listeners: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Kämpfe, J.; Sedlmeier, P.; Renkewitz, F.
key_findings: 97 studies analysed (from 189 articles); global effect is null because specific effects cancel out.
Background music vs none: disturbs reading (all 8 studies negative, mean r = -.11, n = 680), small negative effect on memory, positive on emotional reactions and sports.
Memory for advertisement content: negligible slight negative (r = -.05, 7 studies, n = 930).
Music tempo influences the tempo of activities done while listening.
practical_applications: Music under on-screen text or VO slightly hurts comprehension; music does help mood. Use it, but keep it simple and low under information.
limitations: Psychology of Music 39(4) 424-448; heterogeneous small studies; adults only.

sources.title: The psychoacoustics of the irrelevant sound effect
key_findings: Irrelevant sound effect (ISE): memorising visually presented lists is reliably impaired by background sound that participants are told to ignore, at moderate levels; speech or speech analogues produce by far the largest effects (unfamiliar speech raised serial-recall errors by about 50% on average in the authors' data).
Noticeable spectral change over time is a necessary condition for an ISE; level change by itself is not.
FM-tone study (24 participants, FM rate 0-50 Hz): disruption is non-monotonic with a maximum near 4 Hz (where perceived fluctuation strength also peaks), but no FM tone disrupted as much as speech.

Table 1 re-tabulates earlier studies: music can produce almost equally large effects as speech (signals of sufficient spectro-temporal complexity); Salame & Baddeley (1989) vocal music produced larger effects than instrumental music.
No current model (cognitive or psychoacoustic - fluctuation strength, speech transmission index) captures all the data.
practical_applications: Sung lyrics and choppy, changing music under VO compete with the words more than a steady pad; prefer instrumental, smooth beds.
limitations: Invited review, Acoustical Science and Technology 35(1):10-16; lab serial-recall tasks, not video comprehension.

sources.title: Effects of background music on phonological short-term memory
key_findings: As re-tabulated in Ellermeier & Zimmer 2014 (Table 1): vocal music disrupted serial recall more than instrumental music.
practical_applications: Historical anchor for 'vocal music disrupts verbal memory more than instrumental'.
limitations: Bibliographic only; findings not checked against the original.
Original not read; finding comes only from the Ellermeier & Zimmer 2014 review.

sources.title: Impact of background music on reading comprehension: influence of lyrics language and study habits
sources.authors: Sun, Y.; Sun, C.; Li, C.; Shao, X.; Liu, Q.; Liu, H.
key_findings: N=90 students of one sports university in Shandong (45 habitual music listeners, 45 not); Mandarin pop, English pop, no music: music with lyrics hurt reading comprehension.

90 college students in East China (50 female; 45 habitual music-listeners, 45 non-listeners; 30 per group: Mandarin pop, English pop, no music): music with lyrics reduced reading comprehension vs no music.
Comprehension dropped most when lyrics were in the same language as the text; accuracy was lowest with native-language (L1) lyrics for both listeners and non-listeners.
Non-listeners were hurt more; habitual listeners were much less distracted. Results support the duplex-mechanism account of auditory distraction.
Effect held even though the music was slow-tempo (contrast: Thompson et al. 2012 found fast, loud instrumental music disrupts reading more than slow).
practical_applications: For Thai text-heavy carousels/reels: no lyrics, especially not Thai lyrics, under reading or VO.
limitations: One sample of Chinese students, reading tasks (not video watching); a corrigendum has been published (not read).
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

sources.title: Sound advertising: a review of the experimental evidence on the effects of music in commercials on attention, memory, attitudes, and purchase intention
key_findings: Review (Journal of Media Psychology) of experiments on music in commercials and attention, memory, attitude and purchase intention; findings on recall are mixed.
practical_applications: Music in ads is not automatically positive; fit and attention matter.
limitations: Seen only as a search snippet; title partly from snippet.

sources.title: An ad's musical congruity with the brand fires purchase intent (WARC)
key_findings: Summarises effects of 10 types of music-brand congruity on purchase intent, brand attitude, recall and affect.
practical_applications: Musical fit (genre, tempo, mood matching brand and picture) is the main variable to brief.
limitations: Paywalled trade article; snippet only. Some studies find incongruent music raises attention and recall.

sources.title: Congruence-Association Model and experiments in film music: toward interdisciplinary collaboration
key_findings: CAM: viewers build a coherent narrative from audio and visual channels; structural congruence (shared accents/timing) steers visual attention, association supplies meaning.
practical_applications: Accents in music that coincide with visual accents direct the eye; the music's mood colours how the scene is interpreted.
limitations: Music and the Moving Image 8(2) 5-24; summaries only.

sources.title: Use music and sound effects from the Audio Library (YouTube Help)
key_findings: Creative Commons tracks require crediting the artist in the video description (copy text provided); standard-licence tracks need no attribution.
Audio Library content is copyright-safe on YouTube and won't get Content ID claims; monetisable in YPP.
The page does not state rules for use outside YouTube.
practical_applications: OK for YouTube uploads; for FB/IG/TikTok use only CC BY tracks with credit, or platform libraries.
limitations: Terms change; check per track licence.

sources.title: About CC Licenses
key_findings: Six licences: BY, BY-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC, BY-NC-SA, BY-NC-ND; all require attribution; NC forbids commercial use; ND forbids sharing adaptations; CC0 waives rights (public domain dedication).
practical_applications: Shop content is commercial: avoid NC tracks. Cutting a track to picture may count as an adaptation, so avoid ND tracks for music we edit.
limitations: Not legal advice; whether a sync edit is an 'adaptation' should be checked in the licence legal code.

sources.title: About the Commercial Music Library (TikTok Ads help)
key_findings: Page last updated July 2025: the Commercial Music Library is a pre-cleared global library of 1 million songs, free for businesses to use in content on TikTok.

Businesses cannot use the general music library commercially; the CML is to be used for all commercial TikTok activity - organic content (including duet, react, stitch), video ads and branded content.
Using other users' original sounds or other licensed sounds in business content requires your own licence check.
practical_applications: Business accounts posting promos on TikTok should pick from the CML in-app.
limitations: Help page; detailed CML terms (separate page) not read; use outside TikTok is not granted by this page.

sources.title: Meta Sound Collection terms (as summarised by secondary sources and Instagram help)
key_findings: Secondary summaries: licence covers commercial or non-commercial use but only inside content on Meta products; one Instagram help page says library music is for personal, non-commercial use - conflicting.
practical_applications: Use Sound Collection only for FB/IG content; never export it to TikTok/YouTube; check terms before paid ads.
limitations: Conflicting statements; primary terms not read.

sources.title: Copyright Act B.E. 2537 (1994), English translation
key_findings: s.19: copyright lasts for the author's life plus 50 years; ss.20-22 give other terms (e.g. sound recordings, audiovisual works).
s.4: 'sound recording' excludes a film soundtrack; 'audiovisual work' includes its soundtrack.

s.32 para 1: use is not infringement if it does not conflict with normal exploitation and does not unreasonably prejudice the owner; para 2 lists purposes (research/study non-profit, personal use, criticism with acknowledgement, news, teaching...).
Performers' rights (s.44) last 50 years from the performance/recording (s.49); s.45 remuneration for commercial use of recorded performances.
practical_applications: A shop promo is commercial use: none of the s.32 purposes cover using a popular Thai song in an ad. License it or use cleared libraries.
limitations: Unofficial translation; amendments up to Copyright Act (No. 5) B.E. 2565 (2022) exist (IP Thailand) and were not checked. Not legal advice.

sources.title: Edit to the beat in Final Cut Pro for Mac
key_findings: Final Cut Pro Beat Detection analyses a music clip and shows a beat grid of song parts (big structural transitions), bars and beats; edit points snap to the grid when snapping is on.
It can trim a music clip to the length of a video edit without perceptible breaks; Apple advises a 4/4 clip for the most accurate grid.
Toggle with Clip > Enable Beat Detection (Option-B).
practical_applications: Confirms the craft practice of editing on beat/bar grids; our beat-clip pipeline uses librosa for the same.
limitations: Vendor documentation (Final Cut Pro for Mac); accuracy not independently tested.

sources.title: Processing Fluency and Aesthetic Pleasure: Is Beauty in the Perceiver's Processing Experience?
sources.authors: Reber, R., Schwarz, N., Winkielman, P.
key_findings: Core proposal: the more fluently a perceiver processes an object, the more positive the aesthetic response; beauty is 'objectified', not objective.

Four assumptions: objects differ in fluency (symmetry, figure-ground contrast, goodness of form, prototypicality, repetition, priming); fluency is hedonically marked (positive); people use the feeling as information unless its value is questioned; impact is moderated by expectation and attribution.

Fluency is discounted when people attribute the feeling to an irrelevant source (e.g., background music); fluency that comes as a surprise (expected hard, turns out easy) gives the strongest pleasure, a reading of 'unity in variety'.
Inverted-U for complexity is explained as two opposing mechanisms (salience of the fluency source vs loss of fluency).

Experts prefer more complex/asymmetric stimuli; the authors propose training raises fluency for complex stimuli and experts apply explicit norms of taste, sometimes down-rating simple stimuli despite their ease.
Simplicity is not the same as ease: redundant, contextual patterns can be easier than sparse ones; actual ease must be tested.
practical_applications: Make the main read easy (contrast, clear figure-ground, familiar layout) and put the challenge in meaning, not in decoding.
An 'aha' (looks complex, resolves simply) is the strongest fluency payoff: good for story-carousel final slides.
limitations: Theory/review paper; the authors call the evidence on complexity, expertise and valence 'sparse and sometimes contradictory'.
Mostly lab stimuli (abstract patterns, words); fluency effects on real artworks and ads are smaller and context-dependent.

sources.title: Prototypes Are Attractive Because They Are Easy on the Mind
sources.authors: Winkielman, P., Halberstadt, J., Fazendeiro, T., Catty, S.
key_findings: With random-dot and geometric patterns, prototypicality predicted both categorisation speed (fluency) and attractiveness.
Fluency partially mediated the prototypicality-attractiveness link; some effect of prototypicality remained when fluency was controlled.
Facial EMG: prepared (fluent) prototypes produced quick extra activity over the cheek (smile) muscle, i.e., a genuine mild positive affect, not only a cold judgement.
practical_applications: A recognisable category look (a clear 'eyewear shop' or 'story card' prototype) earns an immediate small liking bonus; deviate from it deliberately, not randomly.
limitations: Abstract lab patterns; small effects; does not test meaningful commercial images.
Beauty-in-averageness for faces may also have other causes (the authors say fluency explains part, not all).

sources.title: Neuroaesthetics
key_findings: Aesthetic experience emerges from interaction of three systems (the 'aesthetic triad'): sensory-motor, emotion-valuation, meaning-knowledge; the systems are not always equally weighted.

Context changes valuation: abstract images labelled 'museum' were rated more attractive than when labelled 'computer-generated', with more medial OFC/vmPFC activity; 'art status', titles and authenticity (original vs copy) modulate responses.
Aesthetic pleasure may reflect 'liking' without 'wanting' (Berridge), a neural reading of Kant's disinterested interest.
Default mode network (DMN) involvement in the most moving artworks is cited from Vessel et al. 2012.

Limits: meaning of individual artworks is fluid and historically contingent; the biggest challenge is reverse inference from brain location to mental process, which should generate hypotheses, not confirm them.
practical_applications: Framing (caption, label, 'handmade', 'by our optician') is part of the aesthetic object; plan it as deliberately as the image.
Treat brain-region claims in marketing ('this lights up the reward centre') as unproven.
limitations: Short review (2014); field has since grown and critiques of small-sample fMRI apply.
Context-label study is cited, not re-analysed here.

sources.title: Move me, astonish me... delight my eyes and brain: The Vienna Integrated Model of top-down and bottom-up processes in Art Perception (VIMAP) and corresponding affective, evaluative, and neurophysiological correlates
sources.authors: Pelowski, M., Markey, P. S., Forster, M., Gerger, G., Leder, H.
key_findings: Per abstract: VIMAP integrates artwork-driven (bottom-up) processing with top-down mechanisms to explain why the same artwork produces very different responses across people.
Per Van Geert & Wagemans 2020: in VIMAP, order and complexity are detected in perceptual analysis and further processed in implicit memory integration.
Per Pizzolante et al. 2024: Pelowski's models frame transformation as expectation-artwork discrepancy that, when resolved, yields insight/epiphany.
practical_applications: Plan for multiple outcomes of one image (facile liking, confusion, rejection, insight) instead of one 'correct' reaction.
limitations: Full text not read; stage details and outcome names unverified here.
Large theoretical model; many links remain to be tested.

sources.title: 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
sources.authors: Hekkert, P., Snelders, D., van Wieringen, P. C. W.
key_findings: Per a CogSci summary (secondary): three studies with consumer products (sanders, telephones, teakettles, cars, phones); typicality and novelty were negatively correlated but each positively predicted preference, suppressing each other's effect.
Typicality and novelty jointly explained about 56% of preference variance in Study 3; central tendency (objective typicality) gave about 60%.
Experts showed weaker typicality-novelty suppression; the hypothesis that experts rely more on novelty was not supported.
Linked to Loewy's MAYA principle (Most Advanced, Yet Acceptable).
practical_applications: New looks should keep a clear category anchor (recognisable layout, product shape) while adding one novel element.
limitations: Original article not read; numbers come from a third-party summary (which itself has one internal inconsistency).
An apparel study reported no negative typicality-novelty correlation (per search summary), so the pattern is category-dependent.

sources.title: Liking versus Complexity: Decomposing the Inverted U-curve
sources.authors: Güçlütürk, Y., Jacobs, R. H. A. H., van Lier, R.
key_findings: 30 participants rated 144 computer-generated grayscale patterns for liking and complexity; objective complexity = compressed file size (r = .946 with perceived complexity).
Two clusters: 20 people liked simpler patterns (r = -.79 with complexity), 10 liked complex patterns (r = .87).
Averaging the two opposite linear functions produced the group-level inverted U; a two-cluster model fit better than a quadratic model.
Both clusters perceived complexity the same way; they differed in liking, not perception.
practical_applications: Do not aim for 'medium complexity for everyone'; choose complexity per audience segment and test.
File size of a compressed PNG/JPEG is a cheap proxy for visual complexity when comparing variants.
limitations: Small, young sample; post hoc clustering; abstract grayscale stimuli only; 1-second exposures.

sources.title: Order, Complexity, and Aesthetic Appreciation
key_findings: Complexity = quantity and variety of information; order = its structure and organisation; following Arnheim, the authors treat them as antagonistic but complementary.
Complexity-liking findings are mixed: inverted U, positive linear (snowflakes, textures) and even U-shaped (solid objects) relations are reported.
Fractal dimension preference typically around D 1.3-1.5 with subgroup differences; Fourier slope about -2 typical of natural scenes and Western graphic art.
Symmetry is usually preferred, but slight asymmetry can be preferred (e.g., Mondrian comparisons); explicit beauty ratings of asymmetry rise with art expertise.

Individual differences: Openness relates to preference for complexity; art training generally relates to preferring complexity; visual working memory capacity predicts preferred complexity; preference for harmony correlates across colour, shape, space and music (Palmer & Griscom 2013).
Authors' view: individuals differ in their preferred balance between order and complexity.
practical_applications: Add order (grid, repetition, alignment, limited palette) when a frame must carry many elements; add variety when an ordered frame feels dead.
Treat complexity preference as audience-specific; order effects are more stable.
limitations: Narrative review (not a meta-analysis), visual modality focus; postprint version read.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: framing credited to Arnheim; open copy is the 2018 accepted manuscript (DOI 10.1037/aca0000224).

sources.title: Visual Complexity and Beauty Appreciation: Explaining the Divergence of Results
sources.authors: Nadal, M., Munar, E., Marty, G., Cela-Conde, C. J.
key_findings: Per search summary and citing papers: divergent complexity-beauty results stem from how studies define and manipulate complexity.
Complexity has at least three dimensions: amount/variety of elements, their organisation, and asymmetry, each relating differently to beauty ratings.
practical_applications: When critiquing 'too busy', say which kind: too many elements, poor organisation, or imbalance.
limitations: Full text not read; details and effect sizes unverified.

sources.title: Back to the inverted-U for music preference: A review of the literature
key_findings: Per abstract summary: of 57 music-preference studies, 50 (87.7%) were classed compatible with an overarching (segmented) inverted-U, 5 mixed, 2 incompatible.
Authors urge caution in dismissing the inverted-U, while acknowledging problems with Berlyne's arousal theory itself.
A citing paper reports a stricter count (Wundt effects found in only 15 of 57), showing classification dependence.
practical_applications: For music beds and pacing, moderate familiarity/complexity is a reasonable default, but verify with the audience.
limitations: Full text not read; 'compatible' is a lenient category; music domain, not visual.

sources.title: Perceptual and Physiological Responses to Jackson Pollock's Fractals
sources.authors: Taylor, R. P., Spehar, B., Van Donkelaar, P., Hagerhall, C. M.
key_findings: Across natural scenes, computer fractals and Pollock paintings, viewers on average preferred mid-range fractal dimension D about 1.3-1.5 (220-participant study cited).
Skin conductance (24 participants) showed the smallest stress rise for D = 1.4 patterns; EEG (32 participants) showed largest frontal alpha changes at D about 1.3.
Gaze paths are themselves fractal (D about 1.4-1.5), proposed link to foraging-like search.
Pollock's own work rose to D about 1.7, above typical viewer preference.
practical_applications: Backgrounds with natural, moderately rough self-similar texture (clouds, foliage, soft wood grain) are a defensible calm-but-alive choice behind products; avoid both flat dead fields and dense high-D noise behind text.
limitations: Review largely of the authors' own programme; small physiological samples (6-32); fMRI preliminary; D alone does not capture complexity; Van Geert & Wagemans note subgroup differences (inverted-U, positive, negative).

sources.title: Implicit and Explicit Evaluation of Visual Symmetry as a Function of Art Expertise
sources.authors: Weichselbaum, H., Leder, H., Ansorge, U.
key_findings: 79 students (psychology and art history), 80 abstract patterns; symmetrical patterns rated more beautiful (est. means 4.24 vs 2.83 on 1-7).
Implicit (IAT) symmetry-positive association (D = 0.55) did not vary with art expertise.
Explicit ratings of asymmetrical patterns rose with expertise, though experts still rated symmetry higher overall.
practical_applications: Symmetry is a safe default for broad audiences (product hero shots, logos); asymmetry reads as 'designed/artistic' mainly to trained viewers.
limitations: Abstract patterns, lab setting, student sample, custom expertise questionnaire, balance not controlled; correlational.

sources.title: The brain on art: intense aesthetic experience activates the default mode network
sources.authors: Vessel, E. A., Starr, G. G., Rubin, N.
key_findings: 16 observers rated 109 paintings 1-4 for 'how strongly does this move you'.
For the most moving works (rating 4), anterior medial prefrontal cortex (a DMN hub) was not suppressed as it was for 1-3 ratings; PCC, hippocampus, substantia nigra also responded more.
