Inter-observer agreement on which paintings moved them was very low (mean pairwise r = .13).
practical_applications: The strongest responses are personal (self-relevant) and idiosyncratic: aim content at a specific audience's lives rather than generic 'beauty'.
limitations: Small fMRI sample (16), typical of the replicability problems described by Turner et al. 2018; no physiological arousal measure.

sources.title: Stronger shared taste for natural aesthetic domains than for artifacts of human culture
sources.authors: Vessel, E. A., Maurer, N., Denker, A. H., Starr, G. G.
key_findings: Per search summary: agreement between observers was high for faces and natural landscapes, low for architecture and artworks.
A second experiment found higher agreement for landscapes than exterior architecture with no reliability difference.
Authors propose natural categories are more uniformly behaviourally relevant, while artifact taste depends on individual experience.
practical_applications: Nature imagery and faces are the 'safer' shared-taste elements; stylised design choices split audiences more.
limitations: Full text blocked (403); numbers not verified here.

sources.title: Aesthetics
sources.authors: Brielmann, A. A., Pelli, D. G.
key_findings: Per press summaries: beauty may be an intense form of ordinary pleasure; beauty and pleasure ratings rise together nearly linearly.
Average features (symmetry, roundness) raise beauty on average, but individual taste differences are large (about half the variance in face attractiveness attributed to personal taste).
practical_applications: Average-based design rules set a floor, not a ceiling; personal relevance drives the top end.
limitations: Only press/secondary coverage read; primer not read.

sources.title: What is interesting? Exploring the appraisal structure of interest
key_findings: Per search summary: interest rests on two appraisals, novelty-complexity and coping potential (ability to understand it).
Four in-vivo experiments supported this; appraisals predicted interest beyond curiosity/openness traits, and did not predict enjoyment.
practical_applications: Make something new AND give the viewer a handle to understand it (caption, familiar character, clear cue): novelty without coping = confusion.
limitations: Full text not read; a dissertation reports inconsistent coping-potential effects.

sources.title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
key_findings: Prototype of awe: perceived vastness (physical or social size) plus need for accommodation (experience does not fit current mental structures).

Five flavouring appraisals: threat, beauty, exceptional ability, virtue, supernatural causality; e.g., vastness without accommodation = deference, accommodation without vastness = surprise; ability without vastness = admiration; virtue = elevation.
Art that is easily graspable may entertain but rarely induces awe; obscurity and challenge raise accommodation (Burke).
Authors state the approach was developed 'in the absence of empirical evidence'.
practical_applications: Awe shots need scale cues (tiny figure vs vast landscape/sky) plus something not instantly understood; a pretty sunset alone gives beauty, not awe.
limitations: Conceptual paper; later empirical work (e.g., Yaden 2019 scale) builds on it.

sources.title: The development of the Awe Experience Scale (AWE-S): A multifactorial measure for a complex emotion
key_findings: Per search summary: six factors - altered time perception, self-diminishment, connectedness, perceived vastness, physical sensations, need for accommodation; structure confirmed in a second sample (N = 636).
Japanese adaptation reportedly kept the six-factor structure.
practical_applications: Checklist for an 'awe' beat: slowed time (hold/slow motion), small self (scale), connection, vastness, bodily cue (chills), something to make sense of.
limitations: Full text not read; journal/DOI not confirmed in this session (listed as 'et al.' to avoid guessing co-authors).

sources.title: Towards a Psychological Construct of Being Moved
key_findings: Three German-language studies (N = 228, 1,683, 901).
Moving episodes mostly involve relationship or critical life events (death, birth, marriage, separation, reunion); sadness (43%) and joy (27%) most often co-reported.
Being moved is a mixed emotion, especially for fiction (positive and negative affect nearly equal); high intensity but low-to-mid arousal; felt as warm, soft, elevating.
Highest appraisals: compatibility with social norms and self-ideals; low appraisal of own causation (observer stance).
practical_applications: Moving story beats come from bonds being tested, lost or restored, watched from a witness position; keep arousal calm (slow pacing, soft sound).
limitations: Self-report, German students only, no physiology; Study 1 scale formatting error.

sources.title: Kama Muta: Conceptualizing and Measuring the Experience Often Labelled Being Moved Across 19 Nations and 15 Languages
sources.authors: Zickfeld, J. H., Schubert, T. W., Seibt, B., ... Fiske, A. P.
key_findings: 19 countries, 15 languages, N = 3,542; KAMMUS scale covering appraisal, valence, sensations, motivation, labels.
Kama muta is a positive social-relational emotion evoked by a sudden intensification of communal sharing.
Typical signs: warmth in the chest, moist eyes/tears, chills/goosebumps, choked up, buoyancy; motivates devotion and moral commitment to communal bonds.
The five facets correlated highly in every sample despite cultural variation.
practical_applications: Design 'heart-warming' beats around a sudden closeness (reunion, unexpected kindness, being included); the emotion transfers across cultures, the specific signals are local (use Thai relational cues).
limitations: Self-report; online-first 2018 version read; published 2019 Emotion 19(3).

sources.title: Aesthetic experiences and their transformative power: a systematic review
sources.authors: Pizzolante, M., Pelowski, M., et al.
key_findings: 23 included articles (12 theoretical, 11 empirical; 13 empirical studies).
Facilitators: empathy, aesthetic sensitivity, openness, expectations, contextual design; process: cognitive discrepancy, emotion, insight; after-effects: self-change, empathy, critical thinking.
Quality: Downs & Black mean 16.2/27; only two studies had active controls; mostly self-report, uncontrolled designs, rare long-term follow-up.
practical_applications: Claims that a post/clip 'changes lives' are not evidence-based; aim for insight moments and measure modest outcomes (saves, comments).
limitations: Authors' strong conclusion exceeds the evidence quality they report; first half of the text read in detail.

sources.title: Small sample sizes reduce the replicability of task-based fMRI studies
key_findings: Resampling 11 tasks: at typical N about 30, replicability of group maps is modest; smallest N with average R-squared > .5 was 36.
Even at N = 121 the conservative voxel Jaccard overlap stays below 0.6; peaks often fail to replicate.
Good test-retest reliability does not guarantee replicability; recommend power analysis, individual-difference approaches and large studies.
practical_applications: Most neuroaesthetics fMRI studies (N 15-30) should be read as hypothesis-generating; never use them as proof in content claims.
limitations: General fMRI, not aesthetics-specific; authors decline a universal minimum N.

sources.title: Global Prevalence of Myopia and High Myopia and Temporal Trends from 2000 through 2050
sources.authors: Holden BA, Fricke TR, Wilson DA, Jong M, Naidoo KS, Sankaridurg P, Wong TY, Naduvilath TJ, Resnikoff S
key_findings: Systematic review/meta-analysis: 145 studies covering 2.1 million participants, combined with UN Population Department and urbanisation data.
2000: 1406 million people with myopia (22.9%; 95% CI 932-1932 million) and 163 million with high myopia (2.7%).
2050 prediction: 4758 million with myopia (49.8%; 3620-6056 million) and 938 million with high myopia (9.8%; 479-2104 million).
Definitions used: myopia -0.50 D or less; high myopia -5.00 D or less (not the IMI -6.00 D cut-off).
practical_applications: Allowed wording: 'นักวิจัยคาดการณ์ว่าปี 2050 ประชากรโลกราวครึ่งหนึ่งอาจสายตาสั้น' — always say 'คาดการณ์', not 'จะเป็น'.
limitations: Projection from regression trends; wide uncertainty intervals.
Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 26875007); full text not read.
High myopia defined at -5.00 D, so the 9.8% is not directly comparable with IMI-defined high myopia.

sources.title: Blindness and vision impairment (fact sheet)
key_findings: At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment; at least 1 billion cases could have been prevented or are unaddressed.
Presbyopia is the main cause of near vision impairment, affecting 826 million people (unaddressed).
Unaddressed: cataract 94 million and uncorrected refractive error 88.4 million cases of distance impairment/blindness.
practical_applications: Use '826 ล้านคนทั่วโลกมีปัญหามองใกล้ไม่ชัดจากสายตายาวตามวัยที่ยังไม่ได้แก้ไข' — not '826 million have presbyopia' (total presbyopia is larger; secondary coverage of the WHO 2019 World report on vision cites ~1.8 billion, not verified here).
limitations: Fact sheet dated 10 Feb 2026; global, no Thai breakdown.
sources.license: WHO terms (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for most WHO content)

sources.title: IMI - Defining and Classifying Myopia: A Proposed Set of Standards for Clinical and Epidemiologic Studies
key_findings: Myopia: spherical equivalent refractive error ≤ −0.50 D when ocular accommodation is relaxed; low myopia ≤ −0.50 and > −6.00 D; high myopia ≤ −6.00 D.
Pre-myopia: ≤ +0.75 D and > −0.50 D in children whose baseline refraction, age and other risk factors make future myopia likely enough to merit prevention.

'There is no clear biological basis in terms of axial length, refraction or other ocular biometric parameter to differentiate high from lower degrees of myopia'; pathologic myopia is defined by structural changes.
practical_applications: Use standard definitions when a script says 'สายตาสั้นมาก' — high myopia = -6.00 D or more.
limitations: Consensus standard for research; other definitions quoted in the paper (e.g. for RAAB surveys) use ≤ −5.00 D for high myopia.

sources.title: Incidence and progression of myopia in secondary school students: Follow-up for 2 years
key_findings: Prospective study of 363 secondary students aged 12-14 in Pathum Thani (82% coverage), examined yearly Sep 2015 - Mar 2017.
Within 19 months the cumulative proportion with myopia (SE ≤ -0.50 D) rose from 24.52% to 31.36%; myopia increased by -0.375 ± 0.247 D per year.
Myopia was not associated with sex (p=0.717) or age (p=0.791); authors state no previous Thai study had shown incidence and progression.
practical_applications: Only Thai figure we may quote, and only as 'การศึกษาหนึ่งในนักเรียนมัธยม จ.ปทุมธานี พบ ~1 ใน 4 มีสายตาผิดปกติ' — never generalise to 'เด็กไทย 25%'.
limitations: Single area, one school population; refraction mostly non-cycloplegic (auto + manifest; cycloplegia only in some cases).
Abstract only (journal page); the 24.52% is myopia in this group, not refractive error in Thai children generally.

sources.title: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults
sources.authors: Singh S, Keller PR, Busija L, McMillan P, Makrai E, Lawrenson JG, Hull CC, Downie LE
key_findings: 17 RCTs, 619 adults; follow-up < 1 day to 5 weeks.
Visual fatigue: may be no difference vs non-blue-filtering lenses at < 1 week (low certainty).
Best-corrected visual acuity: probably little or no effect (moderate certainty, 1 trial, n=156).
Sleep: very uncertain (6 trials, mixed results). Macular health: no trial measured it.
practical_applications: Never claim blue-cut lenses reduce eye strain, improve sleep or protect the retina. Sell them, if at all, as a preference/comfort option with honest wording.
limitations: Short follow-up (< 1 day to 5 weeks); small trials; no meta-analysis possible; long-term outcomes unknown.

sources.title: Are Blue Light-Blocking Glasses Worth It?
key_findings: 'There is no scientific evidence that the light coming from computer screens is damaging to the eyes'; the Academy does not recommend special eyewear for computer use or blue light-blocking glasses.

Eye strain comes from how people use their screens (decreased blinking), 'not by anything coming from the screens'; 'several studies suggest that blue light-blocking glasses do not improve symptoms of digital eye strain'.
Tips: sit about 25 inches (arm's length) from the screen, gaze slightly downward, 20-20-20 breaks, artificial tears when dry; avoid screens 2-3 hours before bed for sleep.
practical_applications: Cite AAO when replacing a blue-light claim with practical screen-habit advice.
limitations: Consumer page; AAO terms forbid copying content into AI programs, so only short paraphrase is kept here.

sources.title: Digital eye strain: prevalence, measurement and amelioration
key_findings: DES (computer vision syndrome) prevalence 'may be 50% or more among computer users'; symptoms fall into accommodative/binocular-stress and external (dry eye) categories.
Cites a US survey of over 10,000 adults with 65% self-reported symptoms (females 69% vs males 60%).
Prevalence estimates vary widely between studies because definitions and questionnaires differ.
practical_applications: Frame screen discomfort as two mechanisms: focusing effort and dry surface (less blinking).
limitations: Narrative review; prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys.

sources.title: The effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision: Testing the 20-20-20 rule
sources.authors: Talens-Estarelles C, Cerviño A, García-Lázaro S, Fogelton A, Sheppard A, Wolffsohn JS
key_findings: 29 symptomatic computer users used webcam software giving personalised 20-20-20 reminders for 2 weeks.
DES and dry-eye symptoms decreased with reminders (p ≤ 0.045) but the improvement 'was not maintained one week after discontinuation'.
No binocular parameter changed except accommodative facility (p = 0.010); no ocular surface/tear film sign changed (p ≥ 0.089).
practical_applications: 20-20-20 may ease symptoms while practised; present as a habit that 'อาจช่วยให้สบายตาขึ้น'.
limitations: Small, uncontrolled before-after design, 2 weeks; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 35963776).

sources.title: 20-20-20 Rule: Are These Numbers Justified?
key_findings: 30 young subjects did a 40-minute tablet reading task four times with 20-second breaks every 5, 10, 20 or 40 (no break) minutes.
Symptoms rose in all four trials (P < .001) but scheduled breaks had no significant effect on symptoms (P = .70), reading speed (P = .93) or accuracy (P = .55).

Conclusion: results 'do not support' 20-second scheduled breaks as a therapeutic intervention; the paper (quoted by Review of Optometry) adds this is not evidence that breaks in general are unhelpful.
practical_applications: Do not present 20-20-20 as proven; suggest real breaks and blinking.
limitations: Single 40-minute sessions in young adults; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 36473088) plus trade-press article.

sources.title: TFOS DEWS II Definition and Classification Report
sources.authors: Craig JP, Nichols KK, Akpek EK, Caffery B, Dua HS, Joo CK, Liu Z, Nelson JD, Nichols JJ, Tsubota K, Stapleton F
key_findings: Definition: dry eye is multifactorial, with loss of tear-film homeostasis as the central concept; tear film instability, hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation and damage, and (for the first time) neurosensory abnormalities are included.

Classification: aqueous-deficient and evaporative dry eye exist as a continuum; diagnosis needs signs and symptoms, and the scheme allows signs without symptoms and symptoms without signs (e.g. neuropathic pain).
practical_applications: Dry eye is a disease to be diagnosed, not something glasses treat; shop content can mention blinking/breaks and refer persistent symptoms.
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 28736335); prevalence figures are in a separate DEWS II report and were not read.

sources.title: Defocus Incorporated Multiple Segments (DIMS) spectacle lenses slow myopia progression: a 2-year randomised clinical trial
sources.authors: Lam CSY, Tang WC, Tse DYY, et al.
key_findings: 183 Hong Kong children aged 8-13, myopia -1.00 to -5.00 D; double-masked RCT DIMS vs single vision.
Progression -0.41 D vs -0.85 D (≈52% slower); axial elongation 0.21 vs 0.55 mm (≈62% less).
21.5% of DIMS wearers had no progression vs 7.4% single vision.
practical_applications: Allowed: 'เลนส์ชะลอสายตาสั้นบางชนิดมีงานวิจัย RCT ว่าชะลอการเพิ่มของสายตาสั้นในเด็กได้ราวครึ่งหนึ่งใน 2 ปี (ในเด็กจีนฮ่องกง)'. Never 'หยุด/รักษาสายตาสั้น'.
limitations: HOYA provided the lenses and spectacles and HOYA staff calculated/manufactured lenses; Chinese children only; 160 analysed (79 DIMS, 81 SV).

sources.title: Spectacle Lenses With Aspherical Lenslets for Myopia Control vs Single-Vision Spectacle Lenses: A Randomized Clinical Trial
key_findings: Wenzhou, children 8-13, SER -0.75 to -4.75 D; HAL vs SAL vs single vision; 157 completed 2 years.
HAL vs SVL: progression -0.66 vs -1.46 D (0.80 D less, ~55%); axial 0.34 vs 0.69 mm (~51%).
Wearing ≥12 h/day: 67% (refraction) and 60% (axial length) slowing; dose-dependent on asphericity and wear time.
practical_applications: Myopia-control lenses only work when worn full-time — say this in any child-myopia content.
limitations: Essilor employed several authors, co-designed the study and analysis; single centre in China.

sources.title: Spectacle Lenses With Highly Aspherical Lenslets for Myopia Control: A Randomized Clinical Trial
sources.authors: Shen J, Hunt C, Young G, Drobe B
key_findings: Double-masked RCT at 9 US sites, children 6-12 years, SER -0.75 to -4.50 D; 159 randomised, 135 (84.9%) completed 24 months.
24-month myopia progression -0.25 D (HAL) vs -0.90 D (single vision): difference 0.64 D, 'a 71% relative reduction'; axial elongation 0.21 vs 0.45 mm, 'a 53% relative reduction'.
Adverse events 11.7% vs 14.6%, none serious or lens related; authors say the findings underlie FDA authorization of the device.
practical_applications: Suggests the effect is not limited to Chinese children — pending verification of the paper.
limitations: Industry trial (Drobe is an Essilor scientist); 2 years only; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 42623028).

sources.title: Interventions for myopia control in children: a living systematic review and network meta-analysis
sources.authors: Lawrenson JG, Shah R, Huntjens B, Downie LE, Virgili G, Dhakal R, Verkicharla PK, Li D, Mavi S, Kernohan A, Li T, Walline JJ
key_findings: 64 RCTs randomising 11,617 children aged 4-18 (60.9% of studies in China/Asia); 12-36 months; certainty very low to moderate. NMA networks poorly connected, so mostly direct pairwise estimates are reported.

At 1 year (control median SER change -0.65 D) SER progression may be reduced by high-dose atropine (MD 0.90 D), moderate-dose (0.65), low-dose atropine (0.38), peripheral-plus spectacles (0.51), multifocal soft contact lenses (0.26) and multifocal spectacles (0.14).
Undercorrected single-vision spectacles: little or no evidence they reduce progression (1 year MD −0.15 D, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.00; 2 years MD 0.02 D).

DIMS (Lam 2020) at 2 years: MD 0.55 D (95% CI 0.38 to 0.72) and axial −0.32 mm; 'inconclusive evidence on whether treatment cessation increases myopia progression'; no economic evaluations of myopia control found.
practical_applications: Position myopia-control lenses as 'หนึ่งในทางเลือกที่มีหลักฐาน' alongside atropine/ortho-K — decided with an eye professional.
limitations: 2023 version read (City, University of London repository copy); later living-review updates not read.

sources.title: Effect of Time Spent Outdoors at School on the Development of Myopia Among Children in China: A Randomized Clinical Trial
sources.authors: He M, Xiang F, Zeng Y, Mai J, Chen Q, Zhang J, Smith W, Rose K, Morgan IG
key_findings: Cluster RCT, grade 1 children in 12 Guangzhou primary schools, Oct 2010 - Oct 2013: 952 intervention, 951 control, mean age 6.6; one extra 40-minute outdoor class each school day plus encouragement of outdoor activity after school.
3-year cumulative myopia incidence 30.4% vs 39.5% (difference -9.1%, 95% CI -14.1% to -4.1%; P < .001).
SER change -1.42 vs -1.59 D (difference 0.17 D, P = .04); axial elongation 0.95 vs 0.98 mm, not significant (P = .07).
practical_applications: Allowed: 'การให้เด็กอยู่กลางแจ้งมากขึ้นช่วยลดโอกาสเริ่มสายตาสั้นได้บ้าง' — a modest, not total, effect.
limitations: Modest effect; China only; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 26372583); compliance figure not read.

sources.title: Time spent in outdoor activities in relation to myopia prevention and control: a meta-analysis and systematic review
key_findings: 25 of 51 articles meta-analysed (23 in children).
Outdoor time protective for incident myopia: clinical trials RR 0.536 (95% CI 0.338-0.850); longitudinal cohorts RR 0.574 (0.395-0.834); cross-sectional OR 0.964.
Trials: myopic shift reduced by 0.30 D after 3 years; but among myopes only, no relationship between outdoor time and progression (R² = 0.00064).
practical_applications: Outdoor time = prevention-of-onset message, not a treatment for a child who already wears glasses.
limitations: Few trials; mix of designs; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 28251836).

sources.title: Interventions to increase time spent outdoors for preventing incidence and progression of myopia in children
sources.authors: Kido A, Miyake M, Watanabe N
key_findings: 5 RCTs (4 cluster-RCTs), 10,733 primary school children mostly in grades 1-2 (aged 6-9).
Incidence: 1 year 7.1% vs 9.5% (RR 0.82, 0.56-1.19, low certainty); 2 years 22.5% vs 26.7% (RR 0.84, 0.72-0.98, moderate certainty); 3 years 30.5% vs 39.8% (RR 0.77, 0.59-1.01, 1 study).

Refraction: MD 0.13 D less myopic shift at 2 years (moderate certainty); authors: interventions 'may potentially reduce the development of myopia' but low certainty makes conclusions on progression difficult. No adverse events reported.
practical_applications: Most conservative wording: 'อาจช่วยลดโอกาสเกิดสายตาสั้น'.
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 38864362); applicability outside East Asia unclear.

sources.title: Ultraviolet radiation (fact sheet)
key_findings: Acute: photokeratitis/photoconjunctivitis (painful, reversible).
Chronic: cataract, pterygium, cancers of/around the eye; possible role in AMD.
Of ~15 million cataract-blind people, 'some 10% may be due to exposure to UVR'.
Advises wraparound sunglasses blocking 99-100% UVA/UVB plus a broad-brimmed hat; water, sand and snow increase UV.
practical_applications: Basis for UV/beach scripts; supports wrap frames and hat advice.
limitations: Global estimate; 10% is an approximate attributable fraction.

sources.title: Global Solar UV Index: A Practical Guide / WHO UV FAQ (ground reflection)
key_findings: 'Grass, soil or water reflect less than 10 per cent of incident UV radiation, sand reflects about 15 per cent, and sea foam about 25 per cent'; fresh snow 'almost doubles a person's UV exposure' (another section of the same page: snow up to 80%).
UV rises about 10% with every 1000 m altitude; light or thin clouds have little effect and may even increase UV; UVA is about 95% of UV reaching the surface.
practical_applications: Beach scripts: reflection is real but modest for water/sand; the bigger factor is time in strong overhead sun and peripheral light.
limitations: Archived WHO FAQ page (undated, Global Solar UV Index era).

sources.title: A review of the epidemiologic evidence linking ultraviolet radiation and cataracts
key_findings: Reviewed against causality criteria; 'the majority of the 22 epidemiologic studies reviewed met most of the epidemiologic criteria for causality and support an association between UV-B and the development of cortical cataract and perhaps posterior subcapsular cataract'.
practical_applications: Say 'UV เป็นปัจจัยเสี่ยงหนึ่งของต้อกระจกบางชนิด' — age remains the main cause.
limitations: Observational evidence; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 12061276).

sources.title: Assessment of the epidemiological evidence that exposure to solar ultraviolet radiation causes cataract
key_findings: Sufficient experimental evidence that artificial UV-B causes cortical opacities in laboratory animals; only limited evidence that solar UV-B causes cortical or posterior subcapsular cataract in humans.
Epidemiological evidence is consistent in suggesting nuclear cataract is not causally associated with solar UV-B.
practical_applications: Counterweight: never say 'แดดทำให้เป็นต้อกระจก' as a flat fact.
limitations: Old review; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 7635000; journal issue dated 1994).

sources.title: Prevalence and risk factors of pterygium: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Rezvan F, Khabazkhoob M, Hooshmand E, Yekta A, Saatchi M, Hashemi H
key_findings: 68 articles, 415,911 participants, 24 countries: pooled pterygium prevalence 12% (95% CI 11-14%); 3% at age 10-20 rising to 19.5% over 80.
Odds ratios: sunlight exposure > 5 h 1.24 (1.11-1.36), rural residence 1.45, outdoor occupation 1.46, male 1.30, alcohol 1.17; sunglasses use 0.47 (0.19-0.57) and smoking 0.84 protective.
Prevalence range 0.07% (clinic-based, Saudi Arabia) to 53% (China).
practical_applications: 'ต้อเนื้อพบมากในคนที่อยู่กลางแจ้งนาน ๆ' is supported; the per-person risk increase is moderate.
limitations: Observational studies; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 29551597).

sources.title: Occupational Exposure to Solar Radiation at Different Latitudes and Pterygium: A Systematic Review of the Last 10 Years of Scientific Literature
key_findings: Cites WHO: population attributable fraction of pterygium due to solar radiation 42-74%.

29 papers (2008-2017): pterygium prevalence rose with mean annual UV index (abstract wording: 'highly increased with latitude and mean annual UV index'); outdoor work, age and male sex are among the most relevant risk factors.
practical_applications: Hua Hin context: fishermen, beach vendors, outdoor workers — good real-life casting for UV stories (without naming real people).
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 29278403); the latitude wording is ambiguous in the abstract, so do not quote it.

sources.title: Optical analysis and reappraisal of the peripheral light focusing theory of nasal pterygia formation
sources.authors: King-Smith PE, Mauger TF, Begley CG, Tankam P
key_findings: Pterygia are far more often nasal (one cited series: 93.6% nasal, 15.5 times more common than temporal); Coroneo's peripheral light focusing (PLF) theory says oblique UV through the temporal cornea is concentrated onto the nasal limbus.

Re-analysis at fixed limbal positions: 'the limbal UV irradiation of the nasal limbus from the PLF was not sufficient to explain the strong nasal location preference'; other explanations such as temporal-to-nasal tear flow should be considered.
practical_applications: Wrap/side coverage advice is reasonable (WHO/AAO also advise wraparound), but don't present 'แสงจากด้านข้างถูกโฟกัส 20 เท่า' as settled.
limitations: Optical modelling study; contested area.

sources.title: How to Choose the Best Sunglasses to Avoid Sun Damage; The Sun, UV Light and Your Eyes (AAO consumer pages)
key_findings: Look for '100% UV protection' or 'UV absorption up to 400nm' (UV400); 'don't be fooled into thinking the darker the lens, the more they'll protect your eyes'.
'Polarization itself does not provide UV protection'; coloured or mirror lenses do not add UV protection; expensive does not mean safer.
Clouds don't block UV; oversize and wraparound frames reduce side entry; wear a broad-brimmed hat; UV is stronger when reflected off water, ice or snow.
practical_applications: Polarised = glare, UV400 = UV — two separate features; good explainer carousel.
limitations: Consumer pages ('How to Choose the Best Sunglasses', 'The Sun, UV Light and Your Eyes'); the news-release URL itself rendered no text. AAO terms forbid copying into AI programs, so paraphrase only.

sources.title: ISO 12312-1:2022 Eye and face protection — Sunglasses and related eyewear — Part 1: Sunglasses for general use
key_findings: ISO catalogue page confirms the 2022 edition: applies to afocal (plano) sunglasses and clip-ons for general use, including road use and driving; excludes sunglasses medically prescribed for attenuating solar radiation, eclipse viewers (ISO 12312-2) and occupational/sport protectors.
Filter categories and the driving rule are known here only through the College of Optometrists' summary of the 2013 edition (see CollegeOptomTints).
practical_applications: Category 4 (very dark) lenses: never advertise as driving sunglasses.
limitations: Standard text not read (paywalled; ISO forbids using its content with AI tools beyond public pages).

sources.title: Tints and driving (clinical guidance)
key_findings: Per BS EN ISO 12312-1:2013: category 0 >80-100% luminous transmittance, 1 >43-80%, 2 >18-43%, 3 >8-18%, 4 >3-8%.

Filters suitable for road use and driving must be category 0-3 (so not category 4), with spectral transmittance ≥ 0.2 × Tv at 475-650 nm and signal-light Q ≥ 0.8 for red and yellow, ≥ 0.6 for yellow, green and blue.
'Sunglass filters with a luminous transmittance of less than 75% are not suitable for road use in twilight or at night.'
practical_applications: Use when making 'เลือกความเข้มเลนส์กันแดด' content.
limitations: UK guidance quoting the 2013 edition of the standard.

sources.title: Methods for Estimating Lens Thickness
key_findings: Sag s ≈ (d/2)² · F / (2000 (n − 1)) with d in mm, F in dioptres: sag rises with power and with the square of diameter, falls as index rises.
Minus lens: edge = s2 − s1 + centre thickness; plus lens: centre = s1 − s2 + edge thickness.
Minimum centre thickness for minus lenses typically 1.0-2.2 mm depending on material and design; rimless/safety may be thicker.
practical_applications: Explain why a smaller, well-centred frame thins a minus lens as much as a higher index does (see README table).
limitations: Thin-lens approximation; manufacturer-era trade article; modern aspheric designs change real numbers.

sources.title: Lens Material Properties (EyeWiki)
sources.authors: Oke I, Sanjiv N, Aggarwal S, Reddy V (AAO EyeWiki)
key_findings: High-index: ≥ 1.60, generally lower Abbe value; lower Abbe → more chromatic aberration (colour fringing in periphery, stronger Rx).
Polycarbonate: superior impact resistance, strong UV absorption, low Abbe; Trivex: high Abbe, light, high impact; CR-39: lower index, blocks ~80% UV untreated.
Reviewed 5 Aug 2026.
practical_applications: 'บางสุด' is not always 'ดีที่สุด' — index trades against Abbe value.
limitations: Few exact numbers on the page.

sources.title: ZEISS finished single vision lens fact sheets (material index, Abbe)
key_findings: 1.59 polycarbonate listed with Abbe 32 (other sources 30-32).
1.74 listed with Abbe vd 32.6 / ve 32 (other trade tables ~33).
practical_applications: Reference numbers for lens-material carousel: 1.50 ≈ 58, 1.56 ≈ 36-43 (varies by maker), 1.60 ≈ 40-42, 1.67 ≈ 31-32, 1.74 ≈ 32-33 — check the exact product sheet before posting.
limitations: Values for 1.50/1.56/1.60/1.67 not read from the sheet this session (2023 PDF 404); figures in the application line are typical trade values to verify.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

sources.title: Transitions XTRActive New Generation (product page)
sources.authors: Nikon Lenswear (Transitions licensee); Shamir Thailand page
key_findings: Manufacturer claim: XTRActive New Generation is 'the only photochromic lens achieving category 2 levels' behind the windshield: 18%-43% transmittance at 23 °C (polycarbonate and 1.5 grey).
Claims category 3 (<18% T) outdoors at 35 °C and 100% UVA/UVB blocking; 'photochromic performance is influenced by temperature, UV exposure and lens material'.
practical_applications: Never sell standard photochromic as 'ใส่ขับรถแทนแว่นกันแดดได้'.
limitations: Manufacturer test conditions; the polarised version was not checked on this page.

sources.title: Self-tinting lenses for more comfortable vision, flexibility and protection (ZEISS)
key_findings: ZEISS: 'a huge amount of UV rays are absorbed by a car's windshield, which has an effect on the lens performance'; PhotoFusion X retains more tint in the car than earlier generations, but 'sunglasses are still recommended for longer trips'.
'Self-tinting lenses darken less in bright sunlight when outdoor temperatures are high', so ZEISS recommends carrying sunglasses in warmer areas.
Darkens in 15-30 seconds and clears in as little as 2 minutes (manufacturer figures).
practical_applications: Hua Hin is hot: tell customers photochromic may not get as dark at the beach at noon as in brochures.
limitations: Manufacturer page; no quantified temperature curve; patent and retailer guides not re-read.

sources.title: Troubleshooting varifocals (CPD article)
key_findings: 'Adaption periods of around two to four weeks should be emphasised to first-time wearers'; expectations (e.g. a narrower reading zone) should be managed at the dispense.
Common remake causes: fitting heights measured off eye level or with slouched posture; check prescription, fitting cross and lens design (trial frame) before blaming the lens.
Manufacturers typically assume a pantoscopic angle of around 8-10° for conventional PALs; more tilt brings the near zone closer and widens the near field.
practical_applications: Progressive content must mention adaptation and correct fitting; no 'ใส่ปุ๊บชัดปั๊บทุกคน'.
limitations: Practitioner CPD article with case examples; gives no non-tolerance rate.

sources.title: The impact of different lenses on visual and musculoskeletal complaints in VDU workers with work-related neck complaints: a randomized controlled trial
key_findings: RCT: 35 VDU workers aged 45-65 from a financial holding in Ghent with neck complaints, VDU progressive (n=18) vs general progressive (n=17).
Both groups improved in visual fatigue and neck pain at 3 and 6 months; 'little difference in effect of the different lenses'; the VDU group rated its lenses more suitable for VDU work.
Cites Horgen et al.: a 1-year RCT of 3 VDU progressive designs vs single vision found a significant neck-pain reduction with one VDU lens type.
practical_applications: Office lenses: present as comfort for long desk work with a wider intermediate zone, not as a neck-pain treatment.
limitations: Small; neck-pain change below the minimal clinically important difference.

sources.title: Guidelines for Appropriate Referral of Persons with Possible Eye Diseases or Injury
key_findings: Prompt referral to an ophthalmologist for: failure to achieve normal acuity; significant eye injury, eye pain or periocular trauma; flashes, recent floaters, halos, transient dimming or distortion, obscured vision, loss of vision, pain in eye/lids/orbit, double vision, excessive tearing.

Also: any visual field loss, media opacities or fundus/optic nerve abnormalities, lid/orbit tumour or swelling or protruding eye, inflammation with or without discharge, strabismus not corrected by glasses, abnormal IOP or glaucoma family history, diabetes without a recent retinal exam, thyroid eye signs.
practical_applications: Red-flag list in FACT_CHECK_WORKFLOW and in any shop post about 'when to see a doctor'.
limitations: US professional guidance (2014 PDF).

sources.title: ZEISS Individual 2 fitting & dispensing guide; ZEISS Individual SV white paper
key_findings: Default pantoscopic tilt 9° and vertex distance 12.5 mm if not measured; fitting height range 13-35 mm; monocular PD measured with pupillometer.
Individual lenses are optimised to measured tilt, wrap and vertex.
ZEISS webinar: 2 mm centration error can reduce binocular field of view by up to 25% (manufacturer claim).
practical_applications: Shop-craft content: 'วัดค่าเฉพาะตัว' (PD, fitting height, tilt) as a real reason a progressive works or fails.
limitations: Older guides (2010-2020); manufacturer figures.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

sources.title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You (AAO)
key_findings: Titanium frames: 'very strong, lightweight and corrosion-resistant' and hypoallergenic; Flexon is a titanium alloy, also hypoallergenic.
Monel (mixed metals) 'may have nickel or other metals that can cause allergic reactions', though most have a protective coating; stainless steel is light, strong, corrosion-resistant and cheaper.

Plastics: zyl (cellulose acetate) easy for opticians to adjust; blended nylon strong and light for sport/wraparound; Optyl becomes malleable when heated; plastic frames break more easily than metal and colour may fade.
practical_applications: Hot car dashboard in Hua Hin can deform acetate — useful care tip.
limitations: AAO consumer page only; the All About Vision page was not reachable, so claims about TR90 and nickel in stainless steel are not verified.

sources.title: Ministry drafts regulation on eyesight-testing and spectacle-fitting businesses
key_findings: 17 Jun 2026: MOPH draft ministerial regulation would make 'กิจการตรวจวัดสายตาประกอบแว่น' a health-business establishment (Health Establishment law).
Shops need a licence; testers must register and complete a specific training course.
Scope: refractive errors (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia) in people aged 12+; no eye-muscle exams; under-12s and eye-muscle problems go to a medical facility/specialist.
Effective 180 days after Gazette publication; existing shops get 180 days to apply. Status: draft (public hearing).
practical_applications: Do not market 'ตรวจสายตาเด็ก' at the shop for under-12s if this rule is enacted; refer to an eye doctor.
limitations: News report of a draft; check Royal Gazette for final text. Confirmed by Thansettakij (17 Jun 2026).

sources.title: Optometry Association complains of delayed professional legislation
key_findings: 18 Jun 2026: Optometry Association of Thailand asked the House health committee to speed up optometry legislation; slow licence renewals; unlicensed people impersonating optometrists.

No optometry council (สภา) is mentioned; Thai news (Khaosod/Matichon snippets) says optometry is a branch of the Art of Healing (พ.ร.บ.การประกอบโรคศิลปะ พ.ศ. 2542) and a draft Royal Decree on optometry was open for comment until 13 Nov 2026.
practical_applications: Only call staff 'นักทัศนมาตร' if they hold the licence; otherwise 'ช่างวัดสายตา/ผู้ตรวจวัดสายตา'. Do not refer to 'สภาการทัศนมาตรศาสตร์' as an existing regulator.
limitations: News; the Art of Healing / Royal Decree detail is from search snippets only.

sources.title: Thai FDA issues medical device advertising regulations
key_findings: Thai FDA announcement B.E. 2568 (2025) on medical device advertising, effective 4 Jan 2025, revokes the B.E. 2564 (2021) announcement; anyone advertising a medical device needs an FDA licence (Form Kor Por. 2), valid up to 3 years.

Prohibited: false or exaggerated benefits, quality, standards, components or source (Section 59(1), Medical Device Act B.E. 2551) and Schedule 1 words such as 'best, excellent, special, miraculous, perfect, completely cured, instantaneous, the safest, No.1, definitely, superior, no side effects'; also endorsement by individuals and comparison with other operators' devices.
Ads must show the advertiser, the ad licence number and warnings; devices exempted by MOPH announcement are outside this rule.
practical_applications: Treat lens-benefit claims (myopia control, blue light) as medical-device claims: no exaggeration, use only manufacturer-approved wording, consider whether Thai FDA ad approval applies (contact lenses clearly do).
limitations: Consultancy summary, not the Gazette text; whether spectacle lenses/frames are exempt was NOT confirmed.

sources.title: Varilux XR series wins the Silmo d'Or (EssilorLuxottica newsroom)
key_findings: Claims 9/10 wearers experienced 'instant sharpness' at all distances and in motion; 95% adapted by day one.
Basis: Eurosyn in-life study, France 2022, n=73 progressive wearers, 2 weeks, sponsored by Essilor.
practical_applications: If quoted: 'จากการทดสอบของผู้ผลิตกับผู้ใช้ 73 คน' — never as independent fact.
limitations: Sponsor study, small n, no independent replication found.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

sources.title: In conversation with Dr Natalia Vlasak about the Miyosmart iQ spectacle lens (AOP Optometry Today)
sources.authors: HOYA Vision Care; AOP Optometry Today
key_findings: HOYA (interview): Miyosmart iQ 12-month RCT in children aged 4-12 showed 'no myopia progression on average' and, per ARVO 2026 results, halted 'clinically relevant myopia progression' in nine out of 10 children.
Previous-generation MiYOSMART slowed progression 'on average by 59% at the 24-month wearing period'; iQ changes: segments closer to centre, segment power +3.5 D to +4.5 D, wider treatment zone.
practical_applications: Use the peer-reviewed Lam 2020 numbers, not '>100%' marketing figures.
limitations: Company statements; iQ data conference-only, not peer-reviewed; the earlier '>100% efficacy' wording and a US approval disclaimer were not on the page read.

sources.title: ZEISS BlueGuard (product page, fact sheet)
key_findings: Claims BlueGuard blocks 'up to 40% of potentially harmful blue light' (BVB metric) with full UV protection, built into the lens material.
'Up to 50% fewer reflections of digital blue light' than ZEISS's own DuraVision Plus BlueProtect coating.
'93% of wearers feel less digital eye strain' and 95% prefer BlueGuard; basis: consumer acceptance survey, n=187 wearers in China, May 2021.
practical_applications: Allowed: 'ลดแสงสีฟ้าบางส่วน สะท้อนน้อยลง (ข้อมูลผู้ผลิต)'. Not allowed: 'ลดอาการตาล้า/ป้องกันจอประสาทตาเสื่อม'.
limitations: Manufacturer page; it says blue-light lenses alleviate DES, which Singh 2023 Cochrane and AAO do not support.

sources.title: Presbyopia (NEI eye conditions page)
key_findings: Presbyopia makes near vision hard for middle-aged and older adults; 'Everyone gets presbyopia as they get older — usually after age 45.'
Cause: with age the lens gets harder and less flexible and stops focusing light correctly; 'Many people have another refractive error in addition to presbyopia.'
It gets worse over time but 'usually stops getting worse after age 65'; managed with reading glasses, prescribed lenses or contact lenses.
practical_applications: Supports 'ทุกคนเป็นได้ แม้เคยสายตาดีหรือสายตาสั้น' and onset 'ราววัย 40 กลาง ๆ ขึ้นไป' (NEI says usually after 45).
limitations: Consumer page; replaces StatPearls (NCBI blocked by a browser check).

sources.title: Analysis of pterygium size and induced corneal astigmatism
key_findings: 77 eyes with unilateral primary pterygium: corneal astigmatism 1.2 ± 0.9 D vs 0.6 ± 0.5 D in fellow eyes (P < 0.0001); with-the-rule 49.4%, against-the-rule 36.4%, oblique 14.3%.
Extension correlated best with astigmatism (r = 0.462), then total area (r = 0.447) and width (r = 0.348).
'Pterygium induced 2 D of corneal astigmatism when its extension exceeded 2.2 mm, width exceeded 5 mm, or total area exceeded 6.25 mm²'.
practical_applications: Supports 'ต้อเนื้อที่ลามเข้ากระจกตาทำให้สายตาเอียงได้'; refer to an eye doctor, do not imply glasses fix it.
limitations: Single-centre, 77 eyes; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 18434847). Replaces 'Kampitak2003Astig': that title actually belongs to this paper and the figures recorded for Kampitak (243 eyes, 2.25 mm) could not be found.

sources.title: Stoicism
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: Virtue (perfected reason) is necessary and sufficient for happiness; health, wealth, reputation are 'indifferents'
Some indifferents are 'preferred' (health) and it is appropriate to select them, but they do not decide happiness
Passions (pathe) are excessive impulses from false judgements; the sage has 'good feelings' (eupatheiai); pre-emotions (propatheiai) happen without assent
Assent is 'up to us' in a way that receiving an impression is not
practical_applications: Stoic characters may still prefer health/comfort; the point is not to stake happiness on them
A first flinch of fear is human (pre-emotion); the story beat is what the character assents to next
limitations: Read through a fetch summariser; long entry, only the first ~100k characters were processed
Author line not captured

sources.title: Epictetus (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Epictetus (c. 55-135 CE), former slave, taught at Nicopolis; wrote nothing; Discourses and Handbook (Enchiridion) come via his student Arrian
Handbook opens: some things are up to us (opinions, impulses, desires, aversions) and some are not (body, possessions, reputation, office)
Prohairesis = faculty of choice/moral character; key practice is testing impressions before assenting
Roles theory: our social 'names' (son, citizen...) point to appropriate acts; life as a play where we do not pick the part
practical_applications: Dichotomy-of-control dialogues for Mint & Tao
Stoicism is role-based and social, not detachment from people
limitations: Year and author of IEP entry not captured
Arrian vs Epictetus authorship debate unresolved

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius
key_findings: Meditations is a private Greek notebook written to himself; title given later by an editor (Casaubon)
Themes: imminence of death, cosmos as a city, acting justly and loving what is allotted, no hatred of others
Draws on Epictetus whom he names
practical_applications: Marcus suits 'notes to self' formats (journal page, pencil notebook) — matches how the text was written
Use his ideas as reminders the character tells themself, not as lectures to others
limitations: First published 2010, revised 2025 per fetch

sources.title: Seneca
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: Works: Letters to Lucilius, On Anger, On the Shortness of Life, Natural Questions
Emotions are judgements; focus on the progressor (proficiens) rather than the perfect sage
Tension: he admits blushing at a humble carriage (Letter 87.4) — gap between knowing and feeling; also wealth and gender/class remarks
practical_applications: 'Progressor' framing fits Slowly Growing: characters who are trying, not perfect
Seneca can be shown as imperfect — honest, relatable

Revised 2024

sources.title: Albert Camus
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: The absurd = gap between the human demand for meaning and the silent world
Myth of Sisyphus ends 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy'; rejects escapes such as hope in an afterlife
The Rebel: 'I revolt, therefore we are'; limits and solidarity over utopian violence
The Plague: fighting a plague with 'common decency'
Camus rejected the existentialist label
practical_applications: Repetitive daily tasks (cleaning lenses, washing cups) as Sisyphus scenes — lucid, not falsely cheerful
Never label Camus 'existentialist' in captions
limitations: Entry year/author not captured

sources.title: Existentialism
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: 'Existence precedes essence' (Sartre): no fixed nature; we define ourselves through choices
Freedom is situated (facticity + transcendence), not 'do anything'
Anxiety reveals open possibilities; authenticity = owning one's projects; bad faith = self-deception that denies facticity or freedom
Beauvoir: willing oneself free is bound up with others' freedom
practical_applications: Mint saying 'I'm just not a person who...' = gentle bad-faith beat; Tao answers with situated freedom
limitations: Entry author/year not captured

sources.title: Aristotle's Ethics
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: Eudaimonia = activity of the rational soul in accordance with virtue, sustained over a life — not a mood
Virtue is a mean between excess and deficiency, relative to circumstances, not a formula
Ethical virtue is built by habituation; completed by practical wisdom (phronesis)
Three bases of friendship: goodness, pleasure, advantage
practical_applications: Small repeated acts as growth = core Slowly Growing theme with a real source
Friendship-of-character is a good frame for Mint & Tao themselves

The 'one swallow' line was not in the processed part — do not quote it from this source

sources.title: Aristotle's Aesthetics (Poetics)
sources.authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: Mimesis is central; plot (mythos) is the most important part of tragedy
Plot needs unity and a size that can be held in memory
Peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) are key sources of emotional effect; should follow probability/necessity
Catharsis meaning is disputed (purgation, clarification, consolation, relief)
practical_applications: A 2-line Mint & Tao story = a micro recognition (anagnorisis): line 2 reframes line 1
Do not claim one fixed meaning of catharsis

sources.title: Zhuangzi
key_findings: Perspectival relativism: daos 'are made by walking them'
Happy fish debate with Hui Shi; useless tree survives because useless
Exemplars are skilled craftsmen (Cook Ding) acting with ease; butterfly dream: 'things change'
Only the Inner Chapters (1-7) are linked to Zhuangzi's own period; text edited by Guo Xiang

sources.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
key_findings: 100 studies from three 2008 psychology journals were replicated with high-powered designs.
35 of 97 replications (36%) were significant in the original direction vs 97% of originals; mean effect size fell from .403 to .197.
By journal/area: JPSP social 23%, JEP:LMC cognitive 48%, Psych Science social 29%, Psych Science cognitive 53% significant replications.
Replication success tracked the strength of the original evidence.
practical_applications: Treat single famous social-psychology findings as provisional; prefer meta-analyses and large replications when writing 'science says' content.
Cognitive effects replicated more often than social ones in this sample.
limitations: One replication per study; sample of three journals only.
Gilbert et al. (2016) technical comment disputed the interpretation; OSC replied.
sources.license: copyrighted (author version posted with AAAS permission)

sources.title: Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings
key_findings: Preregistered replications of 28 findings; each protocol run in ~half of 125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries/territories.
15 of 28 (54%) significant in the original direction at p < .05 (14, 50%, at p < .0001); 21 (75%) had smaller effects than the original; 9 (32%) went in the opposite direction.
Median Cohen's d: 0.60 original vs 0.15 replication; 16 (57%) replications had d < .20.
Little heterogeneity from task order, lab vs online, or WEIRD vs less-WEIRD samples: variation was more attributable to the effect than to sample/setting.
practical_applications: An effect that fails does not usually 'work only in some cultures'; an effect that works tends to work broadly. Relevant when importing Western findings to Thai audiences.
limitations: Only 28 effects; mostly short online/lab tasks.
Read from the LSE author manuscript (accepted version).

sources.title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
sources.authors: Hagger, M. S., Chatzisarantis, N. L. D., et al.
key_findings: Registered Replication Report: 23 labs, total N = 2,141, standardized sequential-task protocol based on Sripada et al.
Ego-depletion effect d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] - small, CI includes zero.
Motivated by an earlier meta-analysis reporting a medium-sized effect and later meta-analyses that questioned its size and flagged possible bias.
practical_applications: Do not write stories or captions claiming 'willpower is a battery that runs out' as fact.
limitations: Critics (e.g. Dang 2016 commentary) argue the e-crossing manipulation may not have been depleting; a null for one paradigm is not proof the theory is wrong in every form.
Read from the KOPS (Konstanz) repository copy.

sources.title: Behavioral priming: it's all in the mind, but whose mind?
sources.authors: Doyen, S., Klein, O., Pichon, C.-L., Cleeremans, A.
key_findings: Experiment 1: replication of Bargh, Chen & Burrows (1996) with automated (infrared) timing and a larger sample found no walking-speed priming effect.
Experiment 2: a walking-speed effect appeared only when experimenters were led to expect slower walking - experimenter expectations helped produce the effect.
Debriefing suggested participants were aware of the primes; authors conclude behavioural priming, while real, involves different mechanisms than usually assumed.
practical_applications: Avoid 'show old-age words and people slow down' type claims; subtle-word social priming is weak evidence.
limitations: Bargh disputed the study publicly; the paper itself was not read in full this session.

sources.title: Reconstruction of a train wreck: How priming research went off the rails
sources.authors: Schimmack, U., Heene, M., Kesavan, K.
key_findings: R-Index analysis of the 12 articles cited in the priming chapter (ch. 4) of Thinking, Fast and Slow: 11 of 12 had R-Index below 50.
Kahneman responded that behavioural priming effects 'cannot be as large and as robust as my chapter suggested' (as quoted in secondary coverage).
practical_applications: Use Thinking, Fast and Slow for the System 1/2 framing and heuristics, but not its social-priming chapter.
limitations: Blog post by the critics themselves, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
key_findings: Existence and edition confirmed (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Background framing for fast intuitive vs slow deliberate thinking; check each specific claim against replication literature (see Schimmack2017).
limitations: Popular book; priming chapter is not well supported by later replications.

sources.title: Assessing the robustness of power posing: No effect on hormones and risk tolerance in a large sample of men and women
sources.authors: Ranehill, E., Dreber, A., Johannesson, M., Leiberg, S., Sul, S., Weber, R. A.
key_findings: N = 200 (original N = 42), experimenter blind to condition, >95% power.
Power posing raised self-reported feelings of power but had no significant effect on hormones or any of three behavioural tasks.
practical_applications: A posture can change how people say they feel, but don't claim it changes hormones or performance.
limitations: Conceptual (not exact) replication.

sources.title: Power posing: P-curving the evidence
key_findings: P-curve of the 33 studies cited by Carney, Cuddy & Yap (2015) did not show evidential value (flat p-curve) once selective reporting is considered.
Original first author Dana Carney later stated she no longer believes power-pose effects are real (separate statement).
practical_applications: Classic example of a viral pop-psych claim to avoid in content.
limitations: Cuddy, Schultz & Fosse (2018) ran their own p-curve on a broader set and claimed evidential value for felt power; critics say it mixed effect directions. Not read directly.

sources.title: Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk
key_findings: Replication of the Kahneman & Tversky (1979) choice items with N = 4,098 (author manuscript) from 19 countries, 13 languages.
Results replicated for 94% of the 17 choice items and 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts; effects were at most attenuated vs 1979.
About a third of participants knew of loss aversion; awareness had only a very modest effect on choices.
practical_applications: Loss framing ('what you lose by squinting every day') is on firmer ground than social priming.
limitations: Hypothetical choices; Thailand not necessarily among the 19 countries (not checked).
Read the Oxford ORA author manuscript ('Not lost in translation'); it tests prospect-theory choice patterns, not the size of loss aversion directly.
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

sources.title: Bad is stronger than good
sources.authors: Baumeister, R. F., Bratslavsky, E., Finkenauer, C., Vohs, K. D.
key_findings: Across everyday events, trauma, relationships, social networks, interactions, feedback and learning, bad events have more impact than good ones.
Bad impressions and stereotypes form faster and resist disconfirmation more than good ones; 'hardly any exceptions' found.
Cites Gottman (1994): stable relationships need at least ~5 positive interactions per negative one.
practical_applications: One bad shop experience outweighs several good ones - service stories should show repair, not only delight.
In Mint & Tao conflicts, one harsh line needs several warm beats to recover.
limitations: Narrative review, not meta-analysis; the 5:1 ratio is Gottman's index cited by the review, not a universal law.

sources.title: Duration neglect in retrospective evaluations of affective episodes
key_findings: Study 1 (32 Ss) and Study 2 (96 Ss) with film clips: duration had small effects on retrospective evaluations.
Evaluations behave like a weighted average of 'snapshots'; a peak & end rule accounted for 94% of variance in an earlier procedure dataset, duration only 3% more.
practical_applications: Endings and the strongest moment dominate memory of a clip or a shop visit: design a clear peak and a warm last beat.
limitations: Authors themselves urge caution about partial correlations; later work (secondary) suggests day-long experiences may not follow peak-end.

sources.title: The psychology of curiosity: A review and reinterpretation
key_findings: Curiosity is a cognitively induced deprivation arising from a perceived gap in knowledge (information-gap theory).
Earlier theories missed why people voluntarily seek curiosity and its intensity, transience, link to impulsivity and tendency to disappoint once satisfied.
practical_applications: Open a specific, answerable gap on slide 1 and close it on the last slide.
limitations: Abstract content known only through secondary pages this session.

sources.title: The wick in the candle of learning: Epistemic curiosity activates reward circuitry and enhances memory
sources.authors: Kang, M. J., Hsu, M., Krajbich, I. M., Loewenstein, G., McClure, S. M., Wang, J. T., Camerer, C. F.
key_findings: Curiosity about trivia questions was an inverted-U function of confidence, peaking near 50% confidence (r = .44 with P(1-P)).
Curiosity correlated with caudate activity (reward anticipation); people paid tokens/waiting time to learn answers.
Higher curiosity predicted better recall of surprising answers 1-2 weeks later.
practical_applications: Best hooks are questions the viewer half-knows ('Why do arms get longer after 40?'), not total mysteries or obvious ones.
limitations: Small fMRI samples; trivia questions, not stories or ads.

sources.title: Nostalgia: Past, present, and future
sources.authors: Sedikides, C., Wildschut, T., Arndt, J., Routledge, C.
key_findings: Nostalgia = sentimental longing for one's past; predominantly positive, self-relevant, social emotion.
Narratives feature the self as protagonist among close others, often with a redemption sequence (bad start -> good end).
Triggered by negative mood and especially loneliness; raises positive affect, self-esteem, social connectedness, and buffers existential threat.
Over 80% of British undergraduates reported nostalgia at least weekly.
practical_applications: Nostalgia content (first pair of glasses, grandparent reading with glasses) should centre on people, not objects, and end on warmth.
limitations: Mostly Western student samples in early work; short review.

sources.title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
sources.authors: Ryan, R. M., Deci, E. L.
key_findings: Three innate psychological needs - competence, autonomy, relatedness - when satisfied yield enhanced self-motivation and well-being.
Focus on social contexts that facilitate vs forestall self-motivation.
practical_applications: Characters grow when they choose (autonomy), get better at something (competence) and feel connected (relatedness); ads that pressure undermine autonomy.
limitations: Abstract-level only this session.

sources.title: Basic psychological need satisfaction, need frustration, and need strength across four cultures
sources.authors: Chen, B., Vansteenkiste, M., et al.
key_findings: Study 1: late adolescents in Belgium and China (N = 685, mean age 17); Study 2: Belgium, China, USA, Peru (N = 1,051, mean age 20).
Satisfaction of each need (autonomy, relatedness, competence) uniquely predicted well-being; frustration of each uniquely predicted ill-being.
Effects were equivalent across the four countries and not moderated by need valuation or need desire.
practical_applications: Supports using SDT needs in Thai content too (cross-cultural, incl. an East Asian sample).
limitations: Students/young adults; no Thai sample; cross-sectional.

sources.title: Maslow reconsidered: A review of research on the need hierarchy theory
sources.authors: Wahba, M. A., Bridwell, L. G.
key_findings: Review of ten factor-analytic and three ranking studies gave only partial support for Maslow.
No clear evidence for five distinct need categories or for a fixed hierarchy; some evidence for two types (deficiency vs growth).
practical_applications: Don't present Maslow's pyramid as proven science in content.
limitations: Old review; title taken from common citation, not confirmed on page this session.

sources.title: Needs and subjective well-being around the world
key_findings: Data from 123 countries: fulfilment of Maslow-type needs correlates with well-being across cultures.
The order in which needs are met has little bearing on their contribution; people report social and self-actualisation needs met even when basic needs are not fully met.
practical_applications: Belonging and respect matter even to customers under money pressure; don't assume 'price first, feelings later'.
limitations: Known only via university press release and coverage this session.

sources.title: Psychology 2e (sections 9.2 Lifespan Theories, 9.3 Stages of Development, 10.1 Motivation, 12.4 Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience)
sources.authors: Spielman, R. M., Jenkins, W. J., Lovett, M. D.
key_findings: Erikson: generativity vs stagnation (30-64) and integrity vs despair (65+); stage theories increasingly replaced by continuous, context-dependent views.

Middle adulthood: visual acuity decreases; crystallized intelligence stable or rising. Late adulthood: fluid intelligence and processing speed decline; networks shrink but remaining friendships stay as close or closer (Carstensen SST).
Motivation: overjustification effect strongest for expected tangible rewards; Yerkes-Dodson; self-efficacy; Maslow criticised for rigid ordering.
Asch: 76% conformed at least once; one dissenter cuts conformity near zero; normative vs informational influence; Milgram 65%, lower when victim closer.
practical_applications: Customers 40+ are in the generativity stage - stories about helping grandchildren/teaching fit.
One honest 'dissenting' voice in a group story is enough to break conformity.
limitations: Intro textbook; page states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and forbids use for training generative AI without permission - paraphrase only, do not copy text.
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per page footer (search snippet of preface said CC BY 4.0 - conflicting)

sources.title: How replicable are links between personality traits and consequential life outcomes? The Life Outcomes of Personality Replication Project
key_findings: Preregistered replications of 78 Big Five trait-outcome associations (median N = 1,504).
~87% replicated in expected direction; effects ~77% as strong as originals.
practical_applications: Big Five is a sound base for character bibles (e.g. Mint high openness, Tao high conscientiousness).
limitations: Cross-sectional self-report online samples.

sources.title: Cautionary comments regarding the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
key_findings: Insufficient evidence for the tenets of and claims about the MBTI.
Forcing continuous traits into dichotomous types weakens construct validity; earlier work reported 5-week retest type stability of 39-76% depending on dichotomy.
practical_applications: MBTI letters may be used as a playful pop-culture hook only, never as science.
limitations: Publisher (Myers-Briggs Co.) and some commentators dispute the reliability critique.

sources.title: Culture and conformity: A meta-analysis of studies using Asch's (1952b, 1956) line judgment task
key_findings: 68 reports, 133 Asch-type experiments, 4,627 participants, 17 countries (97 of the studies from the USA).
Unweighted mean d = 1.06 (median 0.96); strong heterogeneity (Q = 450.8, df 132).
US conformity has declined since the 1950s; collectivist countries tended to show higher conformity than individualist ones (three individualism-collectivism surveys).
practical_applications: In a collectivist context like Thailand, 'what people like us do' may carry extra weight - but test it.
limitations: Unbalanced sample (79 US studies); no Thai data noted.

sources.title: A room with a viewpoint: Using social norms to motivate environmental conservation in hotels
sources.authors: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., Griskevicius, V.
key_findings: Two hotel field experiments on towel-reuse signs.
Exp. 1: descriptive-norm sign ('almost 75% of guests reuse') 44.1% reuse vs standard environmental sign 35.1% (chi2(1, N = 433) = 3.72, p = .05).

Exp. 2: descriptive norms combined 44.5% vs standard 37.2%; provincial norm ('guests in this room') 49.3% vs the other descriptive norms 42.8% (N = 1,318); citizen (43.5%), gender (40.9%) and guest (44.0%) identity norms did not differ from one another.
practical_applications: Real, local social proof ('many Hua Hin customers choose ...') - only when true.
limitations: German replication succeeded (Bohner & Schlueter 2014); a US resort study found the provincial-norm advantage non-significant.
Read from the University of Minnesota Carlson School copy.

sources.title: The Minimal Group Paradigm and its maximal impact in research on social categorization
key_findings: Current Opinion in Psychology 11, 85-89 (short review).
The Minimal Group Paradigm studies social categorization with arbitrary, novel groups and no realistic conflict of interest; it shaped Social Identity Theory and Self-Categorization Theory.
Recent variants extend it beyond in-group favouritism/discrimination to many other research fields.
practical_applications: Simple shared labels ('glasses people', 'Hua Hin locals') can create in-group warmth; avoid out-group mocking.
limitations: Title and details known via search summary only.

sources.title: An integrative model of organizational trust
sources.authors: Mayer, R. C., Davis, J. H., Schoorman, F. D.
key_findings: Conceptual model with research propositions (not an empirical test).
Trust = willingness to be vulnerable to another party, distinguished from trustworthiness and from risk-taking.
Perceived trustworthiness = ability, benevolence, integrity; the trustor's propensity to trust also affects trust.
practical_applications: Shop content should show all three: skill (accurate eye test), care (staff go extra), integrity (honest advice, e.g. 'you don't need new lenses yet').
limitations: Later reviewers question whether all three facets have unique effects.

sources.title: Hope theory: Rainbows in the mind
key_findings: Hope = agency (goal-directed energy) + pathways (planning routes to goals), anchored by goals.
High-hope people generate alternate pathways when blocked; pathways and agency feed each other.
practical_applications: Hopeful stories show a goal, a blocked route, and a new route - not just positive feelings.
limitations: Known via secondary sources; commentaries (Aspinwall & Leaf) question overlap with optimism/self-efficacy.

sources.title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories
sources.authors: Tannenbaum, M. B., Hepler, J., Zimmerman, R. S., et al.
key_findings: 127 papers (9% unpublished), 248 independent samples, N = 27,372.
Average effect on attitudes/intentions/behaviours d = 0.27 fixed-effects [0.25, 0.30]; random-effects d = 0.29 [0.22, 0.35] (attitudes 0.23, intentions 0.31, behaviours 0.27).

Efficacy statements increased effectiveness (95% CI 0.41-0.49 with vs 0.16-0.22 without), but fear appeals without efficacy did NOT backfire on average: significant negative effects in 9/154 low-efficacy vs 3/94 high-efficacy studies (n.s., Fisher p = .54) - the weak, not the strong, efficacy hypothesis was supported.
High vs moderate depicted fear: d = 0.02 [-0.05, 0.09] (21 samples) - no gain from more fear beyond moderate, and no backfire.
More effective when high susceptibility and severity were depicted, for one-time (vs repeated) behaviours, and for audiences that were more female, from collectivist cultures, or young adults.
practical_applications: Fear (e.g. UV / pterygium risk) can persuade, but pair it with a clear, easy action.
limitations: EPPM-specific results and moderators not read this session.
Read the 2015 UIUC dissertation (IDEALS) on which the Psychological Bulletin article is based - same sample counts; published numbers may differ slightly.

sources.title: Putting the fear back into fear appeals: The extended parallel process model
key_findings: Communication Monographs 59(4). Theory paper: integrates Janis, Leventhal and Rogers into the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), based on Leventhal's danger control / fear control framework.

Per the abstract it aims to explain why fear appeals fail (boomerang/curvilinear results), re-incorporates fear as a central variable, and states threat-efficacy relations as propositions for future research.
Standard EPPM summary (secondary): high threat + high efficacy -> danger control; high threat + low efficacy -> fear control (denial, avoidance).
practical_applications: Every scare message needs response efficacy and self-efficacy ('a UV400 lens blocks it; come in for a free check').
limitations: Known via encyclopedia and citing meta-analysis (Bigsby & Albarracin 2021) only.
Only the abstract (via OpenAlex) was read. The threat x efficacy predictions are propositions; Tannenbaum2015 found no average backfire for low-efficacy messages.

sources.title: Empathy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.authors: Stueber, K. (author name not shown in fetched text)
key_findings: Distinguishes emotional contagion, empathy proper (with self-other distinction), cognitive empathy/perspective taking, sympathy/empathic concern, and personal distress.
Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis: empathic concern produces altruistic motivation ('easy escape' studies); critics propose egoistic alternatives.
Prinz and Bloom: empathy is biased toward the near, similar, cute, in-group and identifiable individual; perspective taking has more positive effects than affective empathy alone.
practical_applications: Show one specific person (identifiable) to evoke empathy, but avoid making the audience feel personal distress (they look away).
limitations: Only the first ~100k of ~150k characters read; author name not confirmed on page (first published 2008, revised 2025).

sources.title: Empathy: A review of the concept
sources.authors: Cuff, B. M. P., Brown, S. J., Taylor, L., Howat, D. J.
key_findings: Review of 43 discrete definitions of empathy; eight themes: distinguishing empathy from other concepts, cognitive or affective, congruent or incongruent, subject to other stimuli, self-other distinction or merging, trait or state, behavioural outcome, automatic or controlled.
Separates empathy from related concepts such as sympathy and proposes a new integrated conceptualisation.
practical_applications: Say which kind of empathy a scene targets: feel-with (affective) or understand (cognitive).
limitations: Full text not accessed (core.ac.uk returned 403).
Read from the Northampton repository author version.

sources.title: The origins of attachment theory: John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth
key_findings: Bowlby built attachment theory from ethology, control systems, information processing and psychoanalysis; Ainsworth added the secure-base concept and the first empirical study (Uganda).
Internal working models of self and others let people predict the world; out-of-date models after drastic change can cause problems.
Attachment is not regression - it serves a healthy function in adult life too.
practical_applications: Characters' reactions to separation/loss (a parent's old glasses) follow attachment logic: seeking proximity, protest, then reorganisation.
limitations: Historical review, not evidence synthesis.

sources.title: Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process
key_findings: Applied Ainsworth's three styles to adult romance; adult style distribution roughly matched infancy; styles linked to different love experiences.
practical_applications: Secure / anxious / avoidant as a lens for character dynamics in dialogue stories.
limitations: Early questionnaire studies; later work uses dimensional (anxiety x avoidance) measures (Fraley & Shaver 2000).

sources.title: Cross-cultural patterns of attachment: A meta-analysis of the Strange Situation
sources.authors: van IJzendoorn, M. H., Kroonenberg, P. M.
key_findings: Child Development 59, 147-156: 32 samples from 8 countries, 1,990 Strange Situation classifications, analysed with correspondence analysis.
Intracultural variation was nearly 1.5 times the cross-cultural variation; samples from one country sometimes resembled other countries more than each other.
Avoidant (A) classifications were relatively more prevalent in Western European countries; resistant (C) relatively more frequent in Israel and Japan.
practical_applications: Don't stereotype Thai or 'Asian' families as one attachment type.
limitations: Old, few countries, no Thai sample.

sources.title: Emotional intelligence: New ability or eclectic traits?
sources.authors: Mayer, J. D., Salovey, P., Caruso, D. R.
key_findings: Ability-model authors (Mayer, Salovey, Caruso) agree the term EI is used too all-inclusively and describe much mixed-model ('EQ') research as a 'degenerating research program'.
They cite popular claims as extraordinary: EI 'as powerful, and at times more powerful, than IQ' (Goleman 1995) and 'nearly 90%' of star-performer differences due to EI (Goleman 1998).
They argue a valid, narrower ability concept of EI exists and recommend restricting the term to it.
practical_applications: Use 'EQ' as everyday language for empathy/self-control, not as a measured score that predicts success.
limitations: Proponents with royalty interest in MSCEIT; title from common citation not confirmed on page.

sources.title: Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ
key_findings: Existence confirmed (Bantam Books, 1995). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Popular framing only; the 'matters more than IQ' claim is contested (see Mayer2008_EI).
limitations: Popular science book, mixed-model EI.

sources.title: The Social Animal (12th ed.)
key_findings: Existence and edition confirmed (Worth Publishers). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Readable social-psychology reference for the team; verify specific studies.
limitations: Not read.

sources.title: The positivity effect: a negativity bias in youth fades with age
key_findings: Older adults attend to and remember positive information more than negative (positivity effect); authors argue it reflects motivational change, not cognitive/neural decline.

Socioemotional selectivity theory: limited time horizons shift goals toward emotional meaning and satisfaction; age differences in social-partner preferences were eliminated when time horizons were statistically controlled or experimentally expanded.
Considerable evidence that cognitive load reduces the positivity effect; knowing what reduces/enhances it can inform health and education messages for older people.
practical_applications: For 50+ customers, emotionally meaningful, positively framed messages (seeing grandchildren's faces, reading with ease) may land better than threat-heavy ones.
limitations: PMC page blocked by captcha; title from search summary; cross-cultural generality debated (e.g. Japan vs US).

sources.title: Stereotype embodiment: A psychosocial approach to aging
key_findings: Stereotype embodiment theory: age stereotypes (a) are internalized across the life span, (b) can operate unconsciously, (c) gain salience from self-relevance, (d) work through multiple pathways (psychological, behavioural, physiological).
Experimental and longitudinal studies: positive and negative age stereotypes held by older people have beneficial and detrimental effects on cognitive and physical outcomes.
Central message: the ageing process is in part a social construct.
practical_applications: Never show reading glasses as 'getting old and useless'; show capable, active older people.
limitations: Some supporting experiments used subliminal priming - a method hit by the replication crisis; full text not read (PMC captcha).

sources.title: Patient and economic burden of presbyopia: A systematic literature review
sources.authors: Berdahl, J., Bala, C., Dhariwal, M., Lemp-Hull, J., Thakker, D., Jawla, S.
key_findings: 53 studies; uncorrected presbyopia linked to up to 22% lower QoL score and ~80% difficulty with near tasks (Holden 2008).
Psychosocial: distress and low self-esteem reported; in one Chinese study 15% reported low sense of accomplishment and 7% shame/embarrassment.
Correction rates range from 6% (Africa) to 84% (North America); cost and inconvenience are barriers.
practical_applications: Presbyopia content can name quiet embarrassment (holding the phone at arm's length) with warmth, not ridicule.
limitations: Funded by Alcon with employee authors; English-only, mostly cross-sectional; psychological evidence thin.

sources.title: Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
sources.authors: Simons, D. J., Chabris, C. F.
key_findings: People engaged in a monitoring task often miss an obvious unexpected event; harder tasks produce more misses.
Unexpected events similar to the attended features are noticed more.
practical_applications: In busy frames viewers miss the product; give the glasses the single focus of attention.
limitations: Details via secondary summaries this session.

sources.title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: A 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory
key_findings: Misleading post-event information impairs memory of the original event (misinformation effect).
Warnings help only under limited circumstances; effects stronger when attention is limited.
Young children and the elderly are more susceptible than younger adults; people can come to believe rich false events.
