practical_applications: Memory is reconstructive - flashback scenes can 'change' as characters retell them; never use this to mislead customers.
limitations: Narrative review by the field's leading proponent.

sources.title: Can people feel happy and sad at the same time?
sources.authors: Larsen, J. T., McGraw, A. P., Cacioppo, J. T.
sources.doi_isbn: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
key_findings: Usually people report one or the other, but after Life Is Beautiful, moving out, or graduating many felt both happy and sad.
Affect is typically bipolar in experience but underlying processes are bivariate; later work: making endings salient heightens mixed emotions.
practical_applications: Bittersweet endings ('last day before retirement', 'old frames retired') are a valid, documented emotion state for stories.
limitations: Self-report studies.

sources.title: The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance
sources.authors: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., Savitsky, K.
key_findings: People overestimate how many others notice their appearance (embarrassing T-shirt) and actions; anchoring-and-adjustment explanation.
practical_applications: Addresses fear of 'looking old in reading glasses' or bold frames: others notice less than you think - a kind, true reassurance.
limitations: Student samples; details via secondary summaries.

sources.title: Emotion regulation: Current status and future prospects
key_findings: Process model sorts strategies by where they act in emotion generation (situation selection/modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change/reappraisal, response modulation).
Extended model: regulation as valuation with identification, selection, implementation stages.
practical_applications: A character who reappraises ('it's not age, it's just focus') vs one who suppresses gives two clear arcs.
limitations: Abstract-level only; field still debates what 'emotion regulation' covers.

sources.title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
sources.authors: Green, M. C., Brock, T. C.
key_findings: Introduced 'transportation' - absorption into a story - as a route by which stories change beliefs toward story content.
practical_applications: Stories persuade when immersive; product claims inside a story should be story-true, not a jarring ad break.
limitations: Known via handbook citation only.

sources.title: The extended transportation-imagery model: A meta-analysis of the antecedents and consequences of consumers' narrative transportation
sources.authors: van Laer, T., de Ruyter, K., Visconti, L. M., Wetzels, M.
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 published and unpublished articles.
Storyteller antecedents of transportation: identifiable characters r = .20, imaginable plot .29, verisimilitude .27; receiver: transportability .30, attention .29, familiarity .21; age had no effect.
Effects of transportation: affective responses .57 (large), attitudes .44, intentions .31, beliefs .26, narrative thoughts .20, critical thoughts -.20.
Fail-safe N 80-6,627; studies using the Transportation scale showed smaller effects (.34) than other scales (.56).
practical_applications: Supports story-first carousels/clips as a persuasion format.
limitations: Specific effect sizes not read this session.
Read from the City University accepted manuscript; 43% of studies did not report age and 33% had mean age 18-22.

sources.title: A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking
sources.authors: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., Lauber, E. A.
key_findings: 268 curves from 81 articles: liking rises with exposure then falls (inverted-U).
Existing models do not adequately account for the findings.
practical_applications: Repeat brand elements (wordmark, Mint & Tao) consistently, but vary execution to avoid wear-out.
limitations: Abstract-level only.

sources.title: The identifiable victim effect: A meta-analytic review
key_findings: 41 studies: significant but small effect (r = .05); stronger when the victim bears little responsibility and with money requests.
Later reanalysis (Maier et al. 2023, secondary) found moderate evidence of publication bias.
practical_applications: One named person helps, but the effect is small - don't rely on it alone.
limitations: Abstract-level; publication bias concern.

sources.title: Different languages, similar encoding efficiency: Comparable information rates across the human communicative niche
sources.authors: Christophe Coupé, Yoon Mi Oh, Dan Dediu, François Pellegrino
key_findings: Science Advances. 17 languages incl. Thai; 170 native speakers (10 per language) read 15 short daily-life texts aloud.
Speech rate = canonical syllables / speech duration excluding pauses >150 ms; overall mean 6.63 syllables/s (SD 1.15); individual speakers ~4.3-9.1 syll/s.
Faster languages carry less information per syllable; information rate converges near 39 bits/s.
Information density 4.8 (Basque) to 8.0 (Vietnamese) bits/syllable; secondary sources place Thai among the slower-rate languages.
practical_applications: Upper-bound sanity check for read speech; Thai-specific value is in the supplement (not read) - calibrate from our own TTS audio instead.
limitations: Read speech by students/academics, not TTS or broadcast; Thai per-language syllable rate not found in the main text.

sources.title: Towards an integrated understanding of speaking rate in conversation
sources.authors: Jiahong Yuan, Mark Liberman, Christopher Cieri
key_findings: Interspeech 2006; large English and Chinese telephone-conversation corpora.
English overall average 196 wpm (conversations range 111-291); net rate excluding silences 236 wpm; turn-wise 164 wpm.
Rate rises sharply for turns of 1-7 words, level for ~8-30 words.
Topic shifts English rate ~152 to ~170 wpm; older speakers slower; males ~2% faster; important/unpredictable parts spoken slower.
practical_applications: Very short lines are spoken faster per word; do not estimate duration of 1-3-word lines from a per-word rate.
limitations: Conversation (dialogue), not narration; English/Chinese only.

sources.title: Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation
key_findings: All languages avoid overlap and minimise silence between turns; languages differ in mean response gap within about 250 ms of the cross-language mean.
Same factors predict faster/slower responses in every language.
practical_applications: In written dialogue for TTS/animation, replies should follow quickly; long gaps signal hesitation/dispreferred answers (use deliberately).
limitations: Question-answer pairs only; read via abstract.

sources.title: A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation
sources.authors: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel A. Schegloff, Gail Jefferson
key_findings: Turn-taking is locally managed, party-administered, interactionally controlled and recipient-designed; turn-constructional + turn-allocation components minimise gaps and overlaps.
practical_applications: Real dialogue is short turns, built for this listener, with handover cues (questions, tags); scripted dialogue that is paragraph-long speeches sounds written.
limitations: Foundational theory; read via abstract/summary.

sources.title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking
sources.authors: Herbert H. Clark, Jean E. Fox Tree
key_findings: Cognition (2002). Fillers-as-words: 'uh' announces a minor delay, 'um' a major delay (London-Lund corpus).
Contested: Language Log notes coder perception vs acoustic measurement differences.
practical_applications: A small, deliberate filler/discourse marker can make dialogue sound spoken and signal thinking; in VO narration fillers usually add length without meaning.
limitations: English; citation volume/pages differ across databases (left blank); read via summaries.

sources.title: Variation across Speech and Writing
key_findings: Cambridge University Press. Statistical (multi-feature/multi-dimension) analysis of co-occurring linguistic features distinguishing spoken and written genres.
practical_applications: 'Written style' is a cluster of features (long noun phrases, nominalisations, dense modifiers), not one feature - a checker should combine several signals.
limitations: Book not read; dimension names not confirmed this session.

sources.title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis
sources.authors: Olusola O. Adesope, John C. Nesbit
key_findings: Journal of Educational Psychology 104:250-263.
Spoken+written presentations outperformed spoken-only; did not differ from written-only.
Citing studies report that brief on-screen keywords summarising narration were particularly helpful.
practical_applications: On-screen text = short keywords of the VO, not a full transcript, when visuals also need attention (exception: accessibility captions).
limitations: Learning settings; read via summaries.

sources.title: Reducing verbal redundancy in multimedia learning: An undesired desirable difficulty?
sources.authors: Carole L. Yue, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, Robert A. Bjork
key_findings: Journal of Educational Psychology (2013). On-screen text identical to narration impaired learning; slightly discrepant (abridged) text produced an advantage (per summary).
practical_applications: Subtitles that are shortened versions of the VO are defensible; word-for-word paragraphs over complex visuals are not.
limitations: Read via search summary; title from PDF filename context.

sources.title: Video Captions Benefit Everyone
key_findings: Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences 2(1):195-202.
More than 100 studies: captions improve comprehension, attention and memory; especially helpful in a non-native language.
practical_applications: Burn-in captions on every VO clip (muted feeds, older viewers, accessibility).
limitations: Critics: many studies use foreign-language captions, special populations or self-report; redundancy principle suggests caution (see WatsonLB).

sources.title: 'Video Captions Benefit Everyone': An Investigation
sources.authors: Andrew Watson (Learning and the Brain blog)
key_findings: Argues supporting studies often involve foreign-language captions, at-risk learners, college students or self-report; cognitive load theory suggests caution for typical learners.
practical_applications: Keep captions short and synced; do not add a second competing text layer.
limitations: Blog critique; not peer-reviewed.

sources.title: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov) - 'Write short sentences' and quick-reference tips
sources.authors: Plain Language Action and Information Network (US)
key_findings: Official guidelines for the US Plain Writing Act of 2010.
'Express only one idea in each sentence.'
Archived quick tips: aim for an average of 20 words per sentence, no sentence over 40 words.
practical_applications: Written-copy threshold: avg <=20 words, max 40; for the ear go shorter (see SCRIPT_CHECKER).
limitations: Guideline/consensus, not experimental; English word counts; the 20/40 figure found in archived quick tips, not confirmed in the current page.

sources.title: Content design: Writing for GOV.UK
key_findings: Plain English mandatory; write for a 9-year-old reading age (based on UK average reading age, not a child audience).
Specialist and legal content can and should still be plain; explain needed terms.
practical_applications: Even expert topics (optics, lens tech) get plain wording plus one explained term.
limitations: House style; a '25 words' sentence limit often attributed to GOV.UK was NOT found this session.

sources.title: CDC Clear Communication Index - User Guide and Score Sheet
sources.authors: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
key_findings: 20 items scored 0/1, scaled to 100; 90+ passes.
One main message (a topic is not a message), placed at the top; a call to action for the primary audience; main message and CTA in active voice.
Index is a planning aid; does not replace pretesting with the audience.
practical_applications: SCRIPT_CHECKER rules: single main message, early placement, CTA aimed at the viewer, active voice.
limitations: Health print/web materials; research-based index but scoring thresholds are institutional.

sources.title: Using alternative statistical formats for presenting risks and risk reductions
key_findings: Cochrane review, 35 studies / 83 comparisons.
Natural frequencies understood better than probabilities: SMD 0.69 [0.45, 0.93].
Relative risk reduction perceived larger and more persuasive than ARR/NNT, with no better understanding than ARR; authors warn RRR may mislead.
practical_applications: Health scripts: say '1 in 10 people' (natural frequency), give absolute numbers; avoid 'reduces risk by 50%' without the baseline.
limitations: Mostly hypothetical scenarios; read via abstract.

sources.title: Effectiveness and acceptability of interventions to improve readability of patient healthcare materials: A narrative systematic review
sources.authors: J. Dunnett, J. Holkham, A. Trebacz, C. Baldasera, C. Francis, L. Dawson, R. Swiers, F. Christie-De-Jong
key_findings: Public Health; 30 studies (2014-2024), mostly USA.
Simplified language, structured formatting and visuals improved understanding and preference.
Evidence on adherence and health outcomes mixed; study quality generally low.
practical_applications: Plain language is justified for comprehension; do not promise behaviour change from wording alone.
limitations: Narrative (not quantitative) synthesis; read via summary page.

sources.title: Click bait: Forward-reference as lure in online news headlines
sources.authors: Jonas Nygaard Blom, Kenneth Reinecke Hansen
key_findings: Journal of Pragmatics 76:87-100; 100,000 headlines from ten Danish news sites.
Forward-reference (pronouns 'this', adverbs, definite articles, ellipsis, imperatives, questions) used to create anticipation; strongest in commercial/tabloid media without paywalls.
practical_applications: Detect forward-reference hooks ('this one thing...', 'you won't believe') and require the payoff early in the content.
limitations: Describes usage, does not test effectiveness; Danish corpus.

sources.title: The Upworthy Research Archive, a time series of 32,487 experiments in U.S. media
sources.authors: J. Nathan Matias, Kevin Munger, Marianne Aubin Le Quere, Charles Ebersole
key_findings: Scientific Data 8:195. 32,487 headline/image A/B tests (2013-2015), 150,817 arms, ~538 million assignments; clicks and impressions per arm.
Correction: randomisation likely compromised for ~22% of tests (Jun 2013-Jan 2014).
practical_applications: Headline 'rules' should be tested against data like this, not lore; effects are platform- and era-specific.
limitations: Dataset paper - contains no general headline rule; US 2013-2015 clicks only.

sources.title: Aggregation, Clickbait and Their Effect on Perceptions of Journalistic Credibility and Quality
key_findings: Journalism Practice 14(4):429-446; two online experiments.
Clickbait headlines lowered perceived credibility and quality, but the effect was small; writing proficiency mattered more.
practical_applications: Over-promising hooks carry a small credibility cost; good writing matters more.
limitations: News context; read via abstract.

sources.title: The (Null) Effects of Clickbait Headlines on Polarization, Trust, and Learning
sources.authors: Kevin Munger, Mario Luca, Jonathan Nagler, Joshua Tucker
key_findings: Public Opinion Quarterly 84(1):49-73; MTurk and Facebook-ad samples.
Older people and non-Democrats showed higher preference for clickbait; reading clickbait vs traditional headlines did not change polarisation, retention or media trust.
practical_applications: Clickbait is neither a proven win nor a proven disaster; judge hooks on honesty and match with content.
limitations: US political news.

sources.title: Effects of age and hearing sensitivity on the comprehension of rapid speech (review and related studies, via secondary summary)
sources.authors: Arthur Wingfield and colleagues; related: Gordon-Salant et al.
key_findings: Older adults are especially sensitive to time-compressed (fast) speech; hearing loss adds a further penalty.
Context and inserted pauses between words/phrases reduce age differences.
Lab time-compressed speech overestimates older adults' handling of naturally fast speech (PMC studies).
practical_applications: For 50+ audiences (presbyopia content) slow the VO and insert pauses at phrase boundaries rather than speeding up to fit time.
limitations: Secondary summary of the review plus several PMC primary studies; exact title/citation not verified.

sources.title: Quick Guide: Writing a radio news script
key_findings: Write for the ear (heard once): simple words, short sentences; conversational; lead with the most important point; active voice; round numbers ('nearly two thousand'); title before name; only commas and full stops; read aloud for breath and tongue-twisters; phonetic spellings for hard names.
practical_applications: Directly encoded as VO rules in SCRIPT_CHECKER (numbers, punctuation, read-aloud test).
limitations: Practitioner guidance, English broadcast.

sources.title: Dialogue: The Art of Verbal Action for Page, Stage, and Screen
key_findings: Twelve/Hachette, July 2016. Treats dialogue as action (characters do things to each other with words) across screen, stage, page.
practical_applications: Craft frame for subtext rule: each line should do something (persuade, hide, attack), not report information.
limitations: Book not read (bibliographic); one review says it gives hard rules rather than adaptable advice.

sources.title: Message Design Choices Don't Make Much Difference to Persuasiveness and Can't Be Counted On - Not Even When Moderating Conditions Are Specified
key_findings: 1,149 studies of 30 message-design variations; median main-effect r = .10; prediction intervals frequently include negative effects even under moderators.
Narrative vs non-narrative r = .067, k = 34.
practical_applications: No copy formula (hook type, CTA wording) is guaranteed; the checker flags risks, it does not predict performance.
limitations: First ~100k characters read.

sources.title: Impact of narratives on persuasion in health communication: A meta-analysis
sources.authors: Fuyuan Shen, Vivian C. Sheer, Ruobing Li
key_findings: 25 studies, N = 9,330; r = .063; audio/video narratives significant, print not; detection/prevention yes, cessation no.
practical_applications: Medical-communication scripts: narrative works better for 'go get checked' than 'stop doing X'.
limitations: Read via summaries; substantial heterogeneity (O'Keefe & Hoeken).

sources.title: Similar information rates across languages, despite divergent speech rates (press release)
key_findings: Lay summary of Coupé et al. 2019: ~39 bits/s across languages; 5-8 bits per syllable; faster languages are less dense.
Gives no Thai-specific figure.
practical_applications: Do not transfer an English or Spanish syllable rate to Thai.
limitations: Press release.

sources.title: You won't believe what's in this paper! Clickbait, relevance, and the curiosity gap
key_findings: Relevance-theoretic account of clickbait and the curiosity gap; discusses Blom & Hansen's forward-reference categories (per search summary).
practical_applications: A hook creates an expectation of relevance; if the content does not pay it off, the viewer's effort is wasted - the mechanism behind 'hook must match content'.
limitations: Only the listing/search summary seen; journal and year not verified.

sources.title: Peirce's Theory of Signs
sources.authors: (SEP entry; author not captured in the fetched text)
key_findings: A sign is determined by an Object and produces an effect (interpretant) in a person; it signifies only as it is interpreted.
Icon = signifies by shared quality (portrait, diagram); index = existential/causal link (smoke-fire, weathercock, pointing finger); symbol = convention/habit/law (words, traffic lights).
Peirce came to see pure icons and indices as rare; most signs mix iconic, indexical and symbolic features (hypo-icon, sub-index).
Later typologies (10 and 66 classes) are uncertain even for Peirce and are disputed by scholars.
practical_applications: Classify every visual element by HOW it carries meaning: icons travel across cultures best, symbols least.
An index (steam from a cup, footprints, worn edges) shows a cause and needs little caption; a symbol needs shared convention or a caption.
limitations: Author and revision date not captured.
Only the sections on the triad and typologies were summarised.

sources.title: Course in General Linguistics (excerpt: Nature of the Linguistic Sign)
key_findings: Saussure defines the sign as the whole formed by a concept and a sound-image, and proposes the terms signified (signifie) and signifier (signifiant).
Principle I: the bond between signifier and signified is arbitrary - e.g. 'sister' has no inner link to the French sounds s-o-r; 'ox' is b-o-f on one side of a border and o-k-s on the other.
He raises whether a future semiology should include modes of expression based on natural signs such as pantomime.
From earlier search only (not re-read): a Semiotica critique argues arbitrariness is usually read as symmetrical without justification.
practical_applications: Meaning of a symbol is set by the community that uses it, so the same form can mean different things to Thai vs foreign viewers.
limitations: Read: a course-page excerpt of the English translation (Nature of the Linguistic Sign), not the whole book.
Saussure's model is linguistic; extension to images (via Barthes) is an interpretive move, not an empirical result.

sources.title: Rhetoric of the Image (in Image-Music-Text, trans. S. Heath)
key_findings: Analyses a Panzani pasta ad as three messages: a linguistic message, a coded iconic (symbolic/connoted) message and a non-coded iconic (literal/denoted) message; the literal message supports the symbolic one.

Connoted signs: the half-open string bag spilling provisions = 'return from the market' with the euphoric values of freshness and domestic preparation; tomato, pepper and the poster's yellow-green-red = 'Italianicity', a specifically French knowledge - 'an Italian would barely perceive' it; the name Panzani itself connotes Italianicity by assonance.

All images are polysemous ('a floating chain of signifieds'); text relates to image by anchorage (fixes the reading, has a repressive value; most frequent, common in press photographs and advertisements) or relay (text and image complementary, unity at the level of the story; seen particularly in cartoons and comic strips).
practical_applications: Captions in our posts are anchorage: write them to close off unwanted readings.
Mint & Tao speech bubbles are relay: text carries the plot the image cannot.
limitations: Read in Trachtenberg (ed.) Classic Essays on Photography (1980), Heath translation; essay first published 1964.
Interpretive/theoretical, not empirical.

sources.title: Images in Advertising: The Need for a Theory of Visual Rhetoric
key_findings: Criticises the assumption that pictures simply reflect reality.
Treats visuals as a convention-based symbolic system; many images seen as 'affect-laden' are complex figurative arguments.
Calls for a pluralistic research program on pictures as persuasion; source of 'cultural competency' idea used by McQuarrie & Mick.
practical_applications: Plan images as arguments (claim + evidence + figure), not decoration.
limitations: Theoretical article; abstract only.

sources.title: Figures of Rhetoric in Advertising Language
sources.authors: McQuarrie, E. F.; Mick, D. G.
key_findings: Framework: figurative vs non-figurative; schemes (excess regularity) vs tropes (irregularity); four operations: repetition, reversal, substitution, destabilization.
A rhetorical figure is an artful deviation in the form of a statement.
Preliminary validation data support the distinctions, linked to predicted consumer responses.
practical_applications: Use the same taxonomy for captions and visuals: rhyme/repetition (scheme) is lower risk than pun/metaphor (trope).
limitations: Abstract only; the specific predictions were not read.

sources.title: Visual Rhetoric in Advertising: Text-Interpretive, Experimental, and Reader-Response Analyses
sources.authors: McQuarrie, E. F.; Mick, D. G.
key_findings: Visual figures tested (rhyme, antithesis, metaphor, pun) produced more elaboration and more favourable ad attitude without lower comprehension.
Reader-response interviews matched the text-based analysis.
Effects of visual tropes (metaphor, pun) diminished or disappeared for people lacking the cultural competency to read the (American) ads.
practical_applications: Visual metaphor helps only when the audience shares the code: for foreign tourists, prefer schemes or very common metaphors.
limitations: Abstract only; US ads and samples; a 2003 follow-up (JCR 29(4)) examined directed vs incidental exposure (not read).

sources.title: Beyond Visual Metaphor: A New Typology of Visual Rhetoric in Advertising
sources.authors: Phillips, B. J.; McQuarrie, E. F.
key_findings: Typology built from properties of pictures: visual structure (juxtaposition, fusion, replacement) x meaning operation (connection, comparison) per Lagerwerf2023's summary.
Ordered by complexity: juxtaposition < fusion < replacement (as commonly summarised).
A later student study (search snippet, source not identified) reported juxtaposition prompted more elaboration and fusion was hardest to comprehend.
practical_applications: Template for product metaphors: side-by-side (juxtaposition) for broad audiences; fused object for engaged followers; replacement only with strong context.
limitations: Original article not read; typology described via secondary sources (Lagerwerf2023, a 2018 International Journal of Advertising extension at the URL).
'Connection/comparison' categories confirmed only through Lagerwerf2023's text.

sources.title: The impact of perceived complexity, deviation and comprehension on the appreciation of visual metaphor in advertising across three European countries
sources.authors: van Mulken, M.; le Pair, R.; Forceville, C.
key_findings: Experiment with authentic ads in three European countries, three visual metaphor types.
Hybrids (fusion) were the preferred type.
Deviation from expectation and comprehension raised appreciation; perceived complexity correlated negatively with appreciation.
Follow-up (van Mulken, van Hooft & Nederstigt 2014) proposed a 'tipping point': moderately challenging metaphors appreciated more than very simple or very complex ones.
practical_applications: Aim for 'surprising but solvable': if testers cannot state the intended meaning, simplify.
limitations: Search summary only; author list from bibliography record, title not seen in full; unverified details.
European samples; Lagerwerf2023 did NOT find the inverted U.

sources.title: Conceptual similarity and visual metaphor: effects on viewing times, appreciation, and recall
sources.authors: Lagerwerf, L.; van Mulken, M.; Lagerwerf, J. B.
key_findings: Three experiments (N=65, 73, 73) with 27 juxtaposed object pairs: hyponyms (same kind), visual comparisons (metaphors), unrelated.
Hyponyms identified fastest and liked most; metaphors next; unrelated last.
Longer exposure did not change preference; recall lowest for unrelated pairs; 5 s exposure improved recall.
Fluency theory explained appreciation better than the 'pleasure of solving' view; the inverted U was not found.
practical_applications: In fast-scrolling feeds, easy-to-process pairings win liking; save puzzling metaphors for content people stop to read.
limitations: About 100k of 121k characters read; lab stimuli, not real ads; Dutch-context samples; no culture comparison.

sources.title: Studies in Iconology (Introductory: three levels of meaning)
key_findings: Level 1 pre-iconographic description: forms, figures, objects (primary/natural subject).
Level 2 iconography: conventional subject (who/what story) known through cultural convention.
Level 3 iconology: why a society gave the image that meaning; levels blend in practice.
Critics question the label 'secondary/conventional subject'.
practical_applications: Three-step symbol check: what is literally shown -> which convention it invokes -> what that convention means to THIS audience.
limitations: Panofsky's own text not read; the three-level model is now verified through Lorenz2016_PanofskyModel (textbook chapter read in full). The previously linked Cambridge excerpt is Lorenz's book, not Panofsky's.

sources.title: ISO 9186-1:2014 Graphical symbols - Test methods - Part 1: Method for testing comprehensibility
key_findings: Standard method for measuring how well a symbol variant conveys its intended message without explanatory text: proportion of respondents who understand it correctly.
Part 2 covers perceptual quality, Part 3 referent association; confirmed 2019; a revision (DIS Ed. 3) is in progress.
practical_applications: Basis for our cheap 'does this symbol read?' test: show without caption, ask open question, score correct/partly/wrong.
limitations: Paywalled; acceptance threshold not seen in the standard itself.

sources.title: Safety sign comprehension of fiberboard industry employees
key_findings: 139 fiberboard-industry employees (99.3% male, mean age 32) gave the meaning of 22 common safety signs (ISO 7010 designs): mean comprehension 66.6% (range 22.5%-98.6%); warning signs lowest, prohibition signs highest.
Below 40%: toxic material, automated external defibrillator, overhead obstacle, and 'disconnect mains plug' signs.
Method section: 67% comprehension is the acceptance criterion for safety symbols in ISO 3864 and 85% in ANSI Z535.3-2022.
Earlier studies cited range from 39.2% to 78.4% overall comprehension, attributed to cultural, educational and design differences.
practical_applications: Borrow as a working bar: a symbol meant to carry meaning alone should reach roughly 2 of 3 correct in a small open-ended test; safety-critical messages need text anyway.
limitations: Heliyon 9(6):e16744 (2023), Turkey, one industry, mostly male workers; the ISO/ANSI thresholds are as cited by the author, standards themselves not read.

sources.title: (Cross-cultural replication of Rosen et al. archetypal symbol word-association paradigm) - Behavioral Sciences 3:541
key_findings: German replication of an English-language paradigm reported the archetypal-symbol memory effect was unlikely to be a linguistic artefact (per search summary).
Accompanying dissertation concedes empirical research on archetypes is 'extremely sparse'.
Critiques: Jung's universalism leans on Western esoteric concepts; some archetypes may map to evolved motives (mating, care, status) rather than inherited images.
practical_applications: Treat 'universal archetypes' as a weak hypothesis; rely on broadly shared experiences (mother-child, light-dark, height-power) and still test locally.
limitations: Search summary only; authors not captured; small literature.

sources.title: Cultural Similarities and Differences in Emblematic Gestures
key_findings: Lab blog summary of the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior paper: emblems were catalogued across cultural groups against a standard list of verbal messages; culturally similar gestures carried more basic messages than culturally variant ones.

Three kinds of difference: different forms for the same message (insults exist everywhere); different meanings for the same form (the ring = 'A-OK', 'money' or other messages); culture-unique emblems ('apology' only in South Asia, 'hunger' only in East Asia, 'day after tomorrow' only in the Middle East).
practical_applications: Never let a hand gesture carry the message for a mixed-nationality audience; pair with words or use neutral hands.
limitations: Read only via the lab's own blog summary (Humintell, 9 Jan 2013), read in full; the paper itself not read; which regions read the ring as 'money' is not stated in the summary.

sources.title: 4.4 Nonverbal Communication and Culture (COM110 open textbook)
key_findings: The North American A-OK sign is an obscene gesture in many European cultures; the inverted peace sign (palm inward) is an insult in England and Australia.
Thumbs-up = 'well done' in North America; in Greece and other countries it equals the insulting 'Up yours!' (citing Cotton 2013).
Greek moutza (open palm thrust outward) is an insult; counting on fingers differs between North Americans and other Europeans.
Bowing is more common in Asian cultures; the head nod is an abbreviated bow; nonverbal norms vary with context and individuals.
practical_applications: Avoid thumbs-up / OK as the hero gesture in ads aimed at mixed foreign audiences.
limitations: Open textbook (OER, 2023); country lists not exhaustive. Note: it does NOT mention Brazil - the earlier 'inverted OK obscene in Brazil' claim was not in this source.

sources.title: (Number 4 aversion and number 8 preference in Chinese retail prices)
key_findings: Aversion to 4 plus preference for 8 pushes Chinese prices upward; retailer gains estimated up to 1.40% of 2007 GDP (as reported).
Related: Simmons & Schindler (Nanyang) found Chinese price ads favour 8 and avoid 4; a Singapore study of ~900 ads found ~32% prices ending in 8 (Roschk, Westjohn & Magnusson).
practical_applications: For Chinese-speaking customers, avoid 4 in prices/promo codes; 8 endings are familiar.
limitations: Read via press release (phys.org) summary only.

sources.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles effect: natural experiment on the influence of psychological stress on timing of death
sources.authors: Phillips, D. P.; Liu, G. C.; Kwok, K.; Jarvinen, J. R.; Zhang, W.; Abramson, I. S.
key_findings: Notes Chinese and Japanese consider 4 unlucky; some Chinese/Japanese hospitals omit 4th floor or room 4.
Reported a cardiac death peak on the 4th of the month among Chinese/Japanese Americans.
practical_applications: Evidence that number-4 avoidance is real practice; but do not claim it has health effects.
limitations: Contested: Smith 2002 (BMJ) found no persuasive day effect in California data; a 2003 Medical Journal of Australia Hong Kong study did not support it; McGill OSS summary agrees.
Search summary only.

sources.title: Korean superstitions (Honorary Reporter article)
key_findings: Korean 'four' sounds like 'death'; buildings may label floor 4 as 'F'.
Writing a living person's name in red is taboo (red on memorial wreaths/death records); personal seal (dojang) is the exception.
Shoes as gifts = the recipient will run away; avoid dark/red gift wrap.
practical_applications: Never render a Korean customer's name in red text in a thank-you graphic.
limitations: Volunteer reporter on a government portal; folk-belief reporting, strength of belief today not measured.

sources.title: Swastika
key_findings: Auspicious symbol in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions (prosperity, sun; Buddha's footprints; Japanese manji).
Adopted by the Nazi Party in 1920 (Hakenkreuz); since WWII most Westerners read it as a Nazi symbol.
Germany exempts religious temple uses; ADL calls Hindu/Buddhist temple uses innocuous.
practical_applications: Even in a Thai temple context, crop or avoid the swastika in content for Western audiences; explain if it must appear.
limitations: Search summary across Britannica and other encyclopedias; Britannica page not opened directly.

sources.title: The symbol of the dragon in Eastern and Western cultures
key_findings: Chinese dragon ('loong'): wingless serpentine body with features of carp, tiger and eagle; sacred symbol of good luck, power and wealth, might, wisdom and harmony with nature; believed to bring rain and harvests (Shi Aidong, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences).
Reverence has grown since the 1980s; many Chinese call themselves 'descendants of the dragon'.
Western dragon: fire-breathing, bat-winged antagonist of chaos and evil; Satan in the Book of Revelation; St George legend; Smaug in The Hobbit.
Chinese folklore also has dual good/evil dragons (Heilongjiang black vs white dragon).
practical_applications: Dragon imagery for Chinese New Year is positive for Chinese audiences; for Western viewers frame it as celebratory (colour, dance) not menacing.
limitations: Chinese state media; no audience-perception data. The Olympic-mascot and 2024 'loong' wording-debate claims in the earlier entry are NOT in this article (unverified).

sources.title: Gifts you must avoid giving in Chinese culture, from clocks and shoes to pears, and why
key_findings: Giving a clock (song zhong) sounds like attending a deathbed/funeral (song zhong); strongest with elders; a token payment can neutralise it.
Umbrella (san) sounds like 'separate' (san); chrysanthemums associated with funerals; pears and shoes also on avoid lists.
practical_applications: Gift/promo imagery for Chinese customers: no clocks, umbrellas, white chrysanthemums as 'gifts'.
limitations: Newspaper lifestyle article; search summary only; regional variation not covered.

sources.title: Six National Symbols to showcase Thai Identity to the World
key_findings: On 14 May 2025 the Thai government announced in the Royal Gazette six national symbols to strengthen soft power: Thai elephant (national animal), Ratchaphruek / golden shower tree (national flower), Sala Thai (national architecture), Thai betta fish (national aquatic animal), Naga (national mythical creature), and the Wai (national cultural gesture).

Stated meanings: elephant = strength, endurance, royal and war history; Ratchaphruek = unity, loyalty, prosperity; betta = bravery and elegance; Naga = protection, sanctity, link between human and spiritual realms; Wai = humility and mutual respect.
practical_applications: National symbols are positive identity markers but carry state/royal weight: use respectfully, not as jokes or mascots for discounts.
limitations: News article (31 May 2025) reporting the Gazette notice; Gazette text not read. The earlier entry's 2001 Cabinet date and the list including Garuda, flag and Ramakien are not in this article.

sources.title: The lotus in Buddhism (100 Flowers exhibition)
sources.authors: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco
key_findings: Asian Art Museum: the lotus is one of the most important and recognised Buddhist symbols across all Buddhist cultures; it symbolises purity, 'spontaneous' generation, faithfulness and spiritual awakening.
Thai details (bua luang, merit-making, funeral use) come from earlier search summaries of Thai press, not from this page.
practical_applications: Lotus is safe and positive for Thai audiences in calm/wellness contexts; avoid on feet, floors, trash, or comic contexts.
limitations: Short museum page; Thai-specific uses not verified here.

sources.title: Thailand Lexicon (entries: naga; sai sin; nang kwak)
key_findings: Naga entry: mythical cobra-like serpent, often multi-headed; guardian of the Buddha and protector of earthly waters; symbol of fertility, steadfastness, wealth and abundance; dwells under the earth, in water and in the skies where it makes rain; often rainbow-coloured.
Isaan rocket festivals 'wake the naga' for rain; Nong Khai naga fireballs on the Mekong; naga often shown battling Garuda.

Folk story: a naga disguised as a monk was told it could not be ordained but could guard temples - hence ordination candidates are called 'naag' and nagas line stair rails and roof edges; naga bridges = safe passage over water.
Sai sin and Nang Kwak entries: from earlier search summary only (not in the page read).
practical_applications: Naga/Nang Kwak are folk-religious: fine as respectful cultural reference, risky as cartoon mascots for selling.
limitations: Non-academic travel lexicon; only the naga entry was read in full.

sources.title: The Sacralization of the San Phra Phum (Spirit House) as Manifested in the Community Beliefs of Thai Society
key_findings: Documentary review: San Phra Phum (spirit house) belief has two roots - belief in deities (Phra Phum as tree/community guardian deity, linked to the Four Heavenly Kings of the Mahasamaya Sutta and protective deities in the Ratana Sutta, with offerings in return) and sacred space (originally the burial site of a revered tribal leader or ancestor, later a village guardian shrine).

Buddhism introduced deity belief to replace indigenous guardian/ancestral spirits, giving Phra Phum the character of a deity in a palace (prasat); the sacred space imitates Mount Meru and celestial realms.
Conclusion: the spirit house links humans and nature and represents cultural syncretism for sustainable coexistence.
From earlier search only: Davidson (Chula MA 1996, 893 Bangkok residents) on Phra Phum beside Buddha images; origins disputed.
practical_applications: Spirit houses read as 'home/place protection, respect'; never show people climbing, kicking or mocking one.
limitations: Abstract only; Journal of MCU Philosophy Review 9(2), May-Aug 2026; documentary review, not fieldwork.

sources.title: (Number nine in Thai creative culture) - Journal of Humanities, Naresuan University
key_findings: Number nine is significantly applied in Thai 'creative' culture, linked to astrology/sacredness and its homophone (kao ~ 'step forward' = progress).
Popular sources add: nine monks at blessings, nine auspicious desserts, record lucky-licence-plate auctions (Bangkok Post: ~45m baht).
practical_applications: 9 is a positive number in Thai promos (e.g. 9.9 campaigns, 99 baht) - meaning 'progress'.
limitations: PDF text garbled; title/authors not captured; methods unverified.

sources.title: Ancient Mythological Images and their Interpretation: An Introduction to Iconology, Semiotics and Image Studies in Classical Art History (Chapter 1 excerpt)
key_findings: Panofsky's iconology (first sketched in a 1932 article from a 1931 Kant Society paper, revised in English after 1933) is a three-step interpretive model whose levels he said amalgamate into one 'circle of interpretation'.
Level 1, primary or natural subject matter (phenomenal meaning) = pre-iconographic description of what a viewer can identify from lines and colours using everyday experience.
Level 2, secondary or conventional subject matter = iconographic analysis; Panofsky's example: a dinner table with thirteen guests is likely the Last Supper (needs literary/cultural knowledge).
Level 3, intrinsic meaning or documentary meaning = iconology proper: principles revealing the attitudes of 'a nation, a period, a class, a religious or philosophical persuasion'.
Lorenz notes Panofsky's model changed considerably between 1930, 1932 and the English versions.
practical_applications: Symbol audit: (1) what is literally shown, (2) what convention it invokes for this audience, (3) what worldview it signals.
limitations: Secondary textbook chapter (publisher excerpt) describing Panofsky; Panofsky's own text not read.

sources.title: Audio-Vision: Sound on Screen (trans. C. Gorbman; 2nd ed. 2019 with foreword by W. Murch)
key_findings: 'Added value': the expressive and informative value a sound adds to an image, so that the information seems to come from the image itself.
'Synchresis': the spontaneous, irresistible weld between a sound and a visual event heard and seen at the same time, independent of logic (fight-scene punches).
Sound also 'temporally animates' and 'vectorises' an image (gives it direction toward an expected end).
practical_applications: Any sound placed exactly on a visual event will be read as that event's sound - basis of foley/cartoon SFX and of 'impossible' sounds for drawn characters.
limitations: Film-theory text (tier A as scholarly monograph) but its claims are analytical, not experimental. Read via secondary sources (Basanta 2017, reviews).

sources.title: Shades of Synchresis
key_findings: Quotes Chion 1994: synchresis is 'the spontaneous and irresistible weld' (p.63); strength depends on meaning, context, gestalt and rhythm (pp.63-64); added value (p.5, p.21); vectorisation (pp.13-14).
Notes Chion's frameworks lack a measure of synchresis strength; the author's typology is not empirically tested.
practical_applications: Page-referenced Chion quotes for our docs.
limitations: Artist-researcher essay in eContact! 19.2; informal observations.

sources.title: Interactions in perceived quality of auditory-visual displays
sources.authors: Storms, Russell L.; Zyda, Michael J.
key_findings: 108 participants, 3 automated experiments manipulating pixel resolution / visual noise and audio sampling rate / audio noise.
High-quality audio with high-quality visuals raised perceived VISUAL quality vs visual-only baseline; low-quality audio with high-quality visuals lowered perceived audio quality.
With low-quality visuals, high-quality audio raised perceived audio quality.
practical_applications: Clean, full-band audio makes the same picture look better - spend effort on VO cleanliness and SFX quality, especially for AI/cartoon visuals.
limitations: Presence 9(6) 557-580; 2000-era displays; static image of a radio + music; small effects, lab setting.

sources.title: The influence of video quality on perceived audio quality and vice versa
sources.authors: Beerends, J. G.; de Caluwe, F. E.
key_findings: Video quality contributes significantly to judged audio quality; the video effect on audio judgements was larger than audio's effect on video judgements.
Video quality dominates overall audiovisual quality in non-conversational material.
practical_applications: Balance the Storms & Zyda result: audio helps perceived quality, but a bad picture cannot be rescued by sound.
limitations: JAES 47(5) 355-362; abstract only; sample details unverified.

sources.title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1: Relative timing of sound and vision for broadcasting
key_findings: Subjective tests (Japan, Switzerland, Australia; NTSC and PAL) give detectability thresholds of about +45 ms to -125 ms and acceptability thresholds of about +90 ms to -185 ms on average (positive = sound advanced/early relative to vision).
Recommends overall sound/picture timing tolerance not exceeding +90 ms or -185 ms; final source selection to transmitter input within +22.5 ms / -30 ms.
Annex cites ITU-R BR.265: film sound/picture location within +/- half a frame (about +/-22 ms at 24 fps); the asymmetric tolerance means viewers are more sensitive to sound arriving early than late.
practical_applications: At 30 fps one frame = 33 ms: a hit SFX may sit 0-1 frame early but never more than ~1 frame early; up to ~3 frames late is still undetectable.
limitations: Broadcast lip-sync context (TV chains), not short-form social video; ITU-R page lists BT.1359-1 (11/98) as 'In force' (checked 2026-11-25).

sources.title: Sound alters visual motion perception
sources.authors: Sekuler, R.; Sekuler, A. B.; Lau, R.
key_findings: Two discs moving through each other look like 'streaming'; a brief click at the moment of overlap makes most observers see them 'bounce'.
practical_applications: A single well-timed contact sound changes what the eye sees happen - cheapest way to make cartoon contacts read.
limitations: Nature 385:308; read via abstract-level summaries; effect weaker in older observers (later work).

sources.title: What you see is what you hear (sound-induced flash illusion)
sources.authors: Shams, L.; Kamitani, Y.; Shimojo, S.
key_findings: Abstract: auditory information can qualitatively alter perception of an unambiguous visual stimulus, creating a striking visual illusion - overturning the view that vision always dominates.
Detail from secondary summaries (not in the abstract): a single flash with two or more beeps is seen as multiple flashes.
practical_applications: Rapid SFX can 'multiply' perceived visual events (sparkles, blinks, flickers) - use with care, it can also feel busy.
limitations: Nature 408:788 (2000); abstract read, full letter paywalled.

sources.title: The construct of the multisensory temporal binding window and its dysregulation in developmental disabilities
sources.authors: Wallace, M. T.; Stevenson, R. A.
key_findings: Review: the multisensory temporal binding window (TBW) is the epoch within which stimuli from different senses are likely to be bound; even at delays of a hundred ms or more, subjects still report audio-visual pairs as simultaneous on a high percentage of trials.

Points of subjective simultaneity typically fall in the visual-leading range; TBW size is highly variable between people, but left (auditory-leading) and right (visual-leading) windows correlate within a person.
TBW width depends on stimulus: narrowest for simple flashes/beeps, widest for speech; it recalibrates to environmental statistics and can be substantially narrowed by feedback training.
TBW is altered (wider) in autism, dyslexia and schizophrenia.
practical_applications: Explains why slightly late SFX still fuse but early SFX feel wrong; individual viewers differ.
limitations: Review centred on clinical populations; window widths vary by task (SJ2, SJ3, TOJ). Read via PMC4326640 (Neuropsychologia 64:105-123).

sources.title: The International Affective Digitized Sounds (IADS-2): affective ratings of sounds and instruction manual
sources.authors: Bradley, M. M.; Lang, P. J.
key_findings: Standardised set of 111 everyday sounds rated on valence, arousal and dominance (Self-Assessment Manikin); IADS-1 1999, IADS-2 2007; uneven coverage of valence-arousal space.
practical_applications: Evidence that everyday sounds (screams, laughter, erotic sounds, alarms, birds) carry stable affect - basis of our emotion -> sound table.
limitations: Technical report not read; facts from papers that use IADS (e.g. Stevenson & James 2008).

sources.title: Affective auditory stimuli: characterization of the International Affective Digitized Sounds (IADS) by discrete emotional categories
sources.authors: Stevenson, R. A.; James, T. W.
key_findings: Collected discrete-emotion ratings for the IADS, a database of 111 sounds already rated on valence, arousal and dominance, so sounds can be chosen under both dimensional and categorical theories of affect.
practical_applications: Pick SFX by the discrete emotion they reliably evoke, not by name only.
limitations: Abstract read on Springer page (Behavior Research Methods 40(1):315-321); per-category numbers not read. IADS-E (2018) expands the set.

sources.title: Perceptual bias for rising tones
key_findings: Listeners reliably overestimated the change in level of rising-level tones relative to equivalent falling tones; the bias was stronger at higher levels.
Author proposes a selective advantage (rising intensity can signal an approaching source) and an asymmetry in neural coding of harmonic dynamic intensity change.
From earlier secondary search (not re-checked): replicated in rhesus monkeys (Ghazanfar et al. 2002); a 2026 paper proposes a 'speed prior' explanation.
practical_applications: Risers / crescendos feel bigger and nearer than their dB change; downlifters feel like release - use risers sparingly or they over-promise.
limitations: Nature 395:123-124; abstract read via RePEc; the adaptive explanation is the author's interpretation.

sources.title: The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Craft monograph by a Hollywood foley artist: spotting, cueing, footsteps, props, cloth, sync; one of the first scholarly books on foley.
practical_applications: Foley layers: feet, cloth/moves, specifics (props) - our sfxlib follows the same split.
limitations: Publisher page only; craft knowledge (tier D).

sources.title: Dense Clarity - Clear Density (Transom, 2005)
key_findings: Murch places sounds on a conceptual spectrum from 'Encoded' (clearest example: speech, meaning carried by a code) to 'Embodied' (clearest example: music, sound experienced directly); most sound effects lie between.

'Law of Two-and-a-Half' (first noticed on THX-1138 robot footsteps, 1969-70): within one 'colour' of sound an audience can follow about two-and-a-half layers; at three they congeal into one new 'many' (robots walking in a group); two simultaneous conversations can just be followed, three cannot.

If layers are spread evenly across the spectrum, about five layers per 'moment' (he suggests any five-second section) is the maximum that keeps the mix both dense and clear: one dialogue, one music, one 'linguistic' effect (footsteps), one 'musical' effect (atmospheric tonality), one balanced effect.
Worked out on the Apocalypse Now premixes, where too many good sounds together 'melted into an unimpressive racket'.
practical_applications: Limit simultaneous layers of the same kind; spread layers across the encoded-embodied spectrum (VO + one music + one SFX family).
limitations: Practitioner essay (tier D): his own heuristic from experience, not an experiment; the left-right-brain explanation he offers is speculative.

sources.title: Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
key_findings: Practical and theoretical guide to dialogue, effects, music and ambience for storytelling and emotion; frequently cited by music-psychology papers as one of few sources on combined sound design.
practical_applications: Vocabulary for briefs (texture, rhythm, density, point of audition).
limitations: Bibliographic only; craft.

sources.title: [exact title not confirmed] Kock & Louven 2019 empirical study on sound design and music in moving pictures
key_findings: States that neither music psychology, film psychology nor neuroscience has profoundly explored the power of sound design scientifically.
practical_applications: Honest framing: most sound-design rules are craft, not science.
limitations: Seen only as a search snippet.

sources.title: Hitchcock flicks give your brain tunnel vision (report on Bezdek et al. fMRI study of suspense)
key_findings: Report (2015) on Bezdek et al. (Neuroscience): participants in fMRI watched 10 suspense film clips (3 Hitchcock, plus e.g. Alien) while flashing checkerboards stimulated the visual periphery; in high-suspense moments activity in peripheral parts of the calcarine sulcus dropped and central-field activity rose - attention narrowed to the centre.
The changes were not explained by moment-to-moment visual features (e.g. brightness) but by plot and threat; suspense was rated by a separate group with a slider.
Effects of sound and music were explicitly left untested (Zacks: 'think of Jaws').
practical_applications: Suspense focuses the eye - put the key object in the centre during sound-built tension and silence.
limitations: Science journalism; primary paper not read. fMRI measure, not behavioural probes - the earlier entry wrongly said 'slower responses, missed peripheral probes'.

sources.title: [PhD thesis on silence in film sound] Kingston University
key_findings: Argues a general overview of the uses of silence is lacking in sound and film studies.
practical_applications: Silence design is under-researched: treat our silence rules as craft.
limitations: Snippet only; title not confirmed.

sources.title: Introduction to Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF's): Representations of HRTF's in Time, Frequency, and Space (invited tutorial)
sources.authors: Cheng, C. I.; Wakefield, G. H.
key_findings: Duplex theory (Rayleigh): azimuth from interaural time differences (ITD) and interaural intensity differences (IID); above about 1500 Hz ITD becomes ambiguous (wavelength comparable to head size) and head shadow makes IID the useful cue.

Duplex theory alone leaves a 'cone of confusion' (Hornbostel & Wertheimer 1920), most acute in the median plane where ITD and IID are about zero; HRTF spectral colouring by torso, head and pinna resolves elevation and front/back.
Elevation cues are thought to depend on the pinna, with frequencies near 6-8 kHz important; Blauert: median-plane localisation needs broadband sound.
Measured HRTFs can synthesise spatial sound over headphones.
practical_applications: Phones/earbuds: stereo panning = ILD only; real 3D needs binaural (HRTF) rendering and is lost on a phone speaker.
limitations: Authors at University of Michigan (copy hosted on a University of Maryland lab site); tutorial from about 1999-2001, so newer HRTF personalisation work is not covered; venue not printed on the copy read.

sources.title: Sonic logos: can sound influence willingness to pay?
sources.authors: Krishnan, V.; Kellaris, J. J.; Aurand, T. W.
key_findings: Lab experiment: the number of tones in a sonic logo influenced willingness-to-pay non-linearly.
practical_applications: A short repeated sound signature (motif) carries brand meaning; keep it simple and consistent.
limitations: Journal of Product & Brand Management; snippet only.

sources.title: The impact of the sonic logo's acoustic features on orienting responses, emotions and brand personality transmission
key_findings: Psychophysiology + self-report lab experiment linking sonic-logo acoustic features to orienting response, emotion and perceived brand personality.
practical_applications: Acoustic features of a motif (tempo, pitch contour, timbre) shape the personality the brand seems to have.
limitations: Snippet only; findings not detailed.

sources.title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
sources.authors: Andrew J. Reagan, Lewis Mitchell, Dilan Kiley, Christopher M. Danforth, Peter Sheridan Dodds
key_findings: Sentiment (labMT hedonometer) of 10,000-word sliding windows across 1,327 filtered Project Gutenberg English fiction books.

Three methods (SVD, supervised, unsupervised clustering) converge on six core arcs: Rags to riches (rise), Tragedy/Riches to rags (fall), Man in a hole (fall-rise), Icarus (rise-fall), Cinderella (rise-fall-rise), Oedipus (fall-rise-fall).
Mode 1 (rise/fall) explains 30% of variance; first 12 modes explain 80% (mean-centred).
Hierarchical clustering: Man in a hole ~30%, Tragedy 32%, Oedipus 31%, Rags to riches 5% of corpus.
Highest median downloads: Icarus, Oedipus and two sequential Man-in-a-hole arcs; the most common arcs were not the most popular.
practical_applications: Plan the emotional trajectory of a piece (rise/fall points) separately from its plot events.
Man-in-a-hole (problem then recovery) and double-dip shapes are a defensible default for short problem-solution stories.
limitations: Authors: downloads are 'only a rough proxy for success'.
Measures the emotional valence of the text (syuzhet), not plot; novels 20k-100k words, English, Gutenberg only.
No evidence the arcs transfer to 15-60 s video; extrapolation is CRAFT.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (EPJ Data Science open access)

sources.title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
sources.authors: Tom van Laer, Ko de Ruyter, Luca M. Visconti, Martin Wetzels
key_findings: Journal of Consumer Research 40(5):797-817. Read: accepted manuscript (City Research Online eprint 6755) + the authors' 2015 seminar slides (eprint 18870) with the same tables.
Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes of narrative transportation from 76 published and unpublished articles; inclusion required the Transportation (Green & Brock 2000), Being Hooked or Mysticism scale.
Storyteller antecedents (reliability-adjusted rho): identifiable character .20 (k=16), imaginable plot .29 (k=28), verisimilitude .27 (k=8) - all small.
Receiver antecedents: familiarity .21, attention .29, transportability .30 (medium), education .10, (female) sex .15; age .00 (n.s.; 43% of studies did not report age, 33% had mean age 18-22).

Consequences of transportation: affective response .57 (large), attitude .44, intention .31, belief .26, narrative thought .20, critical thought -.20 (fewer critical thoughts), studies with combined outcomes .36.

Moderator: Transportation scale gives smaller effects (.34) than other scales (.56); the authors attribute the gap to common-method/mood bias and recommend the Transportation scale. File-drawer N 80-6627.
practical_applications: What a storyteller controls (clear character, imaginable plot, plausibility) each has only a small link to transportation; who the audience is (attention, transportability) matters as much.

Once viewers are transported, the link to attitude (.44) and affect (.57) is sizeable - but these are correlations with measured transportation, not the effect of 'using a story' vs not (see BraddockDillard2016, OKeefeHoeken2021).
limitations: Correlational pooled correlations (rho), mostly student samples, Western languages (Dutch, English, French, German, Italian); genre and medium could not be coded as moderators.
sources.license: copyrighted (accepted version in City Research Online)

sources.title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
sources.authors: Melanie C. Green, Timothy C. Brock
key_findings: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 79(5):701-721.
Transportation = absorption into a story combining attention, imagery and feelings; a Transportation Scale was developed and validated (distinct from need for cognition).

Exp 1 (N=97): more-transported readers of 'Murder at the Mall' held more story-consistent beliefs and rated the sympathetic protagonist more favourably. Exp 2 (N=69): highly transported readers circled fewer 'Pinocchios' (false notes).
Exp 3 (N=274) and Exp 4 (N=258) replicated; in Exp 4 instructions that reduced transportation reduced story-consistent beliefs and evaluations.
Labelling the same story as fact or as fiction generally did not change transportation or the beliefs.
practical_applications: Design for absorption: one concrete scene, sensory detail, no interruptions that break the 'story world'.
A story marked as fiction/dramatisation can still shift beliefs - so health facts inside fictional Mint & Tao stories must be correct.
limitations: Lab text stories, US undergraduates; later studies sometimes found transportation did not mediate persuasion.

sources.title: Stories are to entertain: A structural-affect theory of stories
sources.authors: William F. Brewer, Edward H. Lichtenstein
key_findings: Read: University of Illinois Center for the Study of Reading Technical Report No. 265 (Oct 1982); also published in Journal of Pragmatics 6:473-486.
Stories are the subclass of narratives whose primary discourse force is entertainment.

Surprise: critical information early in the event sequence is omitted from the discourse and revealed late, forcing reinterpretation. Suspense: the initiating event (danger) is given and the outcome delayed. Curiosity: a significant event is omitted but the reader knows it is missing (e.g. a mystery), resolved when enough information is given.

In their experiments, suspense, curiosity and surprise versions produced the predicted affect curves; base narratives without such discourse organisations were not rated as stories by most readers, whereas suspense/surprise/curiosity versions were.
practical_applications: Choose deliberately: suspense (show the danger first), curiosity (show that something happened, withhold what/how), or surprise (hide a key fact, reveal at the end).
limitations: Lab texts, US readers; the report summarises experiments detailed elsewhere (see BrewerLichtenstein1981).
sources.license: copyrighted (tech report digitised, open in IDEALS)

sources.title: Brewer & Lichtenstein (1981) - course summary of 'The Trip Home' experiment
sources.authors: David S. Miall (course page summarising Brewer & Lichtenstein 1981)
key_findings: Six versions of a 4-page story (car bomb). Mean liking (7-pt): Base 2.15, Suspense standard 4.85, Foreshadowing 4.30, Misarranged (outcome first) 3.65, No resolution 3.85, Surprise 4.30.
'Is it a story' rating: No-resolution version fell to 2.75 (vs 5.05 standard) - removing the resolution hurt story-ness most.
A plain event sequence without suspense/surprise structure was rated lowest on both.
practical_applications: Never end a story clip without resolution unless it is an explicit series cliffhanger with a known next episode.
Any affect structure beats a flat chronological list.
limitations: Single story, student sample; page is a secondary course summary; curiosity condition not covered on this page.

sources.title: Memory and comprehension of narrative versus expository texts: A meta-analysis
key_findings: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 28(3):732-749. 37 articles, 78 samples, 33,078 participants.
Narrative texts better understood and remembered than expository: overall g = .55 [.31, .79]; comprehension g = .48; memory g = .72.
No moderator significant (age, listening vs reading, content control, delay, test format); heterogeneity I2 = 98%; publication bias signal for memory studies.
practical_applications: Wrap educational facts (e.g. eye-health facts) in a short narrative to improve comprehension/recall, but keep the fact itself explicit.
limitations: Only 28% of effects controlled content; few delayed tests (4), few listening studies (8).
Authors caution against forcing all information into narrative form.

sources.title: Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors
key_findings: Communication Monographs 83(4):446-467.
Narratives had small positive persuasive effects on beliefs, attitudes, intentions and behaviours (secondary sources report r about .17-.23).
Results suggested unidentified moderators.
practical_applications: Stories persuade a little, not magically; combine story with a clear claim and CTA.
limitations: Full text and abstract not reachable (publisher 403; Semantic Scholar elides the abstract; OpenAlex keyless quota exhausted 2026-11-25).

Search summaries quoting the abstract say fictionality moderator analyses gave MIXED results and that medium and research design did not change effect size; secondary summaries disagree on the direction - do not cite a direction.

sources.title: Impact of narratives on persuasion in health communication: A meta-analysis
sources.authors: Fuyuan Shen, Vivian C. Sheer, Ruobing Li
key_findings: Journal of Advertising 44(2):105-113; 25 studies, N = 9,330.
Overall small effect of narrative on persuasion r = .063.
Audio and video narratives significant; print narratives not significant.
Detection and prevention narratives worked; cessation narratives did not.
practical_applications: Narrative video fits detection/prevention messages (e.g. 'get your eyes checked') better than 'stop doing X' messages.
limitations: O'Keefe & Hoeken (2021) reanalysis found substantial heterogeneity.
Read via abstract-level summaries.

sources.title: Message Design Choices Don't Make Much Difference to Persuasiveness and Can't Be Counted On - Not Even When Moderating Conditions Are Specified
key_findings: Frontiers in Psychology; reviews 1,149 studies of 30 message-design variations.
Narrative vs non-narrative: mean r = .067 [.028, .105], k = 34, N = 9,330; 95% prediction interval -.107 to .237 (straddles zero).
Median main-effect r across the 30 variations = .10.
Even under specified moderators, prediction intervals included negative effects.
practical_applications: Treat 'story beats facts' as a modest average bet, not a guarantee; test variants with real audiences.
limitations: Only the first ~100k characters of the article were read.

sources.title: Kishotenketsu and its potential applications to prose writing
key_findings: TEXT: Journal of writing and writing courses 29(2), Oct 2025.
Ki (introduction), sho (development), ten (turn/twist), ketsu (conclusion); 'functions by induction' (Fister-Stoga 1993); Hinds (1982) calls it predominant in modern Japanese prose.
Conflict may exist but is not the driving force; allows passive protagonists, cyclical endings, perspective shift at ten.
Kubota (1997): no definitive academic explanation; Chinese/Japanese scholars advise against exact definitions of zhuan/ten; it is a guide, not a rule.
practical_applications: Calm slice-of-life carousels (Mint & Tao) can use ki-sho-ten-ketsu: no villain, the 'ten' slide reframes everything.
limitations: Literary-craft analysis of two novels; no audience data. Origin claims (e.g. Chinese jueju) are disputed in popular sources.

sources.title: Seeing your life story as a Hero's Journey increases meaning in life
sources.authors: Benjamin A. Rogers, Herrison Chicas, John Michael Kelly, Emily Kubin, Michael S. Christian, Frank J. Kachanoff, Jonah Berger, Curtis Puryear, Dan P. McAdams, Kurt Gray
key_findings: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Life stories with more Hero's Journey elements correlated with more meaning in life and flourishing, less depression.
A 're-storying' intervention increased perceived meaning (six studies, >1,700 people per secondary summary).
practical_applications: The Hero's Journey has evidence as a self-narrative frame (meaning-making), which is different from evidence that it makes better ads or clips.
limitations: Does not test audience response to fiction; read via secondary coverage.

sources.title: Folkloristics in the Twenty-First Century (AFS Invited Presidential Plenary Address, 2004)
key_findings: Per secondary summaries: Dundes criticised Campbell as a non-expert relying on secondhand material and argued a universal archetype harms folklore study.
Toelken (per same summaries): Campbell selected only stories that fit the pattern.
Campbell's corpus centres on male heroes.
practical_applications: Use the Hero's Journey as an optional writing tool, never as 'the universal structure of all stories'.
limitations: Original address not read; only secondary summaries (Wikipedia, blog).

sources.title: The living handbook of narratology - entries 'Narratology' and 'Narrative Constitution'
sources.authors: Jan Christoph Meister; Michael Scheffel (living handbook of narratology, University of Hamburg)
key_findings: Meister, 'Narratology' (rev. 2014): narratology is a humanities discipline dedicated to the study of the logic, principles and practices of narrative representation.

Scheffel, 'Narrative Constitution' (rev. 2013): fabula/sujet comes from Russian formalism (Shklovsky); Tomashevsky: fabula = 'the totality of motifs in their logical causal-temporal chain', sujet = the same motifs in the sequence in which they are presented; later pairs histoire/discours (Todorov), story/plot (Forster).
practical_applications: Separate WHAT happens (fabula) from HOW/ORDER it is told (syuzhet) when planning a clip - the same events can be told as suspense, curiosity or surprise.
limitations: Read via the handbook's print PDFs (archive site).

sources.title: Meet the creator of the Story Spine, an 8-sentence tool to create and analyze stories (NPR interview)
key_findings: NPR interview (2026): Kenn Adams invented the Story Spine, an eight-sentence exercise: Once upon a time / Every day / But one day / Because of that (x3) / Until finally / Ever since then.
Origin: late 1980s, while with Freestyle Repertory Theatre in New York (short-form improv).
Spread to Pixar via improv teacher Rebecca Stockley, who was hired to teach improvisation to Pixar writers.
practical_applications: Fastest skeleton for 15-60 s stories; 'because of that' forces causality instead of 'and then'.
limitations: Craft tool; no empirical test. The 'rule 4 of Emma Coats's 22 rules' link is not stated in this interview (other secondary sources only).

sources.title: Dan Harmon Story Circle (practitioner explainers)
sources.authors: StudioBinder / Reedsy and others, describing Dan Harmon's method
key_findings: StudioBinder (May 2025): 8 steps - You (comfort zone), Need (want something), Go (unfamiliar situation), Search (adapt), Find (get what they wanted), Take (pay a heavy price), Return (back to familiar situation), Change (having changed).
Presents the Circle as Harmon's later reworking of Campbell's Hero's Journey.
practical_applications: Good for 3-10 min episodes (night-optic, series EPs).
limitations: Craft only; practitioner explainer, not Harmon's own text. The page calls Campbell an 'anthropologist' (he was a literature professor/mythologist) - low editorial rigour.

sources.title: What Makes a Super Bowl Ad Super? Five-Act Dramatic Form Affects Consumer Super Bowl Advertising Ratings
sources.authors: Keith A. Quesenberry, Michael K. Coolsen
key_findings: Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice 22(4):437-454.
Content analysis of 108 Super Bowl commercials over two years coded for Freytag five-act form.
Ads with more acts / full five-act form had higher consumer poll ratings (USA Today Ad Meter).
practical_applications: In 30-60 s ads, a complete mini-story (setup, rise, climax, fall, resolution) is associated with higher likability than a fragment.
limitations: Correlational; Super Bowl ads (US, high budget, ~30-60 s); likability poll, not sales. A press summary called story completeness the sole predictor - stronger than the abstract.

sources.title: Story spoilers don't spoil stories
sources.authors: Jonathan D. Leavitt, Nicholas J. S. Christenfeld
key_findings: Psychological Science; three experiments with short stories of three genres (ironic twist, mystery, literary).
Reported that spoiled stories were enjoyed as much or more than unspoiled ones.
practical_applications: Outcome-first (curiosity) structure can work - but see the failed replications.
limitations: Johnson & Rosenbaum (2015) and Levine, Betzner & Autry (2016) found spoilers reduce enjoyment; result is contested.

sources.title: Spoiler replications: Johnson & Rosenbaum (2015) 'Spoiler Alert' (Communication Research); Levine, Betzner & Autry (2016) (Discourse Processes)
sources.authors: Benjamin K. Johnson, Judith E. Rosenbaum; William H. Levine, Michelle Betzner, Kevin S. Autry
key_findings: Both follow-ups failed to confirm 'spoilers don't spoil' and found spoilers reduced enjoyment.
Levine et al.: a mid-story spoiler had no discernible effect; differences in spoiler format (one sentence vs thematic paragraph) proposed as explanation.
practical_applications: Default: do not give away the payoff of a surprise-structured story in the caption/thumbnail.
limitations: Text stories; read via secondary university news and summaries.

sources.title: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013) literary-fiction / theory-of-mind effect (3 labs)
key_findings: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013, Science) across 3 labs, N = 792: no RMET advantage for literary fiction after one passage.
Lifetime fiction exposure still predicted RMET.
Kidd & Castano disputed it; van Kuijk et al. reported a replication largely consistent with the original - mixed.
practical_applications: Do not claim 'one story makes people more empathic' in content.
limitations: Read via BPS digest and summaries.

sources.title: Defining identification: A theoretical look at the identification of audiences with media characters
key_findings: Mass Communication & Society 4(3):245-264.
Identification = experiencing reception and interpretation of the text 'from the inside, as if the events were happening to them'; contrasted with spectatorship (distanced mode).
Distinguishes identification from parasocial interaction, liking/similarity and imitation; identification is internal, imitation is external/behavioural.
Similarity need not be demographic: animated/iconic characters can elicit similarity through shared attributes (e.g. goofy, scared) or similar situations.
practical_applications: Give the viewer a character's goal and point of view in the first beat; faceless characters (Mint & Tao) can still carry identification through clear goals and feelings.
limitations: Theoretical paper - proposes hypotheses, no data.

sources.title: The case of the missing author: just where did the claim that stories are 22 times more memorable than facts alone come from?
key_findings: Could not find the '22x more memorable' claim in Bruner's Actual Minds, Possible Worlds; Aaker states it in a video without a method.
Stanford Women's Leadership page still repeats the figure.
practical_applications: Never quote '22 times more memorable'; cite Mar 2021 (g = .55) instead.
limitations: Blog (mirror URL); a myth-tracing exercise, not research.

sources.title: Narrative stories as mediators for serial learning
sources.authors: Gordon H. Bower, Michal C. Clark
key_findings: Psychonomic Science 14(4):181-182. 24 undergraduates; 12 serial lists of 10 concrete nouns; Narrative Ss wove each list into a story (mean 104 s per list), yoked Controls got the same study time.
Immediate recall: median 99.9% (Narrative) vs 99.1% (Control). Final cued recall of all 12 lists: average median 93% vs 13% - six to seven times more, no overlap between groups.
Authors attribute the effect to thematic organisation that reduces interference between lists.
practical_applications: Linking items into a causal mini-story is a memory aid (e.g. a product's 3 features as one scene).
limitations: Small N, stories generated by the learner (not stories told to an audience), serial word lists.
Gamst & Freund (1978, see GamstFreund1978) found no story advantage with one 30-word list and 5 min study - the effect seems to depend on many lists/interference.
Earlier entry carried the wrong DOI (10.3758/BF03329666 = Gamst & Freund 1978); corrected 2026-11-25.

sources.title: Using narratives and storytelling to communicate science with nonexpert audiences
key_findings: Narratives increase comprehension, interest and engagement for nonexperts (per secondary summaries); can also spread misinformation.
Distinguishes using narrative for comprehension vs persuasion; the ethical question is how, not whether.
practical_applications: Health/optical facts: the story carries attention, the fact must be checked and stated plainly.
limitations: PMC blocked by browser check; read via summaries.

sources.title: Does Oxytocin Increase Trust in Humans? A Critical Review of Research
sources.authors: Gideon Nave, Colin Camerer, Michael McCullough
key_findings: Perspectives on Psychological Science. Evidence does not robustly show human trust is reliably linked to or caused by oxytocin; intranasal OT-trust finding has not replicated well; plasma OT measurement is problematic.
practical_applications: Do not claim 'stories release oxytocin so viewers trust your brand' - neuro-marketing lore.
limitations: About trust experiments, not narrative studies directly; read via abstract summaries.

sources.title: Introduction to Documentary
key_findings: Six documentary modes: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive, performative.
Modes overlap; a mode is a dominant tendency, not a fixed category (per Wikipedia summary quoting Nichols).
practical_applications: Shop/staff mini-docs: observational (watch a fitting), participatory (interview a customer), expository (VO + B-roll explainer).
limitations: Book not read; via encyclopedic/industry summaries (Indiana University Press, 2001; rev. 2010).

sources.title: Emotion-Induced Engagement in Internet Video Advertisements
sources.authors: Thales Teixeira, Michel Wedel, Rik Pieters
key_findings: Journal of Marketing Research 49(2):144-159; facial-expression detection of joy and surprise while viewers watched 30-s ads and could stop (zap).
Joy and surprise affected concentration and retention; effect of joy asymmetric (gains from increases larger than losses from decreases).
practical_applications: Early positive emotion helps keep viewers in short video ads; plan an emotional rise early, not only at the end.
limitations: Lab, 2010-era internet ads; read via abstract/press only.
