sources.title: Freytag's Technique of the Drama: An Exposition of Dramatic Composition and Art (trans. Elias J. MacEwan)
key_findings: Authorised translation from the 6th German edition (Scott, Foresman, Chicago 1900); original Die Technik des Dramas (1863).
Source of the 'pyramid' (five parts commonly listed: introduction/exposition, rising action, climax, falling action/return, catastrophe/denouement).
practical_applications: Five-act form for 30-90 s ads (see QuesenberryCoolsen2014).
limitations: Analysis of 19th-c. five-act tragedy; stage names confirmed via secondary sources only - scan not read.

sources.title: Narrative Processing: Building Consumer Connections to Brands
key_findings: Journal of Consumer Psychology 14(1-2):168-180.

Narratively structured ads elicited more narrative processing than vignette ads; narrative processing related positively to self-brand connections, which related to brand attitudes and intentions (per summaries).
practical_applications: Brand stories should let viewers map the story onto their own life (self-brand connection), not just praise the product.
limitations: Storyboard ads in lab; read via citing papers.

sources.title: Effects of subject-generated stories on recall
key_findings: Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society 12(3):185-188. Two free-recall experiments with a single 30-word list: telling learners to make up a story with the words did not improve mean recall vs standard study instructions, also when study time was varied.
Quotes Bower & Clark (1969) as 93% vs 13% final cued recall and attributes the difference to method (many short lists, interference).
practical_applications: 'Stories help memory' is strongest when many items/lists would otherwise interfere; for one short list of facts the story advantage may vanish.
limitations: Free recall of word lists via the learner's own stories; small student samples.

sources.title: Illustrations of the IPA: Thai
sources.authors: Tingsabadh, M. R. Kalaya; Abramson, Arthur S.
key_findings: Standard Thai has five tones: high, mid, low, rising, falling (khaa mid 'to get stuck', khàa 'galangal', khâa 'I', kháa 'to trade', khǎa 'leg').
Nine vowel qualities; length is distinctive for all vowels.
Only /p t k ʔ m n ŋ w j/ occur syllable-finally; final /p t ʔ/ have no audible release.
Primary stress falls on the final syllable of a word; the last primary stress before the end of a major prosodic group commonly takes extra stress.
/r/ vs /l/ distinction is not robust; many speakers favour [l] for single initial r; as second element of clusters both /l/ and /r/ tend to be deleted.
In polysyllabic words, low and high tones on short-/a/ glottal-stop syllables become mid when unstressed, with loss of the glottal stop.
practical_applications: Lengthen/emphasise the LAST syllable of a word, not the first, when directing emphasis in Thai VO.
Unreleased final stops: a TTS that releases -p/-t/-k sounds foreign.
Do not force tones on unstressed กระ-/ประ-/สะ- prefixes.
limitations: Only pp. 25-26 (vowels, tones, stress, conventions) were read from the scanned PDF; p. 24 and pp. 27-28 not read.
Describes careful Standard (Bangkok) Thai, not regional varieties.

sources.title: Lexical tone and sentence prosody in Thai
key_findings: Tones divide into 'dynamic' (falling, rising: rapid F0 movement) and 'static' (high, mid, low: slow movements).
Citation forms are the 'ideal' tone shapes; in running speech neighbouring tones cause coarticulation (e.g. first of two falling tones falls less far).
Certain unstressed CV syllables with short /a/ are normally toneless or neutralised to mid in running speech.
Three terminal junctures: rising (surprise, doubt, question), sustained (syntactic breaks, final syllable prolonged) and falling (sentence ends).
Sentence-final particles are prime carriers of terminal junctures; their 'lexical' tone is often overridden by sentence intonation (following Henderson 1949).
Sentence accent = syllable lengthening + tone contour approaching the ideal shape + amplitude increase.
practical_applications: Put attitude/question melody on the final particle, not on content words.
Sentence-final content words drop lower in F0: a TTS that keeps a full high 'citation' fall on the last word sounds read-aloud.
Emphasis = length + clear tone shape + loudness, not raised pitch.
limitations: Small corpus (one dialogue, one monologue), mostly auditory; author calls observations preliminary.
Pages 380-385 read; final page with Table 2 and conclusions not read.

sources.title: Using stress to disambiguate spoken Thai sentences containing syntactic ambiguity
sources.authors: Potisuk, Siripong; Harper, Mary P.; Gandour, Jack
key_findings: Stress in connected Thai classified from rhyme duration, mean F0, F0 SD, mean energy and energy SD.
Rhyme duration is a better correlate of stress than nucleus or whole syllable.
Monosyllabic content words are strongly stressed; grammatical words/clitics are weakly stressed unless emphasised.
A bisyllabic noun compound has weak-strong stress, a subject-verb sequence strong-strong: stress disambiguates structure.
practical_applications: Particles and function words (ก็, ที่, ของ, จะ) should be light in VO; content words carry weight.
Compound nouns (e.g. แว่นตา, สายตา) read weak-strong; reading them strong-strong can change parsing.
limitations: Five speakers, read lab sentences; classifier accuracy dropped with speaker-independent normalisation.

sources.title: Intonation in Thai (in Hirst & Di Cristo, eds., Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages, pp. 376-394)
key_findings: Per secondary summaries: three intonation classes in Thai - Fall (finality), Rise (non-finality/question) and Convoluted (contrariness, emphasis) - superimposed on the five lexical tones.
Builds on the author's 1983 Edinburgh PhD thesis 'Intonation in Thai'.
practical_applications: Use three melody labels (fall / rise / convoluted) in voice direction rather than English-style pitch accents.
limitations: Not read; findings come only from search snippets and a computational paper (Charnvivit et al. 2003) that uses the classes.

sources.title: F0 feature extraction by polynomial regression function for monosyllabic Thai tone recognition / intonation pattern recognition (Eurospeech 2003, co-author Luksaneeyanawin)
key_findings: States there are three classes of intonation pattern in Thai: Fall, Rise and Convolution.
practical_applications: Supports the three-class intonation vocabulary for voice direction.
limitations: Only the search snippet was seen; exact title not confirmed.

sources.title: Interaction between tone and intonation in Thai after unilateral brain damage
key_findings: Tones in sentence-final position were significantly lower in F0 than in sentence-initial or -medial position, for normal and brain-damaged speakers.
practical_applications: Expect and allow final lowering; do not 'correct' a TTS that lowers the last word as long as the tone shape is kept.
limitations: Search summary only; sample and clinical focus not checked.

sources.title: Anticipatory tonal coarticulation in Thai noun compounds after unilateral brain damage
sources.authors: Gandour, Jack; Ponglorpisit, S.; Dechongkit, S.; et al.
key_findings: Brain and Language 45:1-20: the falling tone's pitch height and slope were affected by the following tone (anticipatory coarticulation) in noun compounds.
practical_applications: Tone shapes in compounds legitimately differ from citation forms; judge a TTS by whether the word is recognisable, not by matching citation contours.
limitations: Search summary only.

sources.title: Tone features, tone perception, and peak alignment in Thai (as summarised in a citing source)
key_findings: Per a citing source: any actual rise in the high tone is optional in citation form and prohibited in connected speech.
practical_applications: A rising 'high' tone in running speech can be misheard; high tone in connected speech should be high-level/peak late.
limitations: Only the search snippet from a citing document was seen.

sources.title: The Vowels and Tones of Standard Thai: Acoustical Measurements and Experiments (IJAL 28(2), part 3; Indiana Univ. Research Center Publication 20)
key_findings: Foundational acoustic and synthetic-speech perception study of Thai vowels and tones; based on 1960 Columbia dissertation.
practical_applications: Baseline reference for tone shapes and vowel length.
limitations: Bibliographic record only; measurements not read.

sources.title: หลักเกณฑ์การทับศัพท์ภาษาอังกฤษ (Royal Institute English transcription rules, reproduced as DLTV Thai lesson handout, Mattayom 3)
sources.authors: Royal Institute / Office of the Royal Society (rules); DLTV handout compiler
key_findings: Vowels transcribed from the English dictionary pronunciation; consonants by a fixed table.
Silent letters take ์ (horn = ฮอร์น, world = เวิลด์).
ไม้ไต่คู้ used to distinguish from Thai words (log = ล็อก) or to show syllabification.
No tone marks in transcriptions, except where the word would clash with a Thai word (coke = โค้ก, coma = โคม่า).
Double final consonants: drop one in general words (football = ฟุตบอล) but keep both with ์ in technical terms/proper names (cell = เซลล์).
Hyphenated and open compounds are written joined (cross-stitch = ครอสสติตช์, night club = ไนต์คลับ).
Long-established loanwords in the RI dictionary keep their spelling.
practical_applications: RI spelling is a WRITTEN standard and deliberately omits tones: a TTS respelling may add tone marks (spell as said) but subtitles should keep RI/brand spelling.
limitations: Secondary reproduction in a school handout; consonant/vowel tables were referred to but the extracted text did not include them.
sources.license: public educational document (DLTV); rules by ORST

sources.title: หลักเกณฑ์การใช้เครื่องหมายวรรคตอนและเครื่องหมายอื่น ๆ (Office of the Royal Society page)
sources.authors: สำนักงานราชบัณฑิตยสภา
key_findings: Per search summary of the ORST page: ฯลฯ at the end of a list is read 'ละ' or 'และอื่น ๆ'; in the middle (ก ฯลฯ ฮ) it is read 'ละถึง'.
practical_applications: Normaliser: ฯลฯ followed by more text → 'ละถึง'; at end → 'และอื่น ๆ' (or 'ละ').
limitations: The ORST page refused connection; only the search engine summary was seen. Year unknown (0).

sources.title: ฯลฯ - วิกิพจนานุกรม
key_findings: Gives readings 'ละ' (omitting text at the end) and 'ละถึง' (omitting text in the middle); cites no source.
practical_applications: Corroborates the ORST readings.
limitations: Community source, no citations; does not list 'และอื่น ๆ'.

sources.title: HOYA ตอกย้ำผู้นำ ตลาดเลนส์แว่นตา เปิดตัวนวัตกรรมเลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟสุดล้ำ ...
sources.authors: Marketeer Online (press release content from ไทยโฮยา เลนซ์)
key_findings: Brand written 'HOYA (โฮยา)'; Thai company 'บริษัท ไทยโฮยา เลนซ์ จำกัด'.
Progressive lens = 'เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ' (one tag misspells 'โปรแกรสซีฟ').
Presbyopia = 'สายตายาวตามอายุ'; myopia = 'สายตาสั้น'; astigmatism = 'เอียง' ('สายตาสั้นและเอียง').
practical_applications: Brand-verified Thai spelling of HOYA is โฮยา (no tone mark), not โฮย่า.
limitations: Trade media rewrite of a press release; spelling of the spoken tone not shown (RI style omits tone marks).

sources.title: เอสซีลอร์ เปิดตัวนวัตกรรมเลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ “Varilux Comfort® Max” รุ่นล่าสุดเพื่อตอบโจทย์ชีวิตยุคนิวนอร์มอล
sources.authors: บริษัท เอสซีลอร์ ดิสทริบิวชั่น (ประเทศไทย) จำกัด via Vivaldi Integrated PR
key_findings: Issuer is Essilor Distribution (Thailand) itself.
Thai spellings: เอสซีลอร์, เอสซีลอร์ กรุ๊ป, วารีลักส์, วารีลักส์ คอมฟอร์ต แม็กซ์, เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ.
Target group described as having 'ปัญหาสายตายาวตามอายุ'.
practical_applications: Brand-verified readings for Essilor, Varilux and Comfort Max.
limitations: 2020 release; brand spelling of Varilux varies (ส์ here, ซ์ in Naewna 2019).

sources.title: Naewna lady section: Essilor Varilux 60th anniversary / NEW YEAR NEW YOU campaign
key_findings: Spellings: เอสซีลอร์, วารีลักซ์, เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ; website www.essilor.co.th.
practical_applications: Second brand-sourced spelling of Varilux (วารีลักซ์).
limitations: Newspaper reproduction of press content.

sources.title: ZEISS 175 years [PR] (Brand Buffet)
sources.authors: Brand Buffet (PR; quotes MD of Carl Zeiss (Thailand))
key_findings: Body text writes 'ไซส์ส (ZEISS)' and company 'บริษัท คาร์ล ไซส์ส (ประเทศไทย)'; the tag spells 'ไซสส์'.
practical_applications: Brand's Thai written form is ไซส์ส; as TTS input it risks an extra final -t, so a separate spoken respelling is needed.
limitations: Labelled [PR] but issuer not stated explicitly; inconsistent spellings within the page.

sources.title: TH Carl Zeiss General Terms and Conditions (bilingual) - ZEISS asset downloads
key_findings: Per search summary: Thai legal documents name the company 'บริษัท คาร์ล ไซส์ส จำกัด' / 'คาร์ล ไซส์ส (ประเทศไทย)', with a variant 'คารล์ ไซสส์'.
practical_applications: Confirms ZEISS's own Thai form uses ไซส์ส.
limitations: Search summary only; PDF not opened.

sources.title: Daily News article on photochromic ('auto') lenses
key_findings: Body text spells Transitions as 'ทรานซิชั่น' ('เลนส์ทรานซิชั่น', also called 'เลนส์ออโต้'); no brand representative quoted.
practical_applications: Shows common Thai written form; not brand-verified.
limitations: News article, not brand; date not recorded.

sources.title: (How to) อ่านใบตรวจค่าสายตาอย่างไรให้เหมือนผู้เชี่ยวชาญ - หมอแว่น
key_findings: SPH: minus = 'ค่าสายตาสั้น (Myopia)', plus = 'ค่าสายตายาว (Hyperopia)'; unit ไดออปเตอร์.
CYL = 'ค่าสายตาเอียง'; AXIS = 'องศาสายตาเอียง' / 'องศาแกนเอียง'.
ADD = 'ค่า Add', for 'สายตายาวตามวัย (Presbyopia)', +0.75 to +3.00 D.
-2.00 D is 'สายตาสั้นสองจุดศูนย์ไดออปเตอร์' but commonly said 'สั้นสองร้อย'.
practical_applications: Shop VO should say powers in 'hundreds' (สั้นสองร้อย, เอียงเจ็ดสิบห้า) for customers; decimal reading for technical content.
limitations: Practitioner blog of one shop; not an optometry council document.

sources.title: อ่านใบวัดสายตา SPH CYL AXIS ADD PD
sources.url: https://www.putuchon.com/post/อ่านใบวัดสายตา-sph-cyl-axis-add-pd
key_findings: Thai technical glosses: SPH = 'กำลังทรงกลม', CYL = 'กำลังทรงกระบอก', AXIS = 'แกน' (1-180 องศา), ADD = 'กำลังบวกที่เพิ่ม...เพื่อช่วยการมองใกล้', PD = 'ระยะห่างระหว่างรูม่านตาสองข้าง' (มิลลิเมตร).
Minus lens = เลนส์กระจายแสง, plus = เลนส์รวมแสง.
practical_applications: Thai-only glosses for VO when English abbreviations should not be read.
limitations: Practitioner page; no spoken forms given.

sources.title: ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์ - วิกิพีเดีย
sources.url: https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์
key_findings: Optometry = ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์, a โรคศิลปะ profession; practitioner = 'ผู้ประกอบโรคศิลปะโดยอาศัยทัศนมาตรศาสตร์'.
Cites ประกาศกระทรวงสาธารณสุข ฉบับที่ ๒ (พ.ศ. ๒๕๔๖); mentions ราชวิทยาลัยจักษุแพทย์แห่งประเทศไทย.
practical_applications: Use ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์ / นักทัศนมาตร (common) and จักษุแพทย์ in Thai scripts instead of English.
limitations: Article tagged as needing citations; no council document read.

sources.title: Wiktionary entries: myopia, astigmatism, ophthalmology, titanium, acetate, presbyopia, hyperopia
key_findings: myopia UK /maɪˈəʊ.pɪ.ə/, US /maɪˈoʊ.pi.ə/.
astigmatism US /əˈstɪɡmətɪzm̩/.
ophthalmology UK /ˌɒfθə(l)ˈmɒləd͡ʒi/ ~ /ˌɒpθə(l)ˈmɒləd͡ʒi/; US /ˌɑpθə(l)ˈmɑləd͡ʒi/.
titanium US /taɪˈteɪni.əm/ ~ /tɪˈteɪni.əm/; Thai translation ไทเทเนียม.
acetate /ˈæsɪteɪ̯t/.
presbyopia and hyperopia entries had no English IPA.
practical_applications: English IPA basis for RI-style transcription checks.
limitations: Cambridge and Oxford Learner's dictionaries returned HTTP 403, so the planned Tier-B dictionary IPA could not be read; community source.

sources.title: Thai script - Wikipedia (tone rules section)
key_findings: Class lists: high ข ฃ ฉ ผ ฝ ถ ฐ ศ ษ ส ห; mid ก จ ฎ ฏ ด ต บ ป อ; low = the rest.
Tone table by class x (live / dead short / dead long / mai ek / mai tho / mai tri / mai chattawa).
Low class: dead short → high, dead long → falling.
ห นำ before low sonorants (ง ญ น ม ว ย ร ล); อ นำ only in อย่า อยาก อย่าง อยู่.
practical_applications: Lookup table for checking a TTS tone error against spelling.
limitations: Tone section has no inline citations; first 100k characters read.

sources.title: Creating speech register in Thai conversation
key_findings: Register is built from formality-marking particles, pronouns, names, kin terms, titles and pragmatic particles.
Formality is a matter of degree, from the frequency and combination of these signs.
Strangers in unfamiliar situations negotiate a middle register.
practical_applications: Register in a script is set mainly by particle density, pronoun/kin-term choice and titles, not by vocabulary alone.
Shop VO to unknown customers = middle register (polite particle + kin/title terms, no slang).
limitations: Abstract only; four conversations analysed.

sources.title: Syntactic Distribution and Communicative Function of the /kh/ Polite Particles in Thai
key_findings: Article on distribution and function of ครับ/ค่ะ/คะ-family particles (Language and Linguistics 20(1):11-23).
practical_applications: Key reference to read next for particle placement rules.
limitations: PDF is an image scan without text layer; content not read.

sources.title: The Use of the Thai Final Particle Na by Japanese Learners of Thai
sources.authors: Maklai, Sumintra; Ratitamkul, Theeraporn; Sirikanerat, Thanasak
key_findings: Thai National Corpus: นะ has three functions - softening, emphasising, topic marking.
Native speakers and learners used นะ most for emphasis, least for topic marking.
practical_applications: นะ is not only a softener: placed after a topic ('แว่นตัวนี้นะ ...') it marks the topic - useful for natural VO pacing.
limitations: Abstract only; small pair-discussion sample (10+10).

sources.title: Gender-Differential Tendencies in LINE Use: A Case of Thailand
key_findings: 3,384 LINE messages, 13 colleagues: women used final particles (นะ จ้ะ/จ้า ล่ะ) more; men used more stickers.
คะ/ค่ะ is described as used by females; some men reported using kha playfully/flirtatiously with women.
นะ signals that a response is expected and softens the tone.
Differences are socially constructed and shaped by the platform, not determined by gender alone.
practical_applications: Particle choice signals persona, not just biological sex; avoid stereotyped 'female = many particles' writing.
limitations: One workplace chat group; written chat not speech.

sources.title: Thai sentence particles: forms, meanings and formal-semantic variations (Pacific Linguistics A-80)
key_findings: Foundational description of Thai sentence particles including a chapter on the forms and meanings of นะ (per search summary).
practical_applications: Reference for particle meanings beyond craft knowledge.
limitations: Search summary only; PDF not opened this session.
sources.license: CC BY-SA (Pacific Linguistics open archive) - not checked

sources.title: Thai sentence-final imperative discourse particles (JSEALS 15.1)
key_findings: Per abstract snippet: distribution of imperative particles (incl. นะ) depends on illocutionary force and Searlean felicity conditions.
practical_applications: CTA lines: choose imperative particle by speech act (request vs. suggestion vs. urging).
limitations: Search summary only; author name as shown by search, not confirmed on the article page.

sources.title: ระดับภาษาและการใช้ภาษาที่ถูกต้อง (course 113-108 การใช้ภาษาไทยเพื่อการสื่อสาร, week 3)
sources.authors: อ.รักษ์พงศ์ ธรรมผุสนา, Siam University
key_findings: Register = gradation of wording chosen by occasion, relationship and content.
Formal: พิธีการ (ceremony, high literature) and ทางการ/มาตรฐานราชการ (official letters, theses, speeches).
Informal: กึ่งทางการ (polite but not strict; business, people one does not know well or who are older/senior, lectures, light writing) and สนทนา / กันเอง levels.
practical_applications: Shop VO and ads sit at กึ่งทางการ; Mint & Tao dialogue at สนทนา/กันเอง.
limitations: Teaching handout (2011 semester 1/2554); school-grammar taxonomy, not sociolinguistic research.

sources.title: Roles of English in facial cosmetic advertisements in Thai magazines
key_findings: In 100 Thai cosmetic print ads, English is 'not really used for presenting meaning' but to catch attention, enhance product image/value and signal modernity.
practical_applications: English brand/tech words in our ads work as image signals - keep them few and say them clearly; carry the actual message in Thai.
limitations: Abstract only; print ads, one product category.

sources.title: Thai-English Code Mixing and Code Switching in Cosmopolitan Magazine
key_findings: Intrasentential code mixing was the most frequent; no tag switching found (per search snippet).
practical_applications: Thai copy typically mixes single English words inside Thai sentences - the case TTS handles worst.
limitations: Search summary only.

sources.title: Linguistic Devices in Digital Tourism Advertisements by the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT): A Discourse Analysis Perspective
key_findings: 30 TAT digital ads (Facebook, web, YouTube, 2022-2025): lexical selection ~42.5%, speech acts ~17.5%, claiming ~9.9% of devices.
Four strategies: creating atmosphere/identity, directing action, establishing credibility/authority, framing perspectives.
practical_applications: Ad script checklist: one mood/identity line, one clear action line, one credibility line.
limitations: Abstract only; tourism, not retail optics.

sources.title: Socio-cultural factors influencing face manifestation and communicative behaviour in Thai service encounters
key_findings: เกรงใจ (consideration for others) is a key factor in Thai service communication.
Role/socio-economic differences between agents and customers shape communication; agents' customer-facing face can conflict with organisational face.
practical_applications: Shop VO should leave the customer room to decide (no hard push); offers phrased as invitations.
limitations: Abstract only; hotel/travel settings.

sources.title: Understanding Elderspeak: An Evolutionary Concept Analysis (Innovation in Aging)
key_findings: Per search summary: studies disagree whether elderspeak helps or hinders comprehension; exaggerated prosody reduces comprehension.
Elderspeak is generally perceived as patronising; in dementia it increases resistiveness to care.
practical_applications: For older customers: slower, clearer and well-paced speech is fine; sing-song exaggerated pitch and baby-talk terms are not.
limitations: Search summary only (PMC page blocked by bot check); Western care settings; authors not recorded.

sources.title: The text analysis and processing of Thai language text to speech conversion system
key_findings: Thai texts often contain numbers, abbreviations and currency symbols; the two core problems are detecting non-standard words and disambiguating their reading.
practical_applications: Normaliser needs context rules (e.g. 6/6 vision vs 6/6 date).
limitations: Abstract-level record via search only.

sources.title: JaiTTS: A Thai Voice Cloning Model
sources.authors: Karnjanaekarin, J.; Trakuekul, P.; Panitsrisit, N.; Sumanakul, S.; Nitayasomboon, V.; Guntasin, N.; Denkavin, T.; Rutherford, A. T.
key_findings: Handles numerals and Thai-English code-switching without explicit text normalisation.
Short-utterance CER 1.94% vs human ground truth 1.98%; won 283 / lost 58 of 400 pairwise comparisons against commercial systems.
practical_applications: Modern end-to-end TTS can read raw numbers, but explicit normalisation stays the safe default for prices, powers and dates whose reading is a choice (casual vs formal).
limitations: Preprint abstract only; normalisation errors by category not reported in the abstract.

sources.title: Empowering Global Voices: A Data-Efficient, Phoneme-Tone Adaptive Approach to High-Fidelity Speech Synthesis
sources.authors: Geng, Yizhong; Xu, Jizhuo; Liang, Zeyu; Yang, Jinghan; Shi, Xiaoyi; Shen, Xiaoyu
key_findings: Uses Thai as a case study where 'intricate phonetic rules and sparse resources' are addressed via a phoneme-tone adaptive approach; claims state-of-the-art subjective/objective scores.
practical_applications: Confirms that tone-aware G2P is a known Thai TTS weak point; keep respellings that force tones.
limitations: Abstract only; details of preprocessing not read.

sources.title: Exploring Patterns and Challenges in English Word-Final Consonant Pronunciation among Southern Thai EFL Learners
key_findings: Per search summary: 27 undergraduates often dropped English final stops; voiced finals most often mispronounced or omitted; linked to Thai/Southern Thai phonology.
practical_applications: English lines for Thai staff: mark final consonants (price, size, fifty/fifteen) and drill them; avoid words ending in clusters where a simpler word exists.
limitations: Search summary only; small sample; year not confirmed.

sources.title: Metric Units and Everyday Measures (Thai grammar page)
key_findings: Per search summary: ครึ่งลิตร = half a litre; สองลิตรครึ่ง = two and a half litres (ครึ่ง after the unit adds a half).
practical_applications: Normaliser rule: N.5 + unit → N + unit + ครึ่ง (casual).
limitations: Search summary only; site of unknown authority. Needs a reference grammar check.

sources.title: Politeness and pragmatic competence in Thai speakers of English (Newcastle University PhD thesis)
key_findings: Per search summary: for Thai hotel workers speaking English, negative politeness was the chosen strategy in most scenarios.
practical_applications: English staff scripts: indirect, option-giving phrasing feels natural to Thai staff.
limitations: Search summary only; title and author inferred from the file name and snippet, not confirmed.

sources.title: Effect of Camera Angle on Perception of Trust and Attractiveness
key_findings: 12 actors filmed in frontal head-and-shoulder close-ups at 1 m, camera ~30 deg above, at, or ~30 deg below eye level; N=34 viewers (Empirical Studies of the Arts 36, online 2017).
Trust was highest at eye level (M=5.03) vs low angle (M=4.27, p=.007) and high angle (M=4.57, p=.082); low and high did not differ from each other.
No effect of camera angle on attractiveness or on Big-Five personality ratings.

Literature review: earlier findings are heterogeneous (Tiemens 1970 one of three newsreaders; Avery & Long 1976 minor; McCain et al. 1977 higher camera -> higher competence/composure/sociability; Kraft 1987 low=strength, eye=parity, high=weakness; Sevenants 2006 low->potency; Mandell & Shaw 1973 potency; Meridian 1987 no effect).
Authors conclude context and narrative strongly moderate camera-angle effects; Figure 1 lists angles used in prior studies (9-40 deg).
practical_applications: Direct-to-camera trust lines (shop staff, explainer VO with a face) -> eye level by default.
Do not assume low angle = more persuasive for a single talking face.
limitations: Small N (34), students, one context (game-show trust task), 30 deg only.
Large-effect power only (eta_p^2 >= .14).

sources.title: Does it matter to be pictured from below?
key_findings: Three 5-picture stories; the two characters were introduced in high-angle, eye-level or low-angle shots (~35 deg off eye level); linear vs random picture order.
In linear (story) order, low-angle shots raised Potency ratings; no effect on Evaluation or Activation.
In the chess story, the character shown from below was more often chosen as the winner.
In random order (no narrative) no camera-angle effect appeared, contrary to Kraft's (1987) prediction that weaker narrative = stronger angle effect.

Review section: Meyers-Levy & Peracchio (1992) found low angle best for products only under low processing motivation; eye level best under moderate; no effect under high motivation; Meridian (1987) found no effect.
practical_applications: Use low angle on a character only where the story already frames them as the winner/strong one; it reinforces rather than creates meaning.
limitations: Student sample, still pictures, three stories; potency only.
sources.license: open access journal (licence not stated on PDF)

sources.title: The Power of Pictures: Vertical Picture Angles in Power Pictures
sources.authors: Steffen R. Giessner; Michelle K. Ryan; Thomas W. Schubert; Niels van Quaquebeke
key_findings: Four archival studies (six samples) found media tend to depict powerful people from below more than powerless people; a salient power context strengthens this; two experiments found the same for people producing media content.
Explains the verticality-power link with evolutionary (height = formidability), social learning (children look up at powerful parents) and embodiment accounts.
Cites Mignault & Chaudhuri (2003) and Kraft (1987) as evidence that vertical angle shifts dominance judgments.
practical_applications: Picture makers already encode power with vertical angle, so audiences have learned the code; it is a convention reinforced by use.
limitations: Only abstract and introduction (pp. 1-4 of the preprint) read; archival design shows producer behaviour, not viewer effect.

sources.title: The influence of camera angle on comprehension and retention of pictorial events
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018) and Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): slide stories with characters shown from low, eye-level and high (up to ~40 deg) angles; low angles produced impressions of strength, action and superiority, eye level parity, high angles weakness, passivity and insignificance; effects on Potency and Activation, not Evaluation.
Kraft predicted that camera-angle effects grow when narrative structure is weak (later contradicted by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle 2006).
practical_applications: Classic citation for the power reading of vertical angle; use with the replication caveats.
limitations: Not read directly; findings only as reported by the two secondary sources.

sources.title: Judging people in the news - unconsciously: Effect of camera angle and bodily activity
sources.authors: Lee M. Mandell; Donald L. Shaw
key_findings: As summarised by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): a filmed interview with a fictitious appointee, ~12 deg angles; Potency and Activation were higher in low-angle than high-angle conditions; Evaluation did not differ.
practical_applications: Supports a modest potency effect of low angles on a speaking person.
limitations: Not read directly; bibliographic only.

sources.title: The effect of camera angle on source credibility and attraction
sources.authors: Thomas A. McCain; Joseph Chilberg; Jacob Wakshlag
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018): a higher camera angle raised competence, composure and sociability ratings of a TV speaker (opposite to the power convention); credibility was higher when fewer non-eye-level shots were cut in.
practical_applications: For credibility of a speaker, keep most shots at eye level; angle shifts work only sparingly.
limitations: Not read directly.

sources.title: Getting an angle in advertising: The effect of camera angle on product evaluations
key_findings: As summarised by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006): product evaluations were most favourable for low-angle photos and least for high-angle photos only when processing motivation was low; at moderate motivation eye level was best; at high motivation angle had no effect (heuristic-processing account).
A University of Twente thesis (search snippet) reports a failed replication of the need-for-cognition moderation.
practical_applications: Low-angle product hero shots may help fast-scrolling, low-attention viewers; do not expect them to matter to a careful buyer reading specs.
limitations: Not read directly; exact title taken from search results; moderation contested.

sources.title: Some relationships of camera angle to communicator credibility
key_findings: As summarised by Baranowski & Hecht (2018): only one of three newsreaders was rated higher on communicative ability and knowledgeability from a lower vantage point; no difference on authoritative/convincing.
practical_applications: Evidence that angle effects are small and person-dependent.
limitations: Not read directly.

sources.title: A facial-action imposter: How head tilt influences perceptions of dominance from a neutral face
key_findings: Per press release and abstract snippets: five studies, N=1,517; a downward head tilt with forward gaze increased perceived dominance of a neutral face.
Mechanism: tilt creates the illusion of lowered, V-shaped brows (an 'action-unit imposter' for AU4); the eye/brow region is necessary and sufficient.
practical_applications: A camera BELOW a face makes the head read as tilted UP relative to the viewer; a camera slightly ABOVE with the subject looking up into the lens reads as tilted down. Head pose relative to camera can counteract or reverse the expected low-angle 'power' effect (DERIVED).
limitations: Only press summary and abstract fragments read; head tilt is not the same manipulation as camera angle.

sources.title: The many faces of a neutral face: Head tilt and perception of dominance and emotion
key_findings: As cited by Giessner et al. (2011): 3-D modelled faces shown from seven vertical angles; perceived dominance vs submissiveness varied with vertical head/picture angle.
practical_applications: Supports a vertical-angle/dominance link for faces.
limitations: Not read directly; Journal of Nonverbal Behavior 27(2).

sources.title: Facial expression, size, and clutter: Inferences from movie structure to emotion judgments and back
sources.authors: James E. Cutting; Kacie L. Armstrong
key_findings: ~31,000 shots from 24 films (1940-2010): mean shot duration falls from ~8 s for extreme long shots to ~2.5 s for extreme close-ups.
Valence of faces was classified faster when faces were larger (closer scale): ~150 ms faster across scales 1-6 in movie stills; slight rise at ECU.
Clutter magnified the scale effect (~40 ms low clutter vs ~200 ms high clutter); filmmakers hold small-face, cluttered shots longer.
Seven-step shot scale: ELS, LS, MLS, MS, MCU, CU, ECU defined by focal-character size in frame.
practical_applications: Hold wide/cluttered shots longer; close-ups can be short. Emotion beats need the face big and the background clean.
limitations: Happiness/disgust only; reaction time, not felt emotion.

sources.title: Watching More Closely: Shot Scale Affects Film Viewers' Theory of Mind Tendency But Not Ability
key_findings: N=136, animated film 'Father and Daughter'; a SAD close-up of the girl raised spontaneous references to her mental (affective) states vs the long shot (p=.05) and vs a neutral close-up (p=.013).
A neutral close-up did not differ from the long shot; no effect on ToM ability when prompted.
practical_applications: A close-up only adds empathy when the face carries an emotion; a blank close-up is wasted. Relevant to faceless Mint & Tao: the emotional carrier must be posture/props, not a face (DERIVED).
limitations: One film, one emotion, students, animated stimulus; a corrigendum exists.

sources.title: Perspective Distortion from Interpersonal Distance Is an Implicit Visual Cue for Social Judgments of Faces
sources.authors: Ronnie Bryan; Pietro Perona; Ralph Adolphs
key_findings: Faces photographed simultaneously at ~45 cm vs ~135 cm (and 54 vs 120 cm outdoors), normalised for size, expression and lighting.
Close photos lowered trust-game investment and ratings of trustworthiness, competence and attractiveness (pooled trust d=0.24; effects d=0.14-0.36).
Close faces: nose relatively larger, ears smaller, narrower width-to-height ratio; participants did not notice the manipulation; explicit distance info did not change ratings.
Lens distortion was checked and negligible: the effect is camera DISTANCE (perspective), not lens aberration.
practical_applications: Shoot faces wearing glasses from >= ~1.2-1.5 m (longer lens), never arm's-length wide-angle, for trust and attractiveness.
limitations: 18 base faces, white males; online studies uncontrolled; small effects; ratings intercorrelated.

sources.title: The perceptual basis of common photographic practice
sources.authors: Emily A. Cooper; Elise A. Piazza; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: A picture is correct only from its centre of projection (COP); viewers do not compensate for wrong viewing distance: COP nearer than viewing distance -> depth looks expanded; farther -> compressed.

Preferred viewing distance barely depends on focal length (+20% vs +614% needed to match COP) and mostly on print size; intercept ~25 cm; preferred field of view ~22 deg (small prints) to ~36 deg (large).
Explains the 50 mm 'normal lens' rule (focal length ~ format diagonal, 43.3 mm for 35 mm); median of 3,930 Flickr SLR photos = 68 mm.
Recommends LONGER focal lengths for small images viewed close, e.g. phones (~30 cm).
practical_applications: For phone-viewed IG/TikTok, natural-looking people/products favour short-tele looks (~70-100 mm equiv.) more than 24-35 mm (DERIVED from their recommendation).
limitations: Small N in psychophysics (5-19); equations shown as images on PMC.

sources.title: Why pictures look right when viewed from the wrong place
sources.authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath; Ahna R. Girshick; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: Per abstract: perceived shapes in pictures stay nearly invariant over a wide range of oblique viewing angles when binocular cues to the picture surface are available.
Invariance comes from estimating the local surface orientation of the picture, not from geometric information in the picture; the model also explains perceived distortions in wide-angle pictures.
practical_applications: Off-axis phone viewing is mostly tolerated; wide-angle edge distortion is not cured by this compensation.
limitations: Abstract-level access only.

sources.title: The Arrow in the Eye (online book; chapters V 'The Robustness of Perspective' and VIII 'Marginal Distortions')
key_findings: Extends registry record Kubovy1986 (bibliographic). Robustness of perspective: viewed away from the centre of projection a picture should look sheared/magnified, yet viewers rarely notice; contested, with Rosinski & Farber arguing introspection is not evidence.
Leonardo expected pictures to look wrong unless seen from the COP or from >= 20x the largest dimension of the depicted objects.

Marginal distortion: correctly projected off-axis spheres become ellipses and off-axis columns become wider; painters drew spheres as circles and columns at equal widths, giving each its own principal ray; Uccello's Hawkwood mixes viewpoints.
practical_applications: In wide images, draw/accept round things (lenses, heads, plates) as near-circles near the edges; keep key products near the centre.
limitations: Online book; original publisher/year of this version not stated on pages read; relation to the 1986 Cambridge UP book assumed from authorship.

sources.title: Background Surface and Horizon Effects in the Perception of Relative Size and Distance
key_findings: Describes Sedgwick's (1973) horizon ratio: the horizon cuts objects on the same ground at the observer's eye height, so object size can be read as a multiple of eye height without knowing distance; Rogers (1996) found it works with explicit or implicit horizons in pictures.
Equal projected objects below the horizon: the higher one looks larger; this reverses when the lower object is on/above the horizon; holds for photographs.
The perceived horizon is pulled toward the visible end of the ground surface; distance judgments track height in the image.
practical_applications: Basis of the 'heads on horizon' check for AI images; a visible ground edge (floor/sea line) acts as the horizon for viewers.
limitations: Lab stimuli; size judgments not absolute.

sources.title: The visible horizon: A potential source of visual information for the perception of size and distance (doctoral dissertation)
key_findings: As summarised by Ozkan & Braunstein (2010): objects of equal height are cut by the horizon in the same proportion regardless of distance (horizon ratio).
practical_applications: Geometric rule behind the figure-height check.
limitations: Not read; title as commonly cited, not confirmed this session (dissertation, Cornell).

sources.title: Perspective Made Easy: a step-by-step method for learning the basis of drawing
key_findings: Horizon = eye level wherever you are; objects above it are seen from below, below it from above.

Figure-height transfer: line from a new spot through the feet of a known figure to the eye-level line, then back through the head gives the new figure's height (works whether heads are above or below eye level).
Vanishing points placed close together give 'violent', warped perspective (squares look like diamonds); place them far apart.
Circle in perspective = ellipse; the short (minor) axis lies along the cylinder's centre line (axle), the long axis forms a T with it.
Inclined planes vanish above/below the normal VP on a vertical through it (uphill street above the eye level, roofs on a vertical line).
Parallel edges cast parallel shadows to the same VP on a flat surface; sunlight = parallel rays, a nearby lamp fans shadows.
Reflections: upside down, as far below the surface as the object is above, share the object's VPs.
practical_applications: Source for the drawing procedures in PERSPECTIVE_MASTERY.md and the error library.
limitations: Text read via archive.org OCR (first ~100k characters); craft textbook, not perception research.
sources.license: unknown (1939 US edition; Dover reprint copyrighted)

sources.title: How to Draw: Drawing and Sketching Objects and Environments from Your Imagination
key_findings: Library records: Design Studio Press, 208 pp.; early chapters teach accurate perspective grids and ellipses (incl. 'drawing an ellipse on the minor axis') as the base for complex forms.
practical_applications: Standard reference for grids, minor-axis ellipses, environments.
limitations: Contents only from catalogue records; book text not read.

sources.title: ART 110 Week 2: Perspective Theory - Cone of Vision
sources.authors: Brigham Young University-Idaho, Department of Art
key_findings: Cone of vision drawn as 60 deg from the station point (30 deg each side of the line of sight); objects drawn outside it become distorted.
Placing VP1/VP2 on a small format limits the cone of vision.
practical_applications: Teaching convention for the 60 deg cone.
limitations: States that objects outside the cone 'appear blurred' - a simplification; the drawing distortion is geometric (marginal distortion), not optical blur.

sources.title: Perspective (In)consistency of Paint by Text
key_findings: Forensic geometry checks on DALL-E 2 images (~25 per prompt set): vanishing points of parallel lines, shadow-to-object lines meeting at the light's projection, object-to-reflection lines converging.
Kitchen floors had consistent VPs but countertops did not share the floor's VP/vanishing line in all 25 images: locally consistent, globally inconsistent.
All 25 sunny-day cube images had cast shadows inconsistent with one light; reflections failed in 22 of 25 and even plausible ones failed the geometric test.
practical_applications: Exact procedure for our AI-image perspective/shadow/reflection QC.
limitations: Preprint, one model (DALL-E 2), small exploratory sample; newer models may do better.

sources.title: PreciseCam: Precise Camera Control for Text-to-Image Generation
sources.authors: Edurne Bernal-Berdun; Ana Serrano; Belen Masia; Matheus Gadelha; Yannick Hold-Geoffroy; Xin Sun; Diego Gutierrez
key_findings: T2I outputs often default to a flat camera parallel to the ground with the horizon mid-frame.
Prompt words ('shot from below', 'wide angle', Firefly camera tags) give only coarse control; SDXL could not reproduce lens distortion via prompts at all.
Controls roll, pitch, vertical FOV and distortion with a trained conditioning module (57,380-image dataset).
practical_applications: Expect FLUX/Codex to drift toward eye-level, mid-horizon framing; state angle strongly and verify.
limitations: Preprint; camera accuracy shown mostly qualitatively; SDXL backbone, not FLUX.

sources.title: FLUX.2 prompting guide
key_findings: Extends registry record web:docs.bfl.ai:13. Recommends naming camera, lens and film stock for photorealism ('Shot on Hasselblad X2D, 80mm lens, f/2.8'); JSON schema has camera.angle, camera.distance, camera.depth_of_field.
FLUX.2 does not support negative prompts; write 'sharp focus throughout' instead of 'no blur'.
No dedicated perspective guidance.
practical_applications: Use positive camera phrasing; our local model is FLUX.1 schnell, so treat FLUX.2 advice as a hint.
limitations: Vendor docs for FLUX.2, not schnell; no evidence on how precisely numbers are followed.

sources.title: Gpt-image-1.5 Prompting Guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
key_findings: Camera/composition terms (lens, aperture feel, lighting) steer realism more reliably than generic quality words.
Specify framing/viewpoint (close-up, wide, top-down) and perspective/angle (eye-level, low-angle).
For edits: 'preserve the exact layout, proportions, and perspective'; for composites match lighting, perspective, scale and shadows; re-specify details that drift.
Page marked archived; no stated limits for camera control.
practical_applications: Codex prompt wording for angle/lens; keep the real frame photo via -i and state 'preserve proportions and perspective'.
limitations: Vendor guidance, not tested; model version may differ from what Codex uses.

sources.title: Angle of view (photography)
key_findings: Rectilinear lens focused at infinity: alpha = 2 arctan(d / 2f), d = sensor dimension (36 x 24 mm, diagonal 43.3 mm for full frame).
Close focus: use effective focal length F(1+m); with pupil ratio P: alpha = 2 arctan(d / (2F(1+m/P))).
Defines normal lenses as 36-60 mm on 35 mm format (62-40 deg).
practical_applications: FOV table in LENS_OPTICS.md (recomputed by us).
limitations: Community-edited; its table lists 102.7 deg horizontal for 14 mm while the formula gives 104.3 deg - we use the formula.

sources.title: Hyperfocal distance
key_findings: Extends registry record web:en.wikipedia.org:6. H = f^2/(Nc) + f (approx. f^2/(Nc)); focused at H, sharp from H/2 to infinity; example 50 mm f/8 c=0.03 mm -> H ~ 10.5 m.
Historical sources: Kingslake 1951, Derr 1906, Sutton & Dawson 1867, Taylor 1892.
practical_applications: Deep-focus establishing shots, hyperfocal table.
limitations: Community-edited; formulas cross-checked by our own computation.

sources.title: Depth of field
key_findings: DOF ~ 2u^2Nc/f^2 = 2Nc(1 - 1/M_T)^2 (paraxial approximation, u >> f).
Consecutive depths: focus at H -> H/2..inf; at H/2 -> H/3..H.
Same subject size + same f-number -> almost the same DOF regardless of focal length, but background blur differs.
Diffraction limits sharpness at small apertures, mostly relevant in close-up work; background blur disk b = d m_s x_d / D.
practical_applications: DOF reasoning for eyewear close-ups and AI prompt wording.
limitations: Community-edited; macro formula not given there.

sources.title: Depth of focus
key_findings: Depth of focus = tolerance of the sensor/film position (image side); t = 2Nc(1+m), ~2Nc at low magnification; measured in fractions of a mm.
Depth of field depends on focus distance; depth of focus does not; the terms are often confused. Cites Ray (2000) Manual of Photography.
practical_applications: Vocabulary hygiene: never write 'depth of focus' in a prompt when depth of field is meant.
limitations: Community-edited.

sources.title: Depth of Field and Bokeh
sources.authors: H. H. Nasse (Carl Zeiss Camera Lens Division)
key_findings: Image-side depth of focus depends only on the f-number, not focal length.
Object-side DOF is (almost) independent of focal length at the same imaging scale (subject size), because a longer lens is used from proportionally farther away.
This breaks down at large distances, and the maximum blur of a distant background is LOWER for shorter focal lengths than for longer ones even at equal DOF.
Uses circle of confusion z = 0.029 mm = format diagonal/1500 for 24x36; choice of focal length is decided by room, intended perspective and background.
practical_applications: To melt a shop background behind glasses: longer lens from farther away at the same framing, not just a wider aperture.
limitations: Manufacturer white paper; read in part (pp. 1-10 of ~45).

sources.title: Shutter Angles & Creative Control (RED 101)
key_findings: Shutter angle expresses exposure time relative to frame rate (rotary-shutter origin); 180 deg at 24 fps ~ 1/48 s is the common cinema setting.
Smaller angles (e.g. 45 deg) look stuttered/crisp like 1950s newsreels or modern action; larger angles smear motion more and give more light; 360 deg is the limit.
practical_applications: Motion-blur vocabulary for video prompts and for our rig.js motion blur choices.
limitations: Manufacturer tutorial; formula inferred from the worked example.

sources.title: Distortion (optics)
key_findings: Distortion = deviation from rectilinear projection; changes shape without necessarily reducing sharpness.
Barrel (magnification decreases off-axis; wide-angle, fisheye, wide end of zooms), pincushion (increases; older/cheap teles, binoculars), mustache (barrel centre, pincushion edges).
Brown-Conrady radial model with K1, K2 (negative K1 ~ barrel) and tangential terms; corrected with lens profiles (Lightroom, Lensfun, OpenCV).
Perspective distortion is a separate effect: it does not bend straight lines.
practical_applications: Distinguish bent lines (lens) from big noses/converging verticals (position).
limitations: Community-edited.

sources.title: Perspective distortion
key_findings: Linear perspective changes are caused by distance, not by the lens per se; extension (wide/close) vs compression (tele/far) distortion.
85-135 mm on 35 mm format are generally considered good portrait lenses; viewing a wide image closer (or tele image farther) reduces apparent distortion.
practical_applications: Supports 'distance first, lens second'.
limitations: Community-edited; viewing-distance claim marked citation needed there (but supported by Cooper et al. 2012).

sources.title: Vignetting
key_findings: Types: mechanical (hoods/filters), optical (cured by stopping down 2-3 stops), natural cos^4 falloff (not cured by stopping down; ~56% at 30 deg), pixel vignetting.
Cites Ray (2002) Applied Photographic Optics; artistic use to hold the eye centrally.
practical_applications: Subtle vignette in grade keeps eyes on the product; heavy vignette reads 'toy camera/retro'.
limitations: Community-edited.

sources.title: Chromatic aberration
key_findings: Longitudinal (axial) CA: colours focus at different distances; purple/green fringes in out-of-focus areas; reduced by stopping down; typical of long focal lengths.
Lateral (transverse) CA: magnification varies with wavelength; fringes toward edges; not reduced by stopping down; correctable in software by rescaling channels; typical of short focal lengths.
Corrected by achromats (f1V1 + f2V2 = 0), apochromats, low-dispersion glass, diffractive elements.
practical_applications: Detect fringes on metal frame edges in product photos; add only as a deliberate 'vintage lens' cue.
limitations: Community-edited; no discussion of artistic use.

sources.title: Fisheye lens
key_findings: Mapping functions: rectilinear r = f tan(theta); stereographic r = 2f tan(theta/2); equidistant r = f theta; equisolid r = 2f sin(theta/2); orthographic r = f sin(theta).
Circular fisheye (image circle inside frame, black corners; ~8-10 mm on full frame) vs diagonal/full-frame fisheye (12-18 mm).
Uses: action sports, music videos, peepholes, security cameras, domes/VR.
practical_applications: Peephole/door-camera POV look for story clips.
limitations: Community-edited.

sources.title: Forced perspective
key_findings: Uses angular size/relative size to make objects look larger/smaller/closer/farther; LOTR hobbits (moving sets), Hagrid (scaled props), Potemkin Stairs, Disney castles.
Requirements: enough DOF for both planes, matched lighting/contrast (counter aerial perspective), fixed camera at the zero-parallax point - parallax reveals the trick.
practical_applications: Giant-glasses or tiny-character gags in promo shots and puppet clips.
limitations: Community-edited; cites Purves & Lotto 2003, O'Shea et al. 1994, Mather 1996.

sources.title: Reverse perspective
key_findings: Also inverse/Byzantine perspective: farther objects drawn larger, parallels diverge, vanishing points appear in front of the picture; Byzantine and Russian icons, pre-Renaissance art, Cubism, children's drawings.
Why it arose is still debated.
practical_applications: Deliberate naive/folk look; recognise it as an error when unintended.
limitations: Community-edited.

sources.title: Parallel projection
key_findings: Orthographic (rays perpendicular to the plane) vs oblique (rays at another angle; cavalier, cabinet, military types); axonometric includes isometric, dimetric, trimetric.
Parallel lines stay parallel; length ratios along parallels preserved; circles not parallel to the plane become ellipses; no size change with distance.
Cites Krikke (2000) 'Axonometry: A Matter of Perspective', IEEE CG&A; Carlbom & Paciorek (1978).
practical_applications: Isometric infographics of a shop layout; orthographic front/side views for frame spec sheets.
limitations: Community-edited; isometric 30/120 deg and cabinet half-depth not stated on the page (standard drafting convention, flagged DERIVED/CRAFT in our text).

sources.title: La perspective curviligne (English: Curvilinear Perspective: From Visual Space to the Constructed Image, UC Press 1987)
key_findings: Per Wikipedia (search summary): formally codified curvilinear (five-point) perspective: four VPs around a circle (N, S, E, W) plus one at the centre; straight lines curve as in a fisheye; influenced by Escher; van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait cited as an early approximation.
practical_applications: Fisheye/POV panels in carousels and clips.
limitations: Book not read; details from a Wikipedia search summary.

sources.title: Using Blur to Affect Perceived Distance and Size
sources.authors: Robin T. Held; Emily A. Cooper; James F. O'Brien; Martin S. Banks
key_findings: Probabilistic model of how viewers combine defocus blur with other pictorial cues to estimate absolute distance and hence scale; an algorithm adds blur to sharp images to change perceived distance/size (the link to the tilt-shift miniature look is OUR reading; the paper does not use that term) (effect).
Experiment agreed closely with the model; some common blur approximations worked and others did not.
practical_applications: Miniature/diorama look: strong blur gradient consistent with the scene's depth = small scale; inconsistent blur bands fail (DERIVED).
limitations: Abstract only (ACM TOG 29(2), article 19).
Spot-check 2026-11-25: original wording checked; finding corrected to match the source.

sources.title: Contrast as a depth cue
sources.authors: Robert P. O'Shea; Shane G. Blackburn; Hiroshi Ono
key_findings: Per abstract/secondary citations: the lower-contrast region was judged farther, monocularly and binocularly, even when size pointed the other way; contrast acts as a pictorial cue mimicking aerial perspective.
Follow-up O'Shea, Govan & Sekuler (1997, Perception): blur is a depth cue independent of contrast.
practical_applications: Lower contrast/raise value of backgrounds to push them back; keep the product at highest contrast.
limitations: Abstract/search-summary level only.

sources.title: Shot (filmmaking)
key_findings: Field sizes: extreme long, long/wide (often establishing), full, medium long (frame ends near the knees), American/cowboy (upper thighs, holster), medium (around the waist), MCU (more shoulder), CU (shoulder line visible), ECU (chin to forehead or a detail), Italian shot (eyes only), two shot.
Reverse shot = 180 deg turn to the previous image, often with POV/OTS; insert replaces the picture while audio continues.
Cites Bowen 'Grammar of the Shot' 4th ed. 2018, Katz 'Film Directing Shot by Shot' 1991, Ascher & Pincus 1999.
practical_applications: Shared shot-size vocabulary in CAMERA_ANGLE_LIBRARY.json.
limitations: Community-edited; definitions vary across textbooks.

sources.title: Ultimate Guide to Camera Shots
key_findings: Practitioner taxonomy: EWS, WS, FS, MWS (knees up), cowboy (mid-thighs up, from Westerns), MS, MCU (chest up), CU, ECU; single/dirty single, two/three shot, OTS, over-the-hip, POV; eye/low/high/hip/knee/ground/shoulder level, Dutch, bird's eye/overhead (treated as one), aerial.
Stated purposes (craft): EWS isolation/unfamiliarity, low angle power, high angle inferiority, Dutch disorientation, ground level shows what the subject stands on.
practical_applications: Naming conventions for shot lists.
limitations: Craft claims, no evidence; treats overhead and bird's eye as identical.

sources.title: Cutaway (filmmaking)
key_findings: A cutaway interrupts continuous action with a view of something else, usually returning to the original shot; used to adjust pace, hide removed material, join two takes; documentary 'noddies' cover cuts; cites Brown (2012) Cinematography: Theory and Practice.
practical_applications: Cover jump cuts in staff/VO clips with shop-detail cutaways.
limitations: Community-edited; insert vs cutaway not distinguished there.

sources.title: Film Art: An Introduction (9th ed.)
key_findings: Cited by Sevenants & d'Ydewalle (2006, citing the 2004 edition) for the practice of distinguishing mainly three vertical camera positions - high, eye level, low - out of an infinite number of possible angles, and by Baranowski & Hecht (2018, 9th ed. 2010) for the conventional readings (low = dominance, high = vulnerability, eye level for neutral/factual).
practical_applications: Canonical vocabulary reference.
limitations: Not read this session; cited only via the two papers.

sources.title: Striking individual differences in color perception uncovered by 'the dress' photograph
sources.authors: Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Katherine L. Hermann, Bevil R. Conway
key_findings: Free-response survey N=1401 (313 naive): 57% blue/black, 30% white/gold, 11% blue/brown, 2% other.
Women and older people reported white/gold more; some observers switched on re-test (multistable); colour matches showed three peaks = three stable percepts.
Hypothesis: different priors about the illuminant along the daylight locus (cool prior -> white/gold, warm prior -> blue/black, neutral -> blue/brown).

Embedding the dress in scenes with a global warm or cool tint (including the model's skin) flipped most observers: 64% of W/G switched to B/K under warm light, 80% of B/K switched to W/G under cool light.
Larger image size increased W/G reports; blurring decreased them; chronotype trend not significant.
practical_applications: Product colours on the blue-yellow axis (navy, tortoise, brown/blue tints) need unambiguous illumination cues.
A tint applied to the whole scene incl. skin is read as light; check images at thumbnail size.
limitations: Short correspondence + supplement; online sample mostly US; mechanism partly hypothetical.

sources.title: Color Perception: Objects, Constancy, and Categories
key_findings: Natural objects have polychromatic colour distributions; observers estimate object lightness from the brightest parts excluding highlights.
Chromatic and luminance contrast are statistically independent in natural scenes; chroma tends to mark objects while luminance also varies with shading.
Memory colour effect: colour-diagnostic objects (e.g. a grey banana) look tinted toward their typical colour; strongest along blue-yellow; observers most uncertain along the daylight axis.

Constancy indices across 30 years range from near zero to near perfect; >=90% when adaptation is possible or naturalistic cues exist; index rises with publication year r(64)=0.43; appearance vs surface-match instructions matter.
Cues: adaptation and local contrast (major), interreflection/shading, depth, specular highlights, memory colour; full adaptation takes several minutes.
Metamer mismatching (clothing in a badly lit store vs daylight) makes constancy impossible but is rare in natural scenes.
#TheDress pixels lie along the daylight locus; rotating them off-axis reduces individual differences; percept can be primed but not voluntarily changed.
Number of basic colour terms varies by language (11 English/German, 12 Russian, 15 Korean, 5 Himba/Berinmo); category effects are high-level and reduced by verbal interference.
practical_applications: Judge product colour in the plane lit directly but non-specularly; keep cue-rich scenes for true colour; fix green-magenta errors before warm-cool (derived).
limitations: Review; individual claims rest on cited studies not read here.

sources.title: Color constancy
key_findings: Review of human colour constancy in Vision Research 51(7):674-700; excludes colour-vision deficiency and lightness constancy.
Author's site documents constancy indices (incl. Brunswik ratio) and a table of 80 indices from published studies.
practical_applications: Background for why constancy measurements vary with method (see WitzelGegenfurtner2018).
limitations: Full text not read; findings here only from search summaries and Witzel & Gegenfurtner's use of it.

sources.title: Comprehensive color solutions: CAM16, CAT16, and CAM16-UCS
sources.authors: Changjun Li, Zhiqiang Li, Zhifeng Wang, Yang Xu, Ming Ronnier Luo, Guihua Cui, Manuel Melgosa, Michael H. Brill, Michael Pointer
key_findings: CAM16 is a simpler revision of CIECAM02; CAT16 replaces CAT02 for chromatic adaptation alone; CAM16-UCS replaces CAM02-UCS for colour difference.
The 2016 conference version reports CAM16 solves the mathematical problems of CIECAM02 and performs as well or better.
Follow-up work (Gao et al. 2021) compensates the size effect in the CAT16 cone-like space.
practical_applications: Current appearance-model framework; supports the rule 'judge colour in final context and size'.
limitations: Abstract-level only; journal DOI not confirmed in this session; URL is the 2016 CIC conference version (A Revision of CIECAM02 and its CAT and UCS); follow-up only from search summary.

sources.title: Perception of three-dimensional shape influences colour perception through mutual illumination
sources.authors: Marina G. Bloj, Daniel Kersten, Anya C. Hurlbert
key_findings: Chromatic Mach card (magenta and white halves): the white side's perceived colour changes from pale pink to deep magenta when perceived shape flips concave/convex.
Visual system incorporates knowledge of mutual illumination early in colour processing.
practical_applications: Reflected colour (colour bleed) must be consistent with shape; cutouts need ground-colour bounce.
limitations: Abstract/summary level; PDF link returned 404.

sources.title: Practical Pigment Mixing for Digital Painting
key_findings: RGB painting software mixes like light: blue + yellow -> grey instead of green.
Kubelka-Munk (1931) predicts pigment mixing (repeated absorption and scattering) but was never adopted by painting software.
Latent space: RGB as mixture of 4 primary pigments + additive residual, enabling K-M mixing with RGB in/out (Mixbox).
Plain subtractive mixing (as used by CMYK) gives results too dark or wrong in colour compared with K-M.
practical_applications: Do not fake paint overlaps with CSS blend; use AI-painted overlaps or a pigment mixer for watercolour styles.
limitations: Mixbox licence reported as CC BY-NC in secondary sources (not checked).

sources.title: Ein Beitrag zur Optik der Farbanstriche
key_findings: Original two-flux model of light in paint layers (absorption K and scattering S), still widely used in industry.
practical_applications: Theoretical basis for pigment-mixing behaviour vs light mixing.
limitations: Not read; existence and page range from bibliographic records; English translation by S. Westin exists.

sources.title: Color Compatibility From Large Datasets
sources.authors: Peter O'Donovan, Aseem Agarwala, Aaron Hertzmann
key_findings: Analysed Kuler and COLOURLovers themes (>2 million created) and an MTurk rating set of 5-colour themes.
Little evidence that people gravitate to hue templates naturally or that matching a template gives higher scores; themes closely matching templates scored slightly lower.
Preference for hue entropy corresponding to about 2-3 hues per 5-colour theme.
Learned L1-regularised regression over features in several colour spaces predicts theme ratings; demographic groups rate differently.
practical_applications: Treat hue templates as idea generators; limit to 2-3 hue families; judge in context.
limitations: Context-free palettes rated online; interface bias in Kuler data acknowledged by authors.

sources.title: Color Harmonization
sources.authors: Daniel Cohen-Or, Olga Sorkine, Ran Gal, Tommer Leyvand, Ying-Qing Xu
key_findings: Finds the best-fitting harmonic hue template (8 types after Tokumaru et al. 2002 / Matsuda) and shifts image hues toward it with spatial coherence.
practical_applications: Tool for automatic palette unification of AI images; not evidence that templates are preferred.
limitations: Search summary only; PDF download failed in this session.

sources.title: Additivity of colour harmony
sources.authors: Li-Chen Ou, Patrick Chong, M. Ronnier Luo, Carl Minchew
key_findings: Harmony of a three-colour combination can be predicted by averaging the harmony of its three colour pairs (two-colour model).
Experiments in UK and US: 6545 three-colour wheels on a calibrated CRT and 111 interior images; simple and fairly robust predictor; may extend to more colours.
practical_applications: Check multi-colour palettes pair by pair, especially adjacent pairs.
limitations: Abstract only; lab and interior stimuli.

sources.title: Colour harmony
sources.authors: Stephen Westland, Kevin Laycock, Vien Cheung, Phil Henry, Forough Mahyar
key_findings: Review of major colour-harmony theories; asks whether fundamental laws of harmony exist; covers hue circularity, primaries and complementary colours.
practical_applications: Supports treating harmony schemes as conventions to test, not laws.
limitations: Search summary only.

sources.title: Investigation of complementary colour harmony in CIELAB colour space
sources.authors: Forough Mahyar, Vien Cheung, Stephen Westland, et al.
key_findings: AIC 2007 Midterm (Hangzhou) paper: opposite hues in CIELAB do not accurately predict perceived complementary relationships.
practical_applications: Do not treat 180-degree rotation in Lab/OKLCH as an exact complement.
limitations: Conference paper known only from a search summary; URL is the related review record.

sources.title: Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Red on Perceived Attractiveness
sources.authors: Gabrielle K. Lehmann, Andrew J. Elliot, Robert J. Calin-Jageman
key_findings: Adversarial collaboration (original proponent + replicators).
Publication-bias indicators significant for women (and for men without one outlier); effects decline with publication year.
Preregistered studies of women rating men: d=-0.10 vs 0.21 non-preregistered.
practical_applications: Never claim red 'makes' models or products more attractive.
limitations: Discussion section only partly read (page truncated).

sources.title: Color and psychological functioning: a review of theoretical and empirical work
key_findings: Lists effects reported by >=5 labs (red before challenging tasks undermines performance; red in sport; red and attraction; blue light alertness; blue logos and trust appraisals).
Weaknesses: underpowered samples overestimate effects; colour rarely controlled at spectral level; theory either too specific or too general; focus on red.
Concludes it is 'premature to offer any bold theoretical statements, definitive empirical pronouncements'.
practical_applications: Use association language in briefs; avoid applied colour-psychology promises.
limitations: Pre-dates the 2018-2020 meta-analyses that weakened red effects.

sources.title: Limited evidence for the effect of red color on cognitive performance: A meta-analysis
key_findings: 67 effect sizes, 38 samples, 22 publications (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 27(6):1374-1382).
Anagram d=-0.06, knowledge d=-0.04 (n.s.); reasoning d=-0.34 [-0.61, -0.06].
Strong decline effect (early reasoning estimate ~-0.86) and publication bias; bias-adjusted effects near zero.
Casts doubt on a robust colour-priming effect in achievement situations.
practical_applications: Do not cite 'red impairs thinking/focus' in eye-care content.
limitations: Covers red and cognitive tests only.

sources.title: Color Semantics in Human Cognition
key_findings: Colour-concept associations and colour meaning (semantics) are not the same and can conflict.

Color inference framework: pooling inference produces colour preferences (ecological valence; ~80% of variance in average US preferences); assignment inference maps colours to concepts considering the whole set.
Even abstract concepts have systematic colour associations; semantics is flexible and context dependent.
practical_applications: Choose legend/code colours so each concept's best match is distinct within the set; motif colours must not be reused for other meanings.
limitations: Mainly US/Western samples; visualisation context.

sources.title: Color in Complex Scenes
sources.authors: Steven K. Shevell, Frederick A. A. Kingdom
key_findings: In complex scenes an object's colour is not fully determined by the light from that object; chromatic representation also shapes texture, segmentation, depth, motion.
No variant of the equivalent-uniform-background hypothesis explains colour in complex scenes; chromatic variation in the surround alters perceived contrast (Brown & MacLeod 1997).

Cone signals cannot separate illuminant SPD from reflectance; gray-world and brightest-patch estimates miss cues such as specular reflections, shadows, mutual interreflections, luminance-chromaticity correlation.
Cites von Kries (1905) adaptation as classic baseline.
practical_applications: Busy colourful surrounds mute a product; cue-rich lighting supports true product colour.
limitations: Read in part (abstract, constancy section, figure notes).

sources.title: Large shifts in color appearance from patterned chromatic backgrounds
key_findings: Two-chromaticity patterned backgrounds shift perceived colour more than a uniform background of either chromaticity.
Follow-ups explain shifts by S-cone spatially antagonistic receptive fields; assimilation and simultaneous contrast can act together.
practical_applications: Hatching over tints shifts the tint toward the line colour (assimilation).
limitations: Abstract and citing papers only.

sources.title: Neural locus of color afterimages
sources.authors: Qasim Zaidi, Robert Ennis, Dingcai Cao, Barry Lee
key_findings: Recordings from macaque retinal ganglion cells: afterimage signals originate in the retina (slow adaptation of RGC population) and may be modified by cortical processes.
practical_applications: Successive contrast between shots/slides is a low-level effect: preview sequences, not single stills.
limitations: Abstract via search; PMC page blocked by verification.

sources.title: The Brightness of Colour
sources.authors: David Corney, John-Dylan Haynes, Geraint Rees, R. Beau Lotto
key_findings: More saturated stimuli appear brighter at equal luminance (Helmholtz-Kohlrausch); blues and reds brighter than equiluminant yellows/greens, blue slightly more than red.
Bayesian ideal-observer model trained on natural surface statistics reproduces the effect; V1 fMRI responses track brightness, not luminance.
practical_applications: Eye overrates contrast of saturated red/blue text; always measure.
limitations: Effect sizes for humans described qualitatively; fMRI N=3; mechanism one proposal among several.

sources.title: An Opponent-Process Theory of Color Vision
key_findings: Three opponent channels (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white) supported psychophysically with hue cancellation; helped reconcile Hering with trichromacy.
practical_applications: Conceptual basis for complementary afterimages and opponent contrast vocabulary.
limitations: Not read (PDF download failed); later work shows unique hues do not map neatly onto cone-opponent channels (search summary).

sources.title: Computational Color Constancy: Survey and Experiments
sources.authors: Arjan Gijsenij, Theo Gevers, Joost van de Weijer
key_findings: Taxonomy: static methods (gray-world, white-patch, gray-edge; unified in a Minkowski framework), gamut-based, learning-based.
Gray-world assumes the average scene reflectance under neutral light is achromatic; deviations are attributed to the illuminant.
Computational models cannot fully explain human constancy.
practical_applications: Explains why auto-WB fails in one-colour scenes (sea, foliage); shoot a neutral reference.
limitations: 2011 state of the art; deep-learning AWB since then not covered.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - WCAG 2.2
key_findings: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold, ~24px / ~18.5px).
4.5:1 compensates contrast-sensitivity loss of about 20/40 acuity (typical around age 80).
Ratios are not rounded (4.499 fails); logotypes exempt but brand guidelines do not exempt ordinary text; background images with insufficient contrast fail.
practical_applications: Eyewear customers skew older: treat 4.5:1 as floor; measure text over photos on the worst patch.
limitations: Web-oriented; social images apply it by analogy. Year = WCAG 2.2 Recommendation year.

sources.title: APCA in a Nutshell
key_findings: Lc 90 preferred body text; 75 minimum body text; 60 other content text; 45 headlines/large heavy text and detailed icons; 30 absolute minimum other text; 15 minimum non-text.
Developer describes APCA as candidate contrast method for WCAG 3; APCA Readability Criterion maintained separately, still in development.
practical_applications: Supplementary check for text on dark backgrounds.
limitations: Developer's own document; W3C draft says WCAG 3 contrast algorithm is yet to be determined (see W3C_WCAG3_WD).

sources.title: Introduction to the ICC profile format (color.org profile page)
key_findings: An ICC profile provides data to convert between a device colour space and the device-independent PCS based on the CIE 1931 observer; PCS is 'virtual destination for input transforms and virtual source for output transforms'.
Four intents: media-relative colorimetric, ICC-absolute colorimetric (spot colours, proofing), saturation (vendor-specific, charts), perceptual (vendor-specific, photographs).
Current specification v4.4; iccMAX also exists.
practical_applications: Photos perceptual; brand colours relative colorimetric with proof; P3 -> sRGB conversion needs a deliberate intent.
limitations: Overview page, not the normative ICC.1 text.

sources.title: ITU-R BT.709 entry, ICC characterization data registry (with BT.1886 notes)
key_findings: BT.709 defines a camera OETF (4.5L below 0.018, 0.45 power above), not a display EOTF; BT.1886 defines the display EOTF approx. power 2.4 deviating near black.
practical_applications: Export SDR clips as Rec.709; test on real phones because platforms interpret 709 differently.
limitations: Values from search summaries of the registry and secondary pages; ITU PDFs not opened.

sources.title: Color space (MDN glossary) / Apple CGColorSpace displayP3
key_findings: Display P3 uses DCI-P3 primaries, D65 white point and the sRGB transfer function (original DCI-P3: ~6300K white, gamma 2.6).
Gamut about 25% larger than sRGB in area and ~50% in volume (secondary); CSS Color 4 predefines display-p3; color-gamut: p3 media query.
practical_applications: iPhone photos of saturated frames may clip when forced to sRGB; gamut-map deliberately.
limitations: Search summary of MDN/Apple/Wikipedia; Apple page fetch returned only the title.

sources.title: Color Gamut Mapping
key_findings: Survey of 90+ gamut-mapping algorithms and ISO/CIE approaches; chapter on evaluating gamut-mapping algorithms.
Author chaired CIE TC 8-03 and helped create CIE guidelines for evaluating gamut-mapping algorithms.
practical_applications: Clip vs compress decision when moving P3 or sRGB content to print/smaller gamuts.
limitations: Publisher listing only.

sources.title: Final Report of the O.S.A. Subcommittee on the Spacing of the Munsell Colors
sources.authors: Sidney M. Newhall, Dorothy Nickerson, Deane B. Judd
key_findings: Describes a modified and enlarged Munsell solid from 1940 visual estimates (Munsell renotation), defined in the CIE (ICI) system under Illuminant C (JOSA 33(7):385-418).
practical_applications: Munsell H V/C vocabulary is tied to CIE colorimetry; usable in critique and convertible.
limitations: Abstract only; Munsell polar spacing cannot be perfectly uniform (secondary).

sources.title: The Art of Pixar: The Complete Color Scripts and Select Art from 25 Years of Animation
key_findings: Collects the colour scripts of Pixar features; reviews/interviews credit Ralph Eggleston with starting colour scripts on Toy Story (small pastel drawings per scene focusing on basic colour).
Revised 2020 edition with foreword by Eggleston and introductions by Sharon Calahan and Harley Jessup.
practical_applications: Model for one-thumbnail-per-beat colour scripts.
limitations: Book not read; claims from publisher page, reviews and author interview summaries; dates of first colour script differ (1993 vs 1995).

sources.title: Pixar in a Box - The Art of Lighting: Color scripts (Khan Academy)
key_findings: A colour script is a snapshot of the whole film with a frame painted from each scene, showing how each story moment will be lit and its overall colour and value structure (~7 min video).
Series also contains 'The Art of Lighting' and 'Learning Color Science from a Pixar Color Scientist'.
practical_applications: Basis for our per-beat colour-script template.
limitations: Khan Academy page failed to render in fetch; content from secondary listings.

sources.title: If It's Purple, Someone's Gonna Die: The Power of Color in Visual Storytelling
key_findings: Practitioner book on colour in film storytelling (Focal Press).
practical_applications: Craft reference for motif colours; specific claims not usable until read.
limitations: Not read; bibliographic only.

sources.title: O Brother, Where Art Thou? - cinematography by Roger Deakins (American Cinematographer)
key_findings: Shot in summer with lush greens; bleach-bypass/bi-pack tests could not desaturate selectively.

Deakins and Cinesite colorist Julius Friede selected the greens of trees/grass and turned them into 'dry browns and yellows' for the look of 'old, hand-tinted postcards'; little else changed; windows on only a couple of shots.
About 10 weeks in the digital suite; more manipulation added noise/artifacts.
practical_applications: Selective hue-range grading that protects skin; minimal secondaries on AI images.
limitations: Practitioner account; 'first DI' priority disputed (Pleasantville cited as earlier DI timing).

sources.title: ACES documentation - background/overview
sources.authors: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (ACES Central)
key_findings: Scene-referred framework; encodings ACES2065-1 (SMPTE ST 2065-1), ACEScg (linear AP1 for CG/compositing), ACEScct (log AP1 for grading).
Pipeline: input transform -> grading -> optional look -> rendering/output transform to display; ACES 1.3 added gamut compression (secondary).
practical_applications: Composite in linear light, grade, convert to display last.
