limitations: Search summary of the docs and secondary guides.

sources.title: CIE 224:2017 Colour Fidelity Index for accurate scientific use
key_findings: Defines general colour fidelity index Rf with 99 test colour samples and updated colour space; shares calculation framework with IES TM-30-18.
Rf is explicitly not a replacement for CRI Ra (CIE 13.3-1995) for product rating, specification or regulation.
practical_applications: Prefer lamps reported with Rf/TM-30 data for product photography and try-on mirrors.
limitations: Publisher page; full report paywalled.

sources.title: TM-30: What have we learned in the past two years? (DOE presentation)
key_findings: TM-30-15: CAM02-UCS, 99 colour evaluation samples, Planckian/D-series reference; Rf, Rg, 16 Rcs,hj, 16 Rf,hj, colour vector graphic.

Summarising Royer et al. 2016 (Lighting Research & Technology): normalness and preference driven by red chroma + average fidelity; proposed criteria normalness Rf>=80 with 0%<=Rcs,h1<=8%; preference Rf>=74 with Rg>=100 or 0%<=Rcs,h16/h1<=15%.
practical_applications: Light specification for shop try-on and product photography.
limitations: Slide deck summarising peer-reviewed work; original LRT papers not read.

sources.title: ISO/CIE 11664-2:2022 Colorimetry - Part 2: CIE standard illuminants
key_findings: D65 represents average daylight with CCT about 6500 K (6504 K exact after the c2 change); defined as a tabulated SPD, no recommended physical source.
practical_applications: D65 is the white of sRGB/BT.709/Display P3; 'daylight' lamps only approximate it.
limitations: Publisher page and secondary sources.

sources.title: Billmeyer and Saltzman's Principles of Color Technology (3rd ed.) - definitions of metamerism
key_findings: Metamerism: different spectra with identical colorimetric coordinates for a single viewing condition; illuminant metamerism (match fails when light changes); observer metamerism (match fails for another observer).
practical_applications: Explains why frame parts/cases can match in the shop and differ in daylight.
limitations: Definitions quoted second-hand in a mailing-list post; book not read; 4th edition not checked.

sources.title: Colors of the day in Thailand
sources.authors: Wikipedia contributors (plus travel/culture pages in the same search)
key_findings: Sunday red, Monday yellow, Tuesday pink, Wednesday green, Thursday orange, Friday blue, Saturday purple; derived from Hindu astrology (navagraha), linked to Buddha images of the day; birth-day colour treated as lucky; royal ceremonies honour birthday colours.
Details vary between sources (Wednesday day/night).
practical_applications: Optional day-themed content; respect royal associations.
limitations: Tier E; not verified against Thai scholarly sources.

sources.title: Thailand: One-year period of mourning declared
sources.authors: Al Jazeera (and other news reports in the same search)
key_findings: After King Bhumibol's death (13 Oct 2016) the government declared one year of mourning; black and white worn nationwide; black clothing shortages; reports say other subdued colours were later accepted.
practical_applications: Use monochrome/black-white for condolence posts; pause festive palettes during national mourning.
limitations: News summaries; exact official wording not read.

sources.title: Thai Color Terms and Their Structures
key_findings: Thai National Corpus (novels 2008-2017), 13 key colour words incl. separate 'blue' and 'light blue'; 332 non-basic colour terms found.

Applying Berlin & Kay strictly, concludes Thai is at stage 4 with 5 basic terms (white, black, red, yellow, green); blue, light blue, brown, purple, pink, orange, grey treated as non-basic because named after things.
practical_applications: Thai colour words in briefs carry object references; distinguish fa and nam-ngoen explicitly.
limitations: Corpus-linguistic, not perceptual; conclusion conflicts with other Thai studies (9-12 terms).

sources.title: A comparison of Thai and Vietnamese color terms
key_findings: Reports 12 Thai basic colour terms (stage 7 of Berlin & Kay) and 9 Vietnamese.
practical_applications: Shows Thai basic-term count depends on criteria.
limitations: Search summary of repository record only; author's full name not confirmed.

sources.title: Vision & Invention - chapter on colour discord (web edition)
key_findings: Discord = relational effect when a colour's value runs against its natural order (raised toward tint or lowered toward shade) next to another colour; types light, dark, double, muted discord.
Natural order: yellow lightest, violet darkest (after Rood/Carpenter); examples Bonnard, Vuillard, Impressionist light blue/violet shadows.
Use light discord sparingly to enliven; afterimages and simultaneous contrast strengthen discord.
practical_applications: Small value inversions for tension in story scenes.
limitations: Craft text; no empirical support.

sources.title: Okhsv and Okhsl - two new color spaces for color picking
key_findings: HSL lightness 'does not match the perception of lightness well at all for saturated colors'; HSV hue has severe distortions; both built on sRGB without appearance research and not continuously differentiable.
Okhsv/Okhsl keep OKLab hue with cylindrical sRGB mapping; goals (perceptual L/h, cylinder, smooth variation) conflict; sRGB only.
practical_applications: Use Okhsl-style pickers or OKLCH, never HSL S/L to judge equal lightness/vividness.
limitations: Author's blog, not peer-reviewed; publication date not confirmed on page.
sources.license: unknown (blog; code MIT per author, not checked)

sources.title: Perspectives on science and art
sources.authors: Bevil R. Conway; Margaret S. Livingstone
key_findings: Fixations concentrate on regions of high local contrast (citing Reinagel & Zador 1999); eyes attract gaze partly because they hold high local contrast.
Shadows must be locally darker and relatively desaturated to read as shadows (citing Kingdom et al. 2004/2005); their hue can be almost anything.
Faces stay recognisable at low resolution and in simplified/exaggerated forms (citing Sinha et al. 2006); simplified stencil shapes remain recognisable.
Artists were more often strabismic than non-artists in the authors' survey; reduced stereo may favour monocular cues (shading, occlusion, perspective).
Depth from shading need not be globally consistent; viewers accept physically impossible shadows/reflections (citing Cavanagh 2005).
practical_applications: Put the strongest local contrast where the eye should land (focal glasses, a character's head).
Stylised charcoal shadows only need to be darker (and greyer) than their surroundings; their exact geometry is free.
limitations: Short review; value structure (notan) itself is not discussed.
Strabismus link is correlational.

sources.title: Building the gist of a scene: the role of global image features in recognition
key_findings: Scene gist can be computed from a low-dimensional global code of spatial layout (spatial envelope) without first recognising objects.
With brief presentations observers rely on the low-spatial-frequency part of hybrid images; longer viewing shifts reliance to finer content.
Processing runs global-to-local, which does not have to mean a fixed low-to-high spatial-frequency order.
practical_applications: The coarse, blurred, small version of an image (its big value masses) is what a scrolling viewer gets first: design and test it.
Thumbnail/blur checks are a proxy for first-glance reading.
limitations: Read via abstract and preprint excerpts, not full text.
Natural scenes, not illustrations or layouts.

sources.title: From blobs to boundary edges: Evidence for time- and spatial-scale-dependent scene recognition
key_findings: A coarse description (oriented 'blobs' in a spatial arrangement) can initiate scene recognition before object identity is processed.
At ~30 ms masked presentation observers used the low-spatial-frequency part of hybrid images; at longer durations the high-frequency part (as summarised by Oliva & Torralba).
practical_applications: Big value blobs carry the first read; fine line/texture is read later.
A blurred/thumbnail check approximates the first tens of ms of viewing.
limitations: Accuracy figures not seen; summary via abstract and secondary review.

sources.title: The briefest of glances: The time course of natural scene understanding
key_findings: 75%-correct thresholds with masking: global properties (naturalness, openness, depth...) mean 34 ms (19-47 ms); basic-level categories mean 50 ms (30-67 ms).
Global layout properties are available before the scene is named; 20 participants, 548 landscape photos at 256x256 px.
practical_applications: The overall structure of an image (open/closed, deep/flat, light/dark) is read within tens of ms: set it with value masses before detail.
Supports testing images at small size: what survives 256 px and a glance is the design.
limitations: Landscape photographs only; masked lab presentation differs from feed scrolling.

sources.title: How many pixels make an image?
key_findings: Human scene categorisation stays high across low-resolution and multi-megapixel images.
(Secondary summary) Viewers classify scenes and identify several objects at 32x32 pixels.
practical_applications: A 32x32 colour or 64-px greyscale thumbnail is a defensible 'gist' test size: subject and scene type should still read.
limitations: Exact accuracy per resolution not read (full text not accessed).

sources.title: Is it warm? Is it real? Or just low spatial frequency?
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) The Mona Lisa's smile is carried mainly by low spatial frequencies, so it is more visible in peripheral vision and fades when looked at directly.
Later work (Kontsevich & Tyler 2004) tested the claim with noise manipulations.
practical_applications: Soft, low-frequency value shapes can carry mood that survives a glance and the periphery; crisp detail is only seen where the viewer looks.
limitations: Original letter not read; content from press and citing papers.

sources.title: Rembrandt's textural agency: A shared perspective in visual art and science
sources.authors: Steve DiPaola; Caitlin Riebe; James T. Enns
key_findings: Rembrandt varied detail selectively ('textural agency') to guide gaze; with Rembrandt-style renderings of photographed portraits, viewers fixated the detailed eye faster and longer, with calmer eye movements.
Viewers preferred the selectively detailed renderings to the uniformly detailed original photographs (press summary).
practical_applications: Keep the sharpest, finest detail on the focal feature (glasses, a hand, part of a face) and reduce it elsewhere.
Calmer viewing paths come from a single detail peak, not uniform sharpness.
limitations: Abstract and press summaries only; numeric results not read.
Portraits only.

sources.title: Following the masters: Portrait viewing and appreciation is guided by selective detail
sources.authors: Steve DiPaola; Caitlin Riebe; James T. Enns
key_findings: (Abstract excerpt/summaries) Painted portraits differ from photos in that selected regions are rendered in sharper detail; gaze was attracted to and held longer by regions of finer detail and by textural highlighting.
The study set out to separate detail from confounds (meaning, lighting) that usually co-occur with detail.
practical_applications: Detail is a lever separate from value contrast: it can place the eye even when lighting is even.
limitations: Full abstract and results not read; Perception 42(6):608-630 per library record.

sources.title: Measuring visual clutter
sources.authors: Ruth Rosenholtz; Yuanzhen Li; Lisa Nakano
key_findings: Proposes Feature Congestion, Subband Entropy and Edge Density as image-computable clutter measures; clutter = how hard it is to add an item that captures attention.
Colour variability matters for clutter (captured only by Feature Congestion).
A later review reports simple edge density predicting search difficulty about as well as feature congestion.
practical_applications: Edge density (edge pixels / area) is a cheap, evidence-linked clutter proxy for backgrounds behind text or the hero.
limitations: Abstract and repository page only; validated on maps/scenes, not illustrations.

sources.title: Capabilities and limitations of peripheral vision
key_findings: Peripheral vision supports many tasks despite losing much information; a lossy, relatively fixed peripheral encoding may explain the difficulty of peripheral recognition, search, change blindness and gist.
practical_applications: Outside the focal zone viewers get a summary of detail; spend detail where the eye lands and keep the periphery statistically calm.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Visual crowding: a fundamental limit on conscious perception and object recognition
key_findings: Crowding - impaired identification of an object among nearby clutter - limits perception across much of the visual field.
(Secondary) The crowding zone is roughly half the target's eccentricity (Bouma's rule).
practical_applications: Small details (logo, temple engraving, lettering) placed near other detail in the periphery will not be identified; give them space or move them to the focal zone.
limitations: Abstract and secondary statements; Bouma figure from citing reviews.

sources.title: Isophote distance: a shading approach to artistic stroke thickness
sources.authors: Todd Goodwin; Ian Vollick; Aaron Hertzmann
key_findings: Stroke thickness modelled as the image-space distance to the nearest isophote: thicker for nearer and less-curved forms, thinner for distant and highly curved ones; clamped to [Tmin, Tmax].
Reproduced the line weights of illustration examples with few parameters.
practical_applications: Rule set for line weight in pencil/charcoal and rig line art: weight by depth, form size, curvature and light side.
limitations: Graphics method validated by visual comparison, not perception experiments.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: original wording checked; finding corrected to match the source.

sources.title: How to Draw Pictures, Part 4: Line Thickness
key_findings: Line thickness falls with distance and with radial curvature; thick forms get thicker strokes; strokes thicker on the underside of forms lit from above.
Silhouettes usually thicker than interior lines; strokes taper at free ends but not where they pass behind another object.
Artists compress the thickness range and care about relative differences; the author says these trends are observations, not systematic tests.
practical_applications: Direct line-weight checklist for Mint & Tao pencil art and SVG rig strokes.
limitations: Expert blog by a graphics researcher; observations, not experiments.

sources.title: Why do line drawings work? A realism hypothesis
key_findings: Hypothesis: the visual system treats line drawings as approximately realistic renderings; drawing techniques are chosen to convey shape to a human observer.
Argues an edge-detector account (Sayim & Cavanagh 2011) cannot fully explain differences between photo edges and drawn lines.
practical_applications: Draw the lines a plausible shading of the form would produce (contours, creases), not every edge in a reference photo.
limitations: Theoretical paper; abstract and introduction only.

sources.title: What line drawings reveal about the visual brain
key_findings: Lines in standard drawings stand for depth or slant discontinuities; artists omit shadow borders, which would read as false object boundaries.
Line drawings are recognised by infants, people without pictorial culture and chimpanzees - not purely a learned convention.
Junctions carry 3D meaning: T = occlusion, Y = convex corner, X = transparency; contours may end where a smooth surface turns away.
practical_applications: Pencil/charcoal line art: draw occluding contours and creases, end lines where forms turn, keep clean T-junctions at overlaps; use X-junctions (background line continuing through the lens) for glass.
limitations: Perspective article; synthesis, not new experiments.

sources.title: Where do people draw lines?
sources.authors: Forrester Cole; Aleksey Golovinskiy; Alex Limpaecher; Heather Stoddart Barros; Adam Finkelstein; Thomas Funkhouser; Szymon Rusinkiewicz
key_findings: Artists' lines for the same 3D shape largely overlap (75% within 1 mm of another artist's line), especially along occluding contours.
Most non-contour lines lie on large image-intensity gradients and match line-drawing algorithms; 14% were not explained by any local property studied.
practical_applications: Occluding contours are the non-negotiable lines; interior lines go where shading changes fast. Use this to judge AI 'line art' that adds random interior lines.
limitations: Abstract/project page; small artist sample; smooth 3D models, not characters.

sources.title: Stylization and abstraction of photographs
key_findings: Stylises photographs into line-and-region abstractions, keeping detail where viewers' eye movements show meaningful content and removing it elsewhere.
practical_applications: Model for selective detail: keep structure and detail at fixated/meaningful regions, flatten the rest into large regions.
limitations: Abstract and course summary; evaluation details not read.

sources.title: Abstracted painterly renderings using eye-tracking data
key_findings: Uses a few seconds of a viewer's eye-tracking data to decide where a painterly rendering keeps detail; elsewhere strokes are larger and simpler.
practical_applications: Detail allocation can follow where people look; our proxy is the saliency map from analyze_image.py.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Simple line drawings suffice for functional MRI decoding of natural scene categories
sources.authors: Dirk B. Walther; Barry Chai; Eamon Caddigan; Diane M. Beck; Li Fei-Fei
key_findings: Scene category decoded from fMRI activity for line drawings as well as for colour photographs, from V1 to PPA/RSC.
Global scene structure preserved by line drawings is integral to scene-category representation.
practical_applications: Line-art backgrounds for Mint & Tao can carry place (cafe, beach, street) with a few structural lines; texture everywhere is not needed.
limitations: Six scene categories; abstract and press release.

sources.title: Photographic tone reproduction for digital images
sources.authors: Erik Reinhard; Michael Stark; Peter Shirley; James Ferwerda
key_findings: Maps high-dynamic-range scene luminance to a low-range display using ideas from Ansel Adams' Zone System (11 print zones, 0 black to X white; key value; dodging-and-burning).
A simple global operator plus local dodging-and-burning gave good results across many test images (authors' report).
practical_applications: Tonal compression vocabulary: choose the key (where middle grey sits), roll off highlights instead of clipping, keep local contrast at the subject.
limitations: Abstract and summaries; graphics evaluation, not perceptual experiments.

sources.title: Global nonlinear compression of natural luminances in painted art
sources.authors: Daniel J. Graham; David J. Field
key_findings: Paintings cannot reproduce natural luminance ranges; a log-like nonlinearity is a first approximation of how artists compress luminance.
A painter's global compression curve ('artist's look-up table') may be characteristic of a painter; Western observers preferred many such transforms over a plain log transform.
practical_applications: Tonal compression is a style choice: define a 'house curve' per series (e.g. charcoal: lifted blacks, compressed mids) and keep it.
limitations: Conference proceedings; abstract and excerpts.

sources.title: Application of Fourier analysis to the visibility of gratings
sources.authors: F. W. Campbell; J. G. Robson
key_findings: Grating detection thresholds for different waveforms relate through Fourier theory; proposes independent mechanisms tuned to limited spatial-frequency ranges.
(Secondary) The contrast sensitivity function is band-pass, peaking around a few cycles per degree.
practical_applications: Very fine texture at phone viewing distance is near-invisible; mid-scale marks carry most visible contrast.
limitations: Peak value from secondary summary.

sources.title: Does luminance-contrast contribute to a saliency map for overt visual attention?
key_findings: Contrast is elevated at fixated points, but when contrast was modified in natural images no causal contribution of luminance contrast to overt attention was detected; saliency may be computed late.
Parkhurst & Niebur (2004) re-explained the data with second-order (texture) contrast.
practical_applications: Contested note: raw value contrast alone does not guarantee gaze; combine it with detail, meaning (faces, product) and isolation.
limitations: Abstract only.

sources.title: Visual correlates of fixation selection: effects of scale and time
sources.authors: Benjamin W. Tatler; Roland J. Baddeley; Iain D. Gilchrist
key_findings: Image features at fixation contributed similarly across viewing time (unlike Parkhurst et al. 2002).
(Secondary) Edge content and contrast were stronger fixation predictors than colour in these authors' work.
practical_applications: Edges are a stronger gaze lever than hue alone: keep the hardest edges at the focal area.
limitations: Search summary and secondary descriptions only.

sources.title: Colour vision brings clarity to shadows
sources.authors: Frederick A. A. Kingdom; Catherine Beauce; Lyndsay Hunter
key_findings: Colour vision helps identify shadows among other luminance changes; shadows carry shape, depth and movement information once identified.
practical_applications: Shadow masses read best when darker AND slightly desaturated relative to the lit surface; coloured shadows are fine if this holds.
limitations: Abstract and later citations.

sources.title: Prior knowledge on the illumination position
key_findings: Shape-from-shading assumes light from above, biased toward above-left (about 20-30 degrees per a companion paper); one later study found no left bias.
practical_applications: Light flat line-art and charcoal forms from upper-left by default so bumps read as bumps; reverse only on purpose.
limitations: Abstract/secondary; left bias is contested.

sources.title: Face recognition by humans: Nineteen results all computer vision researchers should know about
sources.authors: Pawan Sinha; Benjamin Balas; Yuri Ostrovsky; Richard Russell
key_findings: Familiar faces are recognised at very low resolution (high accuracy at 16x16 blocks in a cited study).
practical_applications: Identity is carried by coarse configuration; for faceless Mint & Tao the coarse silhouette (hair mass, head shape, posture) must carry identity instead.
limitations: Search summary; the caricature result attributed to this paper by Conway & Livingstone was not seen directly.

sources.title: Identification of everyday objects on the basis of silhouette and outline versions
key_findings: Identification of filled silhouettes and outlines of Snodgrass-Vanderwart objects ranged from near zero to perfect depending on the object; norms widely reused.
practical_applications: Silhouette readability is object- and view-dependent: choose the view (pose, angle of the glasses) whose silhouette identifies it, and test it.
limitations: Abstract; full author list not checked.

sources.title: Humans prefer curved visual objects
key_findings: Objects with curved contours were liked more than sharp-angled versions, for real objects and meaningless patterns; authors proposed sharp angles signal threat.
practical_applications: Rounded shapes as the default for friendly characters/mascots and calm promo layouts.
limitations: Abstract; threat explanation later contested (Bertamini 2016).

sources.title: Do people prefer curved objects? Angularity, expertise, and aesthetic preference
sources.authors: Paul J. Silvia; Christopher M. Barona
key_findings: (Via citing papers) Curvature preference held after controlling perceived complexity, using regular and irregular polygons; expertise effects were inconsistent across studies.
practical_applications: Curvature preference is not a reason to avoid angular design for expert audiences; test.
limitations: Paper not reached; content only from Bertamini 2016 and Cotter 2017 citations.

sources.title: Do observers like curvature or do they dislike angularity?
sources.authors: Marco Bertamini; Letizia Palumbo; Tamara N. Gheorghes; Mai Galatsidas
key_findings: Four experiments: curved shapes preferred (about 50 vs 37 on the rating scale), not explained by complexity; curved lines preferred to both straight and angular lines.
Approach to curves but no avoidance of angles in an implicit task; a threat account cannot fully explain the effect.
Cites Leder, Tinio & Bar (2011): curvature preference vanished for negatively valenced objects.
practical_applications: Use curves to add warmth; use angles for energy/tension rather than expecting 'danger' by default.
limitations: Small samples (14-36); some statistic reporting inconsistencies noted on reading.

sources.title: Comparing angular and curved shapes in terms of implicit associations and approach/avoidance responses
sources.authors: Letizia Palumbo; Nicole Ruta; Marco Bertamini
key_findings: IAT: curved polygons associated with positive and safe (and a gender pattern), angular with negative and danger.
A manikin approach/avoidance task did not show the pattern a pure threat account predicts.
practical_applications: Round = positive/safe and angular = negative/danger are measurable implicit associations at the abstract-shape level.
limitations: Abstract; abstract polygons, not characters.

sources.title: How universal is preference for visual curvature? A systematic review and meta-analysis
key_findings: 61 studies, 106 samples, 309 effects, about 11,000 participants: curvature preference g = 0.39 [0.25, 0.52].
Larger with limited presentation time (g 0.75 vs 0.32), meaningless stimuli (0.56) and real objects (0.42); no effect for spatial designs (-0.04); experts small and n.s. (0.13).
Large heterogeneity; no clear small-study bias. Reliable but not universal.
practical_applications: At glance speed (feeds) curvature helps most; for experts and architecture-like layouts it matters little. A default lean, not a law.
limitations: Only continuous measures; culture not tested as a moderator; about two thirds of the full text read.

sources.title: The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems
sources.authors: Aleksandra Ćwiek et al. (incl. Marcus Perlman)
key_findings: 917 speakers of 25 languages (9 families, 10 writing systems): strong overall evidence for the bouba/kiki effect; bouba more consistent than kiki; largely independent of orthography.
practical_applications: Round shapes match soft-sounding names and voices; pair round mascots with soft names/voices, spiky ones with sharp.
limitations: Abstract and press; whether Thai was among the languages not confirmed.

sources.title: Synaesthesia - A window into perception, thought and language
sources.authors: V. S. Ramachandran; Edward M. Hubbard
key_findings: Named the bouba/kiki effect (after Köhler's takete/baluba) and argued that naming is not fully arbitrary.
practical_applications: Historical anchor for shape-sound mapping; use Cwiek2022 for robust evidence.
limitations: Not read; the widely quoted agreement percentage was not verified.

sources.title: Universal aesthetic of fractals
sources.authors: Branka Spehar; Colin W. G. Clifford; Ben R. Newell; Richard P. Taylor
key_findings: (Secondary) Preference for fractal patterns peaks at mid fractal dimension (about 1.3-1.5) across natural, mathematical and painted (Pollock) fractals.
Later work (Spehar et al. 2016; Street et al. 2016) reports individual differences and treats 'universal' cautiously.
practical_applications: Detail density: moderate complexity is liked more than sparse or dense; a texture field should not be maximally busy.
limitations: Paper not read; claims from citing reviews.

sources.title: The glasses stereotype revisited: Effects of eyeglasses on perception, recognition, and impression of faces
sources.authors: Helmut Leder; Michael Forster; Gernot Gerger
key_findings: Faces with full-rim glasses rated less attractive and likeable than without; rimless did not differ; both rated more intelligent and successful; rimless raised trustworthiness.
Glasses drew gaze to the eye region; rimless made faces less distinctive.
practical_applications: Frame visibility changes impressions: full-rim adds intelligence/competence cues; rimless keeps the face's own look. Nothing here on face-shape matching.
limitations: Abstract; European sample.

sources.title: The effect of the shape of eyeglasses on judgements of personality
key_findings: 39 Japanese undergraduates imagined wearing round or square eyeglasses: round -> rated self warmer; square -> more competent and more stubborn.
Face shape was not manipulated; small between-subjects sample; main ANOVA statistics not reported in the text.
practical_applications: Weak, preliminary support that round frames read warm and square frames read competent; face-shape matching advice remains retail convention.
limitations: Very small N; conference proceedings; self-ratings of imagined wear.

sources.title: Is artists' perception more veridical?
key_findings: Artists were as affected by visual context and constancies (size, lightness, shape) as novices; no special access to the retinal image.
Later work (2014) links drawing skill to efficient encoding of object structure; Ostrofsky et al. report a constancy-accuracy correlation (mixed evidence).
practical_applications: Value judged by eye on a colour image is unreliable even for trained artists: check value in greyscale/numerically.
limitations: Search summary of abstracts.

sources.title: Munsell Value (How Color Notation Works)
key_findings: Munsell value runs 0 (black) to 10 (white) in perceptually equal steps; N5 is middle grey; real pigments only approach N0/N10.
practical_applications: Use the 0-10 value vocabulary in briefs; a 5-value plan maps roughly to N2, N4, N5-6, N7-8, N9.
limitations: Search summary of the page.

sources.title: ISO/CIE 11664-4:2019 Colorimetry - Part 4: CIE 1976 L*a*b* colour space
key_findings: Specifies CIELAB coordinates including the lightness correlate L* (cube root of relative luminance with a linear segment near black; 0-100).
practical_applications: Numeric value thresholds can be stated in L*; for neutrals OKLab L = (L*+16)/116 above the dark linear segment.
limitations: Standard text not read; formula as quoted in secondary encyclopedic sources.

sources.title: Plein-air tip: grouping tonal values
key_findings: Organising values into a light group and a dark group is 'an essential composition strategy'; connect darks into one unbroken mass instead of scattered accents; reserve high contrast for what should be noticed.
A simple tonal design reads at a glance and at small size (reply in comments); 'shape welding' merges adjacent similar values.
practical_applications: Mass shadows of figure and furniture into one dark shape in charcoal stories; keep the light group simple.
limitations: Practitioner blog; no tests.

sources.title: Edges (lesson series) and Designing Value Groups (course)
key_findings: (Search summaries) Start from hard edges, then soften transitions and lose edges in shadow to steer the eye to the focal point; squinting groups values and blurs detail.
practical_applications: Edge pass procedure for painted/FLUX images: decide the hard edges first, lose the rest.
limitations: Only search snippets read.

sources.title: Creating Characters with Personality: For Film, TV, Animation, Video Games, and Graphic Novels
key_findings: (Via student papers) Proportion and body shape create visual interest and reveal personality; a widely cited source for shape-language character design.
practical_applications: Practitioner basis for primary/secondary shape design of mascots and Mint & Tao silhouettes.
limitations: Not read; publisher and year not confirmed this session.

sources.title: Physically Based Rendering: From Theory to Implementation, 4th ed. — §9.3 Specular Reflection and Transmission; §11.1 Volume Scattering Processes
sources.authors: Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob, Greg Humphreys
key_findings: Table 9.1 IOR: air 1.00029, ice 1.31, water 1.333, fused quartz 1.46, glass 1.5-1.6, sapphire 1.77, diamond 2.42
Critical angle for air-glass TIR roughly 42 degrees
Conductors use complex IOR; light absorbed within ~0.1 micrometre
Media: sigma_t = sigma_a + sigma_s; transmittance falls exponentially; single-scattering albedo = sigma_s/sigma_t; mean free path = 1/sigma_t
practical_applications: Lens Fresnel/TIR table in LIGHTING_PHYSICS
Volumetric light and fog vocabulary
limitations: Extends registry record PBRT4 (which was bibliographic only): two sections read in full this session; other chapters not read

sources.title: Physically-Based Shading at Disney (SIGGRAPH 2012 course notes v3)
key_findings: Principles: intuitive not physical parameters, as few as possible, 0-1 over plausible range
Parameters: baseColor, subsurface, metallic, specular, specularTint, roughness, anisotropic, sheen, sheenTint, clearcoat, clearcoatGloss
specular 0-1 maps to incident specular 0-0.08 = IOR 1.0-1.8; 0.5 = IOR 1.5 default
Clearcoat fixed IOR 1.5 (polyurethane)
alpha = roughness^2 for perceptual linearity
Diffuse is tinted by subsurface absorption; specular not tinted unless metallic
MERL observations: some woods show specular modulation; fabrics odd grazing response
practical_applications: PBR parameter table; rule: non-metal highlights are white
limitations: Extends registry record Burley2012 (publisher page only); full notes read this session via PDF text extraction; production model, art-directable rather than strictly physical

sources.title: Real Shading in Unreal Engine 4 (SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes)
key_findings: Base material: BaseColor, Metallic, Roughness, Cavity; Specular dropped, non-metal F0 constant 0.04
Variable IOR 'fairly unimportant for nonmetals'
Physically accurate inverse-square falloff windowed: saturate(1-(d/r)^4)^2/(d^2+1)
Sphere and tube area lights via representative point with energy conservation so materials look the same regardless of light size
practical_applications: Falloff explanation; why eyewear lenses are an exception to constant F0
limitations: Real-time production notes (industry); not peer reviewed

sources.title: Background: Physics and Math of Shading (SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes)
key_findings: Absorption, scattering and their combination set appearance; white = high scattering + low absorption
Ordinary diffuse is subsurface scattering at a scale smaller than a pixel
Schlick Fresnel F0 + (1-F0)(1-cos)^5; zones 0-45 / 45-75 / 75-90 degrees; red zone visible only at extreme edges

F0 table (from RTR3): water 0.02, plastic/glass low 0.03, plastic high 0.05, glass high/ruby 0.08, diamond 0.17, iron 0.56-0.58, copper 0.95/0.64/0.54, gold 1.00/0.71/0.29, aluminium 0.91-0.92, silver 0.95/0.93/0.88
Non-metals outside labs mostly 2-5% F0
practical_applications: F0 values in material library; prompt rule against 'highly reflective acetate'
limitations: Course notes hosted on a university teaching mirror

sources.title: Real-Time Rendering, 4th ed.
sources.authors: Tomas Akenine-Möller, Eric Haines, Naty Hoffman, Angelo Pesce, Michał Iwanicki, Sébastien Hillaire
key_findings: Chapters include 7 Shadows, 8 Light and Color, 9 Physically Based Shading, 10 Local Illumination, 11 Global Illumination, 14 Volumetric and Translucency Rendering, 15 Non-Photorealistic Rendering
practical_applications: Pointer for deeper reading on shadows, GI, volumetrics
limitations: Only the book's website/table of contents read; content not read

sources.title: Optics, 5th ed.
key_findings: Standard optics textbook: propagation of light, geometrical optics, polarization, interference, diffraction (chapter list)
practical_applications: Reference for Fresnel/polarization/thin-film interference foundations
limitations: Bibliographic only (publisher listing); dates differ 2016/2017 between listings; no content cited from it

sources.title: Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces
sources.authors: Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li, Kenneth E. Torrance
key_findings: Extends microfacet theory to rough transmission (e.g. etched/ground glass)
Introduces GGX distribution, closer match than Beckmann for some surfaces
GGX later identified with Trowbridge-Reitz
practical_applications: Frosted glass / satin acetate vocabulary; roughness on transmissive materials
limitations: Abstract and secondary descriptions only

sources.title: Measuring and Modeling Anisotropic Reflection
key_findings: Introduces a reflectance measurement device and a mathematical model of anisotropic reflectance, fitted to measured surfaces
practical_applications: Brushed metal/hair anisotropy vocabulary
limitations: Only the abstract was readable; highlight direction vs groove direction NOT confirmed from this source

sources.title: Production Friendly Microfacet Sheen BRDF
key_findings: Cheap, artist-friendly sheen lobe for cloth; layered via albedo scaling
Its distribution ('Charlie') adopted by glTF KHR_materials_sheen
practical_applications: Velvet/fabric sheen parameter in material library
limitations: Search summary only

sources.title: Light Scattering from Human Hair Fibers
sources.authors: Stephen R. Marschner, Henrik Wann Jensen, Mike Cammarano, Steve Worley, Pat Hanrahan
key_findings: Fibre modelled as transparent elliptical cylinder with absorbing interior and tilted scales
Lobes R (surface), TT (transmission), TRT (internal reflection, secondary highlight)
Secondary highlight not present in black hair
practical_applications: Hair highlight rules for characters
limitations: Abstract + secondary excerpts; full paper not read

sources.title: GPU Gems 3, Chapter 14: Advanced Techniques for Realistic Real-Time Skin Rendering
key_findings: Skin: oily layer + epidermis (narrow scatter) + dermis (wide scatter)
Specular F0 = 0.028 from assumed IOR 1.4; skin specular should be white
Red scatters much farther than green/blue (red profile ~16 mm wide in model)
Without SSS skin looks hard and dry; errors cause red glow around shadows, waxy ears
practical_applications: Skin rendering rules and AI artefact checks
limitations: Real-time technique chapter; final ~10% of page not read; author names from general knowledge of the book, page header not quoted

sources.title: KHR_materials_ior (glTF 2.0 extension specification)
key_findings: Default ior 1.5; dielectric_f0 = ((ior-1)/(ior+1))^2 = 0.04 at 1.5
Example IORs: air 1.0, water 1.33, eyes 1.38, window glass 1.52, sapphire 1.76, diamond 2.42

sources.title: The perception of cast shadows
sources.authors: Pascal Mamassian, David C. Knill, Daniel Kersten

Visual system likely assumes a stationary light source
practical_applications: Moving shadow = levitation cue in 2.5D clips; never move the light with the object
limitations: Abstract only

sources.title: Light and Form, Part 1 (Gurney Journey blog)
key_findings: Form principle: analyse nature as geometric solids rendered by tonal contrast
Terms: center light, light/dark halftones, terminator (light tangent to form), highlight (reflection of source, not always at center light), cast shadow
Soft source -> gradual terminator; sun -> strong division
Comments: core usually just past terminator, not always present; darkest spot often the contact crack; 'model the lights or the shadows, not both'
practical_applications: Light-on-form sequence; charcoal three-value plan
limitations: Practitioner blog; some rules come from reader comments endorsed by the author. Gurney2010 book is a separate registry record

sources.title: Elements of Light and Shadow (course notes)

Center light, halftones, terminator, core shadow (darkest part of form shadow near terminator), reflected light, cast shadow, occlusion shadow (darkest, in crevices)
practical_applications: Shadow family table
limitations: Practitioner teaching; no date

sources.title: Water Reflections, Part 1 (Gurney Journey blog)
key_findings: Light tones reflect a little darker because some light enters the water
Water is near-perfect mirror only at a shallow viewing angle; looking steeply down little sky is reflected
practical_applications: Water reflection rules mapped to Fresnel

sources.title: Light — Science & Magic: An Introduction to Photographic Lighting (6th ed. adds Robin Reid)

sources.title: Inverse-square law and the five-times rule for extended sources (CIE 2025 paper by Dotreppe et al.; PetaPixel 2021; photometry teaching notes) — search summary
key_findings: Inverse-square valid only beyond the limiting photometric distance, which depends on source size, intensity distribution, luminance distribution and acceptable error
Minimum test distance 5x largest source dimension for near-Lambertian sources; at 10x radius error ~1%
Ignoring the rule gave deviations up to 32% for task lighting
practical_applications: Large-softbox exception to inverse square
limitations: Search summary across several sources; CIE paper not read

sources.title: A Practical Analytic Model for Daylight
sources.authors: A. J. Preetham, Peter Shirley, Brian Smits
key_findings: Rayleigh extinction ~ lambda^-4, verified experimentally; blue (400 nm) scattered ~10x red (700 nm); low sun yellow/orange from longer path
Haze = more scattering than molecules, less than fog; Mie particles scatter more uniformly -> whitening
Turbidity = (haze+molecular optical thickness)/molecular; linked to meteorological range (contrast threshold 0.02)
Cites psychology: aerial perspective a fundamental depth cue and the only absolute cue for distant unfamiliar objects; Leonardo's observations: horizon whitening, density near ground, hue shift
practical_applications: Aerial perspective, haze and turbidity control in scenes
limitations: Model has known weaknesses addressed by Hosek-Wilkie 2012

sources.title: Precomputed Atmospheric Scattering
key_findings: Real-time Rayleigh+Mie multiple scattering from ground to space
Sky colour in daylight and twilight, aerial perspective for all view/sun directions, earth and mountain shadows as light shafts
practical_applications: Physics behind light shafts and twilight sky
limitations: Abstract only

'if one is to be five times as distant, make it five times bluer'

sources.title: Building Imaginary Worlds: The Theory and History of Subcreation
key_findings: Routledge, New York, 2012, xiv + 394 pp. Treats imaginary worlds as entities in their own right across literature, comics, film, TV, games and the internet, rather than as products of one narrative or medium.
Table of contents (catalogue record) includes a section 'Invention, Completeness, and Consistency' (p. 33ff). Content of that section is reported in BarkerWolf2016.
practical_applications: Use invention / completeness / consistency as the three quality axes of any series world.
limitations: Book not read; existence and structure confirmed via publisher and library catalogue; details come from the Barker review and Wolf's reply.

sources.title: Review and Response: Mark J. P. Wolf, Building Imaginary Worlds (review by Martin Barker; response by Mark J. P. Wolf)
sources.authors: Martin Barker; Mark J. P. Wolf
key_findings: Participations 13(1), May 2016. Barker: Wolf's worlds seek three never-fully-achievable goals: completeness, coherence and consistency; narrative follows a 'principle of economy' while world-building follows an 'encyclopedic impulse' (Wolf p. 8).

Wolf lists four levels at which a world can alter the ordinary: nominal (naming), cultural, natural (species), ontological (rules of the universe); everything not changed is assumed to work as in the real world (people eat, travel takes time, people die).
Wolf (p. 42): casual audiences do not piece together world data but still sense how fleshed-out a world is, which can affect reception.
Wolf (p. 60): deliberate gaps, enigmas and unexplained references keep a work alive because they invite speculation.

Wolf's reply: incompleteness is inevitable, not a requirement; enigmas only work when there is already enough world data for an illusion of completeness, and must be used sparingly - too many and the audience loses interest or feels manipulated.
Barker's critique: Wolf privileges 'encyclopedic' fan engagement over character-driven immersion; Wolf replies few readers study a world without characters they like.
practical_applications: Change as few real-world rules as possible and name them explicitly; leave a small number of planted mysteries, not many.
Build world data for coherence even if most viewers never see it.
limitations: Review-and-reply format; second-hand view of the book.

sources.title: Convergence Culture: Where Old and New Media Collide
key_findings: NYU Press 2006 (revised 2008). Per catalogue descriptions: uses The Matrix as a case where consumers track bits of a story across multiple media channels; chapters on Survivor spoilers, American Idol, The Matrix, Star Wars fan films, Harry Potter fan writing.
practical_applications: Foundational reference for 'transmedia storytelling'; see Jenkins2007 for the short principles.
limitations: Book not read; existence, publisher and year confirmed via MIT CMS page and library catalogues.

sources.title: Transmedia Storytelling 101
key_findings: Transmedia story elements are dispersed across channels, each medium ideally making its own unique contribution.

Transmedia stories are usually built around complex fictional worlds rather than single characters or plots; worlds can support many interrelated stories and invite an 'encyclopedic impulse' to master a world that always exceeds the audience's grasp.

'Additive comprehension' (term credited to Neil Young): each new text adds information that revises understanding of the whole; tension between rewarding followers and staying accessible to newcomers.
Gaps and hints invite fan speculation and elaboration.
practical_applications: Each episode/post should add one new fact about the world (additive), yet stand alone for a first-time viewer.
limitations: Academic blog post by the field's founder; conceptual, no data.

sources.title: Game Design as Narrative Architecture
key_findings: Designers as 'narrative architects': spaces carry narrative potential in four ways: evocative spaces (draw on stories audiences already know), enacted stories (micronarratives held together by broad goals and conflicts), embedded narratives (story information placed in objects and traces for the audience to reconstruct), emergent narratives (systems rich with narrative potential).
Embedded narrative needs redundancy because any single clue may be missed; the world becomes 'a memory palace'.
practical_applications: Put backstory in set dressing (an old photo, a worn chair) and repeat the key clue in more than one form.
limitations: Author web copy is undated; year is the standard citation (published in Wardrip-Fruin & Harrigan, First Person, MIT Press) not shown on the page.
About games; transfer to linear clips is by analogy.

sources.title: Possible Worlds (the living handbook of narratology)
key_findings: Created 2012, revised 2013. Principle of minimal departure: readers imagine a fictional world as close to the actual world as the text allows, changing only what the text requires (Walton: 'reality principle').
Doležel: fictional worlds are radically incomplete; a text's strategies of showing and hiding shape its aesthetic effect.
Storyworlds as modal systems: a textual actual world plus characters' private worlds (knowledge, obligations/desires, fantasies); conflict between these drives plot.
Accessibility typology: fictionalised history (shares real past/geography), realism (keeps natural laws), fantasy (breaks natural laws, keeps logic), nonsense (breaks logic).
practical_applications: State in the bible which real-world rules are suspended; audiences default everything else to reality.
Track each character's knowledge separately (who knows what, when) - a key continuity field.
limitations: Theory entry; not empirical.

sources.title: Transmedia Storytelling: Industry Buzzword or New Narrative Experience?
key_findings: Storyworlds 7(2), 1-19. Asks whether transmedia storytelling is storytelling or mainly a marketing strategy, and whether it is new; contrasts it with adaptation using Jenkins's definition.
practical_applications: A skeptical counterweight: spreading a world over many posts is not automatically a better story; each piece must still work as a story.
limitations: Only the opening excerpt/abstract available; argument and conclusions not read.

sources.title: On Fairy-Stories
key_findings: Per secondary summaries: a successful Secondary World needs the 'inner consistency of reality', which Tolkien places under Art (craft), not imagination alone; it produces Secondary Belief, as opposed to 'willing suspension of disbelief'.
Per secondary summaries: anyone can say 'the green sun'; making a world where it is credible takes labour and skill.
practical_applications: Wonder is cheap; credibility is earned by consistency.
limitations: Primary text not read; only search summaries/study guides. Year of first publication (1947, Essays Presented to Charles Williams) is the standard citation, not confirmed this session.

sources.title: Sanderson's First Law
key_findings: 'An author's ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic.'
Soft systems (vague rules) create wonder and should rarely solve problems; hard systems (clear rules) can solve problems; most writers sit between; prefers rules, costs and laws.
Don't add convenient new powers or laws to fit one situation.
practical_applications: Any special rule in a series (immunity, ghosts visiting at 2 am, a glasses 'power') may only resolve a plot if it was set up earlier.
limitations: Craft essay by a novelist; tier D, not science.

sources.title: Environmental Storytelling: Creating Immersive 3D Worlds Using Lessons Learned from the Theme Park Industry
key_findings: The story is a 'big picture' set of rules guiding every texture and sound; breaking established rules leaves audiences feeling 'cheated'.
Audiences should know 'Where am I?' within about 15 seconds, from environmental clues rather than exposition.
Cause-and-effect vignettes (broken door, crashed vehicle) let viewers infer what happened and what danger is ahead; traces show time passing.
Use light and sparse placement to point at story props; avoid clutter.
practical_applications: First 1-2 seconds of a clip must establish place; one aftermath detail can tell backstory without narration.
limitations: Ex-Disney designer's practitioner article (tier D); the '15 seconds' figure is a rule of thumb.

sources.title: Death in the Afternoon (ch. 16, iceberg passage)
key_findings: As quoted by secondary sources: 'The dignity of movement of an ice-berg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water.'
As quoted: 'A writer who omits things because he does not know them only makes hollow places in his writing.'
practical_applications: Know far more of the world than you show; omit only what you know.
limitations: Primary text not read; quotes from secondary web sources (tier E pages). A different 'seven-eighths' version comes from a later interview; do not conflate.

sources.title: Tablets of Stone or DNA? TV series bibles
key_findings: Journal of Screenwriting 9(1), 3-23 (accepted manuscript read). Bible lengths vary widely: from a 3-page treatment worked up to 10 pages, 5-8 and 20-25 pages, to 50-60 pages (House of Cards) and 79 pages (The Wire); writers define bibles vaguely.

Types: selling bible, writer's bible, season bible (with storyline wall chart), production bible codifying 'case law', format bible for international sales; a 'walking bible' person may hold the memory.
'Less a tablet of stone, and more like a DNA code'; always ask 'which version?'.

Typical contents: premise/concept, place, locations, character biographies, rationale, structure & style, research, production detail (case law), episode storylines. Level of detail depends on what is culturally familiar versus new.
practical_applications: Structure for STORY_BIBLE_TEMPLATE.md: DNA layer + case-law layer + episode layer, versioned.
limitations: Small UK sample of writers and bibles.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: range wording corrected (separate examples).

sources.title: What is the Holocron?
key_findings: Lucasfilm's continuity database, created January 2000 (FileMaker per other sources) when licensed products needed to track new material; before it, lore lived in binders called 'bibles'.
Tracks stories, discrepancies, images, stats, pronunciations, translations, costume variations and behind-the-scenes info; plus style guides, timelines, spelling dictionaries, quote banks and maps.
Over 55,000 entries in 2012 (19,000+ characters, 2,900 species, 5,300 worlds).
practical_applications: Even a tiny studio benefits from one database of entities with IDs, a discrepancy log and a spelling list (Thai/English names).
limitations: Official blog post by the database keeper; 2012 snapshot.

sources.title: Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling - chapter 'Orienting Paratexts'
key_findings: NYU Press 2015. Chapter abstract: digital-era viewers use paratexts (wikis such as Lostpedia, infographics, character charts) to make sense of complex TV's temporality, characters, plot and spatial orientation.
Foregrounds 'forensic fandom' and 'drillability' as modes of spectatorship.
practical_applications: For serial content, publish orienting aids (recap card, character card, map) - the audience will build them anyway.
limitations: Only chapter abstract and examples read.

sources.title: Fictionality and perceived realism in experiencing stories: A model of narrative comprehension and engagement
key_findings: Per search summaries of the abstract: Communication Theory 18(2), 255-280. Distinguishes fictionality, external realism (match to the real world) and narrative realism (internal coherence).

Violations of external and narrative realism are inconsistencies among the viewer's mental models; they can lower online realism evaluations and reduce engagement; knowing a story is fiction does not by itself disrupt model construction.
practical_applications: A fantastical premise is fine; internal contradictions are what break engagement.
limitations: Repository PDF refused connection; only search-snippet abstract fragments available.

sources.title: Situation models in language comprehension and memory
sources.authors: Rolf A. Zwaan, Gabriel A. Radvansky
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 123(2), 162-185. Situation models are indexed on time, space, causation, intentionality and protagonist.
Readers notice when a protagonist's action contradicts an earlier trait (elevated reading times), citing Albrecht & O'Brien.
practical_applications: World facts the audience tracks automatically: when, where, why, goals, who; these are the consistency priorities of a world bible.
limitations: Text comprehension research; video transfer by analogy.

sources.title: Updating a mental model: Maintaining both local and global coherence
sources.authors: Jason E. Albrecht, Edward J. O'Brien
key_findings: Per later papers citing it: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 19(5), 1061-1070. Readers slowed on a locally coherent sentence when it contradicted a backgrounded earlier trait of the protagonist (e.g. vegetarian), showing the trait was reactivated.
Hakala & O'Brien (1995) extended the effect.
practical_applications: Character traits established once stay active in the audience's mind; contradicting them later is noticed even without a recent reminder.
limitations: Full text not read; effect sizes unknown here; reading paradigm, not video.

Painted outdoors, quickly, from the scene; "momentary and transient effects of sunlight"; quick fragmented brushwork; landscapes and everyday life. → impressionism.
From c.1886 (term by Roger Fry, 1910); Cézanne's structured nature, Seurat's scientific colour, Van Gogh/Gauguin's emotional colour and brushwork. → post_impressionism.
Tiny adjacent dabs of pure colour mixing optically (term "pointillism" rejected by Signac); based on Chevreul's 1839 colour-contrast theory; optical mixing reads more luminous. → pointillism.
1890s–WWI; sinuous lines, flowing plant-based organic shapes; sometimes curves inside rigid geometry. → art_nouveau.
1920s–30s (name from 1925 Paris exhibition); fragmented geometric character influenced by cubism; Egyptian/Aztec motifs; streamlined lines of ships, trains, cars. → art_deco.
Dominant 17th-c. style, peak Rome c.1630–80; dynamic movement, bold realism, direct emotional appeal. → baroque_dramatic.
Begins Italy c.1400, revival of classical art; High Renaissance c.1500–30. Page does not discuss perspective — don't cite it for that. → renaissance_realism.
c.1780–1830; emotion over classical restraint; new responses to nature (Constable, Turner); personal feeling. Page does not mention "sublime". → romanticism_landscape.
Early 20th c. Germany (Die Brücke, Der Blaue Reiter); intense non-naturalistic colour, distorted forms, loose thick paint, inner feeling. → expressionism.
c.1905–1910; intense colour often straight from the tube, loose dabs, flattened forms. → fauvism.
Analytical c.1908–12 (subdued earthy tones, fragmented planes, multiple viewpoints); synthetic c.1912–14 (simpler shapes, brighter colour, collage). → cubism.
Breton's 1924 manifesto, "pure psychic automatism"; dreams and the unconscious. → surrealism.
Russia c.1915–1920s; art reflecting industrial modernity; abstract, industrial materials. → constructivism.
School 1919 Weimar → Dessau 1925 → Berlin 1932, closed 1933; equal weight to design, architecture, crafts and fine art. (Page is about the school, not a visual recipe.) → bauhaus_modernist.
1940s–50s New York; action painting (gestural, poured paint) vs colour field (large single-colour areas, contemplative). → abstract_expressionism.
Mid-1950s UK / late-1950s US, peak 1960s; imagery from ads, packaging, comics, film; hard edges, impersonal. → pop_art, vintage_comic_halftone (context).
1960s; purely geometric forms; based on colour theory and perception; effects from subtle to disorienting. → op_art.
Late 1950s–1970s US; plain geometry (squares, oblongs); the object is the reality ("What you see is what you see"). → minimalism.
Relief print carved along the grain; carved-away areas print blank; ukiyo-e printed by hand pressure. → woodcut_print, ukiyo_e_woodblock.
Stencil through stretched mesh, squeegee; photo-stencils; commercial 1920s, artists 1930s, widespread 1950s+. → screenprint_poster.
Paper, photos, fabric, found materials fixed to a support; from papiers collés, early 20th c. → collage_mixed_media.
Paint thick enough to stand out from the surface; Titian/Tintoretto origin; visible strokes. → oil_impasto.
Water-soluble, opaque (paper white doesn't show), more binder + chalk-like fillers. Page does not say "matte". → gouache_flat, storybook_gouache.
